André Greiner-Petter leads a team reporting on a shared task about catching AI-written plagiarism. Their 2025 overview paper describes the PAN 2025 competition task. Plagiarists now use language models to rewrite scientific text from sources. Detectors must find the copied passages and align them with the originals.

The organizers built a large dataset of machine-made plagiarism with three models, Llama, DeepSeek-R1, and Mistral. Four participant teams submitted systems, and all beat the organizer baselines. Simple semantic similarity methods using embedding vectors did surprisingly well on the new data. They reached recall near zero point eight and precision near zero point five. A specialized retrieval model called Linq outperformed every submission. The warning came from old data. Most approaches did far worse on the PAN 2015 dataset, which shows poor generalization. The overview gives task designers a clear benchmark and a caution.
arxiv-2510-07005:
Keyi Ding leads a team separating giant stars from dwarf stars using only brightness measurements. Their 2025 paper serves studies of nearby galaxies, where distant giants are the targets. Milky Way dwarfs in the foreground contaminate those samples badly. A narrow-band filter called NB515 helps, since it senses surface gravity through magnesium features.

The team modeled the filter's response using large libraries of real stellar spectra. On a two-color diagram, dwarfs and giants split apart cleanly. The separation holds even for the reddest, coolest M-type stars, the hardest cases. Machine learning models then sharpened the classification further. A cross-check against known samples gave about eighty-five percent accuracy at their chosen threshold. Earlier uses of the filter focused on metal-poor stars. This work extends reliable sorting to richer, cooler populations. Cleaner giant samples mean cleaner maps of how nearby galaxies are built.
arxiv-2510-07105:
Sorensen and Choi describe a system that learns from human disagreement instead of hiding it. Their 2025 paper reports their entry to the LeWiDi shared task. In many language tasks, raters honestly disagree about the right label. A good system should predict that spread, not just one answer. Their system leans on examples placed inside the prompt itself.

The team first trained their model on many tasks that reward learning from context. They then tuned it further toward each target data set. Showing real rater examples in the prompt proved crucial to success. Their entry won both tasks in the contest overall. Tests that removed parts of the system showed that scale helped too. The work matters for any label task where human judgment varies, from toxicity ratings to medical notes. Modeling disagreement honestly can make such systems fairer and more useful.
arxiv-2510-07505:
Dong and co-authors introduce PEAR, a benchmark that stress-tests planner-executor agent systems for both usefulness and vulnerability. Their 2025 paper targets the dominant design in multi-agent language systems: one agent plans, others execute. Security studies usually probe one attack surface at a time. PEAR evaluates clean task performance and adversarial manipulation together, across many configurations. Four findings stand out. A weak planner damages clean performance more than a weak executor does. Memory is essential for the planner, while executor memory changes nothing measurable on clean tasks, a genuinely surprising asymmetry for system builders.

Performance and robustness trade off against each other: stronger configurations often fall easier. Attacks aimed at the planner mislead the whole system most effectively, since every downstream step inherits the poisoned plan. Higher-utility setups showed greater attack success rates in the experiments. The authors release all code and data.
arxiv-2510-07605:
Luczak, Podsedkowska, and Wieczorek derive variational formulas for quantum entropies on von Neumann algebras. Their 2025 paper treats entropy-like functionals of a general shape: a trace applied to a convex or concave function of a positive operator representing the state. Segal entropy and the Renyi entropy family both fit the template. The setting is semifinite algebras, covering finite systems and many infinite ones with a well-behaved trace.

A structural theme runs through the proofs: the formulas route through abelian subalgebras, the classical corners inside the quantum algebra. Entropy emerges as an extremum over classical snapshots of the state, a satisfying interpretation. The connection gives quantum information theory new handles on entropy in infinite-dimensional settings, where definitions by analogy with matrices can fail silently.
arxiv-2510-07705:
Zhang and four coauthors wrote this 2025 astronomy paper on double-mode RR Lyrae stars. These pulsing stars serve as standard candles for measuring cosmic distances. Double-mode stars pulse in two periods at once, and their distance relation depends less on metal content. Only about three thousand were known worldwide, which limited their use. The authors built an automated screening pipeline to find more of them.

They cross-matched the Gaia catalog of RR Lyrae stars with time-series data from the Zwicky Transient Facility. Period searches, alias suppression, and quality cuts did the screening. The pipeline confirmed many single-mode stars and found nine hundred sixty-nine double-mode stars. Over six hundred of those are new discoveries, a large jump for this rare class. Their distance relation agrees with the one based on the Large Magellanic Cloud. Bigger future surveys should multiply the sample again.
arxiv-2510-07805:
Ding wrote this 2025 algebraic geometry paper on the reducedness of twisted loop groups. Loop groups package a symmetry group into maps from a circle, and they underlie spaces such as affine Grassmannians. Reducedness is a basic sanity property, asking whether the geometry hides nilpotent fuzz. Earlier proofs of the key case leaned on heavy machinery, in recent work. Ding offers a more elementary route along lines set by the Kneser-Tits problem.

The main theorem treats a connected, semisimple, simply connected group over a field of formal Laurent series. For such groups, Ding proves the loop group is reduced. The proof uses only standard results about algebraic groups and group schemes. He follows a line from Beilinson-Drinfeld to Lourenço. An elementary proof matters because later constructions build on these groups. Readers can now check a foundational fact without importing a whole new mathematical framework.
arxiv-2510-08105:
Wang, Liu, Zou, and Wu wrote this 2025 gravitational wave paper tracing oscillations in eccentric black hole mergers to a neglected orbital parameter. The mean anomaly marks where a body sits along its elliptical orbit, long treated as a mere phase. The team's earlier work found oscillations in remnant mass, spin, and recoil as eccentricity varied. Here they decompose waveforms into inspiral, merger, and ringdown. The oscillations persist through every phase.

Initial mass and angular momentum vary smoothly with eccentricity, so they cannot explain the pattern. The radiated energy and angular momentum oscillate instead, matching the remnant quantities. Comparing numerical relativity with post-Newtonian calculations pinpoints the initial mean anomaly as the source. Orbital averaging in standard formulas erases the effect. Sweeping the anomaly through its full range builds an envelope containing all the oscillations. Waveform models ignoring the anomaly can misstate remnant properties at high eccentricity.
arxiv-2510-08405:
Gereon Koßmann, Mario Berta, and René Schwonnek extend routed Bell tests to many parties in a 2025 arXiv paper. Device-independent quantum key distribution promises secrecy based only on observed correlations, not trusted hardware. Long distances hurt it through the detection-efficiency loophole, where missed detections open attack routes. Routed Bell tests counter this by letting one party self-test their device locally.

The authors design a modified setup where both Alice and Bob can self-test locally. Their scheme also covers arbitrarily many local parties, not just two endpoints. They analyze security against attacks using modern robust self-testing tools. In a BB84-type protocol, the key rate varies smoothly with how well the local tests are won. Perfect local Bell tests could in principle beat the detection-efficiency barrier entirely. The rate then faces only standard bit-flip errors, as in trusted-device setups.
arxiv-2510-08505:
Anne Inkenhaag, Andrew Levan, Andrew Mummery, and Peter Jonker revisit a famous cosmic explosion five years on, in a 2025 arXiv paper. AT 2018cow is the prototype luminous fast blue optical transient, a sudden bright event of unknown origin. Rich multi-wavelength data never settled what powered it. Its ultraviolet brightness two to four years later hinted at an accretion disk feeding extra energy.

New Hubble Space Telescope data extend the ultraviolet record to about five years after the explosion. The optical brightness shows no significant fading since the last epoch, and the ultraviolet fades only marginally. These points match published accretion disk models where a low-mass star is torn apart by an intermediate-mass black hole. That agreement supports a tidal disruption origin for AT 2018cow. Interacting supernova models predict different late behavior, and the gap should widen with time.
arxiv-2510-08605:
Nouar Aldahoul and Yasir Zaki build a multilingual multi-agent system to fight adversarial misinformation in a 2025 arXiv paper. False content spreads fast online, threatening public discourse and decisions. Attackers transform misinformation to evade detectors, and some transformation families had never been studied systematically. The authors examine language-switching across six languages followed by translation, among other tricks.

They also study query length inflation before summarization and reformatting claims into multiple-choice questions. Their framework deploys several language model agents with retrieval-augmented generation as a web plugin. Retrieval grounds the agents' checks in external sources rather than model memory alone. The paper argues such plugins can protect factual integrity on real platforms. Feasibility of plugin-based deployment for everyday web use is a central claim. Multilingual coverage spans English, French, Spanish, Arabic, Hindi, and Chinese.
arxiv-2510-08805:
Zaugg and Grzelak speed up a workhorse model of financial volatility, in this 2025 arXiv paper on mathematical finance. The lifted Heston model tracks how market turbulence evolves, storing its memory in a set of linked state processes. Simulating those processes step by step is slow, because accuracy has forced tiny steps across many dimensions. Traders who price options tied to volatility feel that cost directly.

The pair propose a simulation scheme that jumps in large steps instead. It exploits a near-straight-line link between the random driver of the model and its accumulated variance. That link lets them sample the variance from a known distribution, chosen to be the best fit in a precise average sense. Tests showed near-exact accuracy even on coarse time grids. Pricing of volatility options became far cheaper as a result.
arxiv-2510-09605:
Adam Coscia and Alex Endert built VisPile, a visual analytics system for intelligence work, described in a 2025 arXiv paper. Analysts make sense of large document collections by grouping, summarising, and mapping relationships, and the work slows as collections grow. The authors explore how two AI technologies, large language models and knowledge graphs, can help analysts keep pace.

Developed with intelligence community experts, VisPile weaves both technologies into the interface. Analysts sort documents into piles, and the system assists with summarising piles and charting relationships between them. It also helps users validate evidence that the model or the graph produced, keeping a human check on machine output. Six professional intelligence analysts tried the system on a document corpus. The paper describes the tool's design and reports the analysts' feedback on how it supported their sensemaking.
arxiv-2510-09805:
Jeffrey Camlin, the sole author, proposes a way to calm stiff flow equations by stretching time in a 2025 arXiv paper. Continuous-time flow models, in physics and machine learning alike, can develop near-singular behaviour that breaks solvers. Temporal lifting replaces time with a smoothly stretched version of itself, governed by a monotone mapping.

In the lifted coordinate, the method smooths the flow's rough behaviour while keeping its balance laws. Trajectories of hard cases, such as the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations on a 3D torus, become globally smooth. From the machine learning side, temporal lifting acts as a steadying step in continuous time. The author argues it can stabilise physics-informed neural networks and other designs based on latent flows, used in AI systems. The framework also links smoothness theory, the mathematics of when equations stay well-behaved, with methods from representation learning for stiff or turbulent processes.
arxiv-2510-09905:
Fang and co-authors study what they call the personalization trap in this 2025 arXiv paper on language models. When an assistant remembers facts about a user, such as a hard job or a wealthy life, does that memory change how it reads the user's stress? Long-term user memory is now common in AI products.

The team asks how stored personal details shape a model's emotional reasoning, its judgments about what someone feels and why. The concern is that memory may tilt those judgments in unfair or wrong ways. A model might excuse stress in one user and doubt it in another, based only on biography. The paper frames this bias risk as a cost of personalization that designers must measure.
arxiv-2510-10005:
Johnson and co-authors present ChemGen in this 2025 arXiv paper on simulation software. ChemGen is a package that uses code generation to add multispecies thermodynamics and chemical kinetics to physics codes written in C++. Such chemistry lies at the heart of combustion models, yet many physics codes lack it.

Writing kinetics code by hand for each new code is slow and prone to error. ChemGen instead writes the needed code on its own, with the aim of making chemical kinetics easy to add to codes that already exist. The authors frame the package as a bridge between combustion modeling and computational physics. With code writing handled by the tool, modelers can swap chemical schemes without redoing their solver by hand.
arxiv-2510-10305:
Sadykov revisits Mather's stability theorem for smooth maps in this 2025 arXiv paper in singularity theory. A smooth map between spaces is stable if small perturbations leave its shape essentially unchanged. Mather proved that a proper map that is infinitesimally stable, stable under tiny algebraic tests, is truly stable.

Sadykov presents the circle of results around that theorem. The stability of a proper map is equivalent to infinitesimal stability, and both match the Mather normal crossing condition, a geometric test on how the map's critical values meet. The equivalence is a workhorse of singularity theory: it lets geometers certify stability by an algebraic check rather than by testing every perturbation.
arxiv-2510-10405:
Shaikh and Aleksander L. Wysocki study iron atoms on a ferroelectric surface in this 2025 arXiv paper in condensed matter physics. The base is a two-dimensional ferroelectric crystal whose electric polarization can point up or down. Single iron atoms rest on its surface as adatoms.

Using first-principles calculations, the authors trace how flipping the polarization changes the atom's structure, electronic states, and magnetism. Electric control of one atom's magnetic state is a long-sought goal for atomic-scale memory and spin devices. A ferroelectric switch holds its state with no power, so the atom's state would persist on its own. The work maps which traits of the iron atom the switch can in fact control.
arxiv-2510-10605:
MohammadHossein Bateni and four co-authors formalize a budgeting problem that sits inside machine learning practice, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Building a model means evaluating many intermediate candidates: during feature selection, structure search, and parameter tuning. Each evaluation costs resources, and its result steers which candidates to try next. Prior knowledge gives rough quality guesses, but true performance appears only after evaluation. The question is how to spend a bounded evaluation budget wisely.

The team casts this as a general budget allocation problem over unknown value functions. The functions live in a Lipschitz space, meaning their values cannot change too abruptly between nearby points. That smoothness assumption is what makes learning from few evaluations possible in principle. The formalization unifies many ad hoc tuning heuristics under one problem statement, giving researchers a shared language for dividing exploration budgets when every probe is costly.
arxiv-2510-10905:
Ben DalFavero and Ryan LaRose bring error mitigation to quantum computers that are only partly error corrected, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Such machines mix logical qubits, which are protected, with ordinary noisy qubits. Their method, inspired by error cancellation, runs through a new circuit that forms convex combinations of quantum channels. Logical ancilla qubits then serve as a resource that buys down the sampling cost of cancellation.

In the limiting case, logical ancillas reduce the sample complexity to a constant, circumventing lower bounds that constrain all known mitigation techniques. The catch is exponential circuit depth. This trade off leads the authors to conjecture that any mitigation protocol with polynomial or better sampling needs exponential time or space, even with logical qubits available. As a side application, their channel combination circuits simulate open quantum systems with an order of magnitude fewer gates than the current state of the art.
arxiv-2510-11205:
Between scalar and Ricci curvature sits a family of intermediate notions, each averaging sectional curvatures over subspaces of a chosen dimension. Yujie Wu explores the newest such notion in this 2025 arXiv differential geometry paper. The m-intermediate Ricci curvature, introduced by Brendle, Hirsch, and Johne, matches Ricci at one extreme and a multiple of scalar curvature at the other.

Wu shows that if a manifold has non-negative m-intermediate Ricci curvature and admits a stable weighted slicing of order m minus one. The last slice in the chain then has almost non-negative Ricci curvature in the spectral sense. He also proves comparison theorems bounding the diameter and the in-radius for manifolds with such slicings. The free-boundary version covers manifolds with mean convex boundary, extending the results to this setting.
arxiv-2510-12005:
James Cook and four co-authors found the theory of computing in place, where a program must overwrite its own input. Practical algorithms do this all the time to save memory, yet theory lacked an account of its structure. Their 2025 arXiv paper defines inplaceFL, the class of functions computable in log space while rewriting the input tape in place, with no extra output tape.

The results cut both ways. With no assumptions at all, plain logspace computation is not contained in the in-place class. For permutations done in place, the inverse must be easy on average, which pushes integer multiplication and certain tiny circuit scorings outside the class under standard crypto assumptions. Shallower circuit groups, though, run fine in place. With an oracle for a game-like class, the containment flips back. The authors extend this to catalytic computation, where a large borrowed tape must be handed back untouched.
arxiv-2510-12305:
Fernández and co-authors extend nominal signatures with a first order form of dependent sorting, in a 2025 arXiv computer science paper. Nominal techniques give a formal treatment of names and binding, the way variables are tied to their declarations. Many sorted signatures classify expressions by sorts, but classical versions cannot let a sort depend on a term.

Abstraction is eliminated through generalised concretion, an operation like applying a function in the lambda calculus. Expressions are classified by sorts and sort families that respect alpha conversion, the renaming of bound names, while names cannot carry abstraction sorts. This yields a first order dependent sort system. The paper presents its rules and properties, with representation experiments. The system can encode the judgements and inference rules of several calculi. The authors discuss it as a basis for a type theory treating raw expressions and alpha equivalence fully formally.
arxiv-2510-12405:
Negishi and co-authors propose fairer ways to judge whether a generative model produces crystals that are truly unique and novel, in a 2025 arXiv materials science paper. Generative models can sample new chemical compositions with crystal structures quickly, aiding the hunt for functional materials. Uniqueness and novelty scores depend on a distance function between crystals, and the standard one has four flaws.

The standard distance cannot say how similar two compounds are. It cannot separate compositional from structural difference. It reacts discontinuously to small shifts in atomic positions, and its uniqueness scores depend on the order samples are listed. The authors propose two continuous distance functions that in theory overcome all four limitations. Experiments show these distances reveal insights the traditional function misses. The authors offer them as a more reliable basis for evaluating and ranking generative models for inorganic crystals, a step toward trustworthy materials discovery.
arxiv-2510-12505:
Everett, Klinger-Plaisier, and Cotter describe the software behind a framework that tracks how particle distributions evolve in astrophysical jets, in a 2025 arXiv paper. The DIPLODOCUS framework models systems at a mesoscopic scale. It transports particle distribution functions through seven dimensions of phase space, with steady forces and discrete particle collisions. This second paper in the series covers the numerical build, after a first paper on the underlying theory.

The code package, written in Julia, includes a novel Monte Carlo sampling technique for precomputing anisotropic collision integrals. The authors present test cases examining what the package can do on micro scale physics: binary collisions, emissive effects, and outside forces. These effects are the ones key to modeling jetted sources such as active galactic nuclei plus X-ray binaries. The paper is the practical companion to the framework's theory, showing how the math becomes working software.
arxiv-2510-12905:
Mihalache and Mochida connect polygon equations to simplex equations in this 2025 arXiv mathematics paper. Simplex equations extend the famous Yang-Baxter equation from statistical mechanics to higher dimensions. Their polygon cousins extend the pentagon equation from topology and physics. Earlier work linked the two families only in special cases.

First, the authors show that certain commutative pairs of solutions to polygon equations, including their dual versions, produce solutions of higher polygon equations. Next they define a clear compatibility condition between a solution and its dual. Using that condition, they build solutions of the two simplex equations just below the polygon's size. The results extend work by Kashaev and Sergeev and by Dimakis and Müller-Hoissen. They give a bridge between the two families.
arxiv-2510-13005:
Muldrow, Ludden, and Petersen describe a ground testbed for in-space servicing operations in this 2025 arXiv paper, a preprint of a space flight mechanics conference paper. Servicing, assembly, and manufacturing in orbit promise longer-lived space assets. But a robotic arm moving on a free-flying satellite creates complex forces that are hard to test. Real satellites move in six degrees of freedom and cannot be flown in a laboratory.

Their hardware-in-the-loop testbed mounts a six-degree-of-freedom robotic arm on a satellite bus that rides a linear guide rail. The bus and arm move freely along one direction while the arm works. The system lets researchers physically emulate servicing operations. It also validates models of space motion, serial robot manipulation, and contact mechanics against real hardware behavior rather than simulation alone.
arxiv-2510-13105:
Wang and colleagues benchmark whether AI assistants know when to speak up in social settings in this 2025 arXiv paper. As augmented and virtual reality systems enter daily life, an assistant watching first-person video must sense social dynamics and intervene only at the right moment, since constant interruptions disrupt conversation and focus. Current multimodal models largely lack that awareness.

The team built EgoSocial, a dataset of thirteen and a half thousand egocentric video-question pairs designed around intervention in social interaction, spanning cues from broad environment signals to fine personal attention states. Testing leading omnimodal models showed they struggle badly at detecting intervention timing. Their proposed method, EgoSoD, organizes audio and visual cues into a social thinking graph that models participants and interactions dynamically. It improved intervention timing substantially for two tested models and raised overall social interaction scores as well.
arxiv-2510-13605:
Ferreira introduces a new probability distribution for lifetime and income-style data, built from the Lomax family. His 2025 arXiv paper defines the generalized Marshall-Olkin Lomax distribution through a recent generator method. The extra parameters bend the distribution into more shapes than the plain Lomax allows. Its main properties follow easily from those of the base distribution.

Ferreira also builds a regression model for censored data on top of the distribution. Parameters are fitted by maximum likelihood, the standard fit-maximizing method. Simulations check that the estimates behave consistently as samples grow. Three real datasets, covering AIDS and COVID-19 among them, test the model in practice. On those data, the new models beat rivals from two well-known distribution classes. The paper supplies the quantile function and other tools needed for applied use.
arxiv-2510-13805:
Anbajagane builds a simulation-based inference pipeline that adds a three-point lensing statistic to cosmology fits. His 2025 arXiv paper targets weak lensing, where foreground matter bends background galaxy shapes. Standard two-point correlations miss information stored in higher-order shape patterns. The integrated three-point function captures that extra signal.

The pipeline forward-models the shear field with a large suite of N-body simulations. It bakes in systematics like intrinsic galaxy alignment, baryonic feedback, and calibration bias. Synthetic measurements mimic the Dark Energy Survey's third-year data release. Two surprises emerged from validation checks. Source clustering and reduced shear barely affect the new statistic at this survey scale. But the combined data vector's likelihood bends away from Gaussian at large filter sizes. On mock data, adding the three-point statistic improved the key figure of merit by a median 63.8 percent over two-point-only fits, he reports.
arxiv-2510-13905:
Chen and co-authors give language models an explicit mental schema extracted from examples, boosting their science reasoning. Their 2025 arXiv paper builds on schema theory from cognitive science. Humans interpret new problems by activating stored frameworks of earlier ones. In-context learning shows examples but never names the pattern.

Schema-Activated In-Context Learning pulls the reasoning skeleton out of a demonstration first. That schema, a light template of key inferential steps and their links, then scaffolds the new question. Tests use chemistry and physics questions from the GPQA benchmark. A single high-quality demonstration with its schema lifted performance by up to 39.67 percent across the models tried, the authors report. Fewer examples are needed once the schema does the lifting. The authors also find models cannot form such schemas internally on their own. Interpretability improves as a side benefit of the explicit template.
arxiv-2510-14105:
Simon Bortz and co-authors revisit weighted functions of bounded variation, a class of functions flexible enough to include jumps, such as the indicator of a region, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Weighting changes the measure, so lengths and volumes are counted with a density that varies from place to place. The resulting spaces underpin tools from partial differential equations to image denoising.

Depending on the theorem, the authors assume the weight is lower semicontinuous, a mild regularity condition, or satisfies a condition known as A1. Their main contributions include a structure theorem under minimal assumptions. They add a smooth approximation result, showing rough functions can be approached by smooth ones. An embedding theorem locates the weighted space among other function spaces. They prove a weighted Gagliardo-Nirenberg-Sobolev inequality for these functions and a weighted isoperimetric inequality, which relates a region's volume to its boundary size.
arxiv-2510-14405:
Hsiao-Yi Chen, Ryotaro Arita, and Yusuke Nomura develop a first-principles method for spin excitations in magnets whose spins point in swirling, noncollinear patterns, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Approaches model spins as localized arrows on a lattice. Materials with spiral magnetic order need methods derived from the electrons themselves. Green's function techniques were largely confined to collinear magnets.

The authors work in a Wannier basis, a localized electronic representation, and introduce an ansatz potential method that cuts computational cost enough to treat noncollinear systems. Applying the method to the spin-spiral state of the compound LiCu2O2, they reproduce its measured spin-rotation pitch and resolve the magnon dispersion, the energy spectrum of spin waves. Their analysis shows how the spiral structure interacts with on-site exchange splitting, and shows magnetic dipoles on the oxygen ligand ions play a role in mediating ferromagnetic interactions.
arxiv-2510-15005:
Sunny introduces TangledFeatures, in a 2025 arXiv paper, a framework for choosing which inputs a model should use when the candidates are heavily entangled. Feature selection shapes both accuracy and clarity, but most methods chase raw accuracy alone. They degrade when predictors are strongly correlated, each one echoing several others.

TangledFeatures instead picks one feature to speak for each group of entangled predictors. It discards the echoes while keeping the group's power to explain. The chosen subset feeds straight into downstream models, a clearer and more stable basis for analysis than standard selection. The test case is alanine dipeptide, a small molecule, used to predict its backbone torsional angles. The features picked turned out to be meaningful distances between atoms within the molecule. They truly explain how the angles vary, a sign the chosen few carry real information.
arxiv-2510-15205:
Shaw Dalen and the Daedalus Research Team try to give prediction markets the shared math foundation that options markets got from the Black-Scholes model. Their 2025 arXiv paper notes that venues like Polymarket turn scattered opinion into tradable prices for event odds. Yet market makers there lack standard tools to quote prices or hedge risks around shifting beliefs, sudden jumps, and linked events.

The team proposes a model where the traded probability itself moves by diffusion plus jumps, kept consistent with risk-neutral pricing, the convention that prices reflect fair odds. A calibration pipeline strips out market noise and separates smooth drift from jumps, producing a stable surface of belief volatility. They add derivative contracts on variance, correlation, and first passage, modeled on options products. In tests on synthetic and real event data, their model forecast short-term belief variance better than simpler rivals.
arxiv-2510-15605:
Yelda Gülfırat and Mehmet Ünver extend a math language for uncertain judgments, in this 2025 paper. Fuzzy sets grade membership between yes and no. The circular complex kind also carries a second, phase-like dimension, and such tools help when experts give hesitant, conflicting views.

The pair define the circular complex q-rung orthopair fuzzy set, merging two earlier frameworks under one tunable power. At that power set to two it becomes the known Pythagorean version, and at three the Fermatean version. They then build operators that blend many judgments with Gaussian weighting, in both arithmetic and geometric forms. Membership and non-membership grades are integrated in one consistent scheme. The aim is a smoother, statistically grounded way to model uncertainty in group decisions.
arxiv-2510-15805:
Bonnie Rushing and Shouhuai Xu present a metric in a 2025 paper. It measures how well a disinformation campaign engages its targets. Counting views alone is not enough. Their metric weights each kind of engagement. Passive exposure counts less than active sharing. Volume is weighed against how many messages the attackers sent.

The team applied the metric to real campaigns. The campaigns ran across social media platforms. The metric captured the depth of engagement, not just reach. It shows how users actually behaved. The authors offer the framework as a practical tool. Defenders can use it to assess influence operations. They can also use it to plan countermeasures.
arxiv-2510-15905:
Aikaterina Manoli and five co-authors study people who use AI systems for both errands and companionship. Research usually treats assistance and social use apart. Drawing on a survey of about two hundred people and thirty interviews with heavy ChatGPT and Replika users, the team characterises digital companionship as a new kind of human-AI relationship.

Users value humanlike traits such as emotional resonance and personal replies alongside non-human traits such as constant availability and endless patience. Uses blur across brands: Replika serves as a writing helper and ChatGPT as an emotional confidant. Two tensions recur. Users form deep attachments while denying the systems real personhood, and they struggle to fit chatbot bonds into social norms. The findings raise design questions for hybrid, general-purpose AI systems, the team argues.
arxiv-2510-16505:
Lukas Selch leads six co-authors in a 2025 test set for spotting flaws in science papers. Big models that read text and images now help with real research. Yet no one knew if they catch clashes among text, figures, tables, and maths. Their set, PRISMM-Bench, draws flaws flagged by real peer reviewers. It holds 384 such flaws from 353 papers.

Three tasks test if a model can find a flaw, fix it, and match flaw pairs. A strict answer format blocks cheap wins from answer patterns. The team tested 21 top models, both open and closed. Scores ran from about 28 to 54 percent, a low range. The gap shows how far models are from trusted science help.
arxiv-2510-16905:
Yukang Cao, Rahul Moorthy, O. Goktug Poyrazoglu, and Volkan Isler improve robot steering in a 2025 paper. Sampling-based controllers test many possible moves, then pick the best. Older samplers ignore the local map around the robot. That wastes tries on paths blocked by nearby obstacles.

Their sampler, C-Free-Uniform, spreads trial moves evenly through open space. Open space here means the area the robot can actually occupy. It reads the current local map before choosing moves. Built into a path-planning controller, it beat existing methods in cluttered test worlds. It also needed far fewer trial paths to succeed. Even sampling of reachable space, the authors argue, is the key saving.
arxiv-2510-17305:
ZhaoYang Han and five co-authors build a test set for long video grasp by omni-modal models in this 2025 paper. Such models read sight, sound, and text in one pass. Long human clips, like talks and vlogs, pack dense cues in all three. Short-clip tests miss the strain that length adds to grasp.

Their set holds about one thousand long clips from open sources. Six task types span acts inside one event and links across events. A three-step check pipe guards the truth of each test item. Top models still fail at exact time marks in long clips. Long-range cause links also trip them, and merged cues can drop facts.
arxiv-2510-17605:
Time dependent density functional theory is a workhorse for computing how electrons respond to light, but it has long stumbled on states where two electrons are excited at once. Dhyey Ray, Anna Baranova, Davood B Dar, and Neepa T Maitra show that a recent fix, a dressed kernel that varies with frequency, reaches further than expected. Used inside a response reformulated version of the theory, the same kernel stays accurate even under strong fields, far outside the gentle regime where it was developed.

Ray and his co-authors argue the lesson is general: improvements built for the response regime can be carried into harsh, non-perturbative dynamics through the reformulated framework. That widens the reach of a whole family of functional developments that had seemed confined to mild conditions. The paper demonstrates the claim on electron dynamics involving double excitation states.
arxiv-2510-17705:
Dayan Pan, with Zhaoyang Fu and four co-authors, adapts language models to many tasks at once in a 2025 arXiv paper. Full fine tuning can erase old knowledge, a failure called catastrophic forgetting. Lighter tuning methods save resources but often lag on complex multi task mixes. The authors target the attention modules, the parts that weigh which words matter most.

Their mechanism, called CAM, adjusts attention outputs dynamically as tasks change. It boosts task specific features while guarding general knowledge. A hybrid framework pairs one shared full size module with several small specialist modules. A routing strategy blends their knowledge as needed. Across question answering, code generation, and logic tasks, scores rose by close to four percent on average. That beat existing adaptation approaches.
arxiv-2510-17805:
J. E. Hirsch reviews a long-standing puzzle about the Meissner effect in superconductors. The effect is the expulsion of magnetic field when a metal turns superconducting. It was found in 1933 and anchors the field. Most physicists believe the 1957 standard theory fully explains it.

Hirsch lays out that consensus, which rests on the idea of emergence. He then reviews newer doubts about momentum conservation during expulsion. A reductionist view says charge must move radially during the transition. That extra motion mirrors how classical plasmas drag field lines with charges. The review argues the standard theory leaves real questions open.
arxiv-2510-17905:
Monmoy Molla, Masum Murshid, and Mehedi Kalam ask how dark matter made of fermions would change a neutron star from the inside. They vary the dark particle mass and the share of dark matter in the star. Depending on those values, the dark matter settles into a dense core or spreads into a wide halo.

The team tests the model against measured star sizes, heavy two-solar-mass stars, and tidal limits from a merged-star event. Some mass and share ranges fail those checks and are ruled out. The amount of dark matter a neutron star can hold, they find, must stay fairly small.
arxiv-2510-18005:
Mohammad Haidar, Hugo D Nogueira, and J-Ph Karr run high-precision quantum computing simulations of three-body atoms and molecules. Their targets are helium, a negative hydrogen ion, and two small molecular ions, the last pair treated without the usual fixed-nuclei shortcut. The method pairs a compact trial state with a first-quantized description of the particles.

Energies came out with extremely small errors, and the states were limited mainly by arithmetic precision. The scheme avoids flat training landscapes and needs only a few thousand function calls. Quantum chemists get evidence that hard few-body systems, long used as accuracy benchmarks, are within reach of this approach.
arxiv-2510-18105:
Junpeng Hou, Mark M Seidel, and Chuanwei Zhang model how a virus could spread through a quantum network. Quantum links now carry information over long distances with special physical traits. As in classical networks, a spreading infection there could do real harm, so the authors build epidemic tools suited to the quantum case.

Quantum networks looked tougher against infection, with higher outbreak thresholds than matching classical ones. That edge traced mainly to their sparser wiring. At equal average connectivity, the two kinds behaved alike. Network designers get a sober result: the safety comes from sparseness, not from quantum magic.
arxiv-2510-18705:
Peiqin Zhuang and his six co-authors strengthen how transformer models recognize human actions in video. Transformers dominate the field because they gather context across space and time, yet they lag on data sets where the motion itself, not the scenery, defines the action. The authors noticed that an older tool, the cost volume, resembles the affinity matrix inside self-attention but carries far stronger motion information.

Their module builds that affinity matrix in cost-volume style, sampling candidate matches from a sliding window in the next frame around each point. The matrix then serves two purposes: gathering appearance context and supplying explicit motion features. On four widely used data sets the method beat leading approaches, with the clearest gains on the motion-sensitive Something-Something benchmarks, where background clues cannot substitute for tracking how objects actually move.
arxiv-2510-19305:
Chirag Padubidri and three co-authors improve frog counting and occurrence prediction with a deep learning model that uses several data types at once. Knowing where species live guides conservation, but field and citizen science records are patchy, so distribution models must fill gaps from occurrence data and environmental variables.

Their FrogDeepSDM adds data imputation for places where frogs were not recorded, plus balancing methods, to a species distribution model trained on a biodiversity challenge dataset. Balancing cut counting error dramatically in their tests. Better frog maps help conservation groups judge environmental harm and target protection where it counts.
arxiv-2510-19605:
Rachid Benbrik and five co-authors test whether two unexplained bumps in collider data could both be new Higgs-like particles. Experiments at the Large Hadron Collider hint at an extra scalar near ninety-five giga-electron-volts, echoing an older excess at the LEP collider. Separately, the CMS experiment saw an excess near six hundred fifty giga-electron-volts in events with photon pairs and bottom quarks.

The authors check the Next-to-Two-Higgs-Doublet Model, which extends the Higgs sector with two doublets and a singlet. They find regions of the model where a heavy scalar near six hundred fifty giga-electron-volts decays into the known Higgs plus the lighter one, matching both excesses within experimental uncertainty. The scenario makes testable predictions for current and future LHC running.
arxiv-2510-19805:
Carl-Johan Fauvelle Munck af Rosenschöld, Feras M. Awaysheh, and Ahmad Awad benchmark the new generation of in-memory key-value stores that have grown up around Redis. These datastores are core building blocks of cloud-native systems, yet the literature lacked an experimental comparison of the leading alternatives. The study evaluates Valkey, KeyDB, and Garnet under realistic workloads inside Kubernetes deployments.

The measurements cover throughput, tail latency, processor and memory efficiency, and how hard migration from existing systems would be. Clear trade-offs emerged between raw performance, compatibility with the Redis ecosystem, and long-term viability factors like project maturity and community support. The assessment is meant to guide teams choosing a store for the next generation of cloud infrastructure.
arxiv-2510-20205:
Maggie Bai and three co-authors test evolutionary ways to train an artificial intelligence player for the sliding tile game 2048. The game mixes careful planning with random tile arrivals, which makes it a useful testbed for decision making under uncertainty. Two systems are compared: a two-agent setup where one language model refines strategy prompts for another that plays, and a single-agent setup that refines a value function for limited search.

The single-agent system improves steadily, gaining on average more than four hundred points per training cycle with a clear upward trend, and its strategies grow more advanced over time. The two-agent system gains little, which the authors read as a limit of meta-prompting. Rollback features were also tried to guard against declines.
arxiv-2510-20305:
Hassan Firouzjahi revisits bound state perturbations inside a Schwarzschild black hole. These bound states are interior perturbations with an imaginary spectrum that stay regular at the center while their time profile decays exponentially at the event horizon. Using the interior scale factor in the expanding direction as a clock, he rewrites the Regge-Wheeler equation for the problem.

Solving the equation semi-analytically and numerically confirms that bound states exist for scalar, vector, and axial tensor perturbations. For a given angular index above the spin, the count of such states follows a simple difference rule. Firouzjahi derives a universal lower bound on the spectrum that is approached at large angular index, plus an upper bound for the axial case with a steep growth in that index.
arxiv-2510-20405:
Tiago V. Fernandes wrote this doctoral thesis on black hole heat and gravity. They test general relativity, the theory of gravity, at large scales. Black holes seem to have heat traits, such as entropy. Entropy here counts the small states a system can have.

The thesis asks what gives rise to black hole entropy, and if quantum gravity can explain it. Two tools probe the link with heat science. One tool imposes the first law of heat science on a thin shell. The shell is charged, self pulling matter. The other uses a path integral method from quantum gravity. He builds groups of black hole and shell cases with it. He studies shifts between hot matter and black holes. Cases include charged holes in a box or in flat space. One setting is anti de Sitter space, a curved fixed shape space.
arxiv-2510-20505:
Ruiyi Yang and four co-authors introduce RELOOP, a retrieval-augmented generation framework built for multi-step questions over mixed evidence sources. Standard retrieval pipelines stay brittle on such questions and trade accuracy against latency and tool budgets. RELOOP first converts documents, tables, and knowledge graphs into one reversible hierarchical sequence with lightweight structural tags, giving every source a common format.

A head agent guides the search while an iteration agent expands the sequence with structure-respecting moves, gathering just enough evidence before the answer is composed, with an optional loop to resolve contradictions. Experiments on text, table-plus-text, and knowledge graph benchmarks show consistent gains over single-pass, multi-hop, and agentic baselines at high efficiency. One policy serves all formats without per-dataset specialization.
arxiv-2510-20805:
Aron Brenner, Line Roald, and Saurabh Amin study what happens when large data centers shift their power use across regions in response to prices or carbon signals. Such flexibility could help the grid, but very large flexible loads can also game the market in harmful ways.

Using a two level, two zone model that joins grid dispatch with buyer cost cutting, the team finds two failures. Sharp price jumps at generator limits can push load toward higher cost regions just to trigger a price drop elsewhere. Flexible buyers can also blunt the value of new transmission lines by repositioning so flows and costs barely change. The work derives when each failure arises and warns that plain price signals may misstate true system value.
arxiv-2510-20905:
Xingyu Wang and one co-author analyze the global dynamics of heavy tailed stochastic gradient descent in nonconvex loss landscapes. Gradient noise with heavy tails is widely credited for letting training escape sharp minima that generalize poorly, yet theory has mostly covered local behavior.

Machinery from large deviations and metastability theory is adapted to characterize how the algorithm moves between basins over long horizons, and to control that movement. Global understanding opens the door to designing noise that steers training toward flatter, better generalizing solutions on purpose. The work bridges probability theory and the daily practice of deep learning.
arxiv-2510-21205:
Jingyu Wu and nine co-authors search for a repeating rhythm in gamma-ray light from a distant active galaxy cataloged as 4FGL J0309.9-6058. They work with years of data from the Fermi space telescope and test the brightness record with three different timing methods, each sensitive to cycles in uneven data.

All three methods point to a cycle of roughly five hundred fifty days, and a separate Gaussian process check backs the signal. Extending the test over the full Fermi record strengthens the case. A time lag between optical and gamma-ray changes hints that the two kinds of light come from separate regions. Given the year-like period, the team argues that a slowly wobbling jet from the galaxy is the most likely cause.
arxiv-2510-21305:
Jingxuan Kang and three co-authors make nanowire arrays from gallium nitride by a top-down route based on metal dewetting, where a thin metal film breaks into droplets that set the wire pattern. The route is cheap and scales well, but wire width and wire spacing normally move together.

They loosen that link in two ways. First, they vary the surfaces under the film and the metals in it, including gold and platinum, which shifts how the droplets form. Second, they add a sideways etching step that thins the wires while widening the gaps between them. Combined with different starting widths, the two tricks let width and spacing be chosen largely independently over a much wider range than dewetting alone allows.
arxiv-2510-21405:
Aidan Dakhama and three co-authors tune the memory allocators that hand out heap space to running programs, hunting settings that save memory without slowing work down. Their framework, GreenMalloc, searches allocator settings with an evolutionary method and scores candidates quickly with a lightweight stand-in benchmark built from real execution traces.

Promising settings then move to a full system simulator for a case study covering two widely used allocators, the GNU library's malloc and Google's TCMalloc. Across varied workloads, the best settings cut average heap use by up to about four percent with no loss of speed. Even shaved a small amount off run time in the reported results. The approach suits industrial workloads where small memory savings repeat across many machines.
arxiv-2510-21605:
Orest Kupyn, Hirokatsu Kataoka, and Christian Rupprecht teach models to find the most attention-grabbing object in a picture. They use only synthetic training data. Pixel-perfect labels for this task are expensive. Rival subfields each trained their own models on small collections. That fragmented the effort.

Their data engine, S3OD, generates over one hundred thirty-nine thousand high-resolution images. Labels come from diffusion model features and a self-supervised vision model. Generation steers toward categories the current model finds hard. A streamlined decoder predicts several masks at once. That honors honest disagreement among viewers about what stands out. Models trained purely on this synthetic data cut cross-dataset errors by twenty to fifty percent. Fine-tuned versions lead the standard benchmarks.
arxiv-2510-21805:
Zhao Liu leads a ten-author team, with Yichen Zhu, Yiqing Yang, Xiao Lv, Guoping Tang, Rui Huang, Qiang Luo, Ruiming Tang, Kun Gai. Guorui Zhou, in rethinking how recommendation systems generate their next suggestion. Modern generative recommenders encode each item as a short digit code and predict the next code one digit at a time, left to right.

That habit creates two problems: digits of one item are judged without seeing each other, and easy digits get the same training weight as hard ones. DiffGRM swaps the step-by-step decoder for a masked diffusion process that can fill digits in any order with full context. Tailored encoding, training, and decoding steps support the change, and tests across several datasets improved a standard ranking score by roughly seven to sixteen percent over strong rivals.
arxiv-2510-22105:
Yusong Wu and seven co-authors, Mason Wang, Heidi Lei, Stephen Brade, Lancelot Blanchard, Shih-Lun Wu, Aaron Courville, and Anna Huang, study a band that plays along live. Music models can already compose a polished accompaniment for a finished recording, but a streaming partner must listen and answer at the same time, inside the delay limits of real equipment.

Two knobs govern the design: how far the output is allowed to lag behind the live input, and how many frames the model emits per call. Training Transformer decoders across a grid of those settings exposed steady trade-offs. A larger lag improves coherence by closing the recency gap, but demands faster inference to stay inside the budget; longer output chunks raise throughput while degrading the accompaniment. The study charts that frontier for builders of real-time musical partners.
arxiv-2510-22305:
Jianfeng Lu surveys recent mathematics on processes that relax to equilibrium slowly because part of their motion barely feels friction. Such hypocoercive dynamics include the Langevin equation of statistical physics and the Lindblad equation governing open quantum systems. The practical question is quantitative: exactly how fast does the system settle, with constants one can compute.

The overview unifies classical and quantum cases through space-time Poincaré inequalities, a single analytic device that yields convergence estimates on both sides of the quantum divide. Lu then presents a lifting framework, enlarging the dynamics to a bigger space where it mixes faster, that accelerates classical and quantum Markov semigroups alike. Supplies matching upper and lower bounds on the improved rates. The lecture-style synthesis is aimed at readers who want one map of a scattered literature.
arxiv-2510-22705:
Some values stay fixed while a system moves. Finding those values helps in the study of accelerator optics. Lazare Osmanov and Nilanjan Banerjee wrote a 2025 paper on a tool for that hunt. The tool is called AI Poincare. It finds conserved quantities on its own from data.

Their test case is the McMillan system of optics. They score the tool on its count of fixed values. They also check how close its inferred surface lies to true data points. A best range of perturbation size is found. A new neural network design is proposed from the results. Data from a test accelerator at Fermilab were used too. The tool found the right count even with fast signal decay.
arxiv-2510-22805:
Anton Shakov, writing alone in 2025, introduces a new integer sequence. It is a two regular sequence with index A383066. The sequence starts zero, one, one, two, three. He links its counts to divisor counts. Divisors are whole numbers that divide a value evenly.

Shakov proves a key counting claim. The number of times a value m appears equals the divisor count of m squared plus one. That fact yields a generating function. A generating function packs a sequence into one formula. He also discusses other traits of the sequence. One trait links it to the Fibonacci sequence. The work blends sequence theory and number theory.
arxiv-2510-23305:
F Bado and five co-authors measure line broadening and rotation for a large sample of stars from archived ESO/FEROS spectra under the AMBRE Project. Stellar rotation is a fundamental property, yet large uniform catalogs of rotation speeds from high-resolution spectra are still lacking. Broadening of spectral lines serves as a proxy for how fast a star spins.

They estimate broadening by cross-correlating FEROS spectra with AMBRE binary masks, with a specific calibration of a coupling constant. The sample covers FGKM stars. A homogeneous rotation catalog supports studies of stellar aging, activity, and planet host characterization.
arxiv-2510-23405:
Probit J Kalita, Tuhin Malik, Tianqi Zhao, Bharat Kumar, and James M Lattimer look for observable signatures of a quarkyonic phase inside neutron stars. Quarkyonic matter mixes free quarks with nucleons and leptons in the dense core, under beta equilibrium. The authors constrain the model with observations and theory, then run Bayesian inference on it.

They find quarkyonic equations of state can satisfy all current astrophysical observations, strengthening the case for the model beside traditional ones. They then ask what measurements could tell stars with the phase from those without. Future mass, radius, and tidal data may decide the question.
arxiv-2510-23505:
Arthur Le Saux leads a team of eleven researchers presenting MUSIC, a fully compressible code for the interiors of stars and planets. Past simulations changed stellar interior studies, but most codes use the anelastic approximation, which fixes thermal structure and filters out sound waves. Many also use explicit time steps, which severely limit step size.

MUSIC drops those limits, aiming to improve the recipes that one-dimensional stellar codes use for major fluid processes. A compressible, efficient solver can capture convection and waves together, sharpening models of how stars live and oscillate.
arxiv-2510-23605:
Shuhong Zheng, Ashkan Mirzaei, and Igor Gilitschenski present TIRE, a method for generating 3D and 4D content that keeps a chosen subject recognizable. General generators aim for realism and beauty, but they often lose the identity of a specific person or object when the viewpoint changes. Personalizing output from one or a few reference images is well studied for flat pictures, yet still rare for 3D scenes and moving 4D content.

TIRE starts from a 3D asset made by an existing generator, then tracks the subject through rendered video to find regions that drift from the reference. A subject-driven 2D inpainting model repaints those regions step by step, filling in texture that matches the reference. Finally, the fixed views are converted back into a 3D form, a step the authors call resplatting, while keeping the views consistent. In their tests, identity preservation improved clearly over the strongest rival methods.
arxiv-2510-23805:
Xueying Chen and four co-authors wrap a family cancer risk model in a web interface clinicians can actually use. The underlying model, Fam3PRO, estimates a patient's chance of carrying a harmful variant in up to twenty-two hereditary cancer genes, plus future risk across eighteen cancers. It handles many genes and cancers at once and lets users build sub-models, but it shipped only as an R package with no interface.

Their application, F3PI, is built with R Shiny. It gathers family health history, genetic test results, and other risk factors, and draws the family pedigree through a browser tool. The model then returns carrier probabilities and cancer risks, usually within a minute, in interactive and downloadable form. The authors say the interface streamlines data collection that clinics struggle with. By lowering the barrier, it makes risk information more accessible to providers and patients alike.
arxiv-2510-24205:
Telmo Ribeiro and two co-authors present CoMPSeT, a tool for comparing multiparty session types, a way to describe global interaction protocols for concurrent systems. Such choreographic descriptions capture valid patterns of exchange between participants, but many variants exist, each with its own features and quirks. Comparing them by reading papers alone is hard.

CoMPSeT gathers a representative set of examples and lets users combine features, animate protocols, and compare the meaning of concrete cases across variants. The tool is open source, compiled to JavaScript, and runs directly in any web browser. The authors aim to help researchers map the landscape of session types and to support teaching and further design work.
arxiv-2510-24305:
Alexis Forestier and six co-authors report seeing a new crystal form of water ice under conditions like those inside ice giant planets. Using synchrotron X-ray diffraction in laser heated diamond anvil cells, they compressed and heated ice to extreme levels. Above two hundred gigapascals and eighteen hundred kelvin, a hexagonal close packed phase became dominant as the ice entered the superionic regime.

The phase appears more stable than the face centered cubic form through a martensitic transition across a wide pressure range. It also emerges from stacking disorder as the ice cools back toward another phase. The finding may change models of the interiors of Uranus and Neptune.
arxiv-2510-24805:
Alexandre St-Georges leads a team with eight co-authors who fix a flaw in PET scans with no added CT scan at all. PET maps need a fix for how body tissue dims the light as it leaves, or counts come out wrong. That fix is most often drawn from a CT scan, which adds rays, cost, and a chance of misaligned maps.

Their method uses a spread model, trained as a group, to make a fake CT map from the raw PET scan. It works from more than one view of the same scan. On high grade scans, the fake map let them fix the counts with no real CT. That cuts a step for sick folks and clinics alike.
arxiv-2510-25005:
Saptarshi Saha, Dhruv Vansraj Rathore, and Utpal Garain study what if math in systems with loops, where most past tools fail. A what if ask asks how a past case would have gone if a rule had been changed. Most frames draw cause maps as webs with no loops, yet real systems such as body webs loop back on themselves.

Their work sits in that loop case, with cause maps that let a part feed its own past self in a chain. The acts they study are shift and scale acts: soft, plan like changes that move or stretch how a part works. That pair, loops plus soft acts, is the ground the work sets out to cover.
arxiv-2510-25205:
Yuyang Xia, Zibo Liang, Liwei Deng, Yan Zhao, Han Su, and Kai Zheng cut the power draw of self drive stacks with a frame called EneAD. Drive sense work, run by large deep nets, eats the most power in the car, which trims the range of a charge based car. Past squeeze tricks shrink the model but oft drop sense grade a lot.

Their frame works on two sides: how sense data are kept and tuned, and how picks stay firm when sense is lean. More than one sense model is kept on hand, at more than one cost tier. The car can then swap to the tier that fits the road at hand. Range is bought back with no big loss of sight.
arxiv-2510-25405:
Kei Ikemura leads five co-authors on gentle robot manipulation. Yifei Dong, David Blanco-Mulero, and Alberta Longhini helped. Li Chen and Florian T Pokorny complete the team. Their 2025 paper handles deformable and fragile objects. Excess stress can damage such objects irreversibly. Existing solutions need accurate models or special sensors.

Their approach uses vision-based reinforcement learning for control. A stress-penalized reward discourages damaging actions explicitly. Offline demonstrations help bootstrap the learning process. A curriculum moves from rigid proxies to deformables. Policies learned in simulation transferred to real robots. Transfer happened zero-shot, without extra real training. Tasks included picking up and pushing tofu. Learned policies showed damage-aware gentle manipulation behavior. Stress on fragile objects fell substantially, they report. The reduction was about thirty-six percent versus vanilla policies. Task goals were still achieved in evaluations.
arxiv-2510-25505:
Ekaterina Dmitrieva and Petr Satunin study millicharged scalars. Their 2025 physics paper studies resonant production in wave backgrounds. A charged scalar obeys the Klein-Gordon formula here. The background is an electromagnetic plane wave. Its momentum squared is positive in their setup. That case arises in media with refractive index below one.

They reduce the formula of motion to Mathieu form. The Mathieu formula has resonant answers for settings. Those answers grow exponentially in certain ranges. Physically, beams suffer anomalous losses in such media. Electromagnetic fields lose energy through this resonance effect. The authors set constraints on millicharged particle traits. Coupling and mass are constrained by absence of losses. Optical laser beams show no such anomalous losses. Radio beams also show no anomalous losses observed. Those null readings bound how strongly particles couple. Millicharged particles are hypothetical tiny-charge extensions of physics. Resonant production offers a new probe of them.
arxiv-2510-25605:
Oleg Andreev proposes a string description of a four-quark system. His 2025 physics paper studies two quarks and two antiquarks. The system mimics actions in pure SU(3) gauge theory. Gauge and string duality motivates his description. Analytical and numeric studies study string configurations. Rectangular geometries supply the configurations studied here.

As use, two lowest Born-Oppenheimer potentials are studied. Results suggest varied ground state possibilities by geometry. Depending on geometry and quark ordering, states differ. Ground state may be a hadronic molecule state. It may be a tetraquark state instead. A superposition of both is also possible there. For general geometries, asymptotic energy expressions are derived. Tetraquark configuration energy in infrared limit is covered. Results extend to multiquark configurations more generally. Universality of string tension is also showed. Exotic hadron physics benefits from such string models. Tetraquarks remain debated in particle physics tests. Theory guidance on their form is valuable.
arxiv-2510-25805:
Stefano Civelli, Pietro Bernardelle, Nardiena A. Pratama, and Gianluca Demartini test whether giving a large language model a persona changes its content moderation choices. A persona is a role the model is told to adopt. Moderation here means judging whether text or images count as harmful, where fairness and neutrality matter a great deal.

At first the scores look almost unchanged when a persona is added. Closer checks show that personas with different political leanings label harm at different rates, and larger models align more with personas that share their leaning. A follow up task confirms the split, raising concern that persona use can hide bias behind a neutral surface.
arxiv-2510-26205:
Qi Luo, Xiaonan Li, Tingshuo Fan, Xinchi Chen, and Xipeng Qiu benchmark retrieval systems on questions that need a whole corpus, not just a few passages. Retrieval augmented generation fetches text to ground a language model and cut hallucinations. Most benchmarks test local retrieval, where a small set of chunks holds the answer, yet real tasks often ask for corpus level insights, such as the most cited papers in a year.

Their benchmark, GlobalQA, covers counting, extremum queries, sorting, and top k extraction across a collection. Existing methods perform poorly, with the strongest baseline reaching only a very low score in their tests. They propose GlobalRAG, a multi tool framework that preserves structure across the corpus to handle global reasoning.
arxiv-2510-26305:
Hao Fu leads eleven co-authors in a test of whether black hole feedback alone can explain why many galaxies stop forming stars. Supermassive black holes grow by accretion and release energy as active galactic nuclei, which is believed to heat or expel gas and quench star formation. Their semi empirical model, DECODE, grows galaxies by linking star formation to halo accretion through abundance matching, and grows black holes following host growth with empirical feeding patterns.

Fu and the team impose one rule. A galaxy quenches for good when its central black hole nears the limit set by the known link between black hole mass and stellar velocity dispersion. That single condition generates a quenched galaxy fraction consistent with current data in their model, which sharpens the debate with halo driven quenching.
arxiv-2510-26705:
Qiwei Chen and C Ricardo Constante-Amores tame a classic turbulent flow with a learning controller. Rayleigh-Bénard convection is what happens when a fluid is heated from below: warm plumes rise, cool fluid sinks, and heat transport turns turbulent. At high Rayleigh numbers, which measure how hard the flow is driven, direct simulations are too costly for control design.

Chen and Constante-Amores first compress the flow into a low-dimensional model, using standard mode extraction plus autoencoders, then learn its evolution with neural differential equations. A reinforcement learning policy trained on that cheap model was deployed in full simulations. It cut the Nusselt number, a measure of heat transport, by sixteen to twenty-three percent. The policy thickens the thermal boundary layer and damps the bursts that seed convection.
arxiv-2510-26905:
Pedro Antonio Alarcon Granadeno and seven co-authors propose a safety idea for drones in 2025. Drones here are small uncrewed aircraft used on search and rescue flights. Big AI models help them see, infer, and plan, but can also hallucinate. A hallucination is a false output that sounds sure but is wrong. Such errors can also come from broad leaps or missed context.

Their cognition envelope sets bounds on AI choices, like a fence for reasoning. An envelope here is a set limit that a choice must stay inside. A pipeline checks clues from each flight with chance-based reasoning and resource checks. Tests score the clue pipeline across a series of rescue flights. The paper ends with open design and proof tasks for such bounds.
arxiv-2510-27105:
Lei Chang leads four co-authors in proposing a plasma fibre, a waveguide made of plasma rather than glass. The idea borrows from optical fibres, which trap light by total internal reflection. A helicon plasma with a bright core shows spatial and spectral traits much like a fibre, prompting the team to test whether plasma can guide electromagnetic waves the same way.

Theory covers both an ideal step-like density profile and a realistic smooth Gaussian profile. Reflection should occur when the entry angle passes a threshold at the sharp density gradient. Numerical solutions of Maxwell equations with a cold-plasma response agree with the theory. The authors suggest experiments and uses as a reconfigurable component inside existing communication systems.
arxiv-2510-27505:
T. Gayoux, P.-S. Corasaniti, and 154 other co-authors check a hidden risk in the Euclid survey's cluster counts, in a 2025 paper. Euclid, a space telescope survey, will catalog huge numbers of galaxy clusters. Counting clusters by mass can pin down cosmic parameters. The catch: theory counts halos by one mass rule, while observations weigh them by another.

A mapping must bridge the two mass rules. The standard bridge leans on a concentration-mass relation, an assumed link between a halo's size and its inner crowding. On synthetic data from universe simulations, that bridge biased the cosmic answers by more than twice the noise level. A bridge based on halo sparsity, a sparser inner measure, kept bias below the noise in every case they tried. The lesson: the mass bridge must be chosen with care.
arxiv-2510-27605:
Raagini Patki, Nicholas Battaglia, and Rachel Bean propose a fresh probe of gravity on vast scales in 2025. The probe, called the E_G statistic, can split standard gravity from altered forms. Past gauges infer gas speeds from shifts in galaxy light. This work instead rebuilds speeds from a faint sky effect where moving gas shifts the glow left from the early universe.

A new estimator pairs galaxy maps with both a lensing map of that glow and the rebuilt speed field. Forecasts use maps from two ground telescopes and galaxy samples from a major survey tool. The pairing targets the largest scales, where the new speed method is strongest. Joint signals could test gravity with fresh reach.
arxiv-2511-00005:
Alina Chertock, Arsen Iskhakov, and Alexander Kurganov study uncertainty quantification for forward problems with stand-in models built from high-order CWENO interpolation inside random collocation. Traditional spectral methods wiggle near sharp traits, while the seventh-order central weighted essentially non-oscillatory scheme keeps high accuracy in smooth regions and strength near jumps. A ordered contrast with general polynomial chaos methods follows.

Polynomial chaos reaches spectral convergence but is prone to wiggles, motivating the another. Numerical analysis readers get a balanced option when accuracy and strength must coexist. Forward uncertainty quantification supports engineering decisions where inputs are unsure and answers have shocks.
arxiv-2511-00205:
Yuhan Deng and six colleagues present Fix, a design for serverless computing, where code runs on a provider's machines on demand. In Fix, users, programs, and the platform all share one picture of a job: a fixed procedure that runs on known data or on the outputs of earlier jobs. The platform alone moves data across the network.

Because each stage states exactly what data it needs, the provider can plan tasks and transfers ahead and cut idle waiting. The authors frame the design as an end-to-end argument for rented computing. It points toward a service model where customers pay for results, not for effort.
arxiv-2511-00305:
Amrit Gautam, writing for the ALICE Collaboration, outlines the first study of a rare process in ultraperipheral collisions, where two heavy nuclei pass near each other without touching. Light from one nucleus can strike the other and create hadrons, particles built from quarks and gluons. Studying cases where only the new particles appear, with nothing else, probes quantum chromodynamics and resonances born from gluon interactions.

ALICE measured four-pion production in earlier Run 2 data, with hints of two resonances whose nature is still unclear. The upgraded detector in Run 3 opens richer targets: four- and six-pion states and charmonium decays into four hadrons. Gautam lays out the planned program and what it could reveal about dense gluon matter.
arxiv-2511-00505:
Qi Luo, Xiaonan Li, Junqi Dai, Shuang Cheng, and Xipeng Qiu trim the fat from retrieval-augmented generation, the technique that feeds language models outside documents to curb hallucination. As models internalize more knowledge, big external corpora increasingly repeat what the model already knows. Redundancy raises indexing cost, and worse, it can hurt answers to questions the model could handle alone.

Zero-RAG scores each corpus item with a mastery metric and prunes what the model has mastered. This cuts the Wikipedia corpus by about thirty percent and speeds retrieval by about a fifth, with no loss in answer quality. A query router then steers mastered questions toward internal knowledge, and noise-tolerant tuning teaches the model to ignore irrelevant documents. The pruned system leans on the model's own strengths instead of drowning them.
arxiv-2511-00705:
T Stanton and seventeen co-authors chart how fast young galaxies enriched their gas with heavy elements, using the James Webb Space Telescope's EXCELS survey. Sixty-five star-forming galaxies, seen as they were between redshift two and eight, anchor the study. Gas metallicities come from strong-line calibrations tested on this very sample, with direct-method values for nineteen galaxies as a cross-check.

A clear mass-metallicity relation appears in both redshift halves, with steady slopes and only mild growth in overall enrichment between them. Galaxies at redshift three, within the first fifteen percent of cosmic time, already hold about forty percent of the metal content of equal-mass galaxies today. Hints that star formation rate shapes the scatter stay tentative. The offset from locally defined relations confirms these early galaxies lived far from local equilibrium conditions.
arxiv-2511-00805:
Rishita Agarwal and colleagues introduce REaR, a system for answering questions that need data from several tables at once. Most search tools rank tables only by how well each matches the question. They ignore whether the chosen tables can actually be joined together, which later steps require.

REaR splits the job into three stages. First it retrieves tables that match the query, then it expands the set with tables that can join them, using fast precomputed column comparisons, and finally it prunes weak or noisy candidates. The system uses no large language model, yet on BIRD, MMQA, and Spider data it improves retrieval and later SQL accuracy, at lower cost and delay than model based rivals.
arxiv-2511-00905:
Norihiro Iizuka and Simon Lin study a refined measure of multipartite entanglement, called symmetry resolved genuine multi-entropy, in two kinds of random quantum states. The measure tracks entanglement shared among many parties at once, split by the value of a conserved charge.

For Haar random states, the most unbiased random states, they derive explicit formulas in the large system limit under a global charge symmetry. The dependence on subsystem sizes turns out to look much like the case with no conserved charge. Numerical work on spin systems covers both Haar random and graph states. The graph state results show distinctive entanglement patterns, which the authors contrast with the Haar random behavior.
arxiv-2511-01105:
Aaron Dunbrack explores Glass patterns, a little known cousin of the moire patterns that appear when two grids are twisted against each other. Twisting two copies of an ordered crystal gives a long wavelength moire pattern. Twisting a disordered, aperiodic structure instead gives a single moire spot at the rotation center, the Glass pattern.

Across several models, Dunbrack shows these patterns do useful work. They let microscopic parameters be read off from larger scale resistivity measurements. They create an impurity that changes a moire lattice's properties at its center. And they allow domain formation in amorphous magnets. The paper frames Glass patterns as a generic feature of twisted disordered systems and a framework for future theory and experiment.
arxiv-2511-01205:
Yueqiao Jin and colleagues run an experiment on how an artificial intelligence teammate changes moral discussion. Generative AI is increasingly placed as a peer in collaborative learning, but its effect on ethical deliberation was unclear. University students discussed an autonomous vehicle dilemma in groups of three under three conditions.

Some groups were human only, others gained a supportive AI teammate, and others a contrarian one.
