Supportive AI raised the share of grounded, qualified claims and drew reasoning together around care and fairness. Contrarian AI modestly broadened the moral framing and kept value pluralism alive. Both AI conditions reduced drift away from the topic. Final decisions, though, were driven mainly by each participant's starting stance, so the AI reshaped the process more than the outcome.
arxiv-2511-01405:
Vanessa Wirth and colleagues speed up high resolution radar imaging of moving targets. Large aperture millimeter wave MIMO radar can reconstruct near field surfaces in three dimensions and works in any light or weather. The reconstruction is so computation heavy that frame rates suffer, and bandwidth and capture rates are squeezed.

Earlier few tone imaging cut the number of transmitted frequencies, at the cost of range ambiguity and a need to already know roughly where the target sits. Their method, MM-2FSK, extends two tone stepped frequency imaging with a per point depth prior from an external source, which need not be radar. Processing the prior resolves the ambiguities, enabling precise near field imaging of geometrically complex surfaces at reduced cost.
arxiv-2511-01505:
Aprajita Shrivastava, Prasanta Char, Sakshi Gautam, and Sarmistha Banik ask how much the recipe matters when physicists model the matter inside neutron stars. They work in a density-dependent relativistic mean-field framework. Within it, they vary how the couplings between mesons and baryons change with density. They try scalar, vector, and mixed forms, and include exotic Lambda hyperons in the mix.

Most of the new parameter sets give stiffer equations of state, hence larger stars with higher tidal deformability. Adding Lambda hyperons softens the matter again, yet the predicted maximum masses still clear the observed two-solar-mass bar and agree with NICER telescope measurements. The lesson is that coupling choices, often left at defaults, strongly shape what the models say about dense matter.
arxiv-2511-01605:
Daniel Busbib and Ami Wiesel study a classic task in signal work: finding a Toeplitz covariance matrix by Gaussian maximum likelihood. New algorithms often solve this nonconvex task in full when data is rich. Yet the cost surface is oddly hard to move on, and the authors set out to learn why.

They use a Carathéodory form that builds the matrix from steering vectors, set by frequencies and amplitudes. A small case shows that amplitudes alone, on a fixed frequency grid, cannot fit even ideal data. The frequencies must move too. Their main result then shows the curved form adds no false stationary points. Each such point is a true likelihood point. In the ideal case, gradient descent thus finds the true matrix, and extra parameters speed it up in practice.
arxiv-2511-01705:
Edoardo Di Martino, Matteo Cinelli, and Roy Cerqueti improve a basic statistical question: does a dataset have one peak or several? The classic Dip Test answers it, but its statistic is awkward: interpretation depends on sample size, significance needs calibration, and in huge samples it rejects single-peakedness over trivial deviations.

Their Z-Dip measure treats the dip statistic as a random variable under the null hypothesis of one peak and standardizes the observed value, producing scores comparable across datasets of any size. Simulation-based calibration yields a universal decision threshold that closely reproduces Dip Test verdicts without per-size adjustments. Validation on simulated data and more than 88,000 real opinion distributions showed near-perfect agreement with the classical test, with a far more interpretable score.
arxiv-2511-02205:
Kevin Valencia, Thilina Balasooriya, Xihaier Luo, Shinjae Yoo, and David Keetae Park build a learning system for experimental data that arrive from many sensors, unevenly and with noise. Real measurements within each modality are sparse and irregular, yet the modalities are correlated with each other, and which sensors are available changes from place to place and time to time. Models that demand a fixed, complete input grid throw away much of the usable record.

Their framework, OmniField, learns a continuous neural field that is conditioned on whichever modalities happen to be present. A crosstalk block with iterative cross-modal refinement aligns the signals before decoding, enabling reconstruction, interpolation, forecasting, and prediction across modalities without gridding the data first. Across extensive tests it beat eight strong baselines and, under heavy simulated sensor noise, performed close to its clean-input level.
arxiv-2511-02305:
Sushant Pokhriyal and Joel Rosenfeld widen the class of motions that a popular analysis framework can handle. Koopman and Liouville operators turn a nonlinear dynamical system into a linear one acting on functions. That enables identification and prediction methods such as dynamic mode decomposition. Working in reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces gives bounded, well-defined operators, but it also ties the allowed dynamics to the smoothness of the function space, shutting out rough or non-analytic motion.

Their restricted Liouville operator is built over the Hardy space on the unit disk, a classical space of analytic functions. The restriction is arranged to admit a broader family of dynamics than the usual construction. The aim is to keep the operator machinery, and the algorithms that flow from it, available for systems whose behaviour is not smooth or analytic.
arxiv-2511-02605:
Tiberiu-Andrei Georgescu, Alexander Goodall, Dalal Alrajeh, Francesco Belardinelli, and Sebastian Uchitel build safety shields for learning agents. The agents can rewrite their own rules when the world breaks the assumptions they were designed under. A shield watches a reinforcement learning agent and blocks actions that violate a formal specification. Classical shields are frozen: fixed logic, fixed abstraction. When the environment stops behaving as assumed, a frozen shield can make the agent's goals unreachable.

Their framework uses GR(1) specifications, a tractable fragment of linear temporal logic covering safety and liveness. Violations of the environment assumptions are detected at run time, and inductive logic programming repairs the specification online, weakening goals only as much as necessary and in a readable way. In two case studies, a mine pump controller and an arcade game agent, adaptive shielding kept a perfect logical record with near-optimal rewards, while static controllers proved severely suboptimal.
arxiv-2511-02805:
Qianhao Yuan and eight colleagues built MemSearcher, a search agent that keeps its memory small while it works. Typical language model agents paste the whole chat history into every step, so inputs grow long, noisy, and costly. Their 2025 framework keeps only question-relevant facts in a compact memory, holding the context near a fixed size across turns.

Training such an agent is tricky, since each turn runs under a different context. The team answers with multi-context GRPO, a reinforcement learning method that spreads the whole trajectory's reward across all its turns. In tests, MemSearcher beat strong history-stacking baselines on several public data sets. It did so while its token count stayed nearly flat as conversations grew longer.
arxiv-2511-02905:
Mark Dodici, Scott Tremaine, and Yanqin Wu revisit how pairs of stars evolve near the massive black hole at a galaxy's center. Such binaries feed several known phenomena, from hypervelocity stars to mergers. Earlier work said tides plus wobbles driven by the black hole could squeeze a few pairs until they collide. The 2025 paper updates that model with effects the older work left out.

When a pair is driven close, the authors argue, tides should contract the orbit quickly rather than let the stars crash, leaving a very tight binary. Passing stars and vector resonant relaxation then make such close passes far more common. In simulations, one in five binaries a parsec from our own galaxy's center contracts this way, rising to three in five much closer in.
arxiv-2511-03305:
Haoqin Zhao and colleagues harden wireless links against jamming when sensor readings cannot be fully trusted. Most defenses assume clean sensing and act on one time scale, yet real radios face mixed action delays and small reading errors. Neural decision makers are brittle here, since a tiny input shift can flip a choice badly.

Their model plans across several time scales while treating the true state as uncertain within bounds. Two robust schemes keep links working under those bounded errors. One pairs a deep learning method with a worst-case attack step used during training, so the agent learns under pressure. The work aims at steady transmission even when a jammer and faulty sensors strike at once.
arxiv-2511-03405:
Alexandros Vazaios and colleagues merge hindsight replay with tree search learning so failed tries still teach. Search systems guided by neural networks excel at games and classic search, yet sparse rewards starve early training when the network knows nothing. Hindsight replay fixes that by relabeling failed paths as if their end states had been the goal.

Their adaptable version lets builders tune which goals get relabeled, what policy targets are used, and which paths are picked. Tests include equation discovery, where the search must assemble a formula that fits data. Flexible hindsight settings beat fixed ones across the trials reported. The framework gives search learners a dial for turning dead ends into lessons.
arxiv-2511-03505:
Anthony M Gaglione and Dennis Spellman settle a special case of when a matrix group maps into itself only in reversible ways. A group is co-Hopfian when every self-map that stays injective must also cover the whole group. A recent result tied that trait for special linear groups to the same trait in the underlying field, with gaps at small cases.

For the field built by closing the two-element field algebraically, the two-by-two group is shown to be co-Hopfian. That field is plainly co-Hopfian as a ring, so the group result extends the earlier link. The authors then use it to show a named class of groups is not closed under a logic-based sameness, answering a question they posed years earlier.
arxiv-2511-04005:
Yilun Wu, Yi Chen, and Julia Velkovska validate a machine learning method for spotting quenched jets in heavy-ion collisions, where jets lose energy crossing quark-gluon plasma. Many processes shape jet observables at once, and detector effects can confuse the signal, so a jet-by-jet estimate is valuable.

A long short-term memory network trained on jet substructure and parton shower history predicts quenching levels for photon-jet events from the Jewel generator. Predictions correlated strongly with true energy loss. After detector simulation with Delphes, the method still identified quenching in a realistic setting. Tests on momentum imbalance, fragmentation, and jet shape, none used in training, confirmed it learned real quenching features.
arxiv-2511-04205:
Michal Karp is the lead author among seven authors testing whether language models can pass Poland's qualifying examination for the National Appeal Chamber, and whether model judges can grade such attempts. The exam joins a multiple-choice test on public procurement law with a written judgment, and a hybrid retrieval pipeline supported the candidate models.

Several models, tested closed-book and with retrieval support, scored satisfactorily on the knowledge test. None passed the practical written part, however, and model-as-judge evaluations often diverged from the official committee. Hallucinated citations, weak legal argument, and shaky logic were named limits. Automatic judging of high-stakes legal writing looks premature on this evidence.
arxiv-2511-04405:
Benoit Cadorel and two colleagues open a three-part study of complex quasi-projective varieties. Part one uses Nevanlinna theory, a tool for measuring how holomorphic maps spread. The maps run from a lightly ramified cover of the punctured disc into the variety.

For varieties of log-general type with maximal quasi-Albanese dimension, they prove a Big Picard type theorem. As a byproduct, the generalized Green-Griffiths-Lang conjecture follows for this class. This first paper gathers the Nevanlinna-based parts of the series. The results tie hyperbolicity, how maps are restricted, to the shape of a variety's fundamental group.
arxiv-2511-04605:
Fabian Zhou and two colleagues ask what sets the size of quark-gluon plasma in ultracentral collisions. In these head-on nuclear crashes, average particle momentum rises with particle count. Early readings blamed a hotter, denser fireball at fixed volume.

Newer simulations show the volume itself can shift with count for some starting models. The team links that volume change, on paper, to the radial shape of the density field. One-point and two-point functions of the lumpy initial density do the work. They find the volume change stays small when the lumps are narrow, clarifying the momentum signal.
arxiv-2511-04805:
Yushu Zhao and two colleagues compress large mixture-of-experts language models with PuzzleMoE. These models activate only a few experts per input, which scales them cheaply. Storing every expert, though, eats memory and blocks wide deployment.

Dropping or merging experts naively hurts quality at strong compression rates. PuzzleMoE merges experts sparsely by finding element-wise redundancy and specialization in their weights. A dual-mask scheme guides which weights combine and which stay distinct. Bit-packed inference then speeds the shrunken model at run time. The training-free method targets high accuracy under heavy compression. That pairing of merging and packing is the core of the design.
arxiv-2511-04905:
Maksym Luz and a co-author solve a forecasting task for sequences whose pattern repeats by season, with long memory and jumps that scale with level. The true sequence is hidden, and only a noisy, season-linked view of it can be seen.

For known spectra, they give formulas for the error and the traits of the best linear estimates of future values. When spectra are not known for sure, they find the least kind spectra and the robust traits that guard the worst case. The work also covers linked sequences that move together over time.
arxiv-2511-05005:
Dongsu Lee, Daehee Lee, and Amy Zhang present MAC-Flow, a method for teams of agents that must act together. Good team work needs rich joint behavior from past data, plus fast choices in real time, and past methods tended to trade one for the other.

MAC-Flow first learns a flow-based picture of joint acts from offline data. It then squeezes that picture into one-step local policies that keep the team in sync but run fast. Across four test suites with many settings and data sets, it runs far faster than diffusion rivals, about fourteen times faster in the reported tests.
arxiv-2511-05105:
Tim Bauer and a co-author report that some localized fermion states in a chiral spin liquid refuse to mix with other states. Such mixing is a big hurdle for building and steering exotic matter states in quantum simulators.

The states form by wave cancellation at tuned coupling values, in the Yao-Kivelson model, and fill flat bands on a kagome-like lattice. Using a broad Majorana hopping frame, the authors give exact forms for these states in many flux set-ups and in both phases of the model. The set also holds Ising anyons, prized for quantum work.
arxiv-2511-05405:
Lefeng Zhou and co-authors design a Sagnac tractor atom interferometer built on a photonic integrated circuit, a chip that guides light. Atoms ride in twin optical lattices that rotate in opposed senses, formed by evanescent fields from modes in round chip waveguides.

Interference between the counter-rotating atoms can sense rotation with high care. The authors build quantum models of the radial and spin motion in moving frames, which cuts compute cost. They work the design through for rubidium-87 atoms on a sample chip, from field modes to trap shapes, as a plan for a compact rotation sensor.
arxiv-2511-05805:
Winston Chen, Michael Sjoding, and Jenna Wiens ask how to grade an AI model fairly when a treatment in the study changes the very outcome being predicted. Randomized trials solve this by grading on the control group alone, but that wastes the treatment group's data. Trials are costly, so waste matters.

The authors first quantify the bias from naively pooling both groups, and derive when that bias flips which model looks best. Their fix reweights treatment-group cases to mimic the no-treatment world, using nuisance parameters. The reweighted grading is unbiased and uses all the data. On synthetic and real data sets it chose the better model more reliably than the control-only approach, across effect sizes and sample sizes.
arxiv-2511-06005:
Adit Desai, Sudipta Roy, and Mohna Chakraborty examine how vision-language models reason their way into biased judgments about people's jobs. These models read images through statistical associations, not social context, so their stated reasoning can carry bias into downstream uses. The team set out to expose that link.

Five open-source models were asked to predict occupations on the FairFace data set, across many jobs and three prompting styles. Each run produced both a prediction and its reasoning. The reasoning patterns, the authors find, systematically underlie the gaps between demographic groups. Intersectional disparities, where combined traits compound the bias, trace back to those biased chains of thought. They argue model reasoning must be aligned with human values before deployment.
arxiv-2511-06305:
Edwige Cyffers argues, in a position paper, that choosing the privacy budget is not the real weakness of differential privacy. Critics often call the budget hard to interpret and cite that difficulty as a reason to prefer looser data protection methods. Cyffers warns that this framing pushes decision-makers toward unsafe alternatives.

The hard part, the paper contends, is judging privacy risk in a real context, a burden every serious risk method shares. That difficulty comes from the problem itself, not from the definition of differential privacy. Any sound risk estimation method, given current research, should either fit inside the differential privacy framework or explain clearly why it cannot.
arxiv-2511-06805:
Jinhao Chen and four co-authors try to make vision-language models better at solving mathematics problems that involve pictures. Models trained on fixed data sets copied from a teacher learn only static reasoning patterns and struggle with new, harder questions. Their system, called MathSE, instead lets the model improve itself in repeated cycles.

Each cycle runs the model, reflects on its answers, and fine-tunes it using correct reasoning paths it found plus feedback from a separate reward model that judges final outcomes. Over rounds, the training data grows out of the model's own improving attempts rather than a fixed teacher's output. On a suite of hard benchmarks the method gained clearly over its base models, and on one test set it passed a leading open-source rival.
arxiv-2511-07405:
Manon Berriche and colleagues built SPOT, a French dataset for spotting comments that halt or redirect heated online threads. Sociologists call such moments stopping points. They include irony, quiet doubt, or short challenges that counterspeech research often misses.

The corpus holds more than forty three thousand hand-labeled Facebook comments tied to posts flagged as false information, with article and thread context attached. The team turned the idea into a yes-or-no labeling task with clear guidelines. Fine-tuned encoder models beat prompted large models in their benchmarks. Moderation researchers gain a new way to study how ordinary comments defuse false claims.
arxiv-2511-08005:
Huacen Wang and Hongqiang Wang present a two layer electrostatic film actuator with a built in brake for light robots. Motor driven robots can be heavy, complex to control, and need separate braking parts. Thin electrostatic films promise light, flexible motion with accurate open loop positioning, but output force in air has been low.

By placing electrodes alternately on top and bottom layers, the design shrinks effective electrode pitch without harder manufacturing. Actuation stress reaches about two hundred forty one newtons per square metre, roughly ninety percent above earlier three phase designs. Demonstrations include payload handling, a robotic arm, and a dual mode gripper.
arxiv-2511-08205:
Silvie Illesova and co-authors offer a practical three stage route from classic machine learning to hybrid quantum classic workflows. Many practitioners lack quantum training, so jumping straight to quantum models is unrealistic. The setup starts with a classic self training model, then adds a minimal hybrid quantum variant, and finally uses diagnostic feedback from QMetric to refine the design.

On the Iris data set, the refined hybrid model raised accuracy from a low classic value to a much higher quantum assisted one. In the authors reported terms, that is a jump from about zero point three to about zero point nine. Even modest quantum parts, guided by diagnostics, improved class separation.
arxiv-2511-08305:
Ly Tran Ho Khanh and co-authors improve best of many reasoning in language models by steering internal activations toward more diverse solution paths. Sampling several candidate answers helps only when the candidates actually differ, yet models often repeat the same error in slightly different words. Their unsupervised test time method searches for steering vectors that push multiple reasoning trajectories apart at once.

At synchronization points during generation, steering vectors are chosen to maximize the volume spanned by intervened activation sets. That search becomes a Riemannian optimization over products of spheres with a log determinant goal, solved by block coordinate descent. On math benchmarks, diversity and final accuracy both beat plain sampling.
arxiv-2511-08505:
Omri Koshorek and co-authors tackle aggregative questions, the kind whose answer requires gathering facts from many documents and reasoning over the whole set. Retrieval augmented generation usually assumes only a few paragraphs matter per question, so it fails on totals, comparisons, and other corpus wide queries. Their S-RAG approach builds a structured representation of the corpus when documents are ingested, before any question arrives.

At answer time, natural language questions are translated into formal queries over that structure. Two new data sets, HOTELS and WORLD CUP, are introduced to test aggregative skill, alongside a public benchmark. S-RAG substantially outperforms common retrieval systems and long context language models on these tasks.
arxiv-2511-08705:
Marina Anagnostopoulou-Merkouri completes the proof of a generalization of Cameron's base size conjecture, a long-standing question in permutation group theory. A base for a group action is a small set of points whose combined stabilizer is trivial, and the conjecture bounded base sizes for almost simple primitive groups with unusual stabilizers.

The generalized statement allows several different maximal subgroups at once. With seven or more of them, the group always has a regular orbit on the product of the corresponding coset spaces. The same holds with six subgroups except for one named configuration involving the Mathieu group M24 and copies of M23. The proof leans on probabilistic methods and fixed point ratio estimates, building on recent joint work for groups of Lie type.
arxiv-2511-09105:
Shigeki Kusaka and five co-authors compute the cheapest way to poison the alignment of a language model by flipping preference labels. During RLHF or DPO training, human comparisons teach the model what to prefer. An attacker who flips some labels can steer the final policy. This study asks for the minimum number of flips that steering truly needs.

Cast as a convex optimization problem with linear constraints, the attack yields provable lower and upper bounds on its minimum cost. A byproduct is practical: any existing label-flipping attack can be post-processed through their method to need fewer flips for the same poisoning effect. Experiments confirm the savings, largest when the reward model's feature dimension is small compared with the dataset. The results map a fundamental vulnerability in preference-based alignment and hand defenders a yardstick for robustness.
arxiv-2511-09305:
Ryan Martin, Naomi Singer, and Jonathan Williams tackle a quiet weak point in regression work. The weak point is doubt about which variables belong in the model. Frequentist methods lack general confidence sets for model structure, and Bayesian credible sets can miss their promised coverage. Their paper extends the possibilistic inferential model approach to fill that gap.

The extension handles Gaussian linear regression and can include partial prior information about the structure, which also disciplines selection. The authors prove the resulting statements are calibrated against all data-generating processes compatible with the assumptions. In particular, their sets for the unknown structure hit the promised coverage level in finite samples. Two benchmark data sets show how the method compares with existing approaches.
arxiv-2511-09605:
Johannes Kiechle and seven co-authors classify 3D medical scans by looking at them from every direction at once. Tumors and organs rarely align with the standard axial, sagittal, and coronal slicing planes, so plain slice-based models miss their true extent. Worse, most methods average slice features independently, discarding the geometry tying slices together.

TomoGraphView samples cross-sections from directions spread evenly over a sphere around the volume, standard and non-standard alike. A graph neural network then pools features over that spherical arrangement, preserving spatial coherence. The approach builds on 2D foundation-model features while respecting 3D structure. The authors publicly share their code and a user-friendly slicing library for omnidirectional volume analysis.
arxiv-2511-09805:
Albert Leonardo Aguilar Suarez and Gregory Beroza report pervasive label errors in the datasets used to train machine learning models for seismology. Good labels matter as much as good algorithms, so the authors used an ensemble of the PhaseNet and EQTransformer models to audit popular earthquake datasets. They checked 8.6 million examples drawn from eight named datasets used across the field.

Four error types emerged, led by earthquakes with no label at all, then noise samples that secretly contain earthquakes, wrong arrival times, and signals with no earthquake. The average error rate was 3.9 percent, reaching about eight percent in the worst dataset. The authors publish a companion list of flagged examples so training can use only reliable data.
arxiv-2511-09905:
Brian B. Moser and eight co-authors present PRISM, a dataset distillation framework meant to keep synthetic training data diverse. Distillation compresses a big dataset into a small synthetic one, but methods that copy a single teacher model inherit its biases. As distilled size grows, samples turn smooth and alike, hurting generalization to new models.

PRISM splits the supervision: one teacher architecture supplies the logit-matching target, while a changing subset of other architectures handles the batch-normalization alignment objective. On ImageNet-1K it consistently beat single-teacher and recent multi-teacher methods at low and middle images-per-class levels. Feature measurements confirmed richer diversity within each class, and the authors add teacher selection analysis plus a parallel batch scheme for faster synthesis.
arxiv-2511-10105:
Sherjeel Shabih, Lukas Pielsticker, and twenty co-authors present pynxtools, a Python approach that converts experimental materials science data into the standardized NeXus format. Research data often violates findability and reuse principles because every instrument writes its own format. NeXus defines shared storage specifications per technique, and pynxtools supplies a fixed, versioned set of those definitions across methods from atom probe tomography to X-ray diffraction.

A modular plugin system converts data and metadata from instruments and electronic lab notebooks into the unified definitions, validating correctness and compliance along the way. The command-line tool plugs into research data management systems, with the NOMAD platform detailed as an example. The goal is genuine interoperability, so data sets from different techniques can be found, combined, and reused.
arxiv-2511-10405:
Shu-Chiuan Chang and Robert Shrock compute where the zeros of chromatic polynomials pile up for a family of hierarchical graphs. A chromatic polynomial counts the ways to color a graph so that neighbors differ, and its complex zeros reveal deep structure. Their graphs are built by repeatedly replacing each edge with several paths, starting from a simple tree.

The method leans on statistical physics: the chromatic polynomial is a special case of the Potts model partition function. An exact renormalization step relates each graph in the family to the previous one. Iterating it sorts the complex plane into regions of different behavior. The authors chart the boundary curve for many parameter choices and find where it crosses the real axis.
arxiv-2511-10505:
Reza Pirmoradian, M. Hossein Bek-Khoshnevis, Sadaf Ebadi, and M. Reza Tanhayi probe how entanglement is organized in field theories where interactions act across distance rather than only between neighbors. Such nonlocal theories are known to produce volume-law entanglement entropy, meaning entanglement grows with the size of a region instead of just its boundary.

Using numerical lattice simulations, the team measures mutual and tripartite information, which reveal finer structure than entropy alone. They find mutual information reaching across extremely long ranges and a monogamy pattern that behaves unusually as regions move apart. A holographic gravity model reproduces the entropy scaling but predicts none of this shared information. The mismatch suggests these quantum states are too complex for conventional geometric pictures of spacetime.
arxiv-2511-10605:
Thomas Hartke and nine co-authors use ultracold potassium atoms to watch a basic competition in quantum matter: fermion pairing pulling toward superfluidity while magnetism and charge order pull elsewhere. Their system is a spin-imbalanced attractive Hubbard gas, imaged with single-atom resolution across wide ranges of density, magnetization, and interaction strength.

At low imbalance and weak attraction, they find nonlocal fermion pairs mixed with itinerant excess fermions. Stronger interactions produce an effective mixture of hard-core bosons and fermions. As spin doping grows, charge-density wave correlations give way to a Fermi liquid of polarons. Beyond a threshold of imbalance and interaction, evidence appears for combined spin- and pair-density wave order, a possible precursor of magnetized superfluidity.
arxiv-2511-11605:
David Balaban and Adrian Miclăuş describe twin_width_fmi, their solver entered in the heuristic track of the PACE 2025 competition on the minimum dominating set problem. A dominating set is a set of vertices such that every vertex in a graph is either in the set or next to one, and smaller sets are better.

A standard greedy heuristic that repeatedly picks the vertex covering the most uncovered vertices provides the starting solution. Simulated annealing then tries removals and swaps, sometimes accepting worse moves so the search can escape local minima. Their final component, hedom5, follows iterative greedy ideas that alternate building, pruning, and repair, and it was the version submitted to the contest.
arxiv-2511-11705:
Arya Narang measures whether adding a dish's name to its photo helps a neural network estimate calories. Nutrition tracking from images alone is error-prone, and a short text label is nearly free to supply, so even a small gain could matter at scale.

Using the Nutrition5k dataset curated by Google, an image-only convolutional network is compared with a multimodal twin that also reads the dish name. Mean absolute error fell by just over one kilocalorie, about a one and a quarter percent improvement. The gain is real but modest, and the study frames the honest question: when does a second input earn its place in a deployed estimator?
arxiv-2511-11805:
Anna R. Gallazzi and thirteen co-authors dissect how stellar age and metal content scale with galaxy mass in a sample of five hundred fifty-two galaxies seen as they were about seven billion years ago. Data combine the LEGA-C survey at that epoch with the local SDSS sample for comparison.

Splitting galaxies into quiescent and star-forming groups explains the two branches of the age-mass relation, while the metallicity-mass relation shows no such split, though the groups occupy it differently. A high-metallicity sequence holds both quiet and weakly star-forming systems. At lower masses the star-forming relation steepens sharply. Fossil records of this kind reveal how galaxies built their stars across cosmic time.
arxiv-2511-11905:
Maksym Parymuda, Taras Krokhmalskii, and Oleg Derzhko study a flat-band quantum magnet, the spin one-half Heisenberg antiferromagnet on the Tasaki square lattice, near the magnetic field that fully saturates its spins. Flat bands quench kinetic energy, letting interactions dominate and exotic low-temperature states emerge.

Ground states in the relevant magnetization sectors map onto a classical hard-squares problem on an auxiliary lattice, which classical Monte Carlo simulations then explore. The headline feature is an order-disorder phase transition at low temperature just below saturation, falling in the two-dimensional Ising universality class. Flat-band magnetism keeps surprising theorists, and exact mappings like this convert quantum puzzles into solvable classical ones.
arxiv-2511-12105:
Oriane de Leuze and three co-authors examine how electric charge moves through networks of MXene flakes, thin two-dimensional crystals used in sensors and shielding. Most past work looked at single flakes, yet real devices use many flakes joined on a surface. The open question is how much the joins between flakes matter.

Scanning probe tests show each flake holds a near even voltage, while the drop in voltage sits right at the joins between flakes. The team gives numbers for that join resistance. They also track how humidity changes the response at single-flake, multi-flake and network scales, and find the joins lead the sensing behavior as well.
arxiv-2511-12305:
Zhizhen Li and five co-authors present MMSense, a foundation model for wireless sensing that handles many tasks and many kinds of input at once. Large models are already used for channel modeling and beamforming, but most work uses one modality and one narrow goal. Sensing in real settings spans channels, surroundings and people.

MMSense converts image, radar, LiDAR and text data into forms a vision model can share, then fuses them with a gating step that weighs each modality. A vision-language backbone aligns the features and follows task instructions. Extra attention and loss weighting steps aid transfer across tasks. Tests on real wireless datasets beat task-specific and large-model baselines, in their report.
arxiv-2511-12405:
Hyunki Seong and four co-authors present VLA-R, an end-to-end driving framework for open-world settings where a vehicle meets conditions it never saw in training. Unstructured outdoor driving demands strong generalization, which narrow trained models lack. Their system joins open-world perception with a new way to retrieve driving actions.

A frozen vision-language model supplies detection and segmentation features guided by text prompts, with no domain-specific tuning. A small transformer module then merges fine visual detail with language-aligned features. Contrastive learning aligns those features with action representations, so suitable driving behavior can be retrieved for new scenes. Tests on a real robotic platform show strong generalization, in their report.
arxiv-2511-12505:
Allan Lo and five co-authors study rainbow subgraphs in graphs whose edges are colored under a star rule. A coloring of a graph assigns colors to edges. It can fail to be rainbow in two ways: two edges sharing a vertex share a color, or two separate edges share a color. A star coloring forbids the second failure.

The team asks how many colors a star coloring of a large complete graph can use while still avoiding a rainbow copy of a fixed graph. The problem is a special case of generalized Ramsey numbers studied by Axenovich and Iverson. The authors extend those earlier results and pin down the maximum in this star-colored setting.
arxiv-2511-12605:
E. J. Badcock and S. Mughal present M-OWNS, a marching method for modeling how disturbances grow in a boundary layer, the thin flow region near a surface where instability can trigger turbulence. The method factors out a carrier wave from a parabolized stability framework and combines it with a recursive one-way Navier-Stokes projection, which advances the solution downstream step by step.

A resolution analysis shows the factored system can use a coarser downstream step for modes whose wavelength sits near the carrier wave. A fixed-carrier variant, set from the base flow and frequencies alone, matches that accuracy at the same per-step cost and cuts the total solve count severalfold across test cases. The method is validated on incompressible flows.
arxiv-2511-12905:
Tania-Amanda Fredrick Eneye, Ashlesha Malla, and Pawan Paudel test which LinkedIn profile traits predict professional success. Their data cover more than sixty-two thousand anonymized profiles. The outcomes they model are promotions, follower counts, and the rate of career progression. Machine learning models search the profile features for the factors that most strongly track those outcomes, turning the platform's public self-presentation into measurable variables that can be ranked by predictive weight.

Promotions turned out to be highly predictable from profile characteristics, while follower growth proved more complex and harder to model. The authors offer the findings as practical guidance for professionals shaping their profiles and career strategies. The study is compact, with a short abstract. Readers should treat it as an exploratory analysis rather than a causal account: it shows which profile features travel with success in this dataset. Not which changes would cause a career to improve.
arxiv-2511-13005:
Wenqian Ye and four co-authors debias CLIP by choosing its words more carefully. CLIP classifies images zero-shot by matching pictures to text prompts, but it learns shortcuts, naming objects by their usual backgrounds rather than their features, and those shortcuts collapse on out-of-distribution data. Existing fixes fine-tune the model or need advance knowledge of the bias. SAGE needs none of that: after analyzing how spurious bias distorts zero-shot classification, it searches a space of prompt templates and keeps the prompts that push class meanings farthest apart.

No training, fine-tuning, or external annotations are involved, only prompt selection. Across four real-world benchmarks and five backbone models, SAGE consistently improved zero-shot performance and generalization, beating prior zero-shot approaches, with the largest gains in worst-group robustness.
arxiv-2511-13105:
Seungjae Kim, SeungJoon Lee, and MyeongAh Cho blend old and new motion prediction for tracking many objects in video. Tracking-by-detection systems usually predict motion with a Kalman filter, which is fast but assumes near-linear movement. Learned predictors capture curves and turns but generalize poorly and cost more. The authors' analysis found the classical filter still wins in up to a third of cases, even in datasets dominated by nonlinear motion, so neither approach should be discarded.

PlugTrack fuses the two adaptively. A multi-perceptive analysis of each track's motion produces blending factors that decide, moment by moment, how much to trust each predictor. The framework bolts onto existing predictors without modifying them. It posted significant gains on MOT17 and MOT20 and state-of-the-art results on DanceTrack. Classical tools, fused wisely, remain competitive.
arxiv-2511-13605:
Niv Buchbinder and 3 co-authors introduce the submodular objectives chasing problem, where a sequence of constrained maximization tasks arrives over time. Both the objective and the allowed ground set change at each step, and the goal is high solution quality with few changes, called recourse, against an offline benchmark. Many online problems fit this single frame.

For cardinality and partition matroid constraints, their polynomial-time methods reach the optimal approximation factor with optimal competitive recourse. The engine is a new meta-algorithm that maximizes the multilinear extension under general constraints through cutting planes, long a tool for exact minimization. Extra uses include curvature-sensitive static algorithms and communication protocols, widening the reach of the approach.
arxiv-2511-13705:
Alaa Mezghiche hunts for rare cancer subtypes inside kidney cancer gene expression data with an autoencoder and stability-aware clustering. Pan-cancer clustering on a public RNA dataset mostly rediscovers tissue of origin, which serves as a negative control. The real search therefore narrows to kidney cancer cases alone, using the most variable genes.

An autoencoder compresses each tumor into a compact latent vector, and k-means scans cluster counts under a preset discovery rule that demands rarity plus stability across seeds. One small cluster, under seven percent of patients, recurred with high stability and showed coherent marker genes under differential expression tests. The workflow shows how stability checks can certify a rare subtype claim.
arxiv-2511-13905:
Amin Heyrani Nobari and Faez Ahmed offer a simpler engine for topology optimization, the design method that carves material out of a part until only the needed structure remains. The standard solver, MMA, is powerful but complex, while plain projected gradient descent struggles when several constraints act at once. Their PGD-TO framework recasts the projection step as a regularized quadratic problem.

That change removes the need to hunt for active constraints and keeps the math well posed even when constraints clash. A semismooth Newton solver handles the general case, with faster tools for simpler ones. Across four benchmark families, from basic stiffness tasks to multi-material and center-of-mass limits, PGD-TO matches the standard solver's results.
arxiv-2511-14105:
Jin-Peng Zhang and nine co-authors simulate how J/psi particles are produced when protons collide at three LHC-era energies. They use the PACIAE model, which extends the PYTHIA event generator with rescattering among partons and hadrons around the hadronization stage. Both color-singlet and color-octet production channels are included within the NRQCD framework.

Cluster collapse and weak decays of b-hadrons add further contributions. The simulated momentum spectra match experimental data at both mid and forward rapidity. The authors break down how much each mechanism contributes and how those shares move with collision energy and rapidity, including feed-down from heavier charmonium states inside the NRQCD channels.
arxiv-2511-14205:
Minkwan Kim and Yoonsang Lee teach musculoskeletal characters to walk without any motion examples. Their framework, FreeMusco, learns latent representations and control policies together, using the body model itself as a strong prior. Energy-aware, body-adaptive movement emerges from scratch rather than being copied from recordings, and no demonstrations are provided at any stage.

Distinct strategies appear on their own: quadrupedal gaits for a chimp-like body and bipedal gaits for a humanoid one, generalizing across human, animal, and synthetic forms. The learned latent space supports goal navigation and path following. Training uses model-based reinforcement learning with a combined objective and a time-averaged loss that respects the periodic structure of gait.
arxiv-2511-14605:
M. Mirzakhani, R. Mahapatra, and M. Platt characterize a cesium iodide scintillator coupled to a silicon photomultiplier at cold temperatures. Such detectors can hunt rare low energy events. The crystal was polished, shielded from light and background, and read out with a custom amplifier. Response was studied from one hundred kelvin up to room temperature.

A quality measure peaked at one hundred and seventy-five kelvin, marking best photon detection there. Pulse shapes also shifted with temperature. Baseline noise at the optimum implies a threshold near three kiloelectronvolts. Results confirm the system can run at low thresholds. That supports use in rare event and low energy particle searches.
arxiv-2511-14705:
Panpan Qi, Xuanpeng Xiao, and three co-authors combine a machine learning model with a classic nuclear model to predict how readily an alpha particle forms inside a heavy nucleus. That readiness, the preformation factor, strongly affects how fast the nucleus decays by alpha emission. The learning model was trained on nearly five hundred nuclei.

The predicted factors show clear odd-even patterns and dips at closed nuclear shells, as physics would suggest. They also line up with simple quantities tied to decay energy and fragmentation. Feeding the learned factors into the classic potential model sharpens half-life predictions a lot. The hybrid route offers a practical tool for estimating unknown decay rates.
arxiv-2511-15005:
Moses Kiprono builds a mathematical framework for understanding why large language models hallucinate, producing fluent text that is simply not true. The framework treats generation as a probabilistic process and tracks how small errors compound as each new word builds on the last. Tools from information theory, signal analysis, and Bayesian statistics are combined into one lens.

On the measurement side, Kiprono proposes refined uncertainty scores, including versions that track meaning and phase patterns rather than word choice alone. On the remedy side, the work organizes known defenses, such as contrastive decoding, retrieval grounding, factual alignment, and refusing to answer. The aim is a principled map for making language models safer to rely on.
arxiv-2511-15205:
Lixiang Chen, Yongtang Shi, and Liwen Zhang bound the first Steklov eigenvalue of graphs drawn on surfaces with handles. Steklov problems mix interior behavior with boundary data, and on graphs they govern how a network vibrates when only its boundary is driven. For flat, genus-zero graphs a bound was recently proved, and its authors asked what happens when the surface has positive genus.

The new bound grows with the genus and shrinks as the boundary grows, for graphs whose vertex degrees stay bounded. It mirrors a known bound for smooth surfaces, up to a constant factor. Such estimates connect a graph's shape, in the topological sense, to the tones it can sound.
arxiv-2511-15405:
Meimei Liu, Yuqi Zhu, and Giorgio Gratta build a relay microscope from off axis parabolic mirrors with software warping correction. Such mirrors suit specialized optics but introduce field dependent astigmatism. Adding a relay mirror restores near diffraction limited results for an optical tweezers setup. The long path and wide field, however, create severe non uniform warping.

A reduced parameter warping model is chosen from simulation data to avoid overfitting scarce calibration features. Applied to experimental images, the model cuts residual error to a few micrometers in object space. Results improves further when a microscope stage is added. The work shows exotic mirror relays can deliver quantitative imaging. Careful calibration modeling is the enabling step.
arxiv-2511-15505:
Anastasios Petropoulos and Theodore Antonakopoulos present a way to coordinate several processing units on a programmable chip so they can run deep neural network inference together. Inference is the stage where a trained network makes predictions. Their design uses small controller units that follow instructions grouped into load, compute, and store types, with direct links that keep the units in step.

A compiler turns a network model into instruction programs and splits the model into connected pieces matched to the available units. The system can switch at runtime between pipeline sharing and batch sharing without rebuilding the chip. On a standard image network, it reached high compute use and clear throughput gains over earlier designs.
arxiv-2511-15905:
Andreia Chapouto, Guopeng Li, Tadahiro Oh, and Tengfei Zhao prove that solutions of the intermediate long wave equation tend to those of a classic wave equation as water turns shallow. The intermediate equation models long waves at finite depth, and the Korteweg-de Vries equation governs the shallow limit. Convergence is shown in the L2 sense, on both the real line and the circle.

With earlier deep-water work, the result completes the well-posedness and convergence picture in that frame. The proof uses complete integrability, a hidden exact structure, through a Lax pair and a perturbation determinant to control high frequencies. Low frequencies are handled by repeated normal form reductions taken from the limit equation.
arxiv-2511-16005:
Qingao Dong, Mengfei Wang, and eight co-authors build InfCode-C++, an autonomous system that fixes issues in C++ software repositories. Language model agents resolve repository issues well in Python, but C++ resists those systems because overloaded names, nested namespaces, templates, and deep control flow defeat word-based search and shallow navigation. Performance of Python-oriented agents drops drastically on C++ benchmarks.

Two retrieval mechanisms supply precise context: semantic retrieval guided by code intent, and deterministic queries over the abstract syntax tree, the parsed structure of the code. Together they localize faults and support robust patch synthesis in large typed codebases. On a multilingual benchmark C++ subset, the system beat the strongest prior agent by a wide margin.
arxiv-2511-16205:
Qiang Xu, Shengyuan Bai, and three co-authors present ChemO, a benchmark for advanced AI thinking in chemistry. It is built from International Chemistry Olympiad 2025 problems. Chemistry uses a unique multimodal symbolic language of structures and equations. Olympiad tests in math and physics left it as an open test. Two new ideas make automated scoring possible for problems whose answers are drawings or other visual outputs.

Assessment-Equivalent Reformulation turns visual-output problems into formats a computer can grade. A visual aid step splits a model vision from its chemical thinking, for diagnosis. Their ChemLabs multi-agent system mimics expert teams, with agents for splitting the work, perception, thinking, and checking. The top setup scored near the top of the scale, above the judged human gold medal mark.
arxiv-2511-16905:
Bilguun Batsaikhan and Hiroyuki Fukuda ask whether rising entertainment talent in Japan can be spotted before fame arrives. They define a breakout as a sharp rise in public attention, and they try to predict that rise from a mix of Twitter activity and television data. Early spotting matters in advertising, where brands want to sign talent before costs climb.

The pair tests three families of methods: classic time-series tools, neural networks, and blended ensembles that combine several models. On standard error measures, the blended methods beat both of the other families. Looking at breakouts as timed events adds a further check on which approach flags the rise soonest. The study is a practical guide to what social and broadcast signals can and cannot foretell.
arxiv-2511-17105:
Alessandro Agnetis and three co-authors study a scheduling dilemma: choose which jobs to run, and in what order, on a single machine that might fail. Each job costs money to run and pays a reward only if the machine survives long enough to finish it, with success chances that differ by job. The goal is the subset and sequence with the best expected profit.

The authors prove the problem is NP-hard in general, so no fast exact method should exist for all cases. Special cases, where all jobs share a cost or a failure chance, do admit fast solutions. For the general problem they give an integer programming formulation, a dynamic programming method, and two new stepwise exact algorithms. Experiments show the methods handle large instances, and the stepwise algorithms also solve a related partition problem.
arxiv-2511-17305:
Matt Landreman, Humberto Torreblanca, and Antoine Cerfon make it cheap to compute how ferromagnetic steel would disturb the magnetic field inside a stellarator fusion device. Candidate blanket steels are magnetic, and their effect on plasma confinement must be checked, but full finite-element calculations are slow. Because the coil and plasma fields are strong, the steel's magnetization saturates, and its contribution is a small perturbation, two facts the authors exploit.

They represent the steel as an array of point dipoles of known strength, aligned with the main field, so the extra field follows from fast integrals with no equation solving. Checks against commercial finite-element software confirm the accuracy, and the model accepts arbitrary CAD geometry and differentiates cleanly. Applied to equilibria and coil optimization, even a large steel volume changed plasma properties only slightly, and minor coil reshaping fixed the changes.
arxiv-2511-17505:
Chenhua Shi and three co-authors build a fault-tracking pipeline for radio access networks that explains not just what went wrong, but in what order. Mobile operators need the real-world triggers behind service-level breaches before customers notice them. Most tools flag suspicious indicators without reconstructing the causal sequence that turned normal behavior into a fault. This pipeline labels past records as abnormal when tied to breaches, then learns the causal chain leading from normal operation to failure.

In Monte Carlo tests, the method pinpointed the correct trigger sequence with high precision and scaled to millions of data points without slowing down. The authors present causally ordered, high-resolution diagnosis as the step that moves network fault management from reactive troubleshooting toward proactive prevention. It catches the earliest links of a failure chain while there is still time to intervene.
arxiv-2511-17605:
Agnideep Aich, Sameera Hewage, and Md Monzur Murshed test whether fusing clinical and genetic risk scores with copulas, mathematical tools for modeling dependence, sharpens breast cancer risk stratification. Simple linear fusion assumes the two scores relate independently, which their joint behavior may violate. Using the METABRIC cohort, the authors trained clinical and gene-expression classifiers, took out-of-fold risk probabilities for five-year cancer-specific mortality, and fitted four copula families to the paired scores.

The clinical model alone discriminated better than the gene-expression model, and copula fusion did not beat it on standard accuracy measures. Still, patients scoring high on both views had clearly the poorest survival, a pattern competing-risks analysis confirmed, and an external check on independent data found all fusion styles comparable. The authors are candid: copulas describe the dependence interpretably and support joint-group analysis, but superior prediction is not established.
arxiv-2511-17705:
Pengfei Li, Stacy McGaugh, Marcel Pawlowski, Francois Hammer, and J. A. Sellwood ask what the Milky Way's dark matter halo looked like before ordinary matter settled into it. Halos shrink as gas and stars fall in, so the team builds a method that reverses that shrinking step by step.

Applied to new Gaia measures of how fast stars move around the Galaxy, the method gives an odd early halo. Its inner core is too shallow and its outer fall is too steep for standard cold dark matter ideas, and its mass and concentration differ clearly from predictions.
arxiv-2511-17905:
Claus Kadelka reviews canalization as a source of stability in gene regulatory networks. These networks are webs of genes that turn each other on and off and hold a cell's identity steady despite mutations and environmental noise. Discrete models, where each gene is simply on or off, make the math of that robustness tractable.

The perspective gathers the history of the idea, formal definitions inside discrete dynamical models, and measures of stability. It walks through illustrative applications and ends with open challenges where theory meets experiment. Readers get a compact map of how a biological design principle becomes a precise mathematical property.
arxiv-2511-18005:
Shengyuan Wang, Zhiheng Zheng, Yu Shang, and six co-authors present UrbanWorld, a system that generates detailed three dimensional city scenes that match the real world. Building a whole city at high fidelity is hard to scale, and earlier methods fall short on quality, realism, or compatibility with graphics tools.

Their agentic framework uses many multimodal foundation tools to gather real world knowledge, keep robust intermediate forms, and assemble scenes, with rounds of self reflection to limit error build up. In tests it wins most comparisons against baselines for overall perceptual quality. The output fits standard computer graphics pipelines for media and embodied intelligence uses.
arxiv-2511-18105:
Purvish Jajal, Nick John Eliopoulos, Benjamin Shiue-Hal Chou, and three co-authors present AdaPerceiver, a transformer that adapts its width, depth, and token count within a single trained model. Deployed models must fit varied hardware and latency budgets, but most dynamic methods adjust only one of those axes, such as dropping tokens.

A joint training scheme keeps performance strong across the model's many configurations. On image classification it expands the accuracy throughput tradeoff, beating a flexible baseline at higher speed. On segmentation and depth estimation it matches a much larger model with far fewer operations, and a policy can cut computation by about a quarter to a third at equal accuracy.
arxiv-2511-18305:
Raja Kumar, Arka Sadhu, and Ram Nevatia teach vision language models to reason about fine differences between similar categories, such as bird species that look almost alike. Models know a lot of text but often fail to use it for such fine grained recognition, and exact answer rewards encourage memorizing training classes.

Their DiVE-k method turns each training image into a multiple choice question built from the model's own top guesses, then trains it by reinforcement learning to pick correctly. That forces comparison among plausible options and gives a simple checkable reward. On five data sets the method beats prior approaches, especially on new categories.
arxiv-2511-18805:
Yi Xu, Chaofan Fan, Jinxin Hu, Yu Zhang, Zeng Xiaoyi, and Jing Zhang present STORE, a framework for ranking models in recommendation systems. In such systems, huge, sparse, and mixed feature sets strain both representation and computation. Capacity gets forced into embedding layers, causing training pathologies, while attention over all feature tokens becomes costly and diffuse.

STORE tokenizes sparse features into a compact set of stable semantic tokens, rotates the space of static features to improve interactions, and filters out low contributing tokens in attention. Offline experiments and online A/B tests show better click prediction and training throughput, supporting the design for large scale ranking.
arxiv-2511-19205:
Hikaru Kawai and Nobuyoshi Ohta revisit quantum conformal gravity in four dimensions, a theory where scale invariance plays the central role. A known puzzle was a mismatch in beta functions, which track how couplings change with scale, between general quadratic curvature theories and conformal gravity. The gap corresponded to two scalar degrees of freedom.

The authors show the mismatch vanishes once gauge-fixing and ghost terms are added carefully through BRST symmetry, restoring the two scalar modes. Guided by two-dimensional gravity and Liouville theory, they integrate the trace anomaly to build a matching Liouville action. They also state the condition for the BRST symmetry to stay free of anomalies.
arxiv-2511-19305:
Sara Geremia, Domenico De Stefano, and Michael Fop look for core-periphery patterns in collaboration networks at the level of whole communities. Research networks mix communities, hubs, and central cores, and most tools study those patterns one node at a time. Their method starts from a given grouping of nodes, by field or place, for instance.

An objective function then labels each community as core or peripheral, based on how densely and strongly communities connect to each other. Applied to co-authorship among Italian academics in three disciplines, the method reveals a layered core-periphery structure tied to institutions. The grouping choice keeps results readable in social and organizational terms.
arxiv-2511-19405:
Dereck Piche and five co-authors train language model agents to cooperate in social dilemmas instead of exploiting each other. When agents with clashing goals interact, each one's private incentive can wreck the group's outcome. Reinforcement learning, reliable for single agents, pushes multi-agent systems toward defection, and the authors see the same drift in language models.

An opponent-aware method called Advantage Alignment is adapted to steer models toward cooperation that resists exploitation. A group-relative baseline simplifies training in repeated games at language model scale. A new test setting, Trust-and-Split, needs natural language talk to reach high group welfare, and the trained agents fare better across many dilemmas.
arxiv-2511-19505:
Jack Yarndley plans flight paths for spacecraft that carry several propulsion modes. Switching between engines, or mixing an engine with a solar sail, adds flexibility but makes trajectory design much harder. His method uses sequential convex programming, which repeatedly simplifies the problem into convex pieces that solve quickly.

Sparse automatic differentiation extends the linearization step, so many modes can be included without hand-built reformulations and at similar computing cost. New constraints force one mode per time step and cap the total modes used. Tests include a low-thrust trip to comet 67P with a twenty-mode thruster and an Earth-Mars transfer mixing engine and sail.
arxiv-2511-19605:
Chandan Kumar Das and four co-authors simulate magnetic reconnection as the engine of fast gamma-ray flares in blazars, jets of active galaxies aimed near Earth. Those light curves spike too fast for standard shock models. Reconnection, where field lines break and rejoin, is a rival explanation.

Three-dimensional relativistic simulations with the PLUTO code follow turbulent magnetized plasma columns. Current-driven kink instability forms current sheets that spawn plasmoids. A new diagnostic combining structure analysis with reconnection measures finds the active sheets. A small subset aligns with the jet axis, matching the jet-in-jet picture, and such structures could power rapid flares.
arxiv-2511-19705:
Ziteng Sun and six co-authors quantize large language models without any calibration data. Shrinking model weights to fewer bits cuts serving cost, but the usual rounding creates large errors at outlier weights. Existing fixes lean on calibration data, which may be unavailable or barred by privacy rules.

Their method, CafeQ, designs a stand-in loss that can be optimized with no data at all, covering both learned transformations and adaptive rounding. Structured transformations handle single matrices, while paired weights that interact in the graph get dual transformations. Experiments on Gemma 2 models show steady gains, opening quantization to settings where calibration data cannot be used.
arxiv-2511-19905:
Fangyi Chen, Shu Ge, Jian Qian, and Christopher Harshaw design adaptive experiments in a design-based statistics setting. Outcomes and covariates are treated as fixed, and each arriving subject needs a treatment chance and a pair of predictors for an augmented inverse-probability estimator. The goal is to close the gap to an oracle that knew the best fixed choices in advance.

Their Sigmoid-FTRL method handles a non-convex problem by minimizing two convex regrets at once. They prove its Neyman regret shrinks at a rate that no adaptive design can beat under their conditions, so the method is minimax optimal. A central limit theorem and a safe variance estimator also let users build valid confidence intervals from the adaptive data.
arxiv-2511-20305:
He, Lu, Xu, and Chi tune a futuristic antenna system with graph neural networks. Their 2025 paper optimizes RIS-assisted pinching-antenna downlinks. Pinching antennas slide along waveguides to serve users better. A reconfigurable surface of tunable elements shapes reflections too. Jointly setting positions, phases, and beams is hard.

Sum rate and energy efficiency are the twin goals. Power budgets and movable ranges constrain the search. The system's graph structure invites a graph network solution. Their design cascades three specialized sub-networks. The first places antennas from user locations. The second sets surface phase shifts from channel state. The third computes the beamforming vectors. Training is unsupervised, driven by the objectives directly. Three hybrid strategies mix the network with convex solvers. They trade inference time against solution quality. Answers arrive within milliseconds in tests. That speed suits real-time sixth-generation networks.
arxiv-2511-20705:
Bilal Ahmed and Joseph G. Makin propose in 2025 a cheaper way to solve inverse problems with diffusion models, the image generators that start from noise and clean it up step by step. Inverse problems ask the reverse question: given partial or noisy measurements, recover the original signal. Diffusion models make good guides for this, but earlier methods either approximated crudely, needed costly gradient passes, or handled only linear measurements.

Their method, RePS, restarts the sampling process partway, shrinking the approximation errors that build up during generation. It never backpropagates through the score network, its noise predictor, removing a big cost. Tested on the FFHQ and ImageNet photo collections, RePS handled linear and nonlinear tasks. It enlarged images fourfold and filled a masked 128-by-128 box. It restored images with 70 percent of pixels hidden, and removed blur. Across these tasks it converged faster and reconstructed better than existing diffusion-based baselines.
arxiv-2511-20905:
Anna Lyubarskaja and Dominik Rothenhäusler study in 2025 what happens when each dataset is drawn from a slightly different world. In their random unbiased perturbations model, the link between outcome and covariates wobbles randomly from dataset to dataset, averaging out to the truth, while the covariate distribution stays fixed. Unlike adversarial shift, which plans for the worst case, this randomness inflates variance without adding bias. Hospitals or consumer baskets sampled on different days are the motivating picture.

The wobble shrinks the effective sample size: with perturbation strength tau between 0 and 1, n observations carry the information of n divided by (1 + n tau). For local polynomial regression, a new variance term appears with the same bandwidth scaling as ordinary sampling noise. When the perturbation dominates, the best bandwidth follows tau, not n. Matching minimax lower bounds show this effective sample size is a fundamental limit, not an artefact of one estimator.
arxiv-2511-21105:
Pushkal Mishra, Kshitiz Bansal, and Dinesh Bharadia build in 2025 RadarFM, a foundation model meant to give radar the kind of transferable scene understanding that vision-language models gave cameras. Radar perceives through fog, darkness, and long range, yet radar software stays split: each task trains its own architecture. RadarFM instead learns unified scene features from structured spatial language. Captions describe the scene in native radar coordinates, as in 'a stopped bus 20 metres ahead', so language supervises geometry directly.

A hash-aware contrastive objective grades scene similarity by spatial configuration overlap, rather than forcing binary match-or-not decisions. Training data came from the CARLA driving simulator with a realistic radar model, generating large annotated datasets across varied scenarios. The authors also propose localisation-aware metrics that score spatial accuracy beyond ordinary detection measures. The aim is one radar backbone that transfers across detection, segmentation, and occupancy tasks.
arxiv-2511-21205:
Hao-Peng Yan and three coauthors study a black hole sitting inside two exotic surroundings in a 2025 physics paper. One surround is a modified Chaplygin-like dark fluid, a proposed substance blending traits of dark matter and dark energy. The other is a cloud of strings, a web of thin filaments threading the space around the hole. The authors ask how this setting changes what observers could measure.

Yan and his coauthors compute three linked signals. One is the shadow's size. Another is the quasinormal modes, the fading tones the hole rings with after a disturbance. The third is the greybody factors, which state how much Hawking radiation escapes far away. They find the string cloud's strength drives the largest changes in all three signals, while the dark fluid's settings add smaller, patterned shifts. The three signals also track each other at high frequencies, giving observers joint predictions to test.
arxiv-2511-21605:
Alejandro Tabas, Heike Sönnichsen, Sandeep Kaur, Marco Meixner, and Katharina von Kriegstein show the brain keeps a dedicated alarm for sounds that fail to arrive, in 2025. Perception theory explains how brains update beliefs when a feature changes, a higher pitch than expected, via feature prediction errors. But noticing an absence, an expected sound that never comes, needs a different signal, which the team calls the absence prediction error.

Using fMRI in the human auditory system, Tabas and his coauthors designed a paradigm to isolate that signal. Absence prediction errors were encoded in the auditory thalamus and cortex, meaning absence is explicitly represented already in subcortical sensory pathways. Feature prediction errors, by contrast, already appear in the auditory midbrain, while the absence signal does not, implying a separate circuit handles missing stimuli. The results identify a neural mechanism devoted to detecting what is not there.
arxiv-2511-21805:
Kwak and colleagues simulate how spiral arms form in a Milky Way-like galaxy disk sitting inside a halo of dark matter. Instead of stirring the disk by hand, they let structure grow alone and study how resolution, disk stability, and a live halo change what appears. They track spiral patterns labelled m equals 1 through 6, which count how many arms each pattern has.

In well-resolved runs with a live halo, spirals appear in a cascade: many-armed patterns form and fade first, then fewer-armed patterns follow, with the action drifting inward. Raising the particle count tenfold delayed visible spirals by about 0.5 billion years and bar formation by about 1.9 billion years, but did not change the overall path. The three-armed pattern marked when inner-disk angular momentum transport began, ahead of bar formation, while fixed halos produced strong early spirals but no coherent cascade.
arxiv-2511-21905:
Radevych and colleagues connect two major materials-simulation programs. VASP is a widely used first-principles code with a rich library of functionals and pseudopotentials, while EPW specializes in electron-phonon interactions. That coupling between electrons and lattice vibrations governs superconductivity, heat flow, and carrier mobility. Their interface computes interaction matrix elements with VASP's supercell method, then interpolates them inside EPW.

They demonstrate the link on two textbook problems. For magnesium diboride, solving the anisotropic Migdal-Eliashberg equations gave superconducting gap closing temperatures of about 36 kelvin with one functional. The temperatures were 38 kelvin with VASP's PBE and 46 kelvin with a newer functional, bracketing the experimental value of 39 kelvin quoted in the study. For cubic boron nitride they computed carrier mobility with the ab initio Boltzmann transport equation. The result is a route to temperature-dependent properties with VASP's full library.
arxiv-2511-22305:
Fenoglio, Li, Barbiero, and colleagues keep federated learning accurate when every client's data drifts in a different way. Federated training pools many devices' data without centralizing it. A single global model degrades badly when clients' distributions differ, and clustered variants usually must know the shift types and cluster count in advance. Their Flux framework computes privacy-preserving descriptors on each client, clusters clients by descriptor similarity, trains one model per cluster. Even assigns brand-new, unlabeled clients to the right cluster model at test time.

Across four benchmarks, two real-world datasets, and ten baselines, Flux improves accuracy by up to 23 percentage points over the baseline under all four shift types, with overhead comparable to FedAvg. Ablations credit the descriptors themselves: swapping test-time assignment for random clusters costs up to 53 points of accuracy on MNIST in their tables.
arxiv-2511-22705:
St-Onge and colleagues build a floor robot that transfers patients and trains them to stand. Regaining the sit-to-stand motion is key to functional mobility and avoiding rehospitalization. Yet devices split into passive raising aids, moving patients on trajectories without engaging them, and rehabilitation systems, supporting partial bodyweight but unable to adapt training to mobility levels or work outside rooms. The team's two-degrees-of-freedom floor robot adjusts impedance and vertical and forward forces.

Experiments with healthy adults showed the device barely impacts natural sit-to-stand kinematics and delivers precise weight unloading at the centre of mass, up to 61 kilograms at the reported speed. It can add a forward virtual spring helping shift bodyweight onto the feet at seat-off. In transfer mode it lifts patients up to 200 kilograms, retaining raising-aid capability. One limitation surfaced: constrained seating lowered peak velocity, traced to actuator stroke.
arxiv-2511-23205:
Tang and colleagues merge two separate steps of data analysis, dimension reduction and regression, into a single method for problems with many correlated predictors. Their PLS-Lasso builds the partial least squares idea, compressing predictors into latent directions chosen for their link to the response, directly into the Lasso penalty. It comes in two versions, one blending the two goals with a tuning knob and one without it.

Both versions ship with algorithms the authors prove converge to global optima, a guarantee plain Lasso-style methods do not always offer for such blended objectives. Tested against ordinary Lasso on financial index tracking, the task of mimicking an index with few assets, both variants showed promise. Version one proved unstable, winning when the required portfolio was very sparse but fading as the allowed sparsity decreased in their experiments.
arxiv-2512-00105:
Finding interesting patterns in large numerical databases can overwhelm analysts with far too many results. Djawad Bekkoucha and co-authors present a sampling approach for interval patterns in a 2025 journal article. Instead of listing everything, sampling draws a manageable subset at random, weighted by an interestingness measure.

Measures such as frequency or hyper-volume decide which patterns are more likely to be drawn. The authors describe their method as the first sampling approach built for interval patterns in numerical data. It offers data miners a practical way to explore huge pattern spaces without drowning in output. Interval patterns describe ranges rather than single values, which suits sensor and financial data.
arxiv-2512-00605:
Combinatorial bandit problems force repeated choices under constraints, balancing learning with earning. Aurélien Delage and Romaric Gaudel study matroid bandit linear optimization in 2025, exploiting unimodality to gain efficiency. Recent approaches already achieve optimal regret, matching the known lower bound.

Time complexity remains the problem, especially for large matroids or costly membership oracles, as in recommendation systems that must ensure diversity. Unimodality, a single-peaked structure in the problem, can be leveraged to cut computation. The result aims at bandit algorithms that stay optimal in regret while finally running fast enough for real platforms. Matroids generalize independence, covering scheduling, spanning trees, and diversity constraints alike. Unimodality gives the search a peak to climb instead of a plateau to wander.
arxiv-2512-00705:
Seongyeon Park and five coauthors present FlexiWalker, a 2025 computer systems paper on random walks over graphs. Random walks hop from node to node and support many graph analysis tasks. Dynamic walks change their hop chances as the graph evolves, which makes them flexible but hard to speed up.

Most fast CPU and GPU designs rely on precomputed data, which dynamic walks break. Users are left with slow frameworks or hand-tuned code that fits one workload only. FlexiWalker is a GPU framework that adapts at runtime to varied workloads. Its goal is fast dynamic walks without rewriting kernels for each new job.
arxiv-2512-01305:
Jianru Duan studies a torsion invariant for three-dimensional shapes. The invariant is built from L2 methods, which use square-summable data. Sutured decomposition cuts a shape into simpler parts. Duan asks what the invariant can tell about a shape's fibers.

He proves it detects whether a given class is fibered. That means it can tell if the shape is built from a surface swept along a loop. One case is set aside, for closed graph shapes with no curved metric of the right type. Such tests help sort shapes that look alike at first glance.
arxiv-2512-01605:
Anurag and co-authors count the cost of VQE for small molecules. VQE is a hybrid quantum-classic method to find ground-state energies. Those energies drive drug and materials design. Noise and small quantum hardware cap its use today.

The team gauges resources under distinct fermion mappings and Hamiltonian cuts. Each choice shifts qubit counts and circuit depth. Clear counts show which choices save most. That guides chemists to spend scarce quantum time on the setups most likely to yield sound energies. Small molecules are the test bed where quantum chemistry hopes to beat classic methods first, so honest costs there set the field's pace.
arxiv-2512-01805:
