The predictions are checked against CMS measurements of b-jet and B-plus meson production in proton-lead collisions at five point zero two and eight point one six tera-electronvolts. Nuclear modification factors land near one in the probed region, consistent with other estimates. The authors highlight that different cuts on final states can further probe how nuclei reshape parton densities.
arxiv-2602-09105:
Symmetries and their anomalies constrain how quantum field theories flow to low energies, and T. Daniel Brennan and one co-author generalizes those constraints to broken generalized symmetries. Broken ones act on coupling-constant spaces of theory groups and can carry family quirks that limit low-energy phases. This paper extends family-anomaly reasoning to higher-group and non-invertible symmetries.

Anomaly inflow and symmetry topological field theories for such groups are built, with effects on RG flows and low-energy phases. As examples, the authors apply family quirks to four-dimensional QCD-like theories deformed by irrelevant multi-fermion couplings, showing how generalized family quirks carve out allowed low-energy behavior.
arxiv-2602-09205:
Proton-boron fusion needs extreme ion temperatures and strong confinement, making spherical tokamaks with powerful neutral-beam injection leading candidates. Huasheng Xie and ten co-authors develop a reduced multi-fluid equilibrium model for these devices. There, fast toroidal rotation and the proton-boron mass gap drive centrifugal separation and electrostatic polarization that single-fluid magnetohydrodynamics misses. Full multi-fluid models are often numerically stiff, so the reduced model keeps dominant rotation and self-consistent potential while dropping poloidal inertia and pressure anisotropy.

Applied to the experimental EHL-2 and reactor-scale EHL-3B designs, the model shows equilibrium changes governed by the ion Mach number. Below Mach 0.5, multi-fluid effects fade toward the single-fluid limit; above Mach 2, boron piles up on the low-field side and an internal potential near 10 kilovolts appears. Accurate reactor design, the authors conclude, needs multi-fluid physics.
arxiv-2602-09405:
Chen Cheng and Rina Foygel Barber examine a puzzle at the heart of modern machine learning: when does memorizing training data help, and when does it hurt? Working with an overparameterized linear model under general priors in a Bayesian setup, their 2026 paper connects training error to generalization error for arbitrary estimation procedures. The prior distribution, they find, holds determining factors that split optimal behavior two ways.

Sometimes the best generalization demands training error near interpolation relative to noise size, so memorization becomes necessary. Other times it demands training error close to the noise level itself, so overfitting harms. The dividing line falls at noise thresholds set by the prior's Fisher information and variance parameters. The paper thus turns a folk debate into explicit conditions: prior information sets the threshold.
arxiv-2602-09505:
Solving a linear ill-posed operator equation demands regularization, and two classic tools manipulate the spectrum of the pseudo-inverse: Tikhonov regularization and spectral cutoff. Martin Sæbye Carøe and two co-authors introduce a formula interpolating between them in their 2026 paper. One parameter sweeps a family of regularizations with the two classics as limiting cases.

Tuning that parameter to the equation at hand can soften the weaknesses of both endpoints, since neither classic suits every operator. Numerical simulations in signal and image processing demonstrate the approach, showing the interpolated family adapting where pure Tikhonov or pure cutoff would falter. The paper thus turns a binary choice between two regularizers into a continuum with a tunable middle.
arxiv-2602-09705:
A dark energy that changes over time and may cross the phantom divide is hinted at by recent DESI baryon acoustic oscillation data with supernova measurements and cosmic microwave background observations. Bichu Li and Lei-Hua Liu show that adding a non-minimal coupling to the running-curvaton framework lets a single field do two jobs. In their 2026 paper, this one field powers curvature perturbations from the early universe plus phantom-crossing cosmic acceleration late, all free of ghost instabilities.

Using Markov chain Monte Carlo background likelihoods with DESI DR2 data, Pantheon+ supernovae, and a reduced cosmic microwave background prior, the authors constrain the cosmological parameters tightly. Degeneracies among parameters constrain the coupling constants only weakly. A complete analysis at perturbation level using lensing and cosmic microwave background spectra is still needed. One field, two cosmic eras, and a testable path forward define the contribution.
arxiv-2602-09805:
As thought models trade tokens for scores through mulling, search, and fixing, one score cannot tell what tokens buy. Useful thought, repair, or needless bloat all look alike. Daniel Kaiser and three co-authors offer a trace-free test plan in their 2026 paper. It splits token yield using three signals even for closed models: done rate, rightness given done, and made length.

With workload labels at hand, made length is scaled by stated task work, splitting wording extra from workload scaling. Without such labels, an open solver workload scale is tested for staying power under leave-self-out, leave-top-k, and held-out shakes. Tests across fourteen open models on four benchmarks, plus eleven extra models on one benchmark, show yield and extra rankings firm. They beat score rankings, while splitting logic-limited, context-limited, and bloat-limited modes identical under score-per-token.
arxiv-2602-10105:
Two-handed dexterous manipulation needs data that is expensive to collect from real robot hands. A 2026 paper led by Juncheng Mu, with eight co-authors, proposes DexImit, a framework that converts single-camera human manipulation videos into lifelike robot data with no extra information. The pipeline runs in four stages. It reconstructs hand-object interaction at near-metric scale, decomposes subtasks with bimanual scheduling, synthesizes consistent robot trajectories, and augments data for zero-shot real-world deployment.

DexImit can draw on internet videos or generated videos and handles varied tasks, from cutting an apple to making a beverage to stacking cups. By bridging the embodiment gap between human and robot hands, it offers a path to scale robot learning from the vast supply of human video.
arxiv-2602-10205:
Dimer and spin ice models for strip gauge theories offer a lab for interacting quantum strings. A 2026 paper by Gurkirat Singh and Inti Sodemann maps these Rokhsar-Kivelson models onto three quantum chains. The chains: a spin-half XXZ chain, a spin-one chain, and a kinetically constrained fermion chain. Boundary twists map onto transverse string momentum, and Drude weight maps onto inverse string mass per unit length.

Renormalization group phase diagrams show global similarities to full two-dimensional problems plus striking new features. The spin-one chain hosts an unbroken set of degenerate ground states at the RK point, a Bloch sphere without microscopic global symmetry. One model also shows a Landau-forbidden gapless critical point away from that point, plus many local conserved quantities fragmenting the Hilbert space. Our findings highlight spin-chain mappings for exploring unusual dynamics, exotic criticality, and low-energy gauge physics.
arxiv-2602-10305:
Reward shaping speeds reinforcement learning training, but designing good shaping functions for hard continuous control remains largely uncharted. A 2026 paper led by Mateo Juliani, with two co-authors, proposes learning a reward shaping function on its own from offline datasets, even when those datasets carry hidden confounding variables. The method builds on the recently proposed causal Bellman equation, learning a tight ceiling on optimal state values.

That ceiling serves as potentials in the Potential-Based Reward Shaping framework. Tested with Soft-Actor-Critic on several widely used continuous control benchmarks, the algorithm shows strong performance guarantees under hidden confounders. The work marks a solid first step toward confounding-robust continuous control from a causal angle, with training code shared openly.
arxiv-2602-10705:
Sougata Mardanya and ten co-authors predict layer-based topological states in a uranium compound in a 2026 paper. Magnetic topological insulators promise loss-free edge states for energy-fast electronics, but known examples are usually ferromagnets with low ordering heat and stray fields. An antiferromagnetic version with a high Néel temperature has been a long-standing target.

The team studies the van der Waals antiferromagnet UOTe, notable for its high Néel temperature and Kondo physics. Full first-principles study says that two-layer films realize other topological phases depending on layer count, including Chern and axion states. The predictions give lab teams a real material base for loss-free antiferromagnetic electronics.
arxiv-2602-10805:
R. Jafari and Alireza Akbari study how noise reshapes nonequilibrium spin links in a 2026 paper. Without noise, spin link functions cross over from monotonic decay at fast sweeps to oscillatory conduct at slow sweeps. Adding a stochastically driven field changes that picture in systematic ways.

The key sweep velocity at which links change abruptly decreases with noise strength, scaling linearly with the square of noise intensity. When noise intensity and sweep velocity become comparable, stirring chance locks to one half over a finite momentum window, signaling noise-induced maximally mixed modes. A highly oscillatory region emerges in the dynamical phase diagram, with its threshold sweep velocity rising with noise. The results map noise from nuisance to organizer of nonequilibrium phases.
arxiv-2602-10905:
Deyi Kong and three co-authors propose a natural hypergradient method for bilevel tuning in a 2026 paper. Hypergradient estimation bottlenecks on computing or approximating a Hessian inverse. The new method, NHGD, exploits the number structure of the inner problem. It uses the tested Fisher information matrix as an asymptotically consistent surrogate for the Hessian.

That design enables a parallel optimize-and-approximate system: the Hessian-inverse approximation updates synchronously with random inner tuning, reusing slope information at negligible extra cost. The main theory contribution proves high-chance error bounds and sample hardness promises matching state-of-the-art optimize-then-approximate methods, while greatly reducing runs time. The paper offers bilevel tuning that is both rigorous and fast.
arxiv-2602-11105:
Flow-matching models paint and film well, but slowly. Divya Jyoti Bajpai and six co-authors present FastFlow, a plug-and-play inference method that speeds them without retraining. It spots denoising steps that barely change the path and approximates them from earlier velocity values.

Finite-difference extrapolation lets the sampler leap ahead at no extra compute, skipping full network calls at middle steps. A bandit rule decides how many steps are safe to skip before a full call is due, balancing speed against quality. Tests show speedups of more than two and a half times with high-quality output kept. The method works across image, video, and editing tasks.
arxiv-2602-11305:
Aligned models may still fail when safety, values, and culture must align at once. Usman Naseem and six co-authors offer Mis-Align Bench, a unified benchmark for joint misalignment. It builds a large English data set spanning more than one hundred domains, classified into safety, value, and cultural groups, with paired aligned and misaligned replies.

Tests of general, tuned, and open-weight models show a telling pattern. Single-dimension models cover well alone but fail often under joint terms, with lower matching scores than their solo results suggests. The work argues that matching must be judged jointly, since real queries demand all three aspects jointly, and solo benchmarks flatter models that cannot hold them at once.
arxiv-2602-11405:
A dark photon and an axion-like particle may couple to ordinary light through a dark axion portal. Sergei N. Gninenko and six co-authors study that portal's signatures in electron fixed-target tests. Missing energy arises when dark photons are produced and decay invisibly into dark fermions.

Projected sensitivities are derived for two tests, NA64e and LDMX, across two production mechanisms: bremsstrahlung-like pair emission and vector meson photoproduction with invisible decays. New NA64e constraints from a large electron-on-target sample are also derived. Separately, electric dipole moment bounds on electrons, muons, and neutrons constrain CP-violating, fermion-specific couplings through loop effects. The paper maps a portal that fixed-target and precision tests can jointly probe.
arxiv-2602-11905:
Strong convergence for random representations has been extended before, but not to the torsion case, where trace expansions involve fractional powers rather than ordinary Laurent series. Marco Barbieri and one co-author extend the polynomial method for operator-norm bounds in random permutation models to the torsion setting. They frame fraction-power versions of the key hypotheses and prove they lead to strong convergence.

Concretely, for a uniformly random map into the symmetric group, pairing with the standard representation yields a strong approach to the left regular picture. The work also gives explicit near-sharp spectral gaps for related Schreier graphs and a non-Ramanujan limiting case in the modular setting. By pushing the polynomial method into torsion, the paper opens almost Ramanujan behavior to a wider class of random models.
arxiv-2602-12305:
Writing fast CUDA kernels means searching a huge space of low-level tweaks under noisy, costly hardware feedback. Arijit Bhattacharjee led this work with five co-authors, presenting OptiML, an end-to-end frame that turns plain language or input CUDA code into performance-tuned kernels. Optimisation is treated as search under verification, not as one-shot generation.

When input is language, a Mixture-of-Thoughts generator proposes a first runnable kernel. A search optimiser then refines kernels by Monte Carlo tree search over model-driven edits, guided by profiler rewards, with each candidate compiled, checked, and profiled. Tests show verified gains over strong language-model baselines, with clear optimisation paths grounded in profiler evidence rather than guesswork.
arxiv-2602-12605:
PAC-Bayes bounds give strong guarantees on generalisation error, but a related family bounds expected error. Matthias Frey led this work with two co-authors, giving block-sample MAC-Bayes bounds, where MAC stands for mean approximately correct. The family generalises an expectation version of PAC-Bayes bounds, with divergence terms depending only on subsets, or blocks, of training data.

That block structure promises tighter bounds than older bounds. A numerical example illustrates the gain. The original bound stays vacuous for any prior, while the new family gives finite bounds for fitting block sizes. The paper asks whether high-probability versions are possible. It answers no. An example shows no PAC-Bayes bound can do both at once. It cannot vanish faster than one over log n when the MAC-Bayes bound vanishes like n to the minus one half, and depend on allowed error chance in log form.
arxiv-2602-12905:
Object completion networks output static distance fields that reconstruct shape well but resist editing: rescaling them distorts structure. Jelle Vermandere and two co-authors offer a part-aware scaling framework that turns completed shapes into editable objects. Starting from distance and texture fields of leading completion models, the method segments parts automatically, defines user-controlled scaling zones, and interpolates distance, colour, and part labels smoothly.

A repetition strategy handles large deformations while preserving repeating patterns. Tests on Matterport3D and ShapeNet objects show the method beats global and naive selective scaling in visual quality, especially for complex and repetitive shapes. For indoor redesign, simulation, and digital content creation, the payoff is completed objects that can actually be reshaped without falling apart.
arxiv-2602-13405:
Multi-agent systems with chance-driven transitions model controllers, protocols, and cyber-physical infrastructure, but their transition odds are often guessed from data and partly unknown. This paper studies how to check robust plans under that doubt, where groups of agents must meet a time-based goal despite unsure transitions, partial views, and hostile agents. Plans with bounded memory keep the task workable.

The authors frame a robust form of model checking for a chance-based, view-limited extension of Alternating-time Temporal Logic, then map how hard that task is under different kinds of perturbation. That cost map clarifies what robustness demands in multi-agent checking and backs bounded-memory plans in unsure settings. Raphaël Berthon leads the work with three co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13505:
Quantum convolutional codes need polynomial stabilizers that commute while staying sparse and keeping encoding memory small. This paper tackles that design problem with difference triangle sets. The construction builds X stabilizers from a classical convolutional self-orthogonal code based on strong difference triangle supports. It then obtains Z stabilizers by reflecting the triangle indices of X, guaranteeing symplectic orthogonality by design.

That constructive route aims to guarantee a prescribed minimum distance rather than searching for one after the fact. Numerical results demonstrate the construction across a variety of code rates, showing the method works as a practical design tool rather than a one-off example. Vahid Nourozi leads the work with one co-author.
arxiv-2602-13605:
Coupled-cluster theory with one reference usually describes one electronic state, often the lowest-energy state in the reference's symmetry sector. This paper widens the framework so different parts of the cluster operator play distinct roles, from encoding states of other symmetries to letting one ansatz describe several states at once. The result is a new class of downfolding methods whose active-space effective Hamiltonians represent multiple correlated states at once, even when those states overlap the reference.

Three theorems formalize the extension, and standard coupled-cluster downfolding emerges as a special case. A Hermitian variant built on a unitary coupled-cluster representation enables realistic ground- and excited-state simulations while reducing quantum resources required. Karol Kowalski leads the work with one co-author.
arxiv-2602-13705: Arnold Scholz was a number theorist whose life and work are the subject of this article by Franz Lemmermeyer. It is an English translation, with modifications, of an introduction to the correspondence of Hasse, Scholz, and Taussky published in 2016. The piece thus offers English readers a portrait of Scholz through the letters he exchanged with two leading mathematicians of his time.
arxiv-2602-14105:
Naomichi Hatano and one co-author revisit a 2026 arXiv topic in open quantum systems. When a system couples to an infinite environment, non-Hermitian behavior appears, and the one-body problem can be solved in full. That completeness makes the structure of open systems easier to see, the authors argue.

The review first treats potential scattering, defining resonant states under the Siegert outgoing condition. Such states can carry complex energy even though the Hamiltonian looks Hermitian. It then introduces the Feshbach formalism and uncovers a new complete set of states. Because the theory handles any coupling strength, it offers a firm base for later many-body problems.
arxiv-2602-14305:
Aram Hakobyan and two co-authors prove a 2026 arXiv smoothness result for subharmonic functions. The gradient of every bounded subharmonic function is upper semi-continuous, provided its super-level sets can be brushed from outside by uniform C1-Dini domains at each point. That shape touch rule is the key guess.

The idea widens to a class of broad maps, and to edge acts of gradients for Dirichlet problem answers in zones whose edges meet the same rule. The result links a mild edge smoothness rule to gradient smoothness, a useful bridge between shape of zones and analytic traits of answers.
arxiv-2602-14505:
Dennis Gross, writing alone, offers a 2026 arXiv tool for checking and telling sepsis care plans. Safe, clear step-by-step choice-making matters in health care, yet reward-learning plans for sepsis care stay opaque and hard to check. Old chance model checkers work on the full state space, too big for larger choice problems, and cannot tell why a learned plan makes set choices.

COOL-MC wraps the Storm model checker with three adds. It builds only the reached state space under a trained plan, giving a smaller chain fit for checking. It tags states with clinic-meaning atomic marks. It joins telling methods with chance computation tree logic queries to show which traits drive choices across care paths. A case study uses the ICU-Sepsis benchmark from about 17,000 patient records.
arxiv-2602-14705:
Willem Davison and colleagues draw three lessons on long-term motion for perception, asking what the world reveals through movement over time. Point-track estimation gives them a way to learn temporal representations and test them across perceptual tasks, moving beyond the image alone. Their first lesson is that long-term motion carries information about actions, objects, materials, and space, often better than still images do.

Two further lessons, developed in the paper, round out a case for time as a first-class signal in vision. The authors argue that motion over seconds and minutes deserves the same study images have long received. Their work reframes perception as a temporal art, not a snapshot one.
arxiv-2602-14905:
Gabriel J. Cairns, Graham P. Benham, and Ian J. Hewitt model groundwater feedbacks on ice sheets and subglacial hydrology, a coupling most ice dynamics models omit. Sedimentary basins beneath the ice bed discharge or absorb water, shaping the basal hydrological system that modulates many Antarctic glaciers, yet little is known of their effect.

Their idealised glacier model couples sliding to a subglacial system including a sedimentary basin. Exfiltration and infiltration turn out to be controlled by ice sheet and basin shape, with exfiltration promoting sliding and infiltration hindering it. Groundwater thus joins the forces that speed or slow a glacier. Antarctic ice gains a hidden plumbing lesson.
arxiv-2602-15005:
Zhu and colleagues improve cross-domain news recommendation by learning what users truly care about. Recommending news well means inferring needs from mixed signals that reach beyond direct reading, and surface clicks alone miss deeper, reusable interests. The team trains large language models with reinforcement learning to draft lists of interest-driven search queries from cross-domain signals, treating query-list creation as a policy optimization task with several reward signals.

They study two compute levers, inference-time sampling and model size, and find steady gains with more compute in a scaling-like pattern. A final on-policy distillation step moves the learned policy from a large teacher into a compact student fit for production scale. Offline tests, ablations, and large online A/B tests all show gains in interest modeling and downstream recommendation quality.
arxiv-2602-15105:
Schap and colleagues run the first transit survey for exoplanets in the Sagittarius dwarf galaxy stream with TESS. No exoplanet has yet been found outside the Milky Way. The team studies 15176 likely stream members and finds zero planets.

For hot Jupiters of one to two Jupiter radii with periods from under one day to 10 days, the limit is near 1 percent. A second class, with radii of one and a half to two Jupiter radii, yields a limit under one half of one percent. That sits below 47 Tuc's just under six tenths of a percent. A third class yields a limit just under eight tenths of a percent, below M4's just over eight tenths. A future high-efficiency TESS analysis would need 11467 stars to catch one extragalactic planet. Adding more streams could deliver the first such detection, or show that older, metal-poor settings host fewer hot Jupiters.
arxiv-2602-15405:
Nurko and colleagues offer a broad, domain-free setup joining two linked spread nets for sorting in rough settings. One works on the input signal and the other on the sorter's output logits, without needing re-teaching or fine-tuning of the sorter. Routes handle cleanup and sorting as split, stepwise steps, first cleaning the signal and then using a sorter, missing the meaning data in the sorter's output during cleaning.

The paired mix allows shared steering, where the cleaning signal sharpens the class guess and, in turn, the shifting class logits steer the signal rebuild towards telling zones of the surface. The team offers three plans to model the joint spread of the input and the score. They test the joint cleanup tool for picture sorting and auto voice reading. The setup beats older stepwise cleanup rivals, giving strong and pliant gains in sorting scores under varied terms.
arxiv-2602-15705:
Darzi and colleagues build a unified security frame for database-driven cognitive radio networks, where dynamic spectrum sharing through geolocation bases brings serious risks. Those risks include forced place disclosure, place spoofing, and denial-of-service attacks on central services. Existing fixes handle these issues one at a time and lack a unified, regulation-compliant answer under realistic attack conditions.

Their SLAPX frame gives place privacy, user anonymity, checked place, and denial-of-service resilience at once. Private spectrum queries use delegatable anonymous credentials, place checks adapt without revealing exact user place, and verifiable delay functions plus RLRS-based rate limits blunt denial-of-service attacks. Tests and network runs show lower delay and overhead than prior solutions, with strong resistance to spoofing and denial-of-service.
arxiv-2602-15805:
Sznitman and Widmayer consider a steady N-D Galerkin-Navier-Stokes type flow with Brownian forcing and random stirring of freely small strength, serving as taming. As a proof of concept, they show that the steady spread in an open 2D cone from a sister article stands as the ideal limit for the enstrophy-energy process studied here. That holds no matter the stirring strength.

With exact clumping bounds from the sister article, they infer exact ideal clumping bounds. For suitable forcings, those bounds show loss of all but the lowest modes in the ideal limit. The paper connects a concrete 2D cone spread to the ideal limit of a higher-dimensional forced system. It offers a strict bridge between tamed motion and idealised inviscid conduct.
arxiv-2602-16105:
Thinh Hung Truong leads a team of three researchers who test whether large language models grasp GPS coordinates. Such models now drive navigation, robotics, and mapping tools, so skill with real places and coordinates matters more and more. Yet that skill has had little close study. Their benchmark, GPSBench, holds tens of thousands of samples across seventeen tasks. Some tasks test geometric skills like distance and bearing, while others mix coordinates with world knowledge.

Fourteen leading models were tested on raw skill, not tool use. GPS reasoning proves hard, with wide gaps across tasks. Models do better on real-world geographic reasoning than on geometric computation. Knowledge of places fades with scale: strong at country level, weak at city level. Robustness to noisy coordinates points to real coordinate skill, not rote recall. Adding coordinates helps downstream tasks, though fine-tuning trades geometric gains for losses in world knowledge.
arxiv-2602-16405:
Vladislav Efremkin leads three coauthors computing thermal conductivity. In insulating solids below the Debye point, calculating thermal conductivity is hard because classical approaches break down. The authors present a non-perturbative quantum method based on Path Integral Monte Carlo and Green-Kubo linear response theory.

The method is applied to rare gas solids with a Lennard-Jones potential, where quantum effects strongly shape thermodynamic and transport properties. Simulations yield temperature-dependent phonon frequencies, lifetimes, and specific heat. Imaginary time energy current correlations yield thermal transport coefficients using a physical prior. They show that the rise for argon and neon when cold cannot be explained within Peierls-Boltzmann theory using equilibrium line-widths. A distinct transport lifetime emerges from heat-current data. The results present quantum Monte Carlo as a robust approach for heat transport in such solids, beyond classical molecular dynamics.
arxiv-2602-16505:
Sophie Hanna Langbein leads five coauthors on interpreting machine learning survival models. In time-to-event prediction, hazard and survival functions offer natural, interpretable targets, yet their non-additivity hampers standard additive methods.

The authors introduce Survival Functional Decomposition, which splits higher-order effects into time-varying and time-fixed parts, showing when and why additive explanations fail. They then propose SurvSHAP-IQ, extending Shapley interactions to time-indexed functions as a practical estimator for higher-order, time-varying interactions. Together the two methods give an interaction- and time-aware route to explanations across time-to-event tasks.
arxiv-2602-16805:
Yonatan Gideoni, Sebastian Risi, and Yarin Gal test simple baselines against code evolution, a family of methods that search programs by evolving existing code with language models. Code evolution pipelines post impressive scores across domains, yet they are highly complex and rarely compared to simpler alternatives. The paper proposes two simple baselines and tests them against popular pipelines across several domains.

Surprisingly, the baselines match or beat existing methods in every domain tried, from mathematical bounds and agentic scaffolds to heuristic optimization and machine learning competitions. For mathematical bounds, search space matters far more than the exact search algorithm, with simple and complex routes scoring alike given the same space. Prompt-embedded domain knowledge can also inflate apparent sample efficiency. The field gets a caution: complexity must earn its keep against plain baselines.
arxiv-2602-17105:
S. A. Rozhkov led a ten-author team mapping the electronic band structure of sodium potassium antimonide, a multialkali photocathode material. The team paired low-energy photoemission spectroscopy with density functional theory calculations, measuring optical and quantum efficiency spectra plus energy distribution curves across a broad temperature range. Thresholds for several band-to-band transitions showed up in the spectra.

Fine structure in the energy curves revealed two electron groups: fast electrons excited from heavy-hole, light-hole, and split-off valence bands, and photoelectrons trapped in side valleys of the conduction band. From these data the authors pinned down the band gap, spin-orbit splitting, and valley gaps at low temperature, in good agreement with theory. The results should sharpen the grasp of photoemission in this material and aid sturdy spin-polarized electron sources.
arxiv-2602-17305:
Justin Salez, writing alone, proves a clean link between hyper-contractivity and entropy decay in discrete time. For a measure-keeping transition kernel on any probability space, a one-step shrinking estimate with ordered exponents implies a one-step entropy contraction estimate. The shrinking factor is the ratio of those numbers. Neither reversibility nor any regularity is required.

The static implication is both simpler and stronger than the celebrated dynamic relation between exponential hyper-contractivity and exponential entropy decay along continuous-time Markov semigroups. The paper thus gives probabilists a sharp, assumption-light bridge from shrinking to entropy decay, without passing through time-based machinery.
arxiv-2602-17605:
Jowaria Khan and team built a framework for finding hidden environmental targets when sampling is costly, sparse and biased. The driving case is PFAS contamination, which can cause cancer. Experts need high-risk, under-observed regions found under tight budgets. Disaster response and public health work face the same strain.

Their approach fuses active learning, online meta-learning and concept-guided reasoning. A shared notion of concept relevance tracks how factors such as land cover and source proximity shape where a target appears. Relevance-weighted sampling picks the next sites, while relevance-aware meta-batches keep updates diverse as conditions shift. Tests on PFAS discovery show robust target finding under limited data and shifting ground truth.
arxiv-2602-17705:
Zijian Zhang and Linglong Dai survey wavenumber-domain signal work for holographic MIMO systems. Holographic MIMO uses quasi-continuous apertures, a shift in wireless work. With subwavelength antenna spacing, such systems work in both far-field and near-field regimes, where old discrete Fourier transform accounts fail to capture channel traits.

The survey builds on spatial Fourier plane-wave split to model channels in the wavenumber domain, giving a unified, sound basis for fine-grained spatial links and round wave spread. It covers reported methods including signal mixing, channel gauging and waveform designs. It closes with open challenges and future research paths for future wireless systems, offering a map for new hands entering the field.
arxiv-2602-17805:
André Augusto and team expose liquidity exhaustion attacks on intent-based cross-chain bridges. Such bridges let off-chain solvers fill user orders by fronting their own liquidity, improving user experience but creating systemic risks. The paper proposes a new attack class and a replay-based simulation frame.

Analysis of millions of cross-chain intents moving billions of dollars across three major protocols and nine blockchains shows mixed vulnerability. High-profit protocols prove vulnerable under current parameters, with most past attacks profitable at modest mean profit. One protocol stays robust in all tests thanks to low margins and very high liquidity. Another is generally secure but vulnerable under stress. Byzantine attacks can suppress availability everywhere, causing dozens of failed intents and losses up to about a thousand dollars roughly every sixteen minutes. An optimized attack strategy cuts attack costs by up to about nine tenths against the baseline.
arxiv-2602-17905:
Seyed Hossein Alavi and team compare interactive and static formats for persuasive learning, testing games that teach against chats that convince. Interactive chatbots and games persuade and educate on sustainability topics, yet how delivery formats shape learning and outcomes when content stays constant remains unclear. Grounding on arguments and content throughout, the paper compares three delivery modes in a study: static essays, chatbots and text games.

Across subjective measures, the chatbot condition beat the modes and raised felt importance. Yet felt learning failed to align with outcomes. Game players reported learning less than essay readers, yet scored higher on a day-later quiz. Early looks suggest proxies such as word count and chat length relate more to felt experience than to learning. The findings highlight a split between how persuasive experiences feel and what people retain, pointing to trade-offs among hands-on play, real feel and learning in systems.
arxiv-2602-18005:
Mengyuan Lu and team propose a multi-modal sensing residual-corrected graph neural network for millimeter-wave path loss prediction in vehicular links for future intelligent transport systems. The setting becomes an environment sensing path loss graph, with Tx and Rx nodes, Tx-Rx links, and Rx-Rx spatial links. A geometry-driven baseline splits steady trends from random residuals.

Topology-aware graphs and visual detail join through gated fusion to predict the path loss gap from that base. The team built a path loss dataset spanning an urban wide lane, an urban crossroad, and a suburban forking road, matching camera images and scene data to ray-tracing data. It beat empirical and standard baselines, with normalized mean squared error under one hundredth, mean absolute error under six decibels, and mean absolute percentage error near five percent. Few-shot fine-tuning extended it to unseen places.
arxiv-2602-18305:
Krasimir Yordzhev studies an open question about checking whether one language family sits inside another. His 2026 paper asks whether a context-free language is always contained in a group language, a problem Anisimov linked to testing whether finite automata are unambiguous. Finding a fast, polynomial-time check is the goal.

Yordzhev describes context-free languages in an unusual way, through a finite directed graph whose edges carry labels from a specially built monoid. He also defines a semiring whose elements are subsets of that monoid, with product and union as operations. The resulting procedure runs in at most cubic time in that semiring, offering a concrete route toward settling Anisimov's problem.
arxiv-2602-18605:
David V. Stark and two co-authors measure how aging detectors distort brightness. Their 2026 paper uses repeat imaging of a galaxy cluster over seventeen years to examine degraded Charge Transfer Efficiency effects with ACS/WFC on Hubble. They examine how brightness depends on time since installation, location, brightness, and background level.

Global brightness with large apertures proves reliable within about zero point zero five magnitudes. That holds if backgrounds exceed twenty electrons per pixel and sources exceed three hundred electrons per exposure. Smaller-scale measurements can suffer losses above zero point one magnitudes in recent data unless sources sit close to CCD registers or exceed three thousand electrons. Degraded CTE can also create false asymmetries in galaxy light, largely mitigated with sufficient backgrounds and nearby targets. Later-epoch measurements work best with corrected images, though pipeline correction does not always restore charge to its original location.
arxiv-2602-18705:
Simulated classrooms usually hard-code rules into each pupil, which makes social life rigid and hard to align with school values. Wenjing Zhai, with two co-authors, presents EDU-MATRIX in 2026, a society-centric digital twin for secondary education that simulates a social space with a gravitational field rather than a set of isolated people.

An environment context injection engine feeds institutional rules into agents by place and time, a modular logic evolution protocol lets knowledge capsules combine into new ideas. Alignment emerges from each agent's place in the social graph. Run as a twin of a school with 2,400 agents, the system produced clustered, value-aligned behaviour with high dialogue consistency, showing how rules and knowledge interact to shape a school.
arxiv-2602-18805: Vesselin Drensky, writing alone in 2026, surveys the finite basis problem. It asks which families of algebras can be defined by a finite set of rules. He gives many examples that fail this test. He also gives key examples that pass it, along with all their subfamilies. Special focus falls on semigroups, groups, and associative, Lie, and other nonassociative algebras.
arxiv-2602-19105: M. S. Al Ghafri, with two co-authors, characterises nuclear weighted conditional expectation operators on Lebesgue spaces in 2026. The result covers every finite exponent from one upward. A sharp consequence follows for non-atomic measure spaces. There, the zero operator stands alone. No other nuclear weighted conditional expectation operator exists in that setting.
arxiv-2603-01505:
Language models can draft practice tasks for robots, but many drafts break basic physics and cannot be run. Bingchuan Wei, Bingqi Huang, Jingheng Ma, and colleagues close that gap in this 2026 work. Their point is that drafting and checking should not sit in separate stages.

Their loop, FATE, places a general robot agent inside the drafting step itself. It first checks fixed scene facts, such as what objects can do and how a layout fits. Next it tries the task in simulation to see if the robot can in fact do it. When a task fails, a repair step changes the scene or the goal terms to make a valid version. Tests show varied, grounded task sets with far fewer run failures than prior drafting tools.
arxiv-2603-01705:
Berk Guler, Kay Pompetzki, Yuanzheng Sun, and colleagues add hard safety rules to shared robot control. Their 2026 work blends human intent with machine help, a mix that can still yield unsafe moves in clutter. Soft cost terms only nudge a robot away from hazards; they cannot promise safety.

Their frame, BarrierIK, places control barrier functions at the joint-solving layer after commands blend. Barrier functions act as walls that joint solutions may not cross, which gives firm safety bounds. Tests in simulated clutter and in a virtual reality user study compare plain teleoperation with the guarded mix. Violation time falls and clearance from hazards grows, while task success holds steady. Users report more felt safety and trust, and most prefer the guarded mode.
arxiv-2603-01905:
Pradip Kumar builds an abstract frame for placing two special differentials on one punctured surface at once. His 2026 work sits in Riemann surface theory, which studies curved surfaces with complex structure. A configuration datum fixes the combinatorics and carves out a restricted domain of characters, or period data.

Working on a scale-fixed slice of that domain, Kumar assumes three traits: regularity, degeneration detection, and pushability. Under those assumptions, he proves a point exists for any prescribed restricted pair of period data. At that point, one surface carries two meromorphic differentials that realize the pair exactly. The result abstracts a classic extremal-length minimization method of Weber and Wolf. Such frames help geometers build surfaces with tightly controlled analytic data.
arxiv-2603-02005:
Wendi Wang, Jiaxi Yang, Yongkang Du, and Lu Lin debias generated graphs by asking a counterfactual question. Their 2026 work targets graph diffusion models, which can inherit and amplify topology bias from traits like gender or region. Fair generators so far need full labels or joint updates of structure and attributes, which limits general use.

Their model, FairGDiff, asks whether the graph would change if a sensitive trait were different. A causal model links sensitive traits, biased link formation, and the generated structure. The counterfactual answer yields an unbiased treatment estimate folded into both diffusion directions. Generated graphs then stand independent of sensitive traits while keeping structural integrity. Wide tests on real data show a better fairness-utility trade-off than prior fair generators, with scalability intact.
arxiv-2603-02105:
Dhrumil Bhatt, Anakha Kurup, and R. C. Mala present a routing protocol that keeps smart grid sensor networks alive under jamming. Their 2026 protocol, DAMCR, targets reliability, adaptability, and energy efficiency across grid and industrial networks. Radios must hop technologies while attackers try to block the spectrum.

Chaotic frequency hopping spreads signals to resist jamming and add physical-layer security. Link-adaptive power control tunes transmission power to live link quality and remaining node energy. Priority-aware classification separates routine monitoring traffic from urgent fault and protection messages. Simulations mix LoRa, Wi-Fi, and dual-radio nodes under several fading models in a standard tool. Delivery stays near perfect across scenarios, with low latency held even under controlled jamming attacks, beating static single-radio rivals.
arxiv-2603-02305:
Bharath Sambasivam, Kyle Sherbert, Karunya Shirali, and colleagues present a quantum algorithm for time evolution in this 2026 paper. Simulating how a quantum system changes over time is a core task for quantum computers. Their method, TIMES-ADAPT, works inside a small low-energy corner of the full system. A trained unitary first untangles the system's energy states within that corner.

Fixed-depth circuits then carry out the time evolution, with time as a simple dial setting. Two versions cover starting states given in energy terms or in raw qubit terms. Tests use variants of a standard spin model, the Heisenberg XXZ chain. Uses include wave packet motion and energy transport in spin systems. Fixed depth at any time point could ease near-term hardware limits.
arxiv-2603-02405:
Philipp Schröer and Joost-Pieter Katoen present one approach for many goals on random programs in this 2026 paper. Probabilistic programs mix code with chance, and analysts ask varied questions about them. Each question, or objective, once needed its own reasoning machinery. Their trick adds a single reward statement to the language.

A program transformation then applies a chosen function to the total reward. The transformation works from step-by-step differences in reward, keeping it incremental. Moments, threshold chances, budget overruns, and generating functions all become expressible. Every objective reduces to one existing reasoning method for weakest preconditions. The team automated the check in a deductive verifier. Example programs show the single approach handling many objectives cleanly.
arxiv-2603-02605:
Yun-Wen Mao and Roman Krems optimize molecules with very little data in this 2026 paper. Chemical space is vast and discrete, so finding molecules with target properties is hard. Standard machine learning optimizers need large data sets to model that space. Their Bayesian framework works inside a subspace of well over a hundred thousand molecules.

Fewer than two thousand training points suffice for precise optimization. The key is a low-dimensional descriptor that encodes real physics of each molecule. A reliable inverse map turns optimized descriptor points back into valid molecules. On a standard benchmark, entropy targets were hit every time in their tests. Most runs needed under a thousand evaluations to succeed. Zero-point energy targets also scored high success for larger molecules.
arxiv-2603-03205:
Aradhye Agarwal, Gurdit Siyan, Yash Pandya, and colleagues teach tool-using agents to pause, check, and sometimes refuse. A chat model's worst slip is a bad sentence, but an agent's single misstep, opening files or typing credentials, can cause irreversible harm. Their 2026 framework, MOSAIC, makes the safety decision an explicit, learnable step.

Inference follows a loop: plan, check, then act or refuse and replan. Training uses preference comparisons between whole trajectories, avoiding the need for labeled steps and catching safety contrasts that single scores miss. Across three model families and fresh benchmarks covering harmful tasks, prompt injection, and privacy leaks, harmful behavior fell by up to half. Refusals of injected attacks rose, leakage dropped, and benign task performance held or improved.
arxiv-2603-03405:
Shion Matsumoto and three colleagues introduce a new free-energy functional for learning and inference. Two classic objectives, forward and reverse KL divergence, push models in opposite directions, and averages alone cannot explain why. Their 2026 construction, the Surprisal-Rényi Free Energy, is built from log-moments of the likelihood ratio and sits outside the usual family of divergences.

Both KL divergences return as singular endpoint limits of the new functional. Expansions near those limits expose the variance of the log-likelihood ratio as a first-order correction, revealing an explicit mean-variance trade-off. The functional is also the unique minimizer of a weighted sum of KL terms, a Gibbs-style characterization. Finally, it directly controls large deviations of excess code length, giving a precise minimum description length reading. The results clarify the geometry behind the two KL regimes.
arxiv-2603-03505:
Shang Wu and eight colleagues teach a system to rewrite video prompts so the physics comes out right. Leading text-to-video generators make gorgeous clips that break physical law. The authors show the fault lies in thin prompts, not the generators: hand-added physics detail reliably fixes the output, but hand-writing does not scale. Their 2026 framework, PhyPrompt, automates that expert rewriting with reinforcement learning.

Stage one fine-tunes a language model on physics-focused reasoning examples, teaching it to weave in motion and force detail while keeping user intent. Stage two applies group-based policy optimization under a shifting reward: meaning fidelity first, physical commonsense increasingly later. The seven-billion-parameter system beat far larger commercial models on joint success, improving physics and meaning together rather than trading one for the other. Gains also transferred, untouched, to three other video architectures.
arxiv-2605-00005:
Pragya Sharma, Hang Qiu, and Mani Srivastava revisit a settled assumption in distributed real-time computing: that inference must run on the device. Cyber-physical systems use deep neural networks for perception, but local hardware pays heavy energy and computing costs to meet control deadlines. Cloud inference was long dismissed because network delays vary too much for safety-critical loops.

The authors build a formal model of distributed inference latency from sensing frequency, platform throughput, network delay, and task safety limits. They test it on emergency braking for autonomous driving, with simulations using real-time vehicle dynamics. With strong cloud hardware, network and queueing delays are amortized, and the cloud matches or beats on-device inference, holding safety margins more reliably under the conditions they identify.
arxiv-2605-00105:
M Fogliardi and eight co-authors use convolutional networks to read the structure of galaxy clusters from weak lensing maps. Clusters are the most massive bound structures in the universe and key probes of cosmic evolution, but coming surveys will deliver too many for hand analysis. Their networks infer structural parameters from the subtle distortions that a cluster's gravity imprints on background galaxies.

Three architectures are trained on tens of thousands of synthetic shear maps of simulated clusters. Together they predict five parameters at once: virial mass, concentration, substructure count, and the smooth mass fraction among them. On thousands of test clusters, mass estimates stay robust under realistic noise and concentrations are stable, while substructure counts are systematically underestimated. Against traditional profile fitting, the best network is nearly unbiased in mass with fewer systematic errors, offering a scalable route for large surveys.
arxiv-2605-00305:
Tianqi Shi and Jinxin Xue take on Aubry's completeness conjecture, a claim about twist maps and the physics of atomic chains. In the Frenkel-Kontorova model of atoms on a surface, whether the chain conducts or insulates hinges on how rotation numbers vary with a stiffness-like parameter. Aubry predicted that this variation forms a complete devil's staircase, a curve that climbs only in jumps.

The authors present an argument for the conjecture when all minimal configurations are uniformly hyperbolic, the strongly chaotic case. In that regime they argue the rotation number graph is purely singularly continuous, matching Aubry's picture. They also argue the opposite case: when a positive share of orderly KAM tori survives, the staircase is incomplete. The phenomenon is kin to phase locking in circle maps and to steps in the fractional quantum Hall effect.
arxiv-2605-00405:
Kang Yang and 4 co-authors tackle cooperative perception for vehicles and robots whose detectors were trained separately, by different developers, with no joint preparation. In the wild, such agents meet only occasionally and online. Simply fusing their features, the authors find, performs worse than one agent perceiving alone, because the feature languages do not match.

Their module, BOLT, adapts neighbors' features on the fly using the host agent as teacher, needing no ground-truth labels. Confident host features guide the alignment, while neighbors are invited to fill the regions where the host is unsure. The module is tiny by modern standards and plugs into existing systems. On two driving benchmarks it lifted detection scores far above unadapted fusion and consistently beat working alone, across pairing and fusion choices.
arxiv-2605-00505:
Lu Dai and 6 co-authors argue that information retrieval must be rebuilt for its new main reader: the language model. Search feeds chatbots and agents that answer with outside sources, and models can only take in so much at once and have a weakness for noise. Off-topic or false text is no longer a nuisance; it leads to invented answers and broken reasoning.

The authors frame the shift as denoising, raising the density of usable, checked evidence inside a model's window. They sort the field's challenges into four stages: information that cannot be reached, that is hard to find, that is mismatched, and that cannot be checked. A sorting then groups noise-cutting methods across indexing, search, context handling, and checks in agent workflows. The paper closes with denoising work in search-heavy domains such as personal helpers, coding agents, deep research tools, and image-and-text systems.
arxiv-2605-00705:
Martin Bendersky, Salvatore Elia, and Jelena Grbic study the shape and holes of Vietoris-Rips complexes built from hypercube graphs. These complexes turn a graph into a higher-dimensional object whose cohomology, a tool for counting holes, can reveal hidden structure. The authors build a framework that connects the complexes to rings and related objects from algebra.

Their methods yield lower bounds on how connected the complexes must be and the first global upper bounds on a related property. The bounds produce endless families that contradict Shukla's conjecture. They also build explicit cohomology classes from simpler ones and introduce ghost vertices, a new tool for finding and separating such classes.
arxiv-2605-00905:
Anirudh Iyengar Kaniyar Narayana Iyengar and six co-authors present DIAGRAMS, a review framework for reasoning-level attribution in diagram question answering. Answering questions about diagrams, charts, maps, circuits, and infographics requires linking each answer to all visual regions used in the reasoning, not just the region holding the final answer. Building such evidence is slow, and tools often tie their interface to one dataset format.

DIAGRAMS decouples the interface from dataset structures through an internal meta-schema and adapters. Given an image and question, it proposes the regions needed for reasoning, can generate missing questions or regions, and supports human checking and refinement. Across six datasets, suggested evidence agrees strongly with reviewer-final selections.
arxiv-2605-01005:
Tiger Lu and Garett Brown implement coordinates suited to wide binary systems in TRACE, a hybrid integrator inside the widely used REBOUND N-body package. Traditional hybrid integrators perform poorly in this regime, where two bodies orbit far apart while close encounters can still occur between any pair. The new coordinate system supports such encounters across the whole system.

Benchmarks cover planet-planet scattering, stellar flybys, and ZLK oscillations. In wide binary coordinates, TRACE stays qualitatively correct in cases where other hybrid methods fail. In many cases its results are statistically similar to the high-precision IAS15 integrator, with speedups up to about nine times. The authors also give guidelines for when use of these coordinates is appropriate.
arxiv-2605-01105:
Xinfeng Xu and fourteen co-authors develop methods for fitting multi-phase galactic wind models to high-quality outflow observations. Galactic winds shape galaxy evolution, but outflowing gas spans several ionization phases and varies spatially, making model fitting hard. They fit column density profiles using a multiphase, multiscale wind model, identifying three key parameters: initial hot and cool phase mass-loading factors and initial cool-cloud mass.

Good fits are obtained for most galaxies, with tight constraints on the cool-phase loading and moderate constraints on the other parameters. Inferred loadings are mostly of order unity with significant scatter. Interaction between phases lets cool-outflow observations indirectly constrain the hot wind. Predicted trends include cool outflow velocity rising then plateauing with radius.
arxiv-2605-01205:
Quoc Phong Dao and six co-authors introduce Span Representation Alignment for distilling large language models across different tokenizers. Cross-tokenizer distillation transfers knowledge to a smaller student even when they differ, but existing token-level alignment is brittle and sensitive to tokenizer gaps. The authors argue how tokens are grouped into robust views before distillation matters just as much as the matching itself.

Their framework shifts the unit from tokens to tokenizer-free spans, modeled through a physical multi-particle lens. Each span's state is an attention-weighted center of mass that captures semantic information, with salient spans prioritized. A geometric regularizer preserves span structure, and aligned span logit teaching enhances transfer. Cross-architecture experiments show consistent, significant gains over leading baselines.
arxiv-2605-01305:
Himanshu Kumar Dwivedi, Matthias Ehrhardt, and Rajeev combine neural networks with a high-order time scheme to solve fractional equations, a class where the present state depends on the whole past. Such equations often have a sharp kink at the start, which ruins accuracy on even time grids.

Their design, Alikhanov-XfPINNs, pairs the Alikhanov scheme on stretched time grids with a physics-informed network that learns the solution. A flexible activation function speeds training, and the loss is built from the scheme itself, with start and edge rules set as hard or soft limits. A separate time-stepping setup lets them check time errors apart from training errors. Tests on cases with known and unknown exact answers show robust results and large savings in computing time.
arxiv-2605-01405:
Oliver Eggenberger Andersen and four co-authors ask how often a collapsing star forms a black hole partway through its own explosion. In this outcome, called a black hole supernova, the shock revives and the blast starts, but a black hole forms before the explosion finishes.

The team runs 23 long two-dimensional simulations of stars from about 20 to 60 times the Sun's mass, spanning a range of core tightness. Eighteen runs end as black hole supernovae, spread across nearly the whole mass range, with the hole forming between well under a second and a few seconds after core bounce. Final blast energies and hole masses vary widely, and hole mass tracks the carbon-oxygen core mass, though that core alone mispredicts both ends of the range. A three-dimensional check shows how geometry changes the picture.
arxiv-2605-01605:
Zhuoyun Li and eight co-authors locate exactly where a small prompt typo breaks a language model's answer. Robustness work usually grades the whole response, which can hide a drift that hits one key entity, relation, or conclusion while the rest reads fine.

Their framework works at segment level. Clean and perturbed answers are cut into meaning segments, aligned by an optimal-transport objective, and the worst-drifting segments are penalized. An adapter-stability term, guided by how attention reallocates across segments, keeps the low-rank tuning from amplifying those shifts; a PAC-Bayesian view explains why capping adapter growth should transfer to unseen noise. On summarization tests the method hardens models against typos, deletions, synonym swaps, and paraphrases, keeps clean scores competitive, and transfers across data sets better than whole-sequence rivals.
arxiv-2605-01805:
Yu and four colleagues design a learning signal that helps teams of AI agents coordinate. In multi-agent reinforcement learning, several agents learn together toward a shared goal, but each one only sees its own view of the world. A helpful move may pay off for a teammate later, yet the shared team reward gives no direct credit for it. Their framework, MAGIC, estimates how one agent's action shapes its teammates' futures over several steps, then turns only the beneficial effects into extra rewards.

Counterfactual comparisons pit what actually happened against what would have happened under a different action, and an advantage gate steers exploration toward moves aligned with the task. On particle-world tasks and StarCraft micromanagement benchmarks, MAGIC beat leading prior methods, with average relative gains of about twenty-seven percent and ten percent. The result suggests that crediting cross-agent influence step by step builds steadier teamwork.
arxiv-2605-02105:
Ishaan Watts and colleagues show that how a model is pretrained affects how much it forgets during later training and quantisation. Optimisers are usually tuned for the strongest base model, assuming strength alone carries through later changes. The authors argue the shape of the base model, in particular how flat its minimum is, controls what survives updates.

They test three ways to bias training toward flat minima: sharpness-aware minimisation, large learning rates, and shorter rate annealing. Across model sizes and five data sets, all three cut forgetting, by up to eighty percent. At larger scale, a short sharpness-aware phase on an existing one-billion-parameter checkpoint cut forgetting after maths training and after four-bit quantisation.
arxiv-2605-02205:
Mahdi Nouraie, Houying Zhu, and Samuel Muller improve stability selection, a method that picks features by how often they survive resampling. Standard stability selection resamples rows but leaves the design fixed. An irrelevant feature that correlates with relevant ones can then be picked often, breaking the condition behind the false-positive bound.

Their 2D method also varies the design, by adding a grid of injected noise to the inputs and aggregating selection counts over both half-samples and noise levels. At zero noise it reduces to the original method. Input noise acts like a ridge penalty on average, so a jittered Lasso fit can repair some broken designs, though it can also hurt. The paper gives the noise level where a violated feature's statistic vanishes in one case.
arxiv-2605-02405:
Sofianos Panagiotis Fotias and Vassilis Gaganis build closed-loop controllers for carbon storage in rock. Injection and brine output must adapt as the reservoir responds in uncertain ways. Only data that are truly available during operation can be used. The authors cast the task as a decision problem with partial views. They train deep learning controllers in high-fidelity reservoir models.

They compare several policy types, from full-state and well-only designs to history-based and teacher-student variants. That comparison shows the value of past well responses. It also shows the value of full simulator states during training. A latent model pipeline then reuses learned dynamics and retunes controllers under injector failure, leakage, and changed reservoir links. History-based policies recovered nearly all full-state performance.
arxiv-2605-02505:
Sangpil Youm, Leah Jones, and Bonnie J. Dorr revisit semantic role labeling, the task of marking who did what to whom in a sentence. Large language models handle meaning in a hidden way, with few clear structural checks. Older role-labeling tools also face a practical problem: a once-standard framework entered maintenance mode in late 2022, limiting its fit with new encoders.

The authors offer a modern encoder-based system that keeps explicit predicate and argument structure while running inference about ten times faster. Stronger encoders lift accuracy within the same design. A diagnostic method informed by dependency grammar traces span errors and probes how language models react to structural signals. The main gain from those cues, they find, is stability of structure.
arxiv-2605-03305:
Ankit Kumar, Daniel A. Caballero, Hajime Sotani, and Nicolás Yunes develop the first fully relativistic treatment of non-radial oscillations in two-fluid neutron stars whose fluids couple only through gravity. Such oscillations probe star structure and gravity, but prior work lacked a complete relativistic setup for independently conserved currents.

They derive the coupled perturbation equations for the metric and both fluids, with the regularity, surface, and matching conditions needed for a well-posed mode problem. Numerical spectra follow for sample stars, and mode branches are classed by whether the inner or outer fluid dominates, laying groundwork for gravitational wave studies.
arxiv-2605-03405:
Alexander Matyasko, Xin Lou, Indriyati Atmosukarto, and Wei Zhang introduce TsallisPGD, an adversarial attack on semantic segmentation models. Flipping thousands of pixel labels at once is far harder than fooling a classifier, and standard cross-entropy wastes effort on pixels already fooled, overstating robustness.

Their attack uses Tsallis cross-entropy, whose parameter steers gradient focus across pixel confidence levels. No single fixed value wins everywhere, so a dynamic schedule sweeps it during optimization. On three datasets, one validation-chosen schedule gave the best average rank against five rival attacks, on both standard and robust models.
arxiv-2605-03705:
Philipp Czerner, Javier Esparza, and Konrad Winslow present iSMC, a model checker that certifies its own answers through dialogue. Model checking verifies whether a system satisfies a logical property. iSMC handles arbitrary Computation Tree Logic properties with justice requirements. It uses symbolic binary decision diagrams. After solving an instance, it runs a certification step.

The certification rests on interactive proof systems. A dialogue guarantees, with a user-chosen high probability, that the reported answer is correct. iSMC adapts technology from a certified QBF solver presented at CAV 2023, reshaped for CTL model checking. The authors describe it as the first self-certifying model checker of its kind.
arxiv-2605-04505:
Leying Zhang and four co-authors present a framework for judging the quality of generated audio and speech, an area where evaluation methods have lagged behind the fast-improving generators. Standard metrics and general multimodal models often fail to generalise, handle new tasks without retraining, or follow flexible instructions.

Their system connects a frozen high-performance audio encoder to a fine-tuned language model through a trainable adapter, and frames assessment as an instruction-following reasoning task. A broad data pipeline varies sources, tasks, calibrations, and descriptions to build robustness. Across speech, sound, music, and unseen domains, its scores tracked human ratings more closely than rival general models.
arxiv-2605-04705:
Jiangnan Zhu and three co-authors propose a watermarking scheme for 3D medical scans. It protects their ownership and authenticity when they are shared for telemedicine. Such volume data are valuable for diagnosis but easy to copy or tamper with once they travel across networks.

Their method is reversible and leaves the host data untouched. It is a zero-watermarking design. A feature extractor trained with contrastive learning pulls stable, distinctive features from each volume. They are robust to 3D attacks. Watermark bits are embedded by expanding differences between neighbouring voxels. The voxels sit inside small cubes of a wavelet transform. A majority vote during extraction improves reliability, while keeping distortion low.
arxiv-2605-04905:
Mehrab Mahdian, Ferenc Ender, and Tamas Pardy ask whether machine learning models agree on which settings matter most in electrospinning, a sensitive way to make fine fibres. Small changes in operating conditions can alter fibre shape and performance, and many studies trust a single model's ranking of those conditions. That trust may be misplaced, the authors argue.

They trained twenty-one models of many types on ninety-six experiments with polyvinyl alcohol and compared rankings using SHAP values. Models with similar accuracy often ranked features quite differently, showing prediction and explanation are separate qualities. Solution concentration stood out as the most consistent influence across model families.
arxiv-2605-05105:
Gerald Ogbonna, David Bindel, and Lindsay Anderson tackle reducing harmful transients in electric power networks by reshaping the network itself. Reliable operation grows harder as variable renewable generation joins the grid. Their setup uses graph Laplacian matrices, which encode how buses in the network connect, and shows the design problem is convex under stated assumptions.

A matrix condition ensures that steady-state phase angles exist, are unique, and hold together, and it can be added directly as a constraint. On the standard IEEE thirty-bus test system, the method picked out critical links, and dynamic runs showed much smaller transients and better performance measures. A reweighting shortcut explores the trade-off between sparsity and optimality.
arxiv-2605-05405:
James Walsh and four co-authors built GeoQuery, a way to search satellite imagery using plain language. Archives of Earth photos are huge, but picture-based search models cannot understand text queries. Training a joint model needs paired data and computing power that are not available at global scale.

GeoQuery avoids that training with a two-stage trick. It writes text descriptions for a subset of one hundred thousand map tiles, tuned so text distances mirror visual distances. Queries search the text first, then the wider visual archive. On disaster queries it placed floods best, and responders used it during a Brisbane cyclone.
arxiv-2605-05505:
Superconducting radio-frequency cavities need coatings that survive curved shapes. Aaron Gobeyn, Wolfgang Ackermann, and Herbert De Gersem model what uneven coating does to a cavity's quality factor. Their multilayer coatings stack superconductor, insulator, and superconductor, allowing brittle materials that bulk niobium cannot offer.

They generate the thickness unevenness with Gaussian random fields at eight length scales, with over two thousand samples each. Quality factors came out normally distributed, with spread growing as the length scale grew. Mean values barely moved, though in extreme cases the quality factor shifted by a few percent.
arxiv-2605-05705:
Computing integrals with kernel quadrature can beat random sampling, but its tuned weights often go negative and unstable. Satoshi Hayakawa asks whether the speed survives when weights are forced positive. In his setting, a pool of already-scored candidate points must be reweighted to approach a kernel mean.

He shows the problem is governed by the random convex hull the pool generates, not by its plain average. The geometry yields error bounds for positive-weight rules, showing exactly which quantity controls the error. The results clarify when simplex weights keep spectral acceleration and when forcing positive weights costs real accuracy.
arxiv-2605-05905:
Daniel Cortild and Coralia Cartis introduce a new way to add privacy to machine learning training. Objective perturbation protects data by adding random terms to the training goal. The linear version needs bounded gradients, a strong assumption that rules out many modern models.

Their quadratic version instead adds a random quadratic form to the goal. That change creates strong convexity and stability through curvature, so privacy rests on spectral traits of the added term, not on gradient bounds. They prove privacy holds even when the problem is solved only in part. They also give utility bounds on excess risk, compare the method with the linear version, and show modern splitting methods can solve the resulting problems well.
arxiv-2605-06005:
Sarka Liskova and five co-authors build a sign language recognition system that runs on neuromorphic hardware. Recent recognizers are accurate, but their delay and power needs block real time use on small devices. Neuromorphic chips compute with sparse spikes, which suits fast, low power perception at the edge.

Their system pairs a spiking visual attention step, which picks out the region of interest online, with a compact spiking network on the SpiNNaker platform. It targets American Sign Language fingerspelling and was tested on two event based data sets. Accuracy reached 92.27 percent in simulation and 83.1 percent on the hardware itself. The design used just 0.565 milliwatts with a three millisecond delay, the leanest figures among the compared approaches.
arxiv-2605-06305:
Thomas Cory and Axel Küpper use language models to label personal data leaking through web and mobile app traffic. Privacy audits scan outbound HTTP messages for personally identifiable information, but learning based detectors need scarce hand labeled traffic. They also bind tightly to one fixed label taxonomy, so they transfer poorly when definitions of personal data shift across domains or over time.

Their pipeline supplies the taxonomy at runtime instead of baking it into training. Deterministic preprocessing feeds label level classification, targeted value labeling, and output checking stages run by language models. A tool creates synthetic traffic with validated labels, avoiding sensitive real captures for evaluation and prompting examples. Across three label sets of varied scope, the pipeline detected personal data types well and extracted the matching values.
arxiv-2605-06405:
Nam Anh Le studies market making for perpetual contracts on decentralized exchanges, where the funding rate moves as a random state variable. Holding inventory creates two linked effects: price exposure and a funding cash flow that depends on the position. Le turns that coupling into a reduced control problem.

The problem is solved with a monotone finite-difference method for a Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation, and quotes are recovered from value differences. Funding is calibrated on Hyperliquid data for ETH, BTC, and SOL. In holdout simulations the funding-aware method improves mean ETH and BTC results and lowers inventory risk, though the SOL gains are more mixed.
arxiv-2605-06905:
Eshed Gal, Md Shahriar Rahim Siddiqui, Moshe Eliasof, and Eldad Haber propose Conservative Flows, a generative modeling idea that starts from data instead of noise. Standard models transport random noise into samples through a learned flow. Conservative Flows instead run a step-by-step random dynamics that leaves the data distribution unchanged, seeded from data states, and can wrap around any trained flow model as its engine.

Two probability-preserving samplers are built: a corrected Langevin scheme with a Metropolis accept-reject step, and a predictor-corrector flow. Both run directly on existing checkpoints. On a spiral test target, ImageNet, and a flower dataset, the samplers steadily improve over the original generation methods they build on.
arxiv-2605-07305:
Hsin-Ling Hsu and eleven co-authors train medical language models to diagnose actively, the way doctors work in practice. Most model testing is done with complete information given at once, unlike real practice, where doctors order tests and update their thinking over turns. The team finds three common failures: ungrounded test choices, weak updates, and fading coherence.

Their MedAction pipeline builds multi-turn case dialogues through model-environment interaction, filtered by two knowledge-graph metrics for consistency. The resulting dataset holds tens of thousands of such records from thousands of published cases. A fine-tuned open model reached leading open-source results on two testing benchmarks, pushing active testing forward.
arxiv-2605-07505:
Yubin Wu and six co-authors train lightweight agents that operate graphical interfaces through long, branching tasks. Small GUI agents struggle because several different actions can be valid at each state, and fixed demonstrations ignore that freedom. LiteGUI trains on logged interface states with teacher guidance that picks the best-matching valid action at each step.

A second stage mixes action-level supervision with planning-quality supervision, still respecting multiple valid actions. A scalable pipeline produced a matching multi-solution dataset for training and evaluation. Across GUI benchmarks, LiteGUI substantially improved small agents over standard fine-tuning and reinforcement approaches, rivaling much larger models.
arxiv-2605-07605:
Jichuan Yu and six co-authors present BrickCraft, a robot framework for assembling interlocking bricks over long task horizons. Building with bricks mixes big-picture planning, precise spatial grounding, and delicate manipulation, and each new structure seems to demand new skills. BrickCraft instead breaks assembly into reusable primitive moves.

Each step is described relative to a reference brick already in the partial structure, which turns open-ended builds into combinations of a finite skill set. Situated manuals project the intended placement onto the robot's live camera view, guiding the learned skills during execution. Experiments show the system learned proficient assembly from few demonstrations and recombined its skills across diverse long-horizon tasks.
arxiv-2605-08205:
Rajesh Karmakar and Xian-Hui Ge construct a traversable wormhole in a universe with a positive cosmological constant. Adding that constant deforms the geometry in nontrivial ways, and exact traversable solutions are scarce, so the authors work perturbatively around the classic Ellis-Bronnikov wormhole.

Assuming the constant times the throat size squared is small, they derive the first-order metric deformation and map where the approximation holds. Inside that region the shape function takes a de Sitter-like form, the flare-out condition still holds at the throat, and the null energy condition is violated, as traversability demands. The solution gives a controlled starting point for wormholes in an expanding universe.
arxiv-2605-08305:
Siyu Wu, Yulong Ye, Zezhen Xiang, Pengzhou Chen, and coauthors release a benchmark for tuning the knobs of real language model systems. Such systems mix model settings with serving settings, their fidelity choices interact in nonlinear ways, and each configuration costs a different amount to measure, none of which older tuning benchmarks capture.
