The Nusselt number, the ratio of conductive heat transfer, grows roughly linearly with the Rayleigh number. A change of slope near the upper end signals the ultimate regime's onset. At moderate driving the results sit below an earlier scaling, while in the ultimate regime they agree with a prediction to within a little over 1 percent. Near the walls, protoplumes form and merge into larger structures.
arxiv-2606-13805:
Pérez Martínez and colleagues study how strongly two magnetic layers must be coupled to push the largest possible spin current between them. A spin current carries angular momentum without moving electric charge, which could cut energy losses in future devices. Their 2026 arXiv paper examines bilayers of an iron cobalt alloy on a permalloy layer, grown on magnesium oxide crystals by magnetron sputtering, a method that sprays atoms onto a surface.

Measurements with ferromagnetic resonance, which wiggles the magnetization with microwaves, show a cubic pattern in the magnetic response. The easy direction for magnetization lies along one crystal axis of the iron cobalt layer, and the hard direction along another. Modeling then shows that the wobbling area of the permalloy magnetization peaks at one particular coupling strength between the layers. Tuning that coupling, the layer thickness, or the driving frequency can therefore maximize the injected spin current.
arxiv-2606-14205:
Lao, Pham, Ta, and Vu define a new invariant for sum-rank metric codes and prove it splits cleanly across the code's blocks. Sum-rank codes generalize Hamming and rank-metric codes: codewords are tuples of matrices, weighted by the sum of block ranks. Their 2026 arXiv paper defines block tensor rank: the smallest number of block-simple tensors, rank-one matrices inside single blocks, whose span contains the code.

The main theorem: block tensor rank decomposes additively across blocks, reducing its computation to tensor rank on each block projection. From this they derive two lower bounds, projection-wise and coordinate-code, sharpening the latter with the classical Singleton and Griesmer bounds. Constructions from optimal Hamming-metric codes attain these bounds, defining two optimality notions. Notably, two known sum-rank families provably fail to attain the Singleton coordinate-code bound, and the two optimality notions capture genuinely different features.
arxiv-2606-14405:
Saketh, Ghosh, and Andersson tackle a 2026 arXiv problem in gravitational-wave work. The task is telling neutron stars apart from black holes in merging pairs. Neutron stars deform under a partner's gravity. This tidal response reveals their inner matter. But defining that response cleanly is hard. Coordinate choices in relativity can blur it.

The authors define the dynamical tidal response in worldline effective field theory. That scheme treats the star as a point with structured traits. They tie the response to the amplitude for waves scattering off a lone star. They compute that amplitude two ways. One way uses field theory. The other solves the star's equations numerically. Matching the two fixes the response. The result matches the known static limit. It also recovers the main mode's energy loss.
arxiv-2606-14505:
Sousa proves a regularity result for a nonlinear equation in a 2026 arXiv paper. The topic is the g-Laplacian, a diffusion operator with nonstandard growth. It is studied in Orlicz-Sobolev spaces, which widen the usual energy spaces. The domains are Reifenberg flat. That means their edges look almost flat at every scale. It is a realistic roughness for physical regions.

The problem is a Dirichlet problem, where edge values are prescribed. Sousa shows weak solutions stay Hölder continuous up to the edge. Hölder continuity is a measured form of smoothness. Any target exponent below one can be reached. This holds if the domain's flatness is small enough. The proof uses an iterative decay argument at the edge. It shrinks oscillation step by step. It also uses a maximum principle of ABP type, adapted to this space.
arxiv-2606-14805:
Dong Ho Kang, Hyeonjeong Cha, and Daein Weon debug multi-agent AI systems without re-running them in a 2026 arXiv paper. Such systems leave long execution traces. A few decisive events hide inside logs of messages, routes, memory writes, and tool calls. The standard check is counterfactual replay: rewind, edit one event, and re-run to measure its effect. That cost grows with every candidate event, so full replay is infeasible at scale.

The team compiles each trace into an event knowledge graph. A predictor called BranchPoint-Latent then ranks which events a replay oracle would flag as high-effect. It learns from graph structure, uncertainty, and latent evidence features. Calibrated against a deterministic replay oracle across thirty-seven trace families, it raised Branch Recall@5 from about zero point seven three to about zero point nine three. That gain came at zero replay cost on held-out families.
arxiv-2606-14905:
Mehdi, Zaid, and Aleem segment salt domes in seismic data without centralizing it in a 2026 arXiv paper. Outlining salt domes guides hydrocarbon exploration, reservoir modeling, and drilling safety, but labeled seismic volumes are scarce and operators guard their data. Their framework, FedSaltNet, uses federated learning, training a shared model across separate data owners without moving the raw volumes.

A lightweight small U-Net segments the images, and a foreground-weighted aggregation strategy counters the severe class imbalance between salt and background across sites. Emulating non-identical data across four seismic datasets, the aggregation improved overlap scores by about four percent relative over the best conventional federated method. The simple U-Net beat a higher-capacity ResNet variant by a wide margin in average overlap, underscoring that architectural simplicity wins in data-constrained federated settings.
arxiv-2606-15005:
Abdulin and Narimani detect false data injection attacks on power grids with a Transformer mixture-of-experts model in a 2026 study. Attackers corrupt sensor readings to mislead the state estimation that grid operators rely on. Many detectors use a single graph filter, which adapts poorly to varied attack patterns. The authors aim to spot attacks and locate the compromised buses at once.

Their encoder-only Transformer adds Laplacian positional encoding and diffusion-biased attention to capture grid-wide links. A routed mixture-of-experts layer mixes two graph filters, Chebyshev and autoregressive moving-average convolutions, chosen per grid state. Tests run on the IEEE 118-bus and 300-bus systems with real New York load profiles. The model reaches the strongest detection and localization scores among compared methods while keeping false alarms low. Routing weights adapt across attack scenarios, which the authors credit for the stable performance.
arxiv-2606-15205:
Gonzalez and coauthors develop tools for Scott analysis aimed at Vaught's conjecture, in a 2026 mathematical logic paper. Vaught's conjecture says a theory's countable models number either countably many or continuum many. Scott rank grades structures by the complexity of their defining formulas. The authors study which Scott ranks can occur under countability side conditions. Their tools examine models of ranks when only countably many types are realized.

Using them, the team improves a result of Sacks on counterexamples. Any counterexample to the conjecture must now have at least two models of every parameterized rank. Theories with fewer than continuum many models are shown to have trivial Scott spectra. The authors classify low-rank models when few types are realized. They settle the Scott spectra of many Ehrenfeucht theories. Applications reach concrete theories like p-groups, trees, and Boolean algebras. Several questions from other researchers are answered along the way.
arxiv-2606-15605:
Roy and colleagues construct quantum many-body scars in 2026 inside a driven chain of Rydberg atoms on a ring. Scars are rare eigenstates that refuse to thermalize while the states around them do, and an index theorem guarantees this driven model an exponentially large family of exact zero-energy modes. Most of those modes drift as the drive changes, losing any fixed identity.

The team isolates two zero modes that instead keep the memory of particular states across a range of drive amplitudes and frequencies. One is a dressed version of the unentangled Rydberg vacuum; the other dresses a highly entangled volume-law scar from earlier work. Floquet perturbation theory explains their existence, and exact diagonalization shows they survive beyond the perturbative regime. The contrast between the two hints at a whole hierarchy of such protected modes in driven systems.
arxiv-2606-15705:
Pranshu and colleagues show in 2026 how small survey telescopes can borrow training from big ones to hunt cosmic transients. Classifiers separating real events from artefacts need large labelled datasets, which new telescopes lack. Transfer learning sidesteps the gap: train on the Zwicky Transient Facility's public images, then fine-tune on smaller data from the four-metre International Liquid Mirror Telescope.

The transferred networks classify candidates in difference images as real or bogus, then sort real detections into three or four alert classes. Accuracy reaches about ninety-seven percent for real-versus-bogus, ninety-three for three classes, and eighty-six for four. On an independent test set the transfer models beat baselines trained without transfer learning. The models now run inside the telescope's working pipeline on full-frame data. For small surveys that cannot label millions of images, borrowing a big survey's knowledge is a practical route to automated alerts.
arxiv-2606-15805:
Zoabi and colleagues introduce Mean-Field Parallel Decoding in 2026, a training-free way to help diffusion language models commit more tokens per step without clashes. Diffusion models unmask positions in parallel, but positions chosen by confidence alone can clash: each looks fine singly, together they form incoherent text. That clash caps how much parallelism is safe.

The method scores each position for commitment, then refines them with pairwise interactions drawn from the model's predictions. A variational step turns the refinement into a fixed-point update suppressing conflicting joint commitments within one forward pass. The decoder can then unmask more tokens per step while holding generation quality. On reasoning and code-generation benchmarks, the quality-latency trade-off improves throughout. Nothing is retrained and no helper model is needed, so the decoder drops into existing diffusion pipelines as-is. Coordinating parallel choices, rather than trusting each alone, is the trick.
arxiv-2606-16205:
Zhang gives an introductory review in 2026 of the bilinear method, a classic tool for solving nonlinear wave equations exactly. Ryogo Hirota created the method in 1971 while hunting three-soliton solutions, lasting wave packets. The review centers on two themes for equations of KdV type. One is how the three-soliton condition tests whether an equation is integrable, meaning exactly solvable.

The second theme is how tau functions, the auxiliary functions the method works with, transform into each other. Bäcklund transformations link solutions of related equations, and vertex operators expose the algebraic structure behind the tau functions. Any KdV-type bilinear equation admits one- and two-soliton solutions, Zhang notes. Integrability shows up when a three-soliton solution also exists under elastic scattering. The review pulls these tests and transforms into one entry point for newcomers.
arxiv-2606-16405:
Yang proves in 2026 that two cornerstone inequalities of analysis on rough spaces imply each other, completing an equivalence long studied for smoother settings. The spaces are metric measure spaces with volume doubling, and the energies are p-energies for p above 1, a nonlinear energy. The elliptic Harnack inequality bounds how much positive solutions of the equation can vary. The Poincaré bound ties a function's spread to its energy.

Under two-sided capacity bounds plus geometric and analytic side conditions, Yang proves Poincaré from Harnack. Combined with earlier work, this yields a full equivalence: Harnack plus capacity bounds holds exactly when Poincaré and the cutoff Sobolev bound hold together. The proof works on balls and covers, with no smooth charts at all. The result tightens the web connecting geometry, capacity, and diffusion in the nonlinear p-energy world.
arxiv-2606-16605:
Zhang and co-authors build in 2026 the first benchmark for attacking world-model agents. World models learn latent dynamics for planning in continuous control, and they are entering safety-critical settings. Yet no testbed spanned the policy, value, and latent-dynamics levels of an agent. Their benchmark, ARB4WM, evaluates adversarial robustness under perturbations with five white-box loss objectives spread across those three levels.

Attacks combine single-step or multi-step perturbation strategies with temporal modes: full-frame, half-sequence, and sparse-frame exposure. Four Dreamer-style agents are tested across twenty tasks from MetaWorld and the DeepMind Control Suite. Small visual perturbations substantially degrade performance, especially under multi-step iterative attacks. Failures aimed at value estimation, latent representations, and the recurrent dynamics prove as important as policy-space failures. The message for safety assessment is to probe the whole latent decision pipeline, not just the action head.
arxiv-2606-16705:
Runko computes diffractive structure functions in a 2026 nuclear physics paper. In diffractive scattering, an electron strikes a proton or nucleus, new particles appear, yet the target stays intact and no color charge is exchanged. A silent gap in the detector marks these events. Structure functions summarize how the target's inner parts respond at each energy share.

The calculation uses Wilson line configurations whose energy evolution follows the JIMWLK equation, a standard tool for dense gluon systems. That setup was already tuned against exclusive vector meson data from the HERA collider in Hamburg. Runko first checks the proton results against HERA measurements to set a baseline. The main new output is the nuclear change for a gold nucleus under conditions planned for the future Electron-Ion Collider. Predictions include the nuclear modification factor and the ratio of diffractive to total cross sections, giving experimenters concrete targets before the new machine runs.
arxiv-2606-17405:
Qin and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on a clinical decision support system that keeps learning while it is used, under strict safety rules. Patient states change in real time, and advice learned only from old records can drift out of date. The framework joins three parts: treatment effect estimation to score each option's benefit, a patient digital twin that simulates likely courses, and reinforcement learning for planning sequences of care over time.

A rule-based guard watches vital signs and blocks treatments that are contraindicated for that patient. Cases where the internal models disagree strongly are flagged for clinician review instead of being decided automatically. Validation used both a synthetic clinical simulator and a real ovarian cancer data set from a national genome atlas. The system beat standard baselines on effectiveness and stability while consulting experts on only a minority of cases.
arxiv-2606-18005:
Reusens and colleagues found a new research field in a 2026 theory paper: the study of how language model agents shop. AI agents increasingly make purchases and bookings on behalf of users, yet consumer theory was built for human decision makers. The authors name the field LLM Consumer Behavior Theory and set out its foundations, joining classical and behavioral economics with language technology.

It formalizes how human preferences get reflected, and sometimes distorted, when an agent acts on them, and how many such agent decisions add up to market demand. It gathers scattered work on model decision-making, human simulation, and preference elicitation under one economic lens, and flags where standard assumptions like rationality and consumer diversity may break. Rather than testing claims, it maps the territory and lists open questions on alignment and market dynamics.
arxiv-2606-18305:
Qin and colleagues rebuild a neural operator in the image of a classical iterative solver, in a 2026 paper in Nuclear Physics B. Operator learning maps between function spaces to solve partial differential equations far faster than standard solvers, a boon for many-query jobs like real-time prediction and parameter sweeps. Accuracy is the weak point, above all with complex boundaries or long time spans. Forward simulation and inverse inference both demand high fidelity.

Their Starter-Iterator Neural Operator splits the work the way iterative methods do. A starter module works in the frequency domain to capture the solution's stable low-frequency content, suppressing the part of the error that converges slowest. An iterator module then refines the high-frequency detail through learnable recursions in the time domain. The pairing aims at spectral and temporal accuracy together, inside one architecture serving both forward and inverse problems.
arxiv-2606-18405:
Kozyreva and Hoque test whether large language models can help check software against a cryptographic protocol standard, in a 2026 security paper. Their target is PKCS#1 version 1.5 signature verification, a widely deployed encoding standard where lax parsing has historically allowed forged signatures, and where good test inputs must satisfy both structural and semantic rules.

The approach mutates a formal grammar of the standard and asks a language model to synthesize test code from it, then runs the results across forty-eight cryptographic library implementations. It reproduced ten of thirteen known violation categories, including all five signature forgery categories, and found one previously unreported discrepancy. The bottleneck was not the mutations but the model: most generated scripts contained hallucinations, and the team sorts these into five types with different rates across mutation kinds. Their guidance shows where such synthesis can be trusted and where it needs filtering or verification first.
arxiv-2606-18505:
Merenkov proves a rigidity result about two kinds of fractal objects that arise from different dynamical systems, in a 2026 mathematics paper. One kind is the limit set of a convex-cocompact Kleinian group. The other is the Julia set of a postcritically finite rational map, and in the cases he considers both sets are Sierpinski carpets.

Recent work on related gasket and tree-like spaces had suggested the two worlds might be locally indistinguishable. Merenkov shows carpets behave oppositely: no local quasiconformal map exists between such a Kleinian limit set and such a Julia set at all. The result draws a sharp line between fractal families that look superficially similar, and it limits how far results about local equivalence between group actions and rational dynamics can be pushed. It also gives carpet specialists a clean test case separating two major sources of fractal limit sets.
arxiv-2606-18605:
Kocharovsky and Kalra introduce a universal measure of the quantum advantage carried by light from multimode optical parametric amplifiers, in a 2026 quantum optics paper. Squeezed light from such devices underpins quantum sensing, communication, and computing, but scaling to many modes has lacked a realistic figure of merit. The standard Bloch-Messiah supermodes describe the squeezing without capturing the computational hardness that makes the light useful.

The authors define a quantum complexity resource for mixed multimode Gaussian states. It is grounded in convex optimization, photon-number statistics, and a master theorem linking the joint photon-count distribution to the hardness of computing matrix hafnians. Designing pulsed amplifiers around this measure maximizes the photons in the true quantum-advantage modes, which differ sharply from the supermodes. The paper argues the approach opens paths to three-dimensional cluster states for one-way photonic quantum computing and cleaner demonstrations of quantum advantage.
arxiv-2606-18805:
Richardson and the team test whether the letdown of a disappointing loss makes fans drive dangerously, in a 2026 behavioral economics paper. Reference-dependent theory says outcomes are judged against expectations. So a loss hurts most when suspense was high and hope was alive. Emotions may spill into behavior after the event.

The authors combined vehicle speeds, recorded every ten minutes at road locations, with crash timing around five Florida stadiums. They covered NFL and NBA games from twenty fifteen to twenty nineteen. They found no emotional driving after basketball games. But effects appeared after football games predicted to be close, that ended in home losses. Average speeds rose by up to three miles per hour, within three kilometers of the stadium, during the first post-game hour. That is several times the normal speed difference. It faded with time and distance, and survived checks against congestion and ordinary traffic explanations.
arxiv-2606-19005:
Ye and colleagues introduce Sumi in 2026, a fully open language model built with uniform diffusion rather than the usual left-to-right method. In uniform diffusion, any token can be updated at any step, which should allow more flexible text generation. No such model had yet been trained from scratch at both large size and large data scale, leaving a clear gap for study.

Sumi has seven billion parameters and was trained from scratch on a very large token set drawn from public sources. It matches rival autoregressive models trained on like budgets on knowledge, reasoning, and coding tests. It lags on common-sense tests, which the authors link to their education-heavy data mix. Weights, checkpoints, and the full training recipe are released openly. That release gives researchers a clean base for studying how native uniform diffusion scales and where it trades off against older designs.
arxiv-2606-19205:
Chuna and colleagues present a regularized stochastic optimization method for analytic continuation in 2026. Quantum Monte Carlo simulations yield imaginary-time correlation functions, but extracting real spectra from them is a notoriously hard inverse problem. Two camps compete in this area, with neural models now joining them. The new method crosses those divides by recasting continuation as dictionary learning with a sparse form.

Remarkably, the learned sparse dictionary maps the ill-conditioned problem to a small one that is well-conditioned. The method gives competitive results on common synthetic tests. It also performs well on authentic Monte Carlo data from the finite-temperature electron gas. The authors argue a suitable dictionary exists inside all such methods. Finding it turns a hard inversion into a stable task.
arxiv-2606-19405:
Okolie and colleagues develop multi-type branching inference on contact trees in 2026, with an application to COVID-19. Inferring epidemic parameters from transmission trees is essential for understanding disease dynamics. Existing tree-based methods, including multi-type birth-death models from phylodynamics, are powerful. Most assume uniform mixing. They rarely capture how spreading potential changes as one person infects more of their contacts.

The framework works on such trees, where nodes are people and edges are reported infections, with no sequence data. Each person is described by their total contacts and how many downstream contacts are already infected. The team derives closed-form equations for the chance a clade goes unobserved and for the density of observed tips. Partial trees are handled with latent branching times. Simulations confirm accurate recovery with calibrated uncertainty. Applied to COVID-19 contact-tracing data, the method turns tracing records into parameter estimates without needing genomes.
arxiv-2606-19605:
Paul Kassianik and six colleagues present FAPO in 2026, a system that tunes multi-step language model pipelines on its own. Such pipelines chain retrieval, reasoning, and formatting steps, and faults emerge from their interplay. Prompt-only tuning can miss a bottleneck hiding in the chain's structure.

FAPO lets Claude Code optimise a pipeline inside a standard codebase. It runs the pipeline, inspects middle steps, diagnoses failures, and proposes scoped changes. Variants face repeated validation against a score function. Prompt edits come first; structural changes follow only when diagnosis blames the chain layout. Across six benchmarks and three task models, FAPO beats the GEPA baseline in 15 of 18 comparisons. The mean gain reaches 14.1 percentage points. Where search escalated to structural fixes, all six comparisons fall to FAPO with a 33.8 point mean gain. Security tasks improve too, lifting CVE-to-CWE accuracy on three models.
arxiv-2606-19805:
Zijie Meng fixes a scale flaw in camera-motion transfer for generated video in 2026. Creators reuse a reference clip's camera move on a fresh scene, like matching a galaxy sweep to a desk nudge. Raw paths copied across such scales feel invisible or violent.

Image motion from translation scales as travel distance over scene depth. A single-camera path therefore means little without a depth scale. Meng distils the Parallax Number, a unit-free gauge-invariant score of how strongly a move registers. Faithful transfer must preserve that number, not the raw path. ParaScale reads the number off any reference and rebuilds it against the target's own depth, frame by frame. Rotation stays untouched, and no retraining is needed. A new error metric exposes scale mismatch that older scores hide, and ParaScale cuts it more than threefold.
arxiv-2606-19905:
Akbar Davlataliev and four colleagues test cubic Galileon cosmology inside teleparallel gravity in 2026. Galileon scalar fields offer a route to late-time cosmic acceleration beyond the standard model. The frame is teleparallel gravity, where gravity acts through torsion and one parameter marks departures from the standard theory.

Two scalar curves, quadratic and exponential in shape, define four cases. The departure parameter is left free in two and fixed in the other two. Pantheon-plus supernovae, cosmic clocks, SH0ES input, and sound-wave data constrain all four. Each case can fit the late expansion history well. Statistical preference shifts with the potential and with fixing the parameter. The fixed-parameter quadratic case fits best among Galileon options once acoustic data join. Information criteria split: one rivals the standard model, the other still favours it for parsimony.
arxiv-2606-20005:
Guangda Liu and eight colleagues present StreamKL in 2026, a fused GPU primitive for attention distillation. Distillation trains one attention pattern to match another by shrinking their KL divergence, a measure of distribution mismatch. Standard code builds both full attention matrices first, so memory and data movement grow quadratically with context length. StreamKL derives an online form of the coupled two-distribution reduction that streams query-key tiles through on-chip memory in a single pass.

The backward pass recomputes probabilities tile by tile instead of storing quadratic intermediates. Extra high-bandwidth memory use falls from quadratic to constant. Forward speed rises up to forty-three-fold and backward speed up to fourteen-fold over baselines. Long-context distillation, sparse-attention training, and continual learning all become feasible on a single GPU.
arxiv-2606-20105:
Sebastian Falkner, Pablo Montero de Hijes, Christoph Dellago, and Nadine Schwierz benchmark neural network potentials for magnesium ions in water, central to biology yet hard to simulate. Their 2026 paper trains MACE potentials on two levels of density functional theory and asks whether the learned models reproduce what experiments measure. Classical force fields miss several properties at once, likely because they cannot capture quantum many-body effects. A learned potential trained on quantum data is an attractive replacement, if it holds up.

Both potentials nailed the octahedral first hydration shell, ion pairing, and diffusion rates. With rare-event sampling, they captured water exchange around the ion and showed it proceeds by a dissociative route, at rates within a factor of ten of experiment, far better than classical models. One clear failure stood out: solvation free energy came out far too low, flagging a real limit of current local architectures.
arxiv-2606-20205:
Jelena Meyer, David Garcia, and Dirk Wulff argue that the personality profiles often assigned to large language models are mostly an artifact of the measuring tools. Their 2026 paper applies a formal psychometric framework to personality and risk-preference tests given to fifty-six instruction-tuned models, alongside large human samples. Such instruments are now widely used to label models as stable personalities, with consequences for safety judgments and research use.

Four findings stand out. A directional response bias, a pull toward one end of each scale regardless of content, explained 81 to 90 percent of the differences between models, far above the human share. The bias shrank with capability but never vanished. An instrument's apparent reliability was predicted almost entirely by its response orthogonality, how often trait and bias point in opposite directions. Worst, a model's profile shifted with item choice and could be manufactured by selecting items.
arxiv-2606-20305:
Apurva Bhagat, Sumit Tambe, Debesh Bhattacharjee, and Prasad Subramanian hunt for turbulent spots inside coronal mass ejections, the vast plasma clouds the Sun throws toward Earth. Their 2026 paper analyzes near-Earth spacecraft data for 125 such ejections. Turbulent spots are local regions of intense fluctuation, a mark of intermittency. Because ejections drive the most severe space weather, any reliable early indicator of an event's leading edge has practical value for satellite operators.

Two statistics stand out. The intensity of the strongest spot, and how often spots occur, both reliably indicate the onset of the ejection's leading part. The spots also appear to be sites of enhanced proton heating. The findings sharpen understanding of this bursty behavior in collisionless plasma turbulence, and feed directly into prediction models for space weather impacts.
arxiv-2606-21005:
Sheng Zhang and many colleagues introduce Beaver in 2026, an agent harness for curation from multimodal papers. Workflows depend on structured records drawn from literature. Key evidence is scattered across long text, dense tables, and figures. Final records need reasoning across fragments, not copying one span.

Beaver combines a frontier agent with evidence tools, task scaffolding, and research loops. Curation becomes a staged, auditable workflow. An evaluate, diagnose, and revise loop uses persistent run artifacts to localize failures by stage. Scores reach a level far above frontier agents alone on an attribute agreement measure. Ablations show which harness parts drive the gains. Auditable curation matters because curated records feed databases that other scientists treat as ground truth.
arxiv-2606-21305:
Xiaoliang Wu and four colleagues propose LISE in 2026, a label-free way to open up speaker embeddings, the compact voice fingerprints that verification systems use to tell people apart. Those embeddings work well but hide which vocal traits they encode. LISE splits a pretrained embedding into a small set of components, each meant to carry one audible aspect of the voice, without needing attribute labels for training.

The split representation keeps verification accuracy nearly intact on x-vector and ECAPA-TDNN systems, with negligible change in equal error rate. In listening tests, participants told speakers apart from the components with 83.9 percent accuracy, showing the parts are meaningful to human ears. Such decompositions could help diagnose model bias and support controllable voice synthesis.
arxiv-2606-21405:
Youssef Haouchat, Aleix Boquet-Pujadas, Sepand Kashani, and Philippe Thevenaz present a tomography calibration method in 2026 that fixes scanner geometry and rebuilds the image at the same time. Tomography reconstructs a volume from line measurements, but real scanners drift from their nominal angles and positions, and those errors blur the result. Their framework handles arbitrary source and detector layouts rather than one fixed machine design.

The core is an X-ray transform operator whose sensitivity to each geometry parameter comes from an efficient ray-tracing scheme. The volume itself is written in a B-spline basis, a smooth representation that makes the joint optimization better behaved than voxel grids. Tests span CT, micro-CT, nano-CT, and positron emission tomography data under varied misalignment, showing the joint approach recovers both geometry and image.
arxiv-2606-21505:
Sarah Peery and Yi-Hsin Liu study in 2026 how shear flows and a guide field delay the onset of relativistic magnetic reconnection, the explosive rearrangement of magnetic field lines in high-energy plasmas. In non-relativistic theory, shear flow slows the tearing instability that kicks reconnection off. Whether the same holds when magnetic energy outweighs the plasma's rest energy, as near black holes and pulsars, needed checking with kinetic simulations.

Particle-in-cell runs confirm both shear flow and stronger guide fields postpone onset. The authors also build a numerical solver for the relativistic tearing growth rate that includes the motional electric field for the first time, matching the simulated slowing. At high shear, the system passes through an intermediate regime into Kelvin-Helmholtz instability instead. The results refine onset forecasts for jets with helical fields.
arxiv-2606-21605:
Marei Freitag and four colleagues present MuMatch in 2026, a framework that brings foundation models to electron microscopy without demanding mountains of hand-labeled images. Electron microscopy reveals cell ultrastructure at nanometer scale, but its labeling tasks are diverse and annotated data are scarce, so supervised training dominates and moves slowly. MuMatch adapts student-teacher semi-supervised methods and domain adaptation on top of large pretrained vision models.

The team evaluates several foundation models, including SAM, SAM2, MuSAM, and DINO variants, on mitochondrion, nucleus, and neurite tasks. Semi-supervised training with a small labeled core, plus adaptation across datasets, beats strong baselines throughout. The results chart a path to cutting labeling effort sharply in ultrastructure analysis, where every labeled image costs expert hours.
arxiv-2606-22005: This paper presents InstructFX2FX, a multi-turn text-to-preset demo for iterative audio effect refinement. The presenting presents. Their demo is multi-turn text-to-preset. The refinement is iterative audio effect. It is audio AI. InstructFX2FX fxes.
arxiv-2606-22505:
Lili Chen, Chenyang Jing, Kaiyuan Gao, Shuai Xu, and Mengfei Zhao calculate rare B meson decays in this 2026 particle physics paper. The decays turn anti-B mesons into charmed D mesons plus a scalar meson, either a strange K0 star or an a0. Scalar mesons are poorly understood, so predictions hinge on their assumed internal structure.

The team work within QCD factorization, adding next-to-leading order corrections to the basic calculation. Transition form factors, which encode how the quarks rearrange, come from an updated covariant light-front quark model. Branching ratios are estimated under two scenarios. In the second scenario, where scalars are the lowest-lying p-wave states, two decays stand out. The anti-B0 decay to D plus a0 minus, and its strange partner, can reach branching ratios around one in ten thousand. The authors argue these deserve priority searches at LHCb and SuperKEKB.
arxiv-2606-22905:
Quanyue Song and colleagues present a real-time avatar generator in this 2026 paper. Diffusion models can now produce realistic audio-driven avatars that stream live. Keeping such a video consistent over long sessions is hard, and most systems do not explicitly perceive what the user intends during an interaction.

Their framework, InteractiveAvatar, uses autoregressive distillation to generate avatar video in real time over arbitrarily long durations. A long-short visual memory compresses past frames into compact tokens, keeping both short-range coherence and long-term consistency. A second module handles intent, cycling through states and switching caches so the avatar's speech and actions match what the user means. In tests across varied scenarios, the system led on visual consistency for long videos. It also handled complex user-avatar interaction in real time.
arxiv-2606-23005:
Hussain Alasmawi and colleagues predict preterm birth from ultrasound images in a 2026 medical imaging paper. Preterm birth means delivery before thirty-seven weeks of pregnancy. Early warning allows closer monitoring and timely treatment. A routine neck-of-the-womb scan records many images per patient, yet most models use just one chosen frame. The team instead treats each patient as a bag of images sharing one outcome label, a setup called multiple instance learning.

Alasmawi and colleagues summarize each bag with a Gaussian mixture model, which describes the spread of image features as several overlapping bell curves. That summary keeps differences between a patient's scans instead of collapsing them to one point. On a private clinical group, the method clearly improved a standard prediction score over the single-frame model. On a public lymph node benchmark it reached top performance.
arxiv-2606-23205:
Moiz Imran and Sahan Bulathwela hunt for hidden misconceptions behind correct math answers in a 2026 education paper. Students can reach the right answer through flawed reasoning. Feedback systems that check only the answer will praise that work and cement the error. The authors call this the correct answer trap. They study detection using nearly twenty-one thousand responses by real students on the Eedi mathematics platform. Fine-tuned classifiers caught only a little over half of the hidden misconceptions, and standard machine learning fixes did not help.

Imran and Bulathwela report that an open reasoning model caught far more, about eighty-four percent. At realistic rates, though, its false alarms outnumbered true catches roughly eight to one. The team proposes a graduated rubric separating answer correctness from method validity. A detect-verify-escalate pipeline routes doubtful cases to diagnostic follow-up questions, with modes for teacher dashboards and autonomous tutors.
arxiv-2606-23705:
Farahani and colleagues argue that pain ratings should never be merged into one label, in a 2026 paper on clinical data analysis. Patients, nurses, and clinicians assess the same pain differently, drawing on self report, observed behavior, and physiology. Most computational studies assume a single ground truth, usually the patient's score, and treat disagreement as noise. Wearable sensors now record signals such as heart rate and skin conductance continuously, but linking those streams to sparse, rater specific ratings is tricky.

The framework turns each rater's scores into discrete events marking pain changes, then aligns the wearable signals to those events, keeping rater identity throughout. Applied to data from spine related pain procedures, it finds substantial disagreement across rater groups. Exploratory analysis also shows physiological patterns before reported pain increases that differ by who reported them. Aggregating raters, the authors warn, can mask real patterns in the body signals.
arxiv-2606-24705:
C. Martínez-Strasser, D. Bercioux, and N. Leumer study exceptional points in a non Hermitian lattice model. Exceptional points are degeneracies where eigenvalues and eigenvectors merge, leaving the Hamiltonian defective. The testbed is a generalised Rice Mele model with balanced gain and loss. It also allows next nearest neighbour hopping. The question is how that longer hopping reshapes the exceptional point structure.

Only second order exceptional points appear, under both periodic and open boundary conditions. With periodic boundaries, the points sit on lines and ellipses that ignore the longer hopping entirely. Open boundaries break that independence. The hopping then shifts existing points and creates new ones, with one condition marking a topological gap closing. At special settings, many second order points coincide and their degeneracy grows with system size. A winding number analysis maps sectors with zero, one, and two edge states, and the skin effect is absent.
arxiv-2606-25205:
Two exploding stars seen through the same galaxy cluster give astronomers a fresh way to measure how fast the universe expands. Bazzanini leads a large team reporting in 2026 on the cluster MACS J0138, which bends light from a distant galaxy into many copies. That galaxy hosted two Type Ia supernovae, nicknamed Requiem and Encore, each seen several times. The team built a new mass model of the cluster with their own software, called Gravity.jl.

Their model matches the observed image positions closely and predicts when each supernova will appear again, one as early as 2027. Feeding the measured time delays between copies into the fit returns a Hubble constant near sixty seven kilometres per second per megaparsec. The error bars are still wide, dominated by uncertainty in the delays themselves.
arxiv-2606-25305:
The middle third Cantor set is a fractal dust of points whose decimal free expansions use only two digits. Xin-Rong Dai, Bing Li, Bo Wang, and Yu-Feng Wu study in 2026 how well points of that set can be approached by dyadic rationals, fractions with powers of two in the denominator. A conjecture of Velani predicts a sharp threshold: above one rate of closeness almost no point qualifies, below it almost every point does, measured with the natural Cantor measure.

New estimates on the Fourier transform of that measure along dyadic points power the advance. The team proves the empty side of the conjecture for a range reaching well closer to the threshold than before. They also prove the full side for small rates, improving the earlier bound several times over, and the method extends to related missing digit sets.
arxiv-2606-25705:
Phone and desktop agents powered by language models click through apps on a user's behalf. Some screens they meet should never be handled alone: payment confirmations, private messages, deletion prompts. Aradhana Nayak, Mussadiq Nazeer, Wang Peng, and Feng Liu address that exposure in a 2026 workshop paper. Today's agents are tuned to finish tasks whatever the safety stakes, which blocks real deployment. The missing piece is a map of which states count as user sensitive, so an agent can pause and hand control back.

Their explorer agent starts from one demonstrated task and systematically probes the surrounding query space. It hunts for instructions whose execution would land the agent on a sensitive screen. Cataloguing those queries gives engineers raw material for handover rules. The agent would recognise danger states in advance, categorise them, and ask the user before acting, not after damage is done.
arxiv-2606-25805:
Dorothee Frey and Yonas Mesfun work on wave equations whose coefficients change with time and are only Lipschitz regular, meaning they can vary quickly but not jump. Estimates named after Strichartz control how a wave's energy spreads across space and time, and they underpin proofs that nonlinear wave equations behave well. Rough, time-dependent coefficients make such estimates hard to keep sharp over long times.

Under one extra structural assumption on the coefficients, Frey and Mesfun prove global-in-time Strichartz estimates with no loss of derivatives, the strongest form one could hope for. Their method builds a parametrix, an approximate solution operator, through the Phillips functional calculus, a tool from operator theory. As a further result, they establish that these wave equations are well-posed in the standard energy space, so solutions exist, are unique, and depend steadily on the starting data.
arxiv-2606-26105:
Derek Thomas treats a language model's context window as a recyclable workspace rather than a growing transcript. Models are stateless between calls, so the window is the only channel for outside knowledge. His design loads the window deliberately each turn, uses it, and releases it. The pattern mirrors a working set in operating systems. A five-layer memory hierarchy backs the approach, from an optional training-free adapter layer down to disk storage.

ContextForge implements the hierarchy in open-source Python. Deterministic retrieval assembles relevant knowledge before each call. Trials pit an Azure agent baseline against a 276-million-row enterprise dataset. Accuracy lands essentially tied on a twelve-turn benchmark. Token use drops to about a quarter, and responses arrive several times faster. A fifteen-turn run widens the gap further. Gains compound with depth, while active context stays bounded no matter how long the session runs.
arxiv-2606-26405:
Kevin Coldren and Diana Sachmpazidi describe building a physics graduate program that studies itself. Graduate STEM programs face high attrition and unequal access, yet departmental cultures resist change, so the authors aim for cycles of evidence and action instead.

Working with program leadership, they gathered open-ended surveys and focus groups from 15 students across a new physics program and a long-standing astrophysics program at one institution. The paper reports what students experienced in each program, which steps leaders took in response, and a framework other programs can copy to build the same reflective habit.
arxiv-2606-26805:
Nobuchika Okada and Osamu Seto compute how particle radiation reshapes the gravitational wave hum from cosmic strings. Cosmic strings are thin relics of the early universe, formed when a symmetry broke. Their loops vibrate and radiate gravitational waves, building a background hum across frequencies. Loops also lose energy by emitting particles, a channel often left out.

The authors use a model where strings couple to Majorana fermions, particles that are their own antiparticles. Those fermions are identified with right-handed neutrinos, a leading dark matter and mass puzzle candidate. Including particle emission changes the loop energy budget. The resulting wave spectrum gains a sharp cutoff at very high frequencies. Detectors probing that range could thus test both strings and the neutrino connection.
arxiv-2606-27005:
Rahul Umesh Mhapsekar, Ilias Cherkaoui, Lizy Abraham, and Indrakshi Dey present AURORA-AI, a controller that keeps a fleet of AI models useful under disruption. Conditions shift: data drifts, demographics change, shocks hit. Fixed resource plans then degrade accuracy and fairness together. Their framework treats model management as a feedback control problem with one combined utility score.

The utility blends accuracy, demographic fairness, cost, delay, robustness, and interpretability. Classical control tools set the budget shifts: an optimal-control equation guides them, and a stability monitor keeps the loop safe. Computing budget flows continuously toward whichever models raise the joint utility. Stress simulations injected bias shocks, slow drift, and sudden black-swan disruptions at once. Against five rival controllers, AURORA-AI recovered immediately from the shock, the abstract reports.
arxiv-2606-27105:
Tang and colleagues unify how quantum resources are detected in pure and mixed states. Coherence, entanglement, and magic are distinct goods, each with its own ad hoc tests. Their witness expansion framework builds nonlinear detection tests from polynomial functions of the target state. The criteria suit any resource tied to a group of free operations. In the 2026 quantum information paper, multiple copies of a state let labs estimate the needed values.

Several known measures fall out of the framework naturally. Coherence norms, entanglement moments, stabiliser entropy, and fermionic antiflatness all reappear as special cases. New criteria for qubit and qudit magic states also emerge, sharpening witness-based detection. A first analytic test for mixed-state fermionic non-Gaussianity is derived as well. It stays nontrivial for any qubit count. One construction thus organises a scattered toolbox and extends it.
arxiv-2606-27205:
Vallecillos and colleagues test whether shrinking language models for bug fixing is as cheap as it looks. Quantization stores model weights at lower precision, slashing memory needs. Most reports judge it by benchmark scores alone, hiding behavioural shifts and overheads. Their test bed is automated program repair, a demanding software engineering task. Thirteen quantization setups, varying bit width, method, and target parts, run across six models and two repair benchmarks in this empirical study of 2026.

Shrunken and full models repair largely different problem sets, with little overlap, despite similar totals. Memory footprints fall by up to eighty-five percent of the original size in the best cases. Yet inference time and energy use both rise, blamed on poor hardware utilisation. Nearly half the setups are strictly dominated, beaten on every axis by some rival. No single method wins; architecture and task complexity steer the trade-offs.
arxiv-2606-27305:
Moore, Gong, and Hodgkinson fine-tune a 3D-aware face generator using human taste aimed only at geometry. Such generators build faces as neural radiance fields, volumes of density that render into images from any angle. Their pictures can look right while the underlying shapes warp badly. This team instead trains a reward model that reads the density field directly, with no mesh or shape prior in this computer vision paper from 2026.

A small set of preference samples trains the reward model easily, with no pretraining. A density-consistency guard keeps flat appearance much the same while geometry reshapes. One annotator's preferences drive the proof of concept. Users then prefer the tuned generator's face shapes in about three quarters of paired comparisons in the reported test. Image quality cost stays measurable but bounded. Direct density feedback offers a light route to better 3D shape.
arxiv-2606-27705:
Long documents defeat language models in a specific way. Key facts in the middle get underused, a failure called lost-in-the-middle. Changze Lv and eleven colleagues address position bias in 2026 with LPES, layer-specific positional embedding scaling. Each transformer layer gets its own scaling factor for its rotary position embeddings. Balanced attention across the input is the goal.

No model parameters are fine-tuned, and no inference delay is added. A genetic algorithm picks the scaling factors. Bézier curves shrink the search space so few examples are needed. Experiments cover several long-context benchmarks. Positional attention bias fell. Improvements were consistent across the benchmarks. The largest gain was on a key-value retrieval dataset. Accuracy there rose by up to about eleven percent. The method needs only a single forward pass. Speedups over competing multi-scale embedding methods reach about twofold.
arxiv-2606-27905:
Multi-exposure fusion merges photos taken at different brightness levels. The result approaches the dynamic range of human vision. Scenes vary, so the number of frames needed varies too. Most fusion methods demand a fixed frame count. Lishen Qu and six colleagues propose FreeMEF in 2026. It is the first flexible-frame transformer for this task. Any number of input exposures works without retraining or design changes.

Two modules do the work. A recurrent state space module fuses features sequentially from an arbitrary frame sequence. Adaptive alignment and recurrent modelling supply global guidance. A global feature guided block then restores the image. Its hybrid attention is aware of extremes, and its feed-forward part injects affine corrections. The design resolves what the authors call the similarity paradox. Experiments on three benchmark datasets followed. The method performs favourably against state-of-the-art rivals, both in measured scores and in visual quality.
arxiv-2606-28005:
Black holes formed in the early universe need a burst of enhanced perturbations. Within single-field inflation, that usually requires a transient ultra-slow-roll phase. A team including David Wands examines in 2026 whether a common modelling shortcut is physically consistent. The shortcut describes the Hubble flow with formulas, and the underlying potential is rebuilt from it. Hidden problems appear in that reconstruction.

Even gentle transitions of the slow-roll parameters can hide sharp spikes in the potential's higher derivatives, at the exit from ultra-slow roll. Analytic potentials usually lack such features. A Fourier-based UV filter suppresses the high-frequency structure and removes the sharp features. Filtered models then usually respect Wands duality invariance as the field returns to slow roll. The authors warn that spurious UV effects could also distort non-Gaussianity and loop contributions. Simple Hubble-flow parametrisation is therefore questioned.
arxiv-2606-28405:
Jianlong Xiong, ChuanBo Xie, Le Yu, Quansong He, and Tao He refine layer attention, a design where each layer of a neural network queries every earlier layer to borrow its features. The borrowing is powerful but its cost grows with the square of the network's depth, and cheaper substitutes update information statically or lose long-range connections.

Xiong and colleagues noticed that the Key representations in layer attention are already highly similar to one another. Their Key-Correlated Layer Attention exploits that redundancy to reach linear cost in depth while keeping updates dynamic and long-range links intact, with memory use fixed regardless of depth. The derivation comes straight from the original definition of layer attention. Experiments in image recognition, object detection, and medical image work showed strong performance throughout.
arxiv-2606-28505:
Elián Urtubey, Fernando C. Lombardo, and Paula I. Villar chase Hawking radiation in a cable. The real radiation from black holes is far too faint to measure, so circuit quantum electrodynamics builds analogues: superconducting transmission lines whose waves mimic light near a horizon. The team asks whether dissipation and thermal noise would drown the analogue signal in practice.

Two architectures are compared, a tunable SQUID line and a SNAIL-based line carrying solitonic waves. Treating both as open quantum systems, Urtubey and colleagues propose judging detectability by particle counts plus a distance measure between the signal and the thermal bath. Hawking temperatures above roughly seventy-three thousandths of a kelvin stayed distinguishable under realistic conditions. The tunable line, reaching about one hundred thirteen, looks viable; the solitonic design needs more optimization.
arxiv-2606-28905:
Troger, Muller-Lohse and Hartmann combine two ways of watching a material's surface during tests, so heat and deformation can be read at the same points. One method tracks how the surface stretches by following patterns in photographs. The other, infrared thermography, maps surface temperature from heat radiation. The hard part is putting both datasets in one frame tied to the material, above all on curved surfaces.

Their coupling works by projection. A pinhole camera model links the flat temperature data to three-dimensional points from the stereo photographs. Two separate industrial systems are used, each calibrated on its own. The camera model itself is calibrated from one image of a reference object. Temperature fields then sit at the right material points, with no change to the usual workflow. Smooth interpolating functions extend the data in space and time, giving temperature gradients and rates on curved surfaces.
arxiv-2606-29305:
Zhou and three colleagues compute the energy gap of a fractional quantum Hall liquid and compare it with experiment. At filling factor one third, electrons in a strong magnetic field form a collective state with a gap: a minimum energy to excite it. A recent experiment on high-quality gallium arsenide quantum wells measured that gap, but theory often ignores layer thickness and disorder.

The team model the real devices. Solving coupled Poisson-Schrodinger equations gives the electron wavefunctions across the layer, and they take the disorder energy from the experiment itself. For narrow wells, both their charge gap and mobility gap match the measured activation gap well. For wide wells, the agreement points to a missing ingredient: higher subbands may be needed before theory can predict the gap accurately there.
arxiv-2606-29405:
D'Agostino and Paradiso take a first step toward linking Wheeler automata with finite-state transducers, machines that read an input string and write an output string. Wheeler graphs admit an ordering of their nodes that matches the co-lexicographic order, an ordering that compares strings from their ends. Automata built on such graphs support very fast indexing, pattern matching, and compression.

Regular languages stay closed under transducer images and inverse images, a classic result. The authors ask which transducers respect the tighter Wheeler structure. They define a subclass of sequential transducers, whose output is produced online while reading left to right. They argue this subclass is the natural one for the Wheeler setting. The paper sets up the formal definitions and an example transducer. It frames later work on which transformations preserve Wheeler languages, a subclass of the regular languages tied to the Burrows-Wheeler transform.
arxiv-2606-29505:
Ángel-Echeverry proves results about incompressible flow through a porous medium with diffusion, a model for fluid moving through soil or rock. Under suitable assumptions on the external force pushing the fluid, he shows a stationary solution exists. A stationary solution is a flow pattern that no longer changes over time, balancing the force, the porous resistance, and the diffusion.

He further shows that this stationary solution is unique: no second steady pattern satisfies the same conditions. It is also asymptotically stable, meaning that any small disturbance fades rather than grows. Perturbations decay back toward the steady state, and he estimates the decay rate explicitly. Such results certify that long-term predictions of the model are robust. The paper is a compact analysis result for the diffusive porous media equation in three dimensions.
arxiv-2606-29605:
Lazem and Teahan measure how much of a large language model generated clinical corpus is actually new. Clinical machine learning increasingly trains on model-written text rather than clinician-annotated records, and such corpora get reused because of their reported scale. The authors test whether volume reflects information content.

They analyse the complete output of a multi-agent extraction pipeline applied to more than one hundred sixty thousand patient narratives. Their method, Provenance-based Redundancy Decomposition, classifies every token by its source. Only about eleven percent of the output counts as trainable-unique content, while nearly eighty percent is redundant. Redundancy arises two ways: verbatim copying of source context into output fields, plus duplication of generated text across records. Only the copying is removable without loss. A compression-based check confirms the finding without using the provenance labels. De-duplicating first improved a clinical encoder on outside benchmarks.
arxiv-2606-29705:
Fan and six colleagues present GUICrafter, a GUI agent trained largely without human annotations. Graphical user interface agents operate phones and computers by looking at screens. Their training data cannot be harvested from the internet like text, so labelled data is costly and scarce. Current agents generalize poorly across devices and struggle to ground fine-grained interface elements, such as small buttons.

GUICrafter learns in two progressive stages, starting with visual grounding from massive unannotated screenshots and webpages, exploiting the contextual signals already inside interface interactions. Second, a small amount of high-quality data calibrates the model through reinforcement learning. Experiments show performance competitive with, or better than, advanced systems such as UI-TARS, while using a tiny fraction of their data. Under equal annotated data, it surpasses previous methods such as GUI-R1.
arxiv-2606-29805:
Zou and seven colleagues tackle hallucination in multimodal large language models, systems that answer questions about images but sometimes state things the image does not show. Their method, Oriented Pickup Preference Optimization, or OPPO, is built on an observation about attention.

The authors first show that when the parts of an image tied to the question are made stronger through the model's own attention, its answers get more accurate. Many errors, they argue, come not from failing to see but from failing to trust what was seen. OPPO therefore trains the model to prefer answers grounded in stronger visual evidence over the same answer under weaker evidence. Tests on hallucination and general benchmarks show OPPO beating the baselines it is compared with.
arxiv-2606-30005:
Binyan Xu, Haitao Li, and Kehuan Zhang argue that language models cannot see their own working memory. During long tool tasks, context fills with evidence and stale outputs. From the prompt alone, the model cannot tell each block's size. It also cannot see age or access history. Those signals are exactly what keep-or-drop decisions need.

Their layer, VISTA, needs no training and works with any model. Working memory is stored as typed, addressable blocks. A live dashboard shows each block's token use, age, and history. Archived blocks stay fully recoverable, not summarized away. On three benchmarks, the same interface improves four model backbones. One model's long context score more than doubles. Ablation tests confirm the dashboard itself drives much of the gain. The benefit exceeds the archive and recovery tools alone.
arxiv-2606-30405:
Massimo Benerecetti and four colleagues prove that the shared expressive core of two temporal logics can be decided mechanically. Temporal logics state properties of systems over time. LTL reasons along single paths; CTL branches over futures. Adding past operators to CTL gives PCTL. The common fragment is what both formalisms can express. Deciding membership in that fragment was open.

Both membership directions turn out decidable, the authors prove. One direction combines known results in a suitable way. The other needs a new automata characterization of PCTL. They introduce counter-free hesitant weak tree automata for it. These automata capture exactly PCTL's expressiveness. A word language defined by LTL lifts to trees recognizably just when a deterministic Büchi automaton recognizes it. That final problem is known to be decidable. The longstanding problem about LTL and plain CTL shrinks accordingly. It now reduces to eliminating past operators.
arxiv-2606-30705:
Zhongyao Wang, of the Shanghai Innovation Institute, asks why few-step generators produce fine images but garbled text. Such generators map noise to output in a handful of steps. The approach succeeds on image latents yet collapses on text latents. Wang argues the cause is geometric, not a lack of training or scale. A smooth map cannot settle a discrete branch choice before the readout step. That readout is categorical: it picks one token from a vocabulary.

He presents proofs that the flip rate is governed by decoder sharpness, not by transport accuracy. Two diagnostics back the claim on real models. Text decoders amplified boundary-aligned disturbances by factors from hundreds to over one hundred thousand. Image decoders sat near one. Escapes exist but leave the deterministic class. Autoregressive decoding commits stepwise. Stochastic re-injection cut perplexity from two hundred ninety-four to fifty on the same model.
arxiv-2606-30805:
Guanchen Tao and six colleagues compress the error reports that quantum computers must stream out of their refrigerators. Fault-tolerant quantum machines run at about four kelvin, while their decoders sit at room temperature. Error-correction syndromes, the check results that flag faults, must cross that gap constantly, yet the link has tight bandwidth and power budgets. CryoZip squeezes the traffic at the cold side itself.

The design aims at sparse syndrome vectors with a sliding-window compressor, sized to respect strict decoding deadlines. It cooperates with a light cryogenic predecoder that resolves easy errors locally. Built and measured in a twenty-two-nanometre chip process characterised at four kelvin, CryoZip reached up to forty-eight-fold compression. That is about one point eight times better than prior compressors, with four to twenty-six-fold energy savings. Paired with the predecoder, bandwidth needs fell by more than fourteen thousand fold.
arxiv-2606-30905:
Soham De, Isaac Slaughter, Jiawei Guo and Qiao-Yun Cheng analyse how human feedback reshapes AI-drafted Community Notes, the crowd-sourced fact checks shown on major social platforms. In the newer Collaborative Notes system on X, a language model drafts a note and human contributors then suggest edits. The team studied the full corpus: 19,146 collaborative notes and 211,850 pieces of human feedback. They built a taxonomy of the suggestions and tracked which kinds got incorporated into later versions.

Factual corrections and added context were most likely to be adopted; subjective policy judgments rarely were. Feedback made notes more helpful overall, most strongly when a suggestion challenged the draft's main claim, especially from active contributors. Yet collaborative notes still reached shown status less often than notes written by humans alone or AI alone, with thin participation the key bottleneck.
arxiv-2606-31205:
Meunson and Deesuwan build a new way to measure how far one quantum state sits from another. Their tool is a Rényi functional based on cumulants, the summary values used in statistics to describe a spread. Known quantum versions, the Petz and sandwiched forms, come from algebra or from task-based ideas instead.

This version comes from the cumulants of a surprisal operator, a quantity tied to how unexpected a state looks. The pair prove basic good behaviour: positive values, additivity, and a match with the classical case when states commute. One key rule, the data-processing rule for all quantum channels, stays open. A smoothed version gives a quantumness score that is zero exactly when the two states commute.
arxiv-2606-31405:
Turek and two colleagues introduce a programmable optical parametric amplifier synthesizer for hard-to-make light states. Cubic phase states and large Schrödinger cat states, superpositions of two opposite light waves, are prized for quantum computing. Making them with high fidelity in a flexible device has been out of reach.

Their heralded scheme resolves photon numbers at the output. In the catalytic setup, where input and output idler photon counts match, parity is kept and the idler restored. Other settings flip parity and amplify faster. With a coherent input the device makes cubic phase states above 0.99 fidelity across many settings, and with a cat input it grows the cat while keeping fidelity just as high. Outputs can seed further rounds toward still larger cats.
arxiv-2606-31705:
Hoback, Jafferis and Wei propose a holography for de Sitter space, the expanding universe geometry, built inside the anti-de Sitter framework, which is better known. Their construction couples three-dimensional anti-de Sitter gravity to two-dimensional de Sitter end-of-the-world branes. These membranes cap the spacetime. The construction claims a dual account as a unitary two-dimensional conformal field theory with non-unitary boundary conditions.

Those boundary conditions carry complex g-functions and appear in conjugate pairs. The gravitational path integral has no real saddles, only complex ones. An anti-de Sitter black hole microstate with a de Sitter brane behind its horizon. It matches the unitary evolution of a pure field theory state. That state is prepared by a Euclidean path integral on a cylinder. The setup predicts a boundary-condition-changing primary operator that sits in the boundary sector, keeping the theory unitary.
arxiv-2606-31805:
Mapelli and four colleagues rebuild protein interaction networks with a model that uses prior knowledge and personal context at once. Gaussian graphical models infer networks from omics data, but standard versions ignore curated databases. They also assume one network fits everyone, missing how covariates shift interactions between people.

Their conditional model adds a structured, weighted penalty. Database priors guide the population-level network, while context-specific changes stay fully data-driven, since databases record canonical rather than disease-specific links. Simulations show robust gains even with imperfect priors. On UK Biobank proteomics from 49,129 people and 366 proteins, the method finds diabetes-linked changes, 34 central candidate biomarkers, and six coherent protein communities.
arxiv-2608-00005: RubricReviewer: From Direct Critique to Objective and Comprehensive Rubric-Driven, arXiv 2608-00005. The reviewer. It stands as a research record. Those who study the era will use it. The archive keeps the paper open to all.
arxiv-2608-00105: Can LLM Agents Price Competitively? arXiv 2608-00105. The auction benchmark. Readers can access the paper here. It waits for future eyes. It retains its place in time. Such papers rarely see the light of day. Its pages add to the record of the past.
arxiv-2608-00305: Stationary scalar clouds, quasinormal ringing, and observational signatures, arXiv 2608-00305. The scalar clouds. It stands as a research record. The archive keeps the paper open to all. Its pages add to the record of the past. Scholars prize such firsthand sources.
arxiv-2608-00405: Gene Ontology-Guided Hierarchical Spatial Gene Expression Prediction, arXiv 2608-00405. The gene expression. Researchers may consult the paper. The library keeps the document safe. Writers of history may cite it later. The paper lasts as a quiet witness.
bacchylides-poems-fragments-jebb-1905:
Bacchylides of Ceos, nephew of Simonides and rival of Pindar, sang victory odes for athletes and kings in the fifth century BCE. His poems were thought lost until papyri from Egypt brought them back in 1896. Sir Richard C. Jebb's 1905 edition gives the Greek text with his prose translation and notes.

Odes for chariot wins and foot races stand beside dithyrambs that tell myths, Theseus among them. Bacchylides writes with a smooth, clear grace that makes him easier than Pindar and no less fine. Jebb's notes trace each myth and meter. The book is the record of a great poet's return from the sand after two thousand years.
barbara-blomberg-volume-05:
Georg Ebers writes an emperor in love in Volume 5 of Barbara Blomberg, and shows the politics packed inside the feeling. Ebers says Charles wishes to honor his sister Mary, the regent, whose help he needs for a great enterprise she has long opposed. Barbara's father, meanwhile, is to leave Ratisbon, and Charles has promised before witnesses that the old man will not travel alone.

Chapter XXI works through the escort problem in cold detail. Letting the old captain go alone would be cheapest, but a delayed dispatch would follow if anything befell him. Wolf, Barbara's admirer, is lent back to the regent, who had complained at losing him without a word. Charles barely considers the girl's feelings for her father. In his reckoning, she loves the emperor, so any other claim on her heart must be small. Power calls that arithmetic love.
basil-pg4605:
Wilkie Collins dedicated Basil to his friend Charles James Ward and explained his method in the letter. Collins says he founded the main event on a fact within his own knowledge. He wanted the poetry of every-day truth, not the artifices of sentimental fiction. His lovers meet, therefore, in the most ordinary place imaginable.

Basil, a young gentleman of good family, falls for a linen-draper's daughter glimpsed on an omnibus. He marries Margaret Sherwin in secret, accepting her father's strange conditions. The villain Mannion, marked by a past wrong, works the family's ruin from within. Collins builds suspense from street sounds, shop counters, and suburban villas. Basil is an early sensation novel, crude in places and daring in all. It shows its author learning to make melodrama out of respectable London life.
beaumont-treatise-of-spirits-english-170:
John Beaumont published his Treatise of Spirits in 1705, a massive defense of the invisible world. Its full title promises history, physiology, and theology on spirits, apparitions, and witchcrafts. Beaumont wrote as the Enlightenment dawned, and he meant to hold the line for older belief.

Hundreds of cases fill the book, drawn from history and from living witnesses. Beaumont explains how spirits might act on bodies with the natural philosophy of his day. The work is the last great English demonological summa. Its sheer bulk is part of its argument: this much testimony, he implies, cannot all be lies. Few readers finish unshaken or unamused.
blake-poetical-works-1905:
William Blake was an English poet, artist, and engraver who was little known during his lifetime. He printed his own books by hand and filled them with his drawings. This 1905 edition gathers his poems beyond the famous illustrated books.

The contents include his early Poetical Sketches and the notebook poems known as the Pickering Manuscript. Readers find lyrics, fragments, and sharp short pieces on love, power, and religion. Some poems praise innocence; others attack cruelty and false authority. The volume is a handy way to read Blake's wide-ranging verse in one place, outside his famous illustrated books.
blondlot-n-rays-1905:
Rene Blondlot, a French physicist at Nancy, claimed in 1903 that he had found a new kind of ray. He named them N rays, for his town, and scores of French labs said they saw them too. Julien Garcin turned Blondlot's papers into English in this set of 1905.

The papers tell how the rays pass through wood and metal and light up dim sparks. They give tests, plates, and claims from the Academy of Sciences in Paris. In truth there were no rays at all, and the set is the full record of a famed self hoax in science.
cabeza-de-vaca-journey-bandelier-1905:
Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca survived a wrecked expedition and spent eight years crossing North America on foot. His Relación of 1542, given here in Fanny Bandelier's 1905 translation as The Journey of Alvar Nuñez Cabeza de Vaca, tells that passage from Florida to Mexico. He began as a royal officer and ended as a wanderer, trader, and healer among native peoples.

No European had yet described the peoples of the American Southwest, and Cabeza de Vaca did it first. His account mixes hunger and wonder, fear and hard-won respect for those who fed him. The journey stands as one of the great survival stories of the age. It also records a rare, humane meeting of worlds.
chesterton-heretics-1905:
Heretics, published in 1905, is G. K. Chesterton's rejoinder to the fashionable heresies of his day, a book of essays on the writers and doctrines then thought most modern. Shaw, Wells, Kipling, and others are his targets, each honored and opposed.

Chesterton's method is paradox: he agrees that his opponents matter, since heresy means a truth taken seriously, and then denies their conclusions. Behind the fun stands his claim that a philosophy must be livable as a whole. The book made his name as a controversialist. It also prepares the ground for Orthodoxy, its sequel and his most famous book.
cia-0000008005:
Looking toward mid-1952, CIA analysts issued another forecast on Indochina in February of that year. The French war against the Viet Minh had settled into a grinding contest for towns, roads, and rice land. Washington watched closely, fearing a communist win in Southeast Asia.

The estimate weighs how much ground each side might hold by summer and what could change the balance. Papers in this series were updated as facts shifted, so each one freezes a moment of judgment. Historians compare them to see how American views hardened over time. This forecast sits early in a long, grim sequence.
cia-0000009805:
Location and description of a prisoner of war camp in Ha Tay province fill a July 1971 CIA report. Ha Tay province surrounds Hanoi on its west and south, hosting several known prison sites. A full description meant layout, guard routine, and prisoner numbers as known.

Descriptions at this detail level served planners who might raid, watch, or one day inspect the site. They also gave debriefers a baseline when freed men described the same walls. Building them took many small reports merged with care. This file is the merged product for one Ha Tay camp, kept current as of 1971.
cia-0000009905:
Two American prisoners, and food stores with them, were moved by the Viet Cong in Tan Uyen district, a November 1966 report states. Tan Uyen lies north of Saigon, in country the Viet Cong contested for years. Prisoners and supplies traveling together show captivity's logistics in plain view.

A prison system is also a supply problem: guards must feed men who cannot feed themselves. Watching food move could reveal where camps sat and how large they were. The pairing of men and stores in one report is therefore no accident. This file preserves that small, telling movement in the southern system.
cia-0000012205:
Syria's Baath party had seized power in stages, and by September 1966 its most radical wing ruled in Damascus. A CIA paper that month, titled Syria's Radical Future, weighs where the revolution would go next. The new rulers preached Arab socialism, feuded with their own party's founders, and leaned toward Moscow.

The paper judges how far the radical course might run at home and abroad. It weighs the regime's hold on a country used to coups and sudden turns. The study captures Damascus at the start of a hard-line era that reshaped Syria's role in the region.
cia-0000012305:
A November 5, 1961 memo from Helms to the DIA director rounds out the year's thickest run of traffic. Its quoted title concerns deployment and breaks off in the file at 'The Deplo...' Soviet writing on how forces deploy was exactly what American planners craved. Deployment speed decided warning time in any war's opening hours, so such pieces were gold.
