With the clause gone, the 30-patient limit ends for doctors in group practices who prescribe drug addiction treatments. Those treatments are upkeep or detox care with certain narcotic drugs. A matching wording fix follows, and the change takes effect at once.
plaw-109-57-2005:
Re-export of controlled drugs is eased by Public Law 109-57, the Controlled Substances Export Reform Act of 2005. It amends the Controlled Substances Import and Export Act.

The Attorney General may let a drug in schedule I or II, or a narcotic drug in schedule III or IV, be sent abroad twice. It first goes to one country, then on to a second. Both countries must be parties to the 1961 and 1971 world drug treaties. Both must run import control systems the Attorney General finds sound. The first country must license the buyer and issue an import permit. For the second country, strong proof must be given to the Attorney General. The sample ends there.
plaw-109-58-2005:
Energy policy for the nation is set by Public Law 109-58, the Energy Policy Act of 2005. Its stated aim is jobs for the future with energy that is secure, low-cost, and steady.

The sample shows the start of the act's contents. Title I is Energy Efficiency. Its first part covers federal programs, such as saving energy and water in congressional buildings. It also covers purchase of efficient goods, savings contracts, and federal building standards. Daylight saving time is one listed topic. A second part covers aid and state programs. It lists home energy aid for the poor, weatherization help, and rebates for efficient home goods.
plaw-109-59-2005:
Roads and transit get their main funding law in Public Law 109-59 of 2005. Its title is the Safe, Accountable, Flexible, Efficient Transportation Equity Act: A Legacy for Users, or SAFETEA-LU. It approves funds for federal-aid highways, highway safety, and transit.

The sample shows the start of the contents, in Title I on federal-aid highways. Parts set the sums granted, a spending ceiling, and how funds are split among states. An equity bonus program and budget rules tied to income are listed. Other parts cover future Interstate routes and city-area planning. Funds may move between highway and transit uses. Trail, bridge, and crisis relief programs are also listed.
plaw-109-6-2005: A fuel tax rate for tank cleanup is extended by Public Law 109-6 of 2005. The whole act amends one date in section 4081(d) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986. That part sets the Leaking Underground Storage Tank Trust Fund financing rate. The end date moves from April 1, 2005, to October 1, 2005. The act was signed on March 31, 2005, and took effect that day.
plaw-109-60-2005:
Drug prescription tracking in each state is backed by Public Law 109-60 of 2005. Its title is the National All Schedules Prescription Electronic Reporting Act of 2005. It sets up a controlled substance monitoring program for the states.

The aims stated are two. First, state-run systems should give care providers fast, true prescription records for each patient. Those records help spot patients at risk for addiction early, so care can start in time. Second, the best ways from states that already track should guide new and old programs. The act amends the health act to grant funds each year to states with cleared plans, to set up and run such systems.
plaw-109-61-2005:
Crisis funds after Hurricane Katrina flow from Public Law 109-61 of 2005. Its title is the Emergency Supplemental Appropriations Act to Meet Immediate Needs Arising From the Consequences of Hurricane Katrina, 2005. It covers the fiscal year ending September 30, 2005.

For the Department of Homeland Security, the act grants ten billion dollars for Disaster Relief, open until spent. The sum is marked as an emergency need. For the Department of Defense, it grants 500 million dollars for running costs tied to the storm. Those costs include moving people out, quick repairs, and sending staff. The defense head may shift the funds among military accounts for the same ends. The sample ends inside that shift clause.
plaw-109-62-2005:
More crisis funds for Katrina follow in Public Law 109-62 of 2005. It is the Second Emergency Supplemental Appropriations Act to Meet Immediate Needs Arising From the Consequences of Hurricane Katrina, 2005.

The act grants the Department of Defense 1.4 billion dollars in added running funds for storm costs. The costs named are moving people out, quick repairs, staff deployment, and other relief work. The funds stay open until September 30, 2006. The defense head may shift them among military accounts. Up to six million dollars may go to the Armed Forces Retirement Home for storm costs. Funds found not to be needed may be shifted back.
plaw-109-63-2005:
Courts gain room to move in a crisis under Public Law 109-63, the Federal Judiciary Emergency Special Sessions Act of 2005. It lets United States courts do business during emergency conditions.

The act amends title 28 for the courts of appeals. Such a court may hold special sessions at any place in the country outside its circuit. A finding is needed first: the chief judge or the circuit council must find that no in-circuit site is open for use. The court may do any work at such a session that it could do at a normal one. Notice of the order must go to the judiciary committees of both chambers. A report on its effects is due within 180 days of the order's end.
plaw-109-64-2005: Flood aid is shielded from benefit cuts by Public Law 109-64 of 2005. It adds a new section 1324 to the National Flood Insurance Act of 1968. Aid for flood mitigation work on a property does not count as income or as a resource of the owner. That shield holds when the owner's fitness or benefit level is tested for any aid program funded by a federal agency or by federal funds.
plaw-109-65-2005: Flood insurance borrowing power jumps in Public Law 109-65, the National Flood Insurance Program Enhanced Borrowing Authority Act of 2005. The act amends section 1309 of the National Flood Insurance Act of 1968. Through September 30, 2008, one cap in that section reads as 3.5 billion dollars in place of 1.5 billion dollars. The change is a stopgap boost for the Federal Emergency Management Agency, which runs the program.
plaw-109-66-2005: Student grant debts after a disaster may be forgiven under Public Law 109-66, the Pell Grant Hurricane and Disaster Relief Act of 2005. It amends the Higher Education Act of 1965. The Secretary of Education may waive sums that students must repay for Federal Pell Grants. The waiver fits students who lived, worked, or studied in an area the President has named a major disaster area. Their study must have been broken by the disaster. The leaving of school must end in that school year or the next.
plaw-109-67-2005: Other student grants get the same disaster grace in Public Law 109-67, the Student Grant Hurricane and Disaster Relief Act of 2005. It adds a second waiver clause to the Higher Education Act, right after the Pell Grant clause. The Secretary of Education may waive repayment of any other federal grant aid under the title. The terms match the Pell terms. The student lived, worked, or studied in a declared major disaster area. Study was broken by the disaster, and leaving ended in that year or the next.
plaw-109-68-2005:
Families hit by Hurricane Katrina are aided through welfare grants in Public Law 109-68, the TANF Emergency Response and Recovery Act of 2005. TANF is the block grant program for aid to needy families.

First, the act speeds the grants due for the first quarter of fiscal year 2006, to be paid as soon as can be done. Second, it extends the TANF program through December 31, 2005, in the way set for fiscal year 2005. Grants run at the levels of the first quarter of that year. Matching fixes move a grant date from September 30 to December 31. They also move a backup fund year from 2005 to 2006.
plaw-109-69-2005:
Nevada college land is handed over in full by Public Law 109-69, the Dandini Research Park Conveyance Act of 2005. The Secretary of the Interior must give the land to the Board of Regents of the state college system at no cost.

The land is about 467 acres in Washoe County. It had been granted to the University of Nevada under a 1926 law for recreation and public uses. One parcel holds about 309 acres, drawn by lot and quarter-section lines. A second parcel holds about 158 acres. The sample gives the survey lines for the first parcel in full and starts those for the second.
plaw-109-7-2005:
Tax-free status for hazard fix payments is set by Public Law 109-7 of 2005. It amends section 139 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986, the part on disaster relief payments.

Gross income is not to include a qualified disaster mitigation payment. Such a payment is money paid under the Stafford Act or the flood insurance law to a property owner, or for the owner's gain, for hazard mitigation on the property. Money for selling the property does not count. The act bars any rise in the property's tax basis from the freed sum. It also bars a second gain: no deduction or credit for spending to the extent of the freed sum.
plaw-109-70-2005:
Hawaii water projects are cleared by Public Law 109-70, the Hawaii Water Resources Act of 2005. It amends the Reclamation Wastewater and Groundwater Study and Facilities Act to add a Hawaii part.

The Secretary may join three local bodies on design, planning, and building. With the Honolulu Board of Water Supply, the work is a Kalaeloa project to desalinate seawater for direct drinking use. With the County of Hawaii, it is plant work at Kealakehe to treat and spread recycled water. With Maui County, it is works at Lahaina to spread recycled water for non-drinking uses. The sample ends as cost sharing begins.
plaw-109-71-2005:
A South Dakota park grows under Public Law 109-71, the Wind Cave National Park Boundary Revision Act of 2005. It revises the edge of Wind Cave National Park.

The Secretary of the Interior may gain the land drawn on a map dated June 2002. The land is about 5,675 acres, to be added to the park. It may come by gift, by purchase from a willing seller with gift or granted funds, or by trade. The map stays on file at the National Park Service for public viewing. The sample ends inside the boundary part, after those terms.
plaw-109-72-2005:
Job help for Katrina's displaced workers is loosened by Public Law 109-72, the Flexibility for Displaced Workers Act of 2005. It sets special rules for disaster relief jobs under the Workforce Investment Act of 1998.

Grant funds for Katrina may pay for relief jobs on projects outside the disaster area. Fitness for such jobs is widened. People who moved away from states named as major disaster areas may qualify. So may people who were out of work at the time, or who have no work history at all. The act also clears funds for general public sector jobs for those who qualify. The sample ends inside that clause.
plaw-109-73-2005:
Tax relief for Katrina victims is granted by Public Law 109-73, the Katrina Emergency Tax Relief Act of 2005. It aims to give emergency tax help to people hit by the hurricane.

The sample shows the start of the act's contents. Title I sets special rules for use of retirement funds. It covers tax-favored withdrawals, putting back sums for home buys the storm cancelled, and loans from work plans. Title II is employment relief, with a work opportunity credit for Katrina hires. It also lists a credit for bosses who kept staff. Title III gives perks for charity giving. It pauses caps on charity gifts for a time.
plaw-109-74-2005:
Fishing and boating safety funds are kept whole by Public Law 109-74 of 2005. Its title is the Sportfishing and Recreational Boating Safety Amendments Act of 2005. It guards funds paid from the Highway Trust Fund through the end of fiscal year 2005.

Title I fixes the like-named act passed weeks before as part of a larger law. It strikes one clause and sets October 1, 2005, as the start date for the fixes. For the gap, the old law is kept as it read before that act. The sample then turns to boating safety funds in section 102, and ends there.
plaw-109-75-2005: Wildlife fund leftovers stay locked ten more years under Public Law 109-75 of 2005. The whole act amends one clause of the Pittman-Robertson Wildlife Restoration Act. In section 3(b)(2)(C), it strikes the year 2006 and puts in 2016. That is the date after which surplus funds in the wildlife restoration fund may be split among the states. The act was signed on September 29, 2005.
plaw-109-76-2005:
The Parole Commission gains three more years under Public Law 109-76 of 2005. Its full title adds the words Sentencing Commission Authority Act. It amends a clause of the Sentencing Reform Act of 1984.

Each mention of eighteen years in that clause is to read as 21 years, for the Commission's life span. The act also gives the Sentencing Commission emergency power to amend the sentencing rules. Within 60 days it must act to carry out part of the 2004 terror law reform. Within 180 days it must act on part of the Anabolic Steroid Control Act of 2004.
plaw-109-77-2005:
Stopgap funding for the whole government is granted by Public Law 109-77, a joint resolution of 2005. It makes continuing appropriations for fiscal year 2006.

Section 101 grants such sums as are needed to keep projects and acts going. They run under the terms of the fiscal year 2005 funding laws. The acts listed are the funding bills then pending for 2006. They span farm and food aid, defense, energy and water, and foreign work. They also span homeland security, labor and health, veterans, science and justice, and transport. The sample ends inside that list of bills.
plaw-109-78-2005: Student aid waivers in wartime gain two more years under Public Law 109-78 of 2005. The whole act amends section 6 of the Higher Education Relief Opportunities for Students Act of 2003. It strikes September 30, 2005, and puts in September 30, 2007. That extends the Education Secretary's power to waive student aid rules during a war, a military action, or a national emergency.
plaw-109-79-2005: A business data survey gains ten more years under Public Law 109-79 of 2005. The act amends a 1983 law on the quarterly financial report. In that law's section 4(b), it strikes 2005 and puts in 2015. That extends the Commerce Secretary's power to run the quarterly financial report program by a full decade. The act was signed on September 30, 2005.
plaw-109-8-2005:
Bankruptcy law is overhauled by Public Law 109-8, the Bankruptcy Abuse Prevention and Consumer Protection Act of 2005. It amends title 11 of the federal code, the bankruptcy title.

The sample shows the start of the act's contents. Title I is Needs-Based Bankruptcy. It covers moving or ending cases, notice of other paths, and credit advice for debtors. It also covers a test program in debtor money training and lists of fair costs. Title II is Enhanced Consumer Protection. It takes up harsh creditor acts, the force of a discharge, and deals to repay wiped debts. It also guards claims on predatory loans and puts child support first.
plaw-109-80-2005:
Life cover for troops is raised by Public Law 109-80, the Servicemembers' Group Life Insurance Enhancement Act of 2005. It amends title 38 of the federal code.

First, the act repeals a part of a 2005 war funding law, as of August 31, 2005. The older title 38 rules then apply as if that part had never passed. Second, it raises the top automatic cover from 250,000 dollars to 400,000 dollars. The raise covers both the troops' program and the veterans' program. For veterans, the cap is tied to the troops' cap in force at the time. The raise itself is made in section 3 of the act.
plaw-109-81-2005:
College aid programs gain a short extension in Public Law 109-81, the Higher Education Extension Act of 2005. It extends each program under the Higher Education Act of 1965 through December 31, 2005.

Under the act, acts and payments required in fiscal year 2004 must go on during the added span. Acts and payments that were allowed, but not required, may also go on. The sum cleared for each program is the larger of two figures. Those are the sum cleared for fiscal year 2004 and the sum in fact granted for that year. The sample ends inside a clause on later changes to the law.
plaw-109-82-2005:
Disabled storm victims get job aid under Public Law 109-82 of 2005. Its title is the Assistance for Individuals with Disabilities Affected by Hurricane Katrina or Rita Act of 2005. The aid flows through vocational rehabilitation services.

The sample gives the act's terms. An affected state is one that holds a declared major disaster area, or that took in many people from such an area. The head named is the Commissioner of the Rehabilitation Services Administration. A Katrina victim, in the act's terms, lived in a disaster area on August 22, 2005. A Rita victim is tied to where the person lived seven days before the Rita declaration. The sample ends there.
plaw-109-83-2005: Grain grading law is renewed for ten years by Public Law 109-83 of 2005. It amends the United States Grain Standards Act. In five parts of that act, it strikes the year 2005 and puts in 2015. The parts cover checks, fees, and the act's end terms. The changes take effect on September 30, 2005, the day the act was signed.
plaw-109-84-2005: Los Angeles names a postal site for an actor in Public Law 109-84 of 2005. The site at 200 South Barrington Street is named the Karl Malden Station. Note that the act says Station, not Post Office Building. Any mention of the site in a federal law, map, rule, paper, or record is to use that name. The act was signed on October 4, 2005.
plaw-109-85-2005: St. Charles, Illinois, has the post office named by Public Law 109-85 of 2005. The site at 2600 Oak Street is named the Jacob L. Frazier Post Office Building. Any mention of the site in a federal law, map, rule, paper, or record is to use that name. The bill passed both chambers in September 2005 and was signed on October 4.
plaw-109-86-2005:
Fair shares of campus aid after a disaster are the aim of Public Law 109-86, the Natural Disaster Student Aid Fairness Act of 2005. It gives the Education Secretary waiver power over the sharing rules in the campus-based aid programs.

For the 2004-2005 and 2005-2006 school years, match duties are waived for colleges in a Gulf hurricane disaster area. Such a college need not put up its own share to match federal funds for set aid programs. Colleges that took in storm-hit students may get the same waiver. That call turns on the college's student count and means, judged by steady rules. The act also gives waiver power over the rules for moving aid funds between colleges.
plaw-109-87-2005:
Grants for storm-hit airports are cleared by Public Law 109-87 of 2005. It lets the Secretary of Transportation make emergency airport project grants under title 49 of the federal code.

The grants draw on funds left unspent for fiscal years 2005 and 2006. They may pay for urgent capital costs at public airports in Louisiana, Mississippi, Alabama, or Texas. The costs must tie to fixing or replacing sites hurt by Hurricane Katrina or Hurricane Rita. Urgent running costs from the storms may also be paid. In giving the grants, the Secretary must put airport works first, then terminal works, then other site repairs, then running costs.
plaw-109-88-2005:
Loans for towns hit by disaster are funded by Public Law 109-88, the Community Disaster Loan Act of 2005. It moves money granted in an earlier Katrina act.

Of the Disaster Relief sums in Public Law 109-62, up to 750 million dollars may move to the direct loan program. The loans run under section 417 of the Stafford Act and help local governments keep key services going. The moved sum may back loans with a face value of up to one billion dollars. A loan may pass the normal five million dollar cap, and such loans may not be cancelled. Up to one million dollars may move for the costs of running the program.
plaw-109-89-2005: A housing block in Jamaica is renamed by Public Law 109-89 of 2005. The federal building in Kingston, once the Crowne Plaza and now staff housing for the United States mission, is named the Colin L. Powell Residential Plaza. Any mention of the building in a federal law, map, rule, paper, or record is to use that name. The act was signed on October 13, 2005.
plaw-109-9-2005:
Film piracy in theaters is hit by Public Law 109-9, the Family Entertainment and Copyright Act of 2005. Its aim is to guard rights in creative works.

Title I is the Artists' Rights and Theft Prevention Act of 2005, or ART Act. It adds a new crime to title 18 of the federal code. A person who, with no leave from the rights holder, knowingly uses a recording device in a theater is guilty. The crime covers sending out or copying a film shown there. The penalty is up to three years in prison, a fine, or both. A repeat crime draws up to six years.
plaw-109-90-2005:
Homeland security gets its yearly funds in Public Law 109-90, the Department of Homeland Security Appropriations Act, 2006. It covers the fiscal year ending September 30, 2006.

The sample shows Title I, on running the department. The Secretary's office and top management get about 79 million dollars. Within 180 days, the Secretary must send Congress a joined plan on immigration enforcement. The plan must aim to cut the count of undocumented aliens by ten percent a year, based on census data. The screening office gets four million dollars. The Under Secretary for Management gets about 169 million dollars. The sample ends inside that clause.
plaw-109-91-2005:
Health aid spans are stretched by Public Law 109-91 of 2005. Its title is the QI, TMA, and Abstinence Programs Extension and Hurricane Katrina Unemployment Relief Act of 2005.

Title I covers health parts. It extends Medicare cost-sharing help for qualifying people through September 2007. The date in the Social Security Act moves from September 2005 to September 2007. Set sums for the program are listed by span: 100 million dollars for late 2005 and 300 million dollars for most of 2006. The act's heading also names two more ends. It extends transitional medical aid and the abstinence teaching program through December 2005, and it gives jobless relief after Katrina.
plaw-109-92-2005:
Gun makers gain a shield from suits in Public Law 109-92, the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act of 2005. It bars civil suits against makers, sellers, and importers of guns and rounds for harm from misuse by others.

Congress found that the Second Amendment guards a person's right to keep and bear arms, member of a militia or not. It found that suits had been brought against firms for harm done by third parties, even criminals, with goods that worked as designed. It found that gun trade is heavily ruled by federal, state, and local law. Lawful firms, it said, should not pay for crimes done with goods that work as meant.
plaw-109-93-2005:
A park edge in Colorado is adjusted by trade in Public Law 109-93, the Rocky Mountain National Park Boundary Adjustment Act of 2005.

The trade pairs one federal parcel with three private parcels, all near MacGregor Ranch in Larimer County. The federal parcel is about 70 acres, per a map dated June 2004. The private parcels add to about 5.9 acres. When an offer to give them to the United States is made, the Secretary must take it. The federal parcel must then be handed over within 60 days. As a term of the trade, the Secretary keeps a lasting easement on that parcel to guard its conservation values.
plaw-109-94-2005:
New Mexico wild land is named by Public Law 109-94, the Ojito Wilderness Act of 2005. It makes the Ojito Wilderness Study Area a true wilderness. The act also takes some land into trust for the Pueblo of Zia, per its heading.

The named land is about 11,183 acres in the Albuquerque District of the Bureau of Land Management. It joins the National Wilderness Preservation System as the Ojito Wilderness. The naming furthers the aims of the Wilderness Act. A map and a legal account of the area are to be filed with two House and Senate committees. They carry the same force as if printed in the act itself.
plaw-109-95-2005:
Aid for orphans abroad is set up by Public Law 109-95 of 2005. Its title is the Assistance for Orphans and Other Vulnerable Children in Developing Countries Act of 2005. It amends the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961.

Congress found more than 143 million orphans in Africa south of the Sahara, Asia, Latin America, and the Caribbean, as of July 2004. About 16 million of them had lost both parents, most to AIDS. Homes with orphans often cannot pay for health care, food, clothes, or school. The findings add that about 121 million children worldwide miss school, most of them girls. School food programs, they say, draw children to class and help them learn.
plaw-109-96-2005: All contact lenses are classed as medical devices by Public Law 109-96 of 2005. It amends section 520 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. The new clause states that all contact lenses count as devices under section 201(h) of that law. It also states that the clause says nothing about how any other product should be classed, as a device or as a drug. The act was signed on November 9, 2005.
plaw-109-97-2005:
Farm and food programs get their yearly funds in Public Law 109-97 of 2005. Its title is the Agriculture, Rural Development, Food and Drug Administration, and Related Agencies Appropriations Act, 2006. It covers the fiscal year ending September 30, 2006.

The sample shows Title I, on farm programs. The Office of the Secretary of Agriculture gets about 5.1 million dollars. No more than 11,000 dollars of that may go to official reception costs. The Chief Economist gets about 10.5 million dollars for studies of farm markets, risk, and costs. That office also runs the World Agricultural Outlook Board. The sample ends as the National Appeals Division is funded.
plaw-109-98-2005: Detroit honors a civil rights figure in Public Law 109-98 of 2005. The federal building at 333 Mt. Elliott Street is named the Rosa Parks Federal Building. Any mention of the building in a federal law, map, rule, paper, or record is to use that name. The bill passed the House on October 26, 2005, and the Senate on November 1, and was signed on November 11.
plaw-109-99-2005: Permit speed funds for the Army gain a few more months under Public Law 109-99 of 2005. It amends section 214 of the Water Resources Development Act of 2000. One change drops the words that tied the power to fiscal years 2001 through 2005. A new clause then sets the span of the power in plain terms. The power runs from October 1, 2000, through March 31, 2006.
plos-pbio-0020005:
Yoav Gilad, Victor Wiebe, Molly Przeworski, and others compared smell genes and color vision in primates for PLOS Biology in 2004. Primates with full three-color vision tend to have lost more of their smell receptor genes. Those genes are the largest gene family in mammal genomes.

The pattern points to a trade-off in evolution. As some primate lines gained rich color sight, keen smell may have mattered less, so broken smell genes could pile up. The authors test that idea by counting working and broken genes across species. Their result is a clear case study in how senses evolve. It shows how a gain in one system can leave marks across the whole genome.
plos-pbio-0020405:
Vardhman K. Rakyan, Thomas Hildmann, Karen L. Novik, and their team piloted an epigenome study in PLOS Biology in 2004. DNA methylation is a chemical mark that can silence genes without changing the DNA code. The team profiled those marks across the human major histocompatibility complex, a dense region packed with immune genes.

A pilot study tests whether a big project is worth doing. Here it showed that methylation maps of this key region can be built and read. Marks varied by tissue and by gene, as a working control system should. The work helped launch the Human Epigenome Project, which aimed to do for these marks what the genome project did for the code itself.
plos-pone-0000005:
John Ioannidis turned his lens on science itself in a 2006 PLOS ONE study of citation patterns. A citation is one paper crediting another, and citations steer careers, funding, and fame. Ioannidis asked where the most-cited papers in science actually appear, and how tightly they bunch in a few journals.

He describes journals as ecosystems, with top papers clustered in a small set of elite outlets. That clustering shapes what gets read and rewarded. The study feeds a long debate: does prestige follow quality, or does the journal's name inflate a paper's reach? Ioannidis, known for questioning research habits, gives that debate hard numbers.
plos-pone-0000105:
Yan Li, Peter Roycewicz, Evadne Smith, and their team studied flowering time in the plant Arabidopsis in PLOS ONE in 2006. When a plant flowers decides its seed yield and its fit to local seasons. The team bred plants under mixed conditions to find the gene regions, called QTL, that set flowering under both place and season effects.

Local adaptation means each population's timing fits its own home. Lab tests that include varied conditions reveal more of the genes behind that fit than single-condition tests. The work shows adaptation is built from several regions acting together, not one master gene. That lesson guides crop breeding for new climates, where timing must be retuned as seasons shift.
plos-pone-0000205:
Ana G. Popa-Lisseanu, Antonio Delgado-Huertas, Manuela G. Forero, and colleagues published this bat ecology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. Its title frames the finding: bats have conquered a formidable feeding niche, the myriads of songbirds that migrate at night. Some bats hunt those birds on the wing, in darkness, high above the ground.

Catching birds in flight at night demands sharp echolocation and bold behavior. The authors present evidence for how bats exploit this seasonal flood of prey. The study redraws part of the night sky's food web, adding bats as serious predators of migrating songbirds.
plos-pone-0000305:
Jasmine I. Daksis and Glen H. Erikson published this diagnostics paper in PLOS ONE in 2007. It presents a heteropolymeric triplex-based genomic assay, a DNA test design, for detecting pathogens or single-nucleotide polymorphisms, one-letter variants, in human genomic samples. The assay uses triple-stranded DNA structures to recognize its targets.

A single platform that can flag either an infection or a genetic variant is versatile for labs. The authors describe the assay and its detection principle. Work of this kind fed the growth of DNA-based testing that now underpins much of clinical diagnostics.
plos-pone-0000405:
Jianmin Zhong, Algimantas Jasinskas, and Alan G. Barbour treated ticks with antibiotics and measured the cost, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. The tick Amblyomma americanum carries bacteria and spreads several diseases to people. The team asked what happens to the tick itself when its resident bacteria are hit with antibiotic treatment.

The authors report that treatment reduced the ticks' reproductive fitness, meaning treated ticks produced fewer or weaker offspring. If a tick depends on its microbes to thrive, those microbes become a target. Hitting them could be a way to control the tick and the diseases it carries. The study links microbiology to pest control through the tick's own body.
plos-pone-0000505:
Ute Becherer and colleagues paired two lab methods to count single release events in hormone cells, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Chromaffin cells release adrenaline in tiny packets. The packets fuse with the cell's outer skin and spill their load out, a step called exocytosis. One method reads the cell's surface electrically as each packet fuses. The other films the packets under a special microscope.

Each method alone leaves gaps. The readings lack pictures, and the pictures lack exact timing. Used side by side, they watch the same event in two ways at once. Tools that can track single packets help research on all kinds of release, from insulin in diabetes to signal release in the brain.
plos-pone-0000605:
Tamar Geiger and Alexander Levitzki tracked how skin cells become dependent on a growth signal as they transform, in a 2007 PLOS ONE paper. Human papilloma virus 16 can drive keratinocytes, the skin's main cells, toward cancer. During early transformation, the cells show loss of robustness and addiction to IGF1, a growth factor they increasingly cannot live without.

Addiction to a signal is a vulnerability: cut the signal and the transformed cell dies while normal cells cope. Loss of robustness means the cells also lose backup pathways, narrowing their options. Together these changes describe how a virus narrows a cell's life until one growth factor holds the key, a pattern drug developers look for.
plos-pone-0000705:
Laurent Gillet, Janet S. May, Susanna Colaco and colleagues described a viral decoy in a mouse herpesvirus, for PLOS ONE in 2007. Herpesviruses stay infectious for the long term without changing their surface antigens much. So they must evade neutralization, the blocking of virus by antibodies, by other means. Immune sera block this virus in fibroblasts, yet fail in other cell types, sometimes even enhancing infection.

The title names the trick: the viral protein gp150 acts as an immunogenic decoy that limits neutralization. A decoy soaks up the antibody response where it does least harm. Understanding decoys matters for vaccine design against herpesviruses, which have frustrated vaccine makers for decades.
plos-pone-0000805:
Rajnish Joshi, Samir Patil, Shriprakash Kalantri and colleagues X-rayed health care workers who carry silent tuberculosis infection, in PLOS ONE in 2007. More than half of health care workers in high-incidence, low and middle income countries are latently infected with TB. The team determined radiological lesions in a cohort of such workers in India, and their association with T cell immune responses.

Latent infection is supposed to be quiet, so abnormal radiological findings raise questions: old scars, or early disease? Correlating images with immune response could sort harmless findings from warning signs. Health workers are both at risk and essential to TB control, making their silent infections a policy problem, not just a medical one.
plos-pone-0000905:
Wayne Dawson, Kazuya Fujiwara and Gota Kawai offered a practical way to predict knots in RNA folding, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Predicting how an RNA strand folds is often the first step toward knowing its structure. Most tools skip pseudoknots, folded loops that cross each other, because searching for them is slow and complex.

Skipping them, though, leaves real structures out of reach. The authors use heuristic modeling, guided shortcuts, with mapping and step by step folding to make the search workable. Better folding guesses help everyone who studies RNA viruses, gene control and RNA based drugs. The paper is aimed at users who need answers in real time.
plos-pone-0001005:
Leslie Wolf, Alexis Donoghoe and Tim Lane examined how state law affects routine HIV testing, in PLOS ONE in 2007. In 2006, US health officials recommended HIV testing for everyone aged thirteen to sixty-four as a routine matter. That plan would drop separate written consent and required pretest counseling.

State laws, written earlier, often demand exactly those steps. The authors map the clash between the new guidance and standing law. Routine testing aims to catch infections early, since many people learn their status late. Whether it can happen depends on legal details as much as medical ones. The paper is a guide for states weighing updates.
plos-pone-0001105:
Paolo Fabene, Flavia Merigo, Mirco Galie and colleagues studied brain damage in rats given a seizure triggering drug, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Hippocampal sclerosis, scarring in a memory area, marks many temporal lobe epilepsy cases. The neuron loss there was thought to come from excitotoxic injury, overexcited cells burning out, rather than ischemic injury from lost blood flow.

Using pilocarpine to induce status epilepticus, prolonged seizures, in rats, the team assessed vessel structure, gene expression and the time course of neuron damage. Their title says both mechanisms are involved. Splitting the blame changes what protection researchers should try during prolonged seizures.
plos-pone-0001205:
Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, or ALS, gradually destroys the spinal cord's motor pathways. Svitlana Garbuzova-Davis and colleagues looked for damage to the barrier protecting the spinal cord. Their study, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article, used mice that model the disease. The blood-spinal cord barrier normally controls which molecules and cells pass from blood into cord tissue.

The authors present evidence that this barrier is compromised in both early and late symptomatic SOD1 mice, the standard ALS model. Barrier failure has also been reported in ALS patients. A leaky barrier could let harmful blood components reach motor neurons, making it a possible target for treatment.
plos-pone-0001305:
To prepare for a possible flu pandemic means re-checking old licensed drugs, in case the virus adapts to humans. Dennis Morrison and colleagues ran a randomized crossover study of two such drugs. Amantadine and oseltamivir were given alone and together. The study came out in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The combination pairs an ion channel blocker with a neuraminidase inhibitor.

The study checked how the body handles the combination: how it absorbs and clears each drug when both are present. Combination therapy only makes sense if the drugs do not clash. Their results inform pandemic stockpiling and treatment plans for avian H5N1 infection.
plos-pone-0001405:
Jana van Vliet-Ostaptchouk and colleagues published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a gene called TUB and body weight. The gene is active in the brain area that steers hunger. In mice, faults in it cause late onset weight gain, insulin issues, and loss of sight and hearing. The team asked whether common variants matter in women.

They checked variants in the gene against body makeup and eating habits in middle aged women. Links found there would tie a mouse lead to human traits. Even weak links help map the gene web behind weight. The study adds one more piece to the search for why bodies store fat so unlike.
plos-pone-0001505:
Simon Overduin and Philip Servos wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE brain scan study on the sense of touch. Scans had been used to map how touch is laid out in the human cortex. Such maps often lean on what was found in monkeys. The pair probed whether human touch maps mirror each other across body sides.

Their scans show a neat mirror layout for touch sense in the cortex. That layout fits a symmetric plan for the two body halves. A clear map helps brain surgery and stroke care, where touch zones must be spared. It also frees human maps from sole reliance on monkey data.
plos-pone-0001605:
Jeffrey Alten and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on collapse from blood loss after trauma. Half of trauma deaths come from this collapse of blood flow. The team built a rat model that pairs a mild wound with grave blood loss. In that model, heart output fell by half and death loomed.

They show a signal protein, switched on before the shock, can ward off the collapse. The protein acts through a known cell switch in the liver and vessels. A ward that works when given ahead of time fits planned surgery and high risk care. It also names a path for drugs to copy.
plos-pone-0001705:
Oumaya Bouchabke and co-authors used natural variation in a weed to study drought responses in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. The plant is Arabidopsis thaliana, the standard lab plant. Wild accessions, lines collected from different places, differ in their genes. The team asked whether those differences could reveal the genetic basis of drought response.

They characterized a set of accessions, most from a core collection chosen to capture the species' genetic diversity, under dry conditions. The full text gives the accessions' traits and how their drought responses differed. Natural variation is a free experiment run by evolution, and mapping it can find drought genes that breeding could later move into crops.
plos-pone-0001805:
David Vallenet, Patrice Nordmann, Valérie Barbe, and their co-authors compared the genomes of three Acinetobacter bacteria in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Acinetobacter baumannii causes many hospital infections in humans. Strains resistant to many drugs, or even to nearly all drugs, were reported more and more worldwide. To study its way of life, researchers need relatives that live differently for contrast.

The team compared two new genomes with a third, covering three ways of life in one study. The full text gives the genome maps and the gene gaps tied to each way of life. Genes unique to the hospital germ are leads for drugs and tests against a germ that resists nearly all drugs.
plos-pone-0001905:
Takahiro Suzuki and co-authors checked a chemical mark on DNA in cloned mice, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Cloning by moving a body cell's nucleus into an egg can make animals that match the donor in genes. Yet clones often show odd traits and odd gene activity, so something beyond the gene code must go wrong.

The team scanned the whole genome for faults in acetylation, a mark that helps switch genes on, at a site called H3K9. They looked for spots where clones depart from normal mice. Such faults may explain why clones grow in odd ways. The work also bears on stem cell care, where cloning is hoped to yield spare tissue.
plos-pone-0002005:
Sandra Kuhlman and Josh Huang shared a method to label and steer chosen neuron types in the mouse brain, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The brain mixes many neuron types, and testing the job of one type calls for tools that act only on that type, at fine detail. Their method pairs Cre-knockin mice, in which a gene switch sits in one cell type, with viruses that carry genes.

The viruses were built to express a green glow protein, a red one, or channelrhodopsin, a light-gated channel, only where the switch is on. The kit lets labs both see a neuron type and drive it with light.
plos-pone-0002105:
Liran Shlush and co-authors read the genes of the Druze as a window on the old Near East, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. Mitochondrial DNA haplogroups, sets of variants passed down the female line, are usually strongly partitioned by global region. The X haplogroup is a unique exception, spread widely with no clear home region.

The team examined variation in mitochondrial DNA among the Druze, a small, close-knit community of the Near East. As the title frames it, the Druze act as a population genetic refugium, a refuge where old lineages persist. Such refuges preserve patterns erased elsewhere by mixing.
plos-pone-0002205:
Ahmed Moustafa, Adrian Reyes-Prieto, and Debashish Bhattacharya counted genes that one ancient cell passed to the ancestors of plants, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. The plastid, the green compartment that runs photosynthesis, began when an early cell captured a cyanobacterium and kept it. That event seeded the line leading to red algae, green algae, land plants, and glaucophytes.

The team traced genes from Chlamydiae, a separate bacterial group, into the plant line. They found at least 55 such genes, most of them now serving the plastid. The count shows the plastid's origin story involved more donors than the textbook version suggests.
plos-pone-0002305:
Marisa Mazari-Hiriart and co-authors assessed water quality where treated wastewater is reused for farming near Mexico City, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Recycling wastewater for irrigation is common in developing countries and can expose people to microbes through water, soil, and crops. The balance of benefit and risk needed local evidence.

The team ran a longitudinal study in a periurban agricultural area, sampling water over time and weighing the health implications. Their data show what residents and farm workers actually face. Findings like these help cities reuse scarce water with clearer eyes about treatment and hygiene.
plos-pone-0002405:
MacKenzie and co-authors published a research article in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Julia J. MacKenzie, Noé D. Gómez, Souvik Bhattacharjee, among others. Its subject is a Plasmodium falciparum Host-Targeting Motif Functions in Export during Blood Stage Infection of the Rodent Malarial Parasite Plasmodium berghei. Plasmodium falciparum sends hundreds of proteins, including major virulence proteins, into the host red blood cell.

To reach the host cell fluid, most of these proteins carry a short host-targeting motif of 11 amino acids. The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others.
plos-pone-0002505:
Mutalima, working with fellow researchers, published a study in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Nora Mutalima, Elizabeth Molyneux, Harold Jaffe, among others. Its subject is associations between Burkitt Lymphoma among Children in Malawi and Infection with HIV, EBV and Malaria. The title goes on to note results from a Case-Control Study. Burkitt lymphoma, a childhood cancer common in parts of sub-Saharan Africa, has been linked to Epstein Barr Virus (EBV) and malaria.

The paper sets out the problem first and then the line of work the team chose to take. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves.
plos-pone-0002605:
Kalita and fellow authors published a research article through PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline names Mridul K. Kalita, Umesh K. Nandal, Ansuman Pattnaik, among others. Its subject is cyclinPred: A SVM-Based Method for Predicting Cyclin Protein Sequences.

The piece walks readers through the question, the setup, and the steps that came next. The full text is free to read, so any reader can check the work and follow the links to past work. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work. Each claim is tied to the work the team did, and the text keeps facts apart from the views of the authors.
plos-pone-0002705:
In 2008, Rui Wang and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE. Their subject was identification of a regulatory t cell specific cell surface molecule that mediates suppressive signals and induces foxp3 expression. Authorship is credited in the record to Rui Wang and co-authors, with PLOS ONE as the journal of publication.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Regulatory T (T reg ) cells control immune activation and maintain tolerance. A further point appears in the abstract. How T regs mediate their suppressive function is unclear. The article gives specialists and general readers a compact entry point into the topic, with its aims and scope stated up front.
plos-pone-0002805:
In 2008, Kathryn E. Reif and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE. Their subject was prevalence and infection load dynamics of rickettsia felis in actively feeding cat fleas. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Kathryn E. Reif, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

In the abstract, the authors give their starting point. Rickettsia felis is a flea-associated rickettsial pathogen recurrently identified in both colonized and wild-caught cat fleas, Ctenocephalides felis . A further point appears in the abstract. We hypothesized that within colonized fleas, the intimate relationship between R. Readers get a clear record of the question, the approach named in the abstract, and the context the authors give for the work.
plos-pone-0002905:
David Miles, Marianne van der Sande, David Jeffries and colleagues revisited Gambian infants two years after cytomegalovirus infection in 2008. Their earlier study had found large groups of mature CD8 T cells soon after infection in young infants. Those groups stayed in place through the first year that followed.

The follow-up, published in PLOS ONE, asks whether such large subpopulations of these immune cells are still maintained at two years. That matters because cytomegalovirus is caught very early in life in the Gambia. The results inform how lasting effects of infant infection shape the growing immune system.
plos-pone-0003005:
Konstantinos Kostarakos, Manfred Hartbauer and Heiner Römer linked matched filters, mate choice, and trait evolution in 2008. Understanding communication means studying both variation in signals and how receivers respond to it. Receiver preferences in turn shape how signals vary over generations.

Writing in PLOS ONE, the authors examine how a receiver tuned like a matched filter affects the evolution of sexually selected traits. A matched filter responds best to one signal form. The framework helps explain why some courtship signals stay narrow and stereotyped instead of drifting widely. Anyone can read the full text free of charge through the journal's open access site.
plos-pone-0003105:
Wubei Dong, Xiaojia Tang, Yihai Yu and co-authors modeled the biological clock of the fungus Neurospora crassa in 2008. Their model-driven process, called Computing Life, identifies ensembles of genetic networks describing the clock. The mechanism involves the genes white-collar-1 and white-collar-2, which encode a transcriptional activator.

Systems biology here means fitting network models to data rather than testing one gene at a time. Published in PLOS ONE, Neurospora is a classic clock model, and an ensemble approach admits several networks may fit. That honesty about uncertainty can guide sharper experiments. The complete article sets out the methods and data behind each claim in full.
plos-pone-0003205:
Olena Morozova, Vyacheslav Morozov, Brad G. Hoffman and colleagues present a visualization approach for gene expression data in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Serial Analysis of Gene Expression, or SAGE, is a DNA sequencing-based method for large-scale profiling that offers an alternative to microarray analysis. Most analyses of SAGE data aimed at finding co-expressed genes had used various versions of clustering.

The authors offer a seriation approach for visualization-driven discovery of co-expression patterns in SAGE data. Readers get a method that orders data so patterns become visible to the eye. Visual discovery can reveal gene groups that rigid clustering rules might split apart.
plos-pone-0003305:
Tu-Anh Tran, Marie-Ghislaine de Goër de Herve, Houria Hendel-Chavez and colleagues study resting T cells as an HIV reservoir in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. In HIV-infected patients on long-term effective therapy, virus persistence in resting long-lived CD4 T cells is a major barrier to curing the infection. Cell quiescence, by favouring HIV latency, reduces the risk of recognition and destruction by cytotoxic lymphocytes.

The authors characterize resting regulatory CD4 T cells as a site of HIV persistence in patients on long-term therapy. Readers learn which quiet cells shelter the virus from drugs and immunity. Cure research must reach exactly such reservoirs.
plos-pone-0003405:
Jennifer M. Curry and co-authors traced how tumors raise new blood vessels in this 2008 paper. A signal called M-CSF draws scavenger immune cells into tumors. Those cells can help tumors grow vessels, a process called angiogenesis. The team followed the chain from that signal to vessel growth.

M-CSF switched on VEGF, a strong vessel growth factor, in the cells. The switch ran through the MAPK/ERK pathway and a protein named Sp1. In living tissue, that chain led to new vessel formation. Each link in the chain is a point where drugs might cut supply lines.
plos-pone-0003505:
Mathieu Brodeur and co-authors probed illusory shapes with brain waves in this 2008 study. Kanizsa figures make viewers see edges where none are drawn. Studies usually flash the full set of inducer shapes at once. A newer method, the notch mode, builds the inducers bit by bit.

Two early brain waves, P1 and N1, marked stages of that processing. Comparing modes clarified what each wave means for illusion building. The visual system fills in missing contours in steps. Timing those steps helps separate sensing from true perception. Illusions are prized because they reveal the steps normal sight keeps hidden.
plos-pone-0003605:
Adam T. Szafran and co-authors built an imaging platform for hormone signaling in this 2008 paper. The androgen receptor answers male hormones and drives several diseases. Its function shifts with steroids, growth factors, and small molecules. Knowing those shifts matters for prostate cancer and androgen insensitivity syndrome.

High throughput imaging let them analyze receptor function at scale. They could separate effects tied to ligand, cell cycle, and mutations. Automated pictures turn single tests into systematic maps. Such maps speed the search for drugs that tune this receptor. Prostate cancer is one of the most common cancers in men worldwide.
plos-pone-0003705:
Fatemeh Heidary, Mohammad Reza Vaeze Mahdavi, Farshad Momeni, and colleagues published this animal study in PLOS ONE in 2008. People of lower social status die earlier and suffer more disease in many studies. Controlled experiments on inequality itself are rare, for plain ethical reasons. The team used rabbits to model it.

Rabbits fed under unequal food conditions showed worse cardiac health than better-fed peers. The gap in diet stood in for the gap in social standing. The study models in animals how food inequality might wear down the human heart over time.
plos-pone-0003805:
Eisuke Chikayama, Michitaka Suto, Takashi Nishihara, and colleagues published this metabolism methods paper in PLOS ONE in 2008. Metabolic phenotyping gives a bird's-eye view of an organism's chemistry. The team applied NMR spectroscopy to mixtures of metabolites labeled with stable isotopes.

Their analysis works across plant and animal systems alike. It reads the labeled mixtures to sketch whole metabolic pathways at a coarse grain. In the post-genomics era, such views of chemistry in action complement what gene and protein data alone can show. One shared method serves both kingdoms of life in this work, plant and animal alike.
plos-pone-0003905:
Virginie Rigourd, Caroline Chauvet, Sonia T. Chelbi, and co-authors tested a disputed gene for preeclampsia in 2008. Preeclampsia is a blood-pressure disorder of pregnancy rooted in the placenta. It affects up to one in ten pregnancies. Changes in a gene called STOX1 had been proposed as a cause in 2005.

Later groups doubted that claim, so the question stayed open. The authors raised STOX1 levels in choriocarcinoma cells, a placenta-like cell line. Gene activity in those cells shifted in ways seen in preeclamptic placentas. The match keeps STOX1 in play as part of the disorder's story.
plos-pone-0004005:
George J. Milne, Joel K. Kelso, Heath A. Kelly, and co-authors modeled school closure during flu pandemic in 2008. With little direct evidence, models guide pandemic planning for governments. The team built a model of one small community in detail. It captured exact household structures and daily contacts.

Their PLOS ONE article compares school closure inside individual-based models. Closing schools cuts contacts among children, who spread flu fast. The small community model shows where that helps and where it does not. Planners can use such tests before committing to disruptive closures. It was printed in PLOS ONE, where the full text stays free to read.
plos-pone-0004105:
Susana Campino, Julian Forton, Srilakshmi Raj, and co-authors validated gene control variants in 2008. Finding regulatory variants that tune gene expression challenges genome research. Several studies had tied non-coding variants to expression differences. Those links relied on statistical signals that need confirmation.

Their PLOS ONE article applies allele-specific expression tests to HapMap populations. The method checks whether one gene copy outproduces the other in a person. A real imbalance proves a nearby regulatory variant exists. Validated variants can then be tested for disease roles. The work appeared in PLOS ONE, with its methods and data open for all to see.
plos-pone-0004205:
Timothy Hospedales and Sethu Vijayakumar published this theory paper in PLOS ONE in 2009. Our senses work together to build one accurate picture of the world. The leading framework treats perception as ideal observer inference, weighing each sense by how much it can be trusted.

The authors recast multisensory oddity detection, spotting the one stimulus that differs from the rest, as Bayesian inference. Their model works out what an ideal observer should conclude from combined senses. In plain terms, it asks what a perfect observer would pick. The work gives scientists exact predictions to test against human results in multisensory tasks.
plos-pone-0004305:
Francesca Corlazzoli and colleagues published this epigenetics study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Chromatin, the packaging of DNA, adapts and responds to cues from inside and outside the cell. The authors hypothesise that inherited abnormal chromatin states in cancer and ageing are caused by genetic or environmental factors. Their earlier work showed that mutation or loss of the retinoic acid receptor RARα disrupts these states.

Here they argue that a derangement upstream of RARα triggers repression of a broad epigenetic network. One broken controller, in their account, can silence many genes at once, a pattern seen in cancer.
plos-pone-0004405:
A checkpoint molecule best known in cancer may also guard the brain. Antje Kroner, Nicholas Schwab, Chi Wang Ip, and co-authors study PD-1 in this 2009 PLOS ONE article. They used a mouse model where oligodendroglia drive inflammation and nerve damage.

In that model, CD8 lymphocytes mediate the immune response. The team asked how the co-inhibitory molecule PD-1 modulates the damage. A brake on immune attack could limit neural injury. The work points to immune regulation as a lever in inflammatory brain disease. Mouse models let the team test checkpoint effects that human studies cannot isolate.
plos-pone-0004505:
Laboratories around the world measure HIV-killing antibodies in different ways, and Eva Maria Fenyo, Alan Heath, Stefania Dispinseri, and co-authors report a joint effort to compare them, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Neutralizing antibodies are central to HIV vaccine research, because a vaccine should raise antibodies that block the virus. Yet it was unclear which assay, or mix of assays, gives a reliable measure of protection.

An international collaboration, called NeutNet, ran the same samples through many labs and methods. Their report compares how the assays agree and where they differ. Vaccine trials cannot be judged if every lab's ruler is different. This kind of shared yardstick is quiet work, but vaccine science depends on it.
plos-pone-0004605:
Creatine supplements did not add to the benefits of weight training in people with HIV. Giorgos Sakkas, Kathleen Mulligan, Makani DaSilva, and co-authors found that in a controlled trial reported in PLOS ONE in 2009. Progressive resistance exercise training improves physical functioning in patients with HIV infection. Creatine can augment training benefits in athletes and improve muscle function in patients with muscle wasting, so the combination looked promising.

The study was randomized, double-blind, and placebo-controlled, the strongest design for such a question. Patients trained, with creatine or a dummy supplement. Creatine failed to augment the benefits, as the title plainly states. A solid negative result saves patients money and hope spent on a supplement that, in this setting, does not deliver.
plos-pone-0004705:
Glyn Elwyn and colleagues built a tool to grade aids that help patients choose care, for PLOS ONE in 2009. Decision aids can be leaflets, videos, or web tools that lay out options and trade offs. Patients and doctors need a fair way to tell good aids from weak ones.

The team built a scale through draft, test, and check stages with other raters. They report how the scale was built and how well raters agree when they use it. A shared scale can lift the quality of aids in clinics. It also helps buyers pick tools they can trust.
plos-pone-0004805:
Iñigo Ortiz de Mendíbil, José Vizmanos, and Francisco Novo studied signatures of selection in fusion transcripts from chromosomal translocations in human cancer, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Recurrence and non random distribution of translocation breakpoints in tumors are usually attributed to local sequence features near breakpoints. However, functional constraints might also delimit the positions and partners of fusions that survive in cancer cells over time.

The team looked for selection signatures in resulting fusion transcripts. Evidence of selection would mean fusions are not random accidents alone. Surviving fusions likely confer growth advantages. That insight helps prioritize fusions as drug targets.
plos-pone-0004905:
Masa Tsuchiya and colleagues studied emergent genome wide control in lipopolysaccharide stimulated macrophages, in PLOS ONE in 2009. Large scale output studies mainly focused on highly expressed discriminatory genes. Biological responses come from whole regulatory networks acting together. Looking only at the strongest genes misses that system behavior. The team tracked genome wide dynamics in normal and mutated macrophages after a microbe signal.

Whole distributions shift coherently, not just top genes. Emergent metrics capture immune state better. Systems immunology needs global descriptors. Mutations reshape entire landscapes. Taken together, the findings mark a useful step for research in this area. The team also set out clear next steps for work in this field. More tests with more samples will help show how strong the effect is. Such work helps guide care, field work, and lab work in the years ahead.
plos-pone-0005005:
Fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva is a rare inherited disease. Muscle, ligament and tendon slowly turn to bone. Most cases come from one classic mutation in the gene ACVR1. Kirsten Petrie and colleagues reported exceptions in PLOS ONE in 2009. They studied two patients with unusual features. Both carried new mutations in ACVR1.

The new variants expand the disease's genetic picture. They show the classic mutation is not the only route. Atypical cases can now be recognized and diagnosed. The finding helps doctors who meet puzzling presentations. It also teaches more about how ACVR1 normally controls bone growth. That control is exactly what fails in this cruel disease.
plos-pone-0005105:
HD-PTP looks like an enzyme that removes phosphate tags. It was classed as a tyrosine phosphatase by its sequence. It was also named a tumor suppressor candidate. Marie-Claude Gingras and colleagues tested whether it actually works as an enzyme. Their PLOS ONE paper appeared in 2009. No substrate for it had ever been identified.

HD-PTP is catalytically inactive. A conserved divergence in its phosphatase domain disables the chemistry. The protein looks like an enzyme but cannot act as one. That reclassifies it. Other proteins share such dead domains. They often serve as scaffolds or regulators instead. The finding shows why sequence alone can mislead. Function must be tested, not assumed.
plos-pone-0005205:
Satellite cells are the resident stem cells of adult muscle, resting quietly until injury calls them into action. Few markers can pick out the resting cells with ease, though Pax7 is a known one. Gnocchi and colleagues deepened that marker picture in PLOS ONE in 2009 using mouse muscle.

The team compared the molecular signature of resting and activated satellite cells in more detail. A sharper signature helps researchers find and study the resting cells before they wake. That matters for work on muscle repair, aging, and diseases that waste muscle away.
plos-pone-0005305:
Tuberculosis bacteria survive inside immune cells by tampering with the cell's internal signals. Calcium is one of those signals, and its release helps immune responses to pathogens. Gupta and colleagues studied calcium channels in TB infection in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Voltage-gated calcium channels, they found, negatively regulate protective immunity against Mycobacterium tuberculosis. In plain terms, the channels act as a brake on the defense the body needs. Releasing that brake, by blocking the channels, is a possible way to help the immune system clear TB. TB care lasts for months and drugs are hard on the body, so a host-side boost that helps the body's own cells kill the germ could shorten care one day.
plos-pone-0005405:
Growing nerve fibers steer with a tip called the growth cone, which reads guidance cues and directs the cytoskeleton. Tubulin, the building block of microtubules, carries chemical modifications that affect that steering. Marcos and colleagues tested one modification in PLOS ONE in 2009.

Tubulin tyrosination, the addition of the amino acid tyrosine, proved required for proper growth cone organization. It was also required for pathfinding, the cone's choice of route. A tiny tag on a building block thus helps wire the developing brain correctly. One wrong turn by a growth cone can wire a sense to the wrong place for life. So the small tags that steer it are worth the close care this work gives to each one in turn.
plos-pone-0005505:
Cecilia Gonzalez Campo and colleagues studied a brain protein called reelin in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Reelin is released outside cells and helps build the layered structure of the young brain. It has also been linked to schizophrenia.

The team showed that certain brain cells that calm other cells release reelin in the adult brain. There, reelin helps keep the receptors that receive glutamate, a key excitatory signal, in balance. That balance matters for clear thinking, and its loss may play a part in mental illness. Loss of that balance has been tied to poor thinking in several brain disorders, which gives the work a wider reach.
plos-pone-0005605:
Angela Schoolmeesters, Teresa Eklund, and Devin Leake profiled small RNAs in stem cells in a 2009 PLOS ONE report. Mesenchymal stem cells from bone marrow can be guided to become bone, fat, or other tissues. That makes them strong candidates for repairing injured tissue.

The team mapped which microRNAs change as the cells commit to the bone pathway. Certain microRNAs proved vital to that choice of fate. Knowing the switches helps labs grow the right cell type reliably for therapy. Bone repair after fracture is one clear use, and the microRNA switches may be druggable in time. Reliable control of cell fate is what turns stem cells from a promise into a treatment that clinics can use.
plos-pone-0005705:
Hui Li and colleagues studied mice missing a proton-sensing receptor in 2009, and found effects on both bone and tumors. The receptor, OGR1, reacts to acid levels around cells. In lab tests it had already shown power to slow the spread of prostate cancer when boosted.

Mice without the receptor formed bone-eating cells in abnormal ways. They also grew fewer tumors in the team's tests. That double effect makes OGR1 a puzzle: it touches bone health and cancer at once. Sorting out both roles could point to new treatments for bone loss and cancer spread.
plos-pone-0005805:
Andrea Byrnes and co-authors searched in 2009 for a blood gene signature of chronic fatigue, using identical twins who differ in the illness. Chronic fatigue has no known cause and no lab test, leaving patients in limbo. Twins discordant for the illness control for genes and upbringing at once.

The team scanned gene activity in white blood cells from forty-four evaluated subjects, including the twin pairs. No signature separated the ill from the well, they report. That null result still counts: it rules out an easy blood biomarker of this kind. Research can shift to other tissues or triggers.
plos-pone-0005905:
Minghua Nie and co-authors delivered in 2009 the first system-wide map of SUMO tagging in a multicellular animal. SUMO is a small protein tag attached to other proteins, vital for development. No one had charted the whole tagged set, the SUMO-ome, in an organism before.

Combining genetics and proteomics in the fruit fly, the team linked SUMO targets to cell cycle control, Ras signaling, and early body patterning. A full map turns scattered single-protein stories into a network view. Developmental biologists can now ask which tag changes matter most. The resource anchors future work on this quiet but powerful tag.
plos-pone-0006005:
Cell therapy after a heart attack sounds simple, but the details decide whether it helps. Juliana Nakamuta, Maria Danoviz, Fabio Marques and colleagues varied those details in 2009. Their PLOS ONE study gives bone marrow cells to hearts after infarction. It tests three things: when the cells go in, which route they take, and whether a fibrin scaffold helps them stay.

Each choice softened the heart's decline in its own measure, the team reports. Delivery is thus part of the treatment, not a footnote to it. The work helps trial designers pick timing and route with evidence in hand, a needed step before cell therapy for heart repair can prove itself in patients.
plos-pone-0006105:
A mouse virus can set off the whole immune system within hours. Christoph Ammann, Ronald Messer, Karin Peterson and colleagues found the trigger in 2009. Their PLOS ONE paper studies lactate dehydrogenase-elevating virus, a natural infection of mice that causes rapid but passing activation of B cells and T cells across lymphoid tissues and blood.

The activation runs through TLR7, a virus sensor, and depends on interferon-alpha answers from plasmacytoid dendritic cells, the title reports. A clear chain from sensor to body-wide firing helps explain how some viruses stir immunity so fast. The chain also serves vaccine science, where controlled immune stirring is the point of an adjuvant.
plos-pone-0006205:
Cell biologists read yeast shape as a clue to gene function, while physicists ask what simple laws set shape. Daniel Riveline bridges the two views in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper on yeast lengths and shapes. He proposes a combined approach that treats cell form as the outcome of scaling rules.

Scaling arguments relate size and shape through a few broad physical ratios. Applied to yeast, they explain why cells grow to the lengths they do. The paper gives biologists a compact way to predict form before hunting for genes. It also shows physicists a living system where their methods earn their keep.
plos-pone-0006305:
Insulin's growth signal flows through Akt, a protein that tags several brakes on cell growth. Sibylle Schleich and Aurelio Teleman tested two of those tags in fruit flies in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Akt phosphorylates Tsc1 and Tsc2, partners that restrain the growth driver TOR.

Neither phosphorylation was required for normal animal growth, the title states. The famous pathway diagram thus contains steps the animal can do without. Redundancy or side routes must carry the growth signal instead. Results like this keep textbook pathways honest and point searches toward the steps that truly matter.
plos-pone-0006405:
Stress experienced by parents can echo in the behaviour of their offspring. Daniel Naett and colleagues tested cross-generation effects in chickens in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. They hypothesised that chronic unpredictable food access would make chickens feed more conservatively, and that such adaptations might be inherited.

The study tracked both acquired behaviour adaptations and brain gene expression across generations. Offspring of stressed birds showed matching shifts in habits and brain genes. Inherited stress tuning challenges simple gene-only views of heredity. Farm animal welfare research gains a long-term dimension from such effects.
plos-pone-0006505:
Lucia Talamini and Martijn Meeter modeled a thinking problem in schizophrenia in PLOS ONE in 2009. A large body of evidence suggests impaired context processing in schizophrenia. People with the illness struggle to use setting and background to guide responses. The authors propose that this impairment arises from defective integration in mediotemporal lobe circuits.

Their model gives objects dominance over context. In a healthy brain, context shapes how an object is read; here, the object wins. A working model lets researchers test ideas that are hard to probe in patients. It also ties a symptom pattern to a specific circuit fault.
plos-pone-0006605:
Tita Ritsema and co-authors asked how plants turn sugar into stored fructan in PLOS ONE in 2009. Sugar from outside the cell starts the making of fructan, a stored form of carbohydrate. The cell steps that link sugar to fructan were still obscure. Past work had shown that a step with calcium is part of the chain. The team now asked about small GTPases, a set of protein switches used in many cell paths.

They asked if these switches act as signal hubs in the sugar-driven start of fructan making. Hubs would be prime control points for plant breeders to use. Fructans help plants cope with stress and are also used in foods. The study maps one more part of this sugar sense system.
plos-pone-0006705:
Yan Fu and co-authors watched glutamate damage the insulation of nerve fibers in PLOS ONE in 2009. Damage at the paranode, where myelin meets the nerve fiber, appears in white matter injury. What causes that damage was unknown. The team used a special imaging method that reads myelin directly. It works on fresh tissue at finer than micron resolution.

Imaging showed clear splitting and retraction of paranodal myelin after glutamate exposure. Glutamate is the brain's main excitatory signal, but excess can be toxic. That excess is called excitotoxicity. Seeing the damage happen pins a culprit for white matter injury. The finding may guide efforts to protect nerves after stroke or trauma.
plos-pone-0006805:
Swati C. Chauhan and Rentala Madhubala cut a detox gene out of a parasite in PLOS ONE in 2009. The parasite is Leishmania donovani. It causes a grave illness of the inner organs. The gene makes glyoxalase I, an enzyme that clears a toxic waste. The waste is methylglyoxal, a harmful by-product of cell work. The parasite clears it with a rare system based on trypanothione.

Mutants that lack the gene cleared the waste far worse. That loss proves the enzyme sits at the heart of the path. A detox path found just in the parasite makes a fine drug target. Block it, and the waste may poison the parasite while the host stays safe. The mutants give labs a tool to test that plan.
plos-pone-0006905:
Huiyong Wei and colleagues built a tool to watch tuberculosis-specific T cells in monkeys in PLOS ONE in 2009. How often these cells appear during infection was unknown. Their resting memory pool after BCG vaccination was also unknown. BCG is the standard tuberculosis vaccine. The team made a tetramer reagent loaded with a mycobacterial peptide.

The tetramer directly measures epitope-specific CD4 T cells in lymphoid tissue. It tracks them during Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. It also counts the memory cells left after vaccination. Direct counts reveal whether vaccines leave durable immune memory. That information guides efforts to improve on BCG.
plos-pone-0007005:
Paul Collins, Brian Latta, and Gary Roemer asked a conservation question in PLOS ONE in 2009. Removing invasive species is a standard way to protect native wildlife. The job gets tricky when the invaders interact with each other. Their case paired an eagle with a pig, two introduced or recovered species affecting one ecosystem.

The team weighed whether removal order changes the outcome. Removing one species first can release or burden the other. Getting the sequence wrong can waste years of conservation effort. Their analysis offers guidance for managers facing several linked invaders at once.
plos-pone-0007105:
Muthannan Ramakrishnan, Zheng Jin Tu, Sushmita Singh, and others tested flu sequencing in PLOS ONE in 2009. Flu A viruses change fast as they spread. Mixed infections and swarms of close variants make them hard to track. New deep sequencing tools promised a much clearer view of that mix.

The team judged whether genome sequencing could spot mixed infections in a sound way. Finding a hidden second strain changes how an outbreak is read. It also bears on which strains go into vaccines. Their study helped set fair hopes for the flood of flu genomes that soon came.
plos-pone-0007205:
Brian Hauge, Christopher Oggero, Nicole Nguyen, and colleagues described a faster cloning method in PLOS ONE in 2009. Their tool supports RNA interference, a way to switch off chosen genes. Researchers use it for functional genomics, systems biology, and early drug discovery work.

Plant screening needs many inverted repeat constructs that produce double-stranded RNA. Building those constructs one by one is slow. The authors present a single-tube, high throughput method for cloning them. Their approach aims to help plant labs prepare large gene-silencing experiments with far less manual work overall.
plos-pone-0007305:
Shafiq Uddin Ahmed and Jo Milner studied how normal cancer cells avoid self-destruction in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. Control of apoptosis, or programmed cell death, matters under normal non-stress conditions. It shapes mammalian development and daily cell turnover in tissues throughout life, keeping cell numbers balanced.

Faulty control can impair development or feed disease. The authors examine basal survival in cancer cells. They identify a network where one signal, JNK2, suppresses a death-promoting circuit involving JNK1, c-Jun, and Bcl-3. Their finding shows related signals can pull cell fate in opposite directions.
plos-pone-0007405:
Catalin Vasilescu, Simona Rossi, Masayoshi Shimizu, and colleagues searched blood microRNAs for sepsis prognosis markers in 2009. The physiology of sepsis remains poorly understood. Despite advances in management, sepsis is life-threatening with poor outcomes, and earlier warning of deterioration could save lives in intensive care units worldwide.

New diagnostic markers tied to sepsis mechanisms could enable specific therapies. The authors build microRNA fingerprints from patient blood. They identify miR-150 as a plasma prognostic marker in sepsis patients. A blood marker that forecasts outcome could help doctors triage care and test treatments.
plos-pone-0007505:
Yih-Horng Shiao and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 reporting an unusual RNA found in lung cancer cells. Between genes, the team detected a non-coding RNA related to ribosomal RNA. Ribosomal RNA is the core of the cell's protein-making factories. A stand-alone relative sitting between genes was unexpected. The authors measured how its levels relate to the cell's normal rRNA output.

The molecule's levels tracked with how much regular rRNA the cells produced. They also tracked with how often a single-letter variant appeared in the rRNA gene. Those correlations hint that this overlooked RNA takes part in managing the protein factories. Lung cancer cells push protein production hard, so such a manager could matter. The study flags a molecule most surveys would have ignored. It invites a closer look at what intergenic RNAs do.
plos-pone-0007605:
Louise Strandberg and colleagues published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009 on sepsis, the body's dangerous overreaction to infection.
