Sepsis is often caused by gram-positive bacteria, especially Staphylococcus aureus. Few effective therapies exist, so knowing what predisposes patients matters. Obesity was their suspect. The team fed mice a high-fat diet for a long period, then induced sepsis and compared the outcomes with lean mice.

The chronically fat-fed mice died more often. Their immune response to the infection was disturbed as well. Chronic overeating thus does more than strain the heart and metabolism. It rewires immunity in ways that show up when infection strikes. That link helps explain worse sepsis outcomes in obese patients. The study gives the clinic a mechanism to think with: diet history as immune history.
plos-pone-0007705:
Matthew Hirsch and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It describes a method for editing genes with a virus called AAV. Short pieces of single-strand DNA, called oligonucleotides, can guide precise changes. The virus triggers a brief DNA damage response in the cell it enters.

During that response, the cell's repair tools rebuild the viral genome into circular forms. The authors harness that moment to steer small, targeted edits into DNA. The technique, called recombineering, offers a gentle way to rewrite short stretches of genetic code. Such tools matter for gene therapy research.
plos-pone-0007805:
Jingxian Liu and Jianxing Song published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It finds a new way to study proteins that clump together. Protein aggregation inside the body is linked to many human diseases. Yet clumped proteins will not dissolve, which blocks close study of the process.

The authors took insoluble mutants of the SH3 domain, a common protein part. They dissolved them in salt-free water, against expectations. Then they used NMR to read the proteins' structure in detail. The trick opens aggregation itself to high-resolution study. That could reveal how clumps form and how to stop them.
plos-pone-0007905:
David Mutch and co-authors published a study in PLOS ONE in 2009. It profiles body chemistry after a common weight-loss operation. Roux-en-Y gastric bypass surgery brings weight loss and better insulin sensitivity. It also cuts related illnesses such as diabetes and heart disease.

The many metabolic adaptations behind those gains are still being mapped. The team used metabolite profiling on patients after surgery. They identified candidate markers that reflect the clinical adaptations. Such markers could tell doctors which patients are responding well. They may also reveal how bypass surgery resets metabolism, beyond simple restriction of food.
plos-pone-0008005:
Rodrigo Suarez and colleagues mapped smell wiring in a small Madagascan mammal for PLOS ONE in 2009. The lesser tenrec uses a vomeronasal system to read scent signals from its own kind. In most mammals, two cell groups in that system send their wires to strictly split zones of the brain.

In the tenrec, the two groups' wires mix and even swap zones, ending together in single target balls. That merged map breaks a rule long thought fixed for mammals. Odd wiring like this is a gift for science: it shows which parts of the smell map can bend as species evolve.
plos-pone-0008105:
Vijaya Kolachalama and colleagues modeled drug flow from stents at artery forks in PLOS ONE in 2009. Stents that leak drugs are now standard for propping open clogged arteries. Forks, where one artery splits in two, are the hardest spots to dose evenly.

Their model showed blood flow itself boosts how much drug settles from the stent into the fork walls. Flow, long treated as a mere carrier, is an active part of dosing. Stent designs that work with the flow, rather than ignoring it, should coat forks more evenly and heal them better.
plos-pone-0008205:
Hannah E. Jones and colleagues examined bacteria in fetal membranes in a PLOS ONE study from 2009. Infection inside the womb may help trigger early labor. It may also play a role when membranes rupture too soon. Many bacteria linked to early birth are hard to grow in the lab. So the team turned to molecular methods instead.

They compared membranes from very preterm births with those from births at term. Both the frequency and the mix of bacterial species differed between groups. Such data help clarify how hidden infection relates to early delivery. They may guide efforts to prevent preterm birth.
plos-pone-0008305:
Deverick Anderson and his team wrote in PLOS ONE in 2009 about wound germs that resist drugs. Some germs that infect a wound after surgery can shrug off a key drug, methicillin. These germs are called MRSA, a form of the germ Staphylococcus aureus. What MRSA itself adds to harm and cost was not well known. Past work gave mixed answers on that point.

The team ran a matched study of 659 surgical patients in more than one center. Each sick patient was matched with a like patient for a fair test. They weighed both health results and money costs tied to the drug-proof germs. Clear counts help wards judge how much it is worth to stop such germs.
plos-pone-0008405:
Alan C.-N. Wong, Thomas J. Palmeri, Baxter P. Rogers, and colleagues asked how the way a person learns about an object changes the brain's picture of it, in PLOS ONE in 2009. That experience reshapes object representations in the visual cortex was already known. What was not known is whether the kind of learning matters. Learning can take many forms, and each might leave a different mark on the cortex.

The team used contrasting training programs to teach people about objects, then measured the cortical patterns that followed. How the objects had been learned changed how the visual cortex represented them. Two people can thus look at the same object while their brains file it differently. The result matters for teaching and for retraining vision after brain injury.
plos-pone-0008505:
James Thomas and co-authors study a fertility gene in a 2009 PLOS ONE paper. The gene is PRDM9, also called Meisetz. In mice, mismatched forms of PRDM9 can cause hybrid male sterility. That sterility can isolate populations and may help form new species. Mice lacking PRDM9 are sterile in both sexes. Their meiosis, the cell division that makes sperm and eggs, stalls early.

The author traces how fast PRDM9 has evolved across species. Its change is described as extraordinary in speed and pattern. Rapid change fits a gene caught in an evolutionary arms race. The paper helps explain hybrid sterility and speciation.
plos-pone-0008605:
Sarah Huber and co-authors study immunity in Darwin's finches in a 2010 PLOS ONE paper. Invasive parasites are a major threat to island animal populations. Darwin's finches of the Galapagos face introduced pox virus and nest flies. The fly Philornis downsi harms nestlings in their nests. The team developed assays for parasite-specific antibody responses in the medium ground finch. That finch is Geospiza fortis, a classic Darwin species.

They find invasive parasites trigger acquired immunity in the finches. Birds exposed to the parasites mount antibody defenses. Such ecoimmunity may help finches persist under new parasite pressure. It also shows island species can adapt immunologically, not just genetically.
plos-pone-0008705:
Ronan Murray, James Robinson, Jodi White, and colleagues reported a dangerous pairing seen during the flu pandemic. Their 2010 PLOS ONE article describes pneumonia caught outside hospitals. The culprits were pandemic H1N1 flu together with MRSA, a drug-resistant staph germ. Bacterial lung infection has long been a known flu complication. Resistant staph made that complication harder to treat.

The authors describe the co-infected patients and their illness course. Two germs at once can turn a flu case fatal fast. Quick recognition matters because standard antibiotics may fail against MRSA. The report warns clinics to suspect this pairing early.
plos-pone-0008805:
Davide Corti, Johannes Langedijk, Andreas Hinz, and colleagues mined HIV patients' immune memory for rare antibodies. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. A vaccine against HIV remains a central unmet goal. A few infected people make antibodies that neutralize many viral strains. Those rare antibodies mark weak spots on the virus. Memory B cells store the recipes for them.

The team screened memory cells and isolated new monoclonal antibodies. Some neutralized a broad range of HIV-1 strains. Each broad antibody teaches vaccine designers what shape to imitate. The work brings an antibody-guided vaccine closer to reality.
plos-pone-0008905:
Hui Yang, Chao Liu, Yongwang Zhong, and colleagues showed the Huntington protein jamming a cell disposal machine. Their study appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Huntington disease comes from an overlong repeat inside the huntingtin protein. How that change kills brain cells remains uncertain. Expanded huntingtin stresses the cell's protein-folding compartment. The disposal system, which shreds worn proteins, may be part of the story. An enzyme called gp78 tags proteins for that shredding.

Huntingtin bound a domain of gp78 and blocked its work. It stopped gp78 from gripping both ubiquitin tags and the p97 helper. A jammed disposal route could poison neurons over years. The block names a fresh target for Huntington therapy.
plos-pone-0009005:
Mohammed Ali and co-authors tested a suspected helper in HIV's escape from human cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Human cells fight HIV with tetherin, a protein that pins new virus particles to the cell surface. HIV answers with its protein Vpu, which defeats tetherin somehow. The protein CAML was a candidate partner in that counterattack.

The team removed or added CAML and watched virus release. Tetherin worked the same with or without CAML present. So CAML does not tune the restriction on HIV-1 particles. Ruling out a plausible suspect narrows the search for how Vpu really works.
plos-pone-0009105:
Brian Layden and co-authors surveyed a huge family of cell receptors in embryonic stem cells, in PLOS ONE in 2010. G protein coupled receptors are the largest receptor family in the body. They had barely been studied in embryonic stem cells. Knowing which signals steer these cells is vital for cell replacement therapy.

The team focused on Gs-alpha signalling, one arm of the family. That pathway proved to play a real role in stem cell behaviour. Mapping active receptors shows which chemical levers labs can pull. Such levers could guide stem cells into the tissues doctors need.
plos-pone-0009205:
Lin Chen, Wanliang Shi, Hui Li, and co-authors published this infection study in PLOS ONE in 2010. It brings together two public health problems: opioid use and tuberculosis. Both can harm the lungs, but how they do so was unclear. The study asks how the two insults interact inside the body.

The team gave mice long-term morphine and infected them with the tuberculosis bacterium. They report that a sensor protein called Toll-like receptor 9 plays a critical role in what followed. With both insults present, lung cells died by apoptosis, a tidy form of cell suicide. The finding ties an immune sensor to the extra damage seen when the two problems combine.
plos-pone-0009305:
Carmen Blanco-Aparicio and co-authors published this breast cancer study in PLOS ONE in 2010. A signaling protein called AKT shows up at high levels in many human breast cancers. That rise usually follows faults in the PTEN/PI3K pathway, a control circuit for cell growth. How extra AKT actually pushes tumors to form was the open question.

Using mouse models, the team explored what stronger AKT activity contributes to mammary tumors. Their work separates AKT's own push from the effects of the broken pathway around it. Knowing which part drives growth matters, because drugs that block AKT are judged by exactly that. The study maps AKT's share of blame in tumor formation.
plos-pone-0009405:
Claude Saegerman and co-authors published this animal disease investigation in PLOS ONE in 2010. Bluetongue virus serotype 8 was first reported in northern Europe in August 2006. It swept through herds in 2007 and 2008, hitting sheep and cattle hard. Where and when the virus first entered remained unknown.

The team worked backward from herd records and outbreak data. They estimated the most likely time and place the virus entered Belgian ruminants. Pinpointing an introduction helps officials understand how the disease crossed into new territory. That knowledge sharpens surveillance at the borders where the next incursion may land.
plos-pone-0009505:
Stephanie Soscia and colleagues offered a new view of a protein tied to Alzheimer's disease in PLOS ONE in 2010. The protein, amyloid beta, builds up in the brains of patients. It is often treated as waste with no normal job. Yet it binds to many partners in the body. The team tested whether it can act against microbes.

In their tests, amyloid beta killed a range of germs, much like known defense proteins do. That suggests the protein has a real role in the brain's defenses. Plaques might then be the leftovers of an immune fight gone too far. The idea reframes how Alzheimer's damage may begin.
plos-pone-0009605:
Amber Hartman and a large team published a full genome in PLOS ONE in 2010. The microbe is Haloferax volcanii, strain DS2. It belongs to the archaea, the third domain of life beside bacteria and eukaryotes. It thrives in very salty water where most life cannot. Labs use it as a model for archaeal biology.

Sequencing its complete genome gives the full list of its genes. Researchers can now plan experiments against a known map instead of guessing. The genome also supports comparisons with other salt loving microbes. Such comparisons show how life adapts to extreme salt, heat, and dryness.
plos-pone-0009705:
California mice sing in ultrasound, pitches too high for people to hear. Matina Kalcounis-Rueppell and colleagues compared those calls in wild mice and lab-raised mice. Their comparison appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. The mice belong to the species Peromyscus californicus. Ultrasound calls are also hard to study without special microphones.

The calls serve as markers of behavior in many studies. If life in a lab cage changes the songs, lab results may not match wild behavior. The team measured how the two groups' calls differed. Their findings give researchers a wild baseline for reading mouse behavior.
plos-pone-0009805:
Shinji Hadano leads the team behind a 2010 PLOS ONE study linking two genes in ALS, a disease that kills motor nerve cells. Loss of the ALS2 gene causes some young-onset forms. Its protein helps move cargo inside cells and may protect nerves from faulty SOD1, another ALS gene.

Mice with one faulty SOD1 type grew worse when ALS2 was also missing, losing weight and movement and dying sooner. Their spinal cords held swollen fibers, clumps of misfolded protein, and backed-up waste bags. Cell tests showed faulty clearing of that waste. The authors propose that jammed cell clean-up makes the SOD1 harm worse.
plos-pone-0009905:
Gene studies produce sprawling datasets, and judging which analysis methods work best is hard. Christopher Cabanski and colleagues proposed a standardized score for that judging. Their method appeared in PLOS ONE in 2010. Different methods can give different answers from the same data.

The score is called SWISS MADE, short for Standardized Within Class Sum of Squares. It evaluates both methodologies and dataset elements on one yardstick. A shared yardstick makes comparisons between studies fairer. The tool helps analysts pick methods that truly fit their data. Fair scores keep method fights honest.
plos-pone-0010005:
Srikanth Chiliveru, Svend Birkelund, and Søren Paludan published cell work in 2010. They studied how fibroblasts sense Chlamydia pneumoniae. That bacterium lives inside host cells. Fibroblasts are common connective tissue cells. When they detect germs, they can switch on interferon-stimulated genes, a set of defense genes that slow infection.

The authors asked which sensors inside the cell detect this bacterium and trigger those defense genes. They pointed to receptors that sense nucleotides, the building blocks of DNA and RNA, inside the cell. The result helps map how the body spots a germ that hides within its own cells.
plos-pone-0010105:
The authors were Guy Lahat, Quan-Sheng Zhu, Kai-Lieh Huang, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study named vimentin as a possible cancer drug target. Vimentin is a structural filament found in many connective tissue cells. In active cells it also helps with adhesion, movement, survival, and signaling through constant rebuilding.

The team drew evidence from lab cell work and mouse tumors grown from human tissue. Soft tissue sarcomas were among the cancers in view. If vimentin can be attacked safely, cancers that depend on it might gain a new treatment option.
plos-pone-0010205:
The authors were Claudia Molins, Mark Delorey, Brook Yockey, and others. Their 2010 PLOS ONE study compared tularemia germs in mice. The type A form of Francisella tularensis causes serious human disease. Genetic typing splits type A into three distinct groups, called clades A1a, A1b, and A2.

Human case data hinted those clades differ in how severe illness becomes. The team tested virulence, the power to cause disease, in mice for each clade. Confirmed differences would help doctors read a patient's infecting strain as a clue to likely outcomes. The report appeared in 2010.
plos-pone-0010305:
Yoshiyuki Kumada and Shuguang Zhang grew gum ligament cells in designer scaffolds in 2010. Periodontal ligament fibroblasts hold teeth in their sockets and repair gum tissue. The team built two peptide scaffolds, mesh-like gels that self-assemble, with short active motifs attached. Those motifs include RGD, a cell-gripping signal found in body proteins, to invite cells to settle.

In three-dimensional scaffolds, the human cells made large amounts of type I and type III collagen. They did so without any extra growth factors added. Their PLOS ONE result supports scaffold-only approaches for dental tissue repair.
plos-pone-0010405:
Eric Blalock and co-workers tracked aging markers in mice given a diabetes drug long-term, for PLOS ONE in 2010. Pioglitazone helps restore insulin response in type 2 diabetes. It works through a master switch for fat and sugar handling. Reports had suggested such drugs might also slow brain aging in Alzheimer's models. The team measured aging signs in both body and brain after long treatment.

Long use lets benefits and harms both show up honestly. The study read out many markers rather than one, giving a broad picture. Drugs taken for years by millions deserve that kind of checking. Results here inform debates about repurposing diabetes drugs for brain protection. Aging, the authors remind us, is a whole-body process worth measuring widely.
plos-pone-0010505:
Rong Lu and co-workers tracked long-term effects of a Salmonella protein inside living animals in PLOS ONE in 2010. Salmonella infection is common and can linger, raising risks of bowel disease and cancer. One bacterial protein it injects into our cells is AvrA. Evidence suggested AvrA does many jobs, from calming inflammation to altering cell growth. Most studies, though, were in dishes rather than whole animals.

Studying chronic effects in vivo shows what months of exposure do to the gut. That timescale matches the human risks under debate. If one bacterial protein nudges tissue toward disease, it becomes a target for prevention. The study extends AvrA research into realistic, long-term settings. It bridges infection biology and chronic disease research.
plos-pone-0010605:
Orlaith Fraser and Thomas Bugnyar watched ravens after fights, in PLOS ONE in 2010. After a conflict, an uninvolved bird sometimes approaches the loser and stays close. In primates, that kind of contact is often read as comfort.

The ravens did approach recent losers more than other flock members. The contact also seemed to lower later stress and further attacks. The authors weigh comfort against simpler explanations, like seeking safety. Even with care, the pattern looks much like consolation. Finding it in birds suggests concern for others runs deeper in evolution than once thought.
plos-pone-0010705:
Hans Supèr, August Romeo, and Matthias Keil modeled how the brain separates objects from backgrounds, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Seeing a mug on a table feels instant, yet the brain must decide which edges belong to the mug. That border assignment is a core step in vision.

Their model solved the task in one forward pass, without signals looping back. Local edge cues fed a network that assigned borders and split surfaces. The output matched key features of human perception. A forward-only design is simpler to build into machines, so the model interests both brain science and computer vision.
plos-pone-0010805:
Preethi Srikanthan and colleagues combined national survey data on muscle, fat, and blood sugar, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Sarcopenia, the loss of muscle with age, often occurs in the same bodies as obesity. Each condition alone is tied to insulin resistance, the core fault of type 2 diabetes. Whether the pair is worse than the sum was the open question.

In the third National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey, people with both low muscle and obesity had the worst insulin resistance. Their blood sugar control was also poorer than in either condition alone. Muscle is not just for strength; it is a sugar sink. Keeping muscle while losing fat may matter more than weight alone suggests.
plos-pone-0011005:
Vyacheslav Gurevich and Yona Kassir published this yeast development study in PLOS ONE in 2010. Meiosis, the cell division that makes spores in yeast and eggs and sperm in animals, runs on a cascade of gene regulators switching each other on in sequence. The authors asked a basic control question: does completing the program require each regulator to reach a strong level?

Surprisingly, meiosis tolerated drastic changes in the amounts of its three consecutive positive regulators. The timing of early gene activity did not set when DNA copying began. But the timing of the middle activator did set when nuclear division started. Switching it on early forced division early. That broke coordination with DNA copying. Gurevich and Kassir uncover a design switch, from judging amounts to judging timing, that makes a developmental program run robustly.
plos-pone-0011105:
Hubbe, Neves and Harvati tackled human origins in PLOS ONE in 2010. How and when people first settled the Americas is still argued over. The authors tested rival ideas about migration routes, timing and the spread of early groups across the New World.

By weighing those scenarios against the available evidence, the study shows which accounts fit best. The question matters because this was one of the last great moves of humans across the globe. A clearer picture helps link skull form, genes and climate in one story. It also guides where future digs and studies should look.
plos-pone-0011205:
Drumond, Nieto, Trigo and colleagues traced Brazilian rainfall in PLOS ONE in 2010. The dry northeast of Brazil depends on seasonal rains that begin far from the region itself. Using a method that follows air parcels backward, the team identified the main sources of moisture for both the pre rainy and rainy seasons.

Ocean and land sources fed the region in different shares across the seasons. Knowing where rain water comes from improves drought forecasts. Millions of farmers plan planting around those forecasts. The study links distant seas and forests to the fate of a semi arid region's harvests.
plos-pone-0011305:
Gawlik, Remacle, Shiryaev and colleagues built an ultra sensitive sensor in PLOS ONE in 2010. Furin is an enzyme that cuts proteins, including some used by anthrax toxin to enter cells. The team built a light based sensor able to report furin at extremely low levels on cell surfaces.

Such sensitivity reveals enzyme activity that older tests would miss entirely. Tracking furin could matter for following how anthrax protective antigen is processed. The sensor also suits studies of other diseases where furin plays a part, including some viral infections. Biodefense gains a sharper tool for detecting a key step in toxin action.
plos-pone-0011405:
Simon Zeller and co-authors grew genetically modified wheat under varied conditions in 2010 to measure how genes and environment interact. A wheat line carrying an added gene may thrive in one field and disappoint in another, because soil, weather, and pests all change what the gene does. Regulators often judge such wheat from trials in a narrow set of conditions.

Their field work showed that the added gene's effects on the plant shifted with the environment in which it grew. The same line could look beneficial in one setting and neutral or costly in another. That variability carries a clear lesson for approval and farming alike. A transgene should be judged across the range of conditions where farmers will actually grow it, not from a single favorable trial.
plos-pone-0011505:
Dineke Frentz and co-authors compared in 2010 the rulebooks doctors use to read HIV drug resistance. HIV mutates to dodge drugs, and genotypic tests read the virus's DNA changes to predict which drugs will still work. Several interpretation systems translate the same DNA into advice, and they sometimes disagree, leaving doctors unsure which to follow.

The team tested how well each system predicted patients' actual viral outcomes over time on treatment. A head-to-head comparison on real outcomes, not opinion, tells clinics which rulebook best forecasts whether a drug combination will hold. Choosing the better interpreter can mean fewer failing regimens and less resistance built by trial and error. The study serves everyday HIV care directly: the test is only as good as the rules that read it.
plos-pone-0011605:
Erica Larson and Alexander Idnurm traced the history of a fungal gene in PLOS ONE in 2010. The gene, called leuA, makes an enzyme fungi need to build leucine, an amino acid that humans and animals cannot make. Because people lack this pathway, it has been proposed as a target for antifungal drugs.

Larson and Idnurm found the gene in a group of early fungi and compared its history across species. The evidence points to two separate origins for the same enzyme in fungi. Finding that nature arrived at the same tool twice reshapes how researchers read fungal evolution and judge drug targets.
plos-pone-0011705:
Sean Rands modelled how effort by single animals sharpens what a whole group knows, in PLOS ONE in 2010. By foraging carefully or scanning for predators, an animal improves its own picture of the surroundings. Group members can also tap the shared pool of information that others gather.

Rands asked how much private effort is worthwhile when public information is also available. His model shows when extra individual work pays off for the group as a whole and when it does not. The result helps explain how social animals balance doing their own work against copying neighbours.
plos-pone-0011805:
Daniel Casasanto and Kyle Jasmin analysed the hand gestures of politicians speaking, in PLOS ONE in 2010. Body-specificity theory holds that people with different bodily traits form different mental representations, even for abstract ideas. An earlier test found right- and left-handers associate good things with their dominant side.

The authors tracked spontaneous gestures during positive and negative political speech. Speakers' hands added their own commentary, favouring one side for good content and the other for bad. The pattern links handedness, gesture and abstract value, suggesting the body quietly shapes how politicians, and voters, frame good and bad.
plos-pone-0011905:
Christopher Record and colleagues compared in 2010 the three-dimensional structures of the four human MST kinases. These enzymes, related to the yeast Ste20 kinase, help control cell death, cell growth, and cell polarity. Their faulty regulation has been linked to prostate and colorectal cancer, yet the four family members are switched on in different ways.

A side-by-side structural comparison shows where the four enzymes match and where their shapes part company. Those differences explain how one family can serve several control jobs without mixing signals. For drug design, the map highlights which pockets are shared and which are unique enough to target a single member.
plos-pone-0012005:
Kerstin Johannesson and co-workers examined in 2010 the indiscriminate mating of male marine snails. In promiscuous species, males gain from mating often, since each mating may add offspring. Females gain little past an optimal number of matings, and extra ones can cost them, setting up a sexual conflict.

The study asks whether male snails' refusal to be choosy, mating with partners of little benefit, reflects that conflict compromising their behavior. Males that cannot afford to pass up chances may waste effort or even mate with the wrong targets entirely. The snails make a tidy test of how far selection pushes males toward quantity over judgment.
plos-pone-0012105:
Seiichi Kanzaki, Akira Yamaguchi, Kayoko Yamaguchi, and co-authors examined the thymus gland in mice with a storage disease, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The mice model Sandhoff disease, in which a missing enzyme lets fatty material build up in cells, slowly harming the brain. The thymus, a small gland that trains immune cells, had drawn the team's interest in earlier work on these mice.

They describe how the gland changes as the disease advances in this model. Immune changes are easy to overlook in a disease known for nerve damage, yet they may shape how the illness unfolds. Mapping them gives researchers a fuller picture of the disease and more places to look for ways to slow it.
plos-pone-0012205:
Rea Tschopp, Abraham Aseffa, Esther Schelling, and co-authors surveyed cattle tuberculosis where herds, wildlife, and herders meet in southern Ethiopia, in PLOS ONE in 2010. The disease is well documented in Ethiopia's highland cattle but had never been studied among the pastoralist herds of the South Omo region. There, cattle, wild animals, and people live in unusually close contact.

Their survey measured how common the disease is at that busy crossroads. Bovine tuberculosis can pass to people through milk and close contact, so the number sets the risk for herding families too. First measurements in an unstudied region are what control programs, and honest advice to herders, are built on.
plos-pone-0012305:
Owen Woodward, Yun Li, Shengqiang Yu, and co-authors identified a cut piece of the polycystin-1 protein in PLOS ONE in 2010. The inherited disease behind this protein fills kidneys with cysts until they fail, and it traces to faults in either of two genes. Polycystin-1 is a huge membrane protein, and the team found it is clipped to release a fragment with a job of its own.

The fragment, called P100, controls how calcium enters cells through a store-operated route, by working with the calcium sensor STIM1. Calcium mishandling is a leading theory for why cysts form. Each piece of this pathway clarified brings the disease's first cause closer to a druggable step.
plos-pone-0012405:
David Rosen, Santosh Putta, Todd Covey and colleagues profiled single leukemia cells to map how they answer DNA damage, in a 2010 PLOS ONE study. Acute myeloid leukemia varies hugely between patients, and drug response varies with it. Using a method that reads signals inside many single cells, the team compared damage responses with each sample's growth pathway profile.

Distinct patterns of damage response and cell death lined up with Jak/Stat and PI3 kinase pathway states. Those links suggest which patients' leukemias might yield to which drugs. Single-cell profiling of this kind moves leukemia care toward matching treatment to the signaling habits of each patient's cancer.
plos-pone-0012505:
Erum Khan, Mehreen Kisat, Nabil Khan and colleagues reviewed dengue fever cases in Pakistan across 2003 to 2007, in a 2010 PLOS ONE retrospective study. Dengue's pattern in Pakistan had changed greatly over two decades, and small local studies disagreed with each other. A pooled national picture was needed to plan hospital and mosquito control responses.

The team assembled patient records to describe who fell ill, where, and with what clinical features. Their profile shows the age and seasonal patterns outbreaks followed in those years. Solid baseline data like this let health officials spot when a new season breaks pattern and demands a faster, bigger response.
plos-pone-0012605:
Carpaneto, Koepsell, Bamberg and co-authors examined a protein that moves sugar through maize plants. Most higher plants ship sucrose, a sugar, from leaf to root and grain. The gate for that trip in maize is a transporter named ZmSUT1, driven by protons crossing the cell membrane.

Their 2010 study measured tiny electric charges that shift as the gate opens and closes. Both sugar and protons changed those charge movements, revealing steps in how the transporter works. Understanding this gate matters for crop science, because sugar flow sets how well a plant fills its grain.
plos-pone-0012705:
Huo, Yao, Wang and co-authors shrank tumours in mice with a virus cocktail carrying part of the telomerase gene. The fragment, hTERTC27, comes from the tail end of human telomerase, an enzyme most cancers switch on. Earlier work showed the fragment curbs HeLa cell growth and tumour formation.

Their 2010 study gave the cocktail under the skin of mice with melanoma and saw growth held back. Using a piece of the cancer's own machinery against it is an elegant trick. The result supports more work on this fragment as a cancer treatment base.
plos-pone-0012805:
Reitzel, Behrendt and Tarrant watched daily clock genes respond to light in a sea anemone. Circadian rhythms run the day-night cycles of behaviour and body function in most animals. Nematostella vectensis, a simple anemone, sits near the root of the animal family tree, making its clock a clue to the clock's origin.

Their 2010 study found rhythmic gene activity tied to light in this simple animal. A working clock in such an early branch suggests the animal clock is truly ancient. That reshapes the story of how timekeeping evolved.  Daily cycles were tested under changing light schedules too.
plos-pone-0316505:
Akine Eshete and six colleagues listen to people living with diabetes in North Shoa, Ethiopia. Their 2026 study is phenomenological, meaning it centres lived experience. Government programmes exist, yet daily self-care still falls short for many patients. The authors wanted the barriers described in patients' own terms. Interviews ran through July 2024 across four districts.

Twenty patients and five healthcare workers took part. Participants varied by age, sex, work, and diabetes type. Conversations were recorded, transcribed, and coded with qualitative software. A thematic framework organised the codes into subthemes and main themes about self-care practice. Such ground-level accounts show where clinic advice collides with real life. They give programme designers specific friction points to fix, rather than generic calls for more education.
plos-pone-0320105:
Saha Roy and colleagues, in a 2026 study, ask how filling in missing values in medical data changes what artificial intelligence models learn. Gaps are common in health records, and the way they are filled can tilt results. The team compared six ways of handling missing data across common prediction methods.

Two tasks were tested: spotting COVID-19 and predicting which patients would get worse. In a general screening group, a method that fills gaps by chained estimates gave the best results, lifting detection and revealing hidden viral coinfections. In an intensive care group, using only complete records looked stronger at first, but that edge came from bias: sicker patients were tested more, so their records were fuller. The authors warn that the right fix for missing data depends on the care setting, and the wrong one can mislead doctors.
plos-pone-0324305:
Schepisi and colleagues, in a 2026 study, track emergency department visits for mental health crises across three large Italian areas before and during COVID-19. More than five million residents were followed from 2018 to 2021. The question was not only whether visits changed, but whose changed most, since the pandemic hit the poor hardest and services shrank at the same time.

Before the pandemic, first crisis visits were more common among the most deprived residents, women, the youngest and oldest, and immigrants. When COVID arrived, visits fell, and the fall grew steeper with deprivation: the worse off the area, the bigger the drop. Age gaps in visit rates narrowed as middle-aged groups fell most. The authors read the pattern as unmet need, not improved health: those with the greatest barriers stayed away most, a warning for how services should reopen after a crisis.
plos-pone-0324405:
Lei Du and colleagues surveyed three hundred thirteen flight attendants at Tibet Airlines about leadership style and service quality. They studied spiritual leadership, a style built on vision, hope, and caring for staff, and asked whether it lifts the service passengers receive. Questionnaires measured leadership, how meaningful attendants found their work, how engaged they felt, and how well they served.

All four measures rose together. The chain of influence was clear: leadership fed a sense of meaningful work, which fed engagement, which fed service performance. Each link also helped on its own. Airlines compete on cabin service, so evidence that a values-driven leadership style pays off through staff meaning and energy has direct management value.
plos-pone-0332005:
José Paulo Rodrigues dos Santos and co-workers survey Swiss adults about cryonics, the practice of freezing a legally dead body in hope of future revival. Switzerland hosts a major facility, yet public views there were unmeasured. Their 2026 study asks close to two hundred fifty adults about awareness, ethics, and personal interest in signing up.

Most respondents backed the right to choose freezing when done to high medical standards, and few wanted legal bans. Personal interest stayed a minority taste, though about one in five reported real interest or intent. Wanting a longer life and prior familiarity drove openness more than age or gender. The snapshot shows a permissive public that mostly watches the practice from a distance.
plos-pone-0334305:
Kelly Ormond and colleagues surveyed a representative sample of nearly four thousand Swiss adults about gene editing as medical treatment. Presented with seven treatment options, only a small minority rejected editing outright, while about a third accepted every option. Support was strongest for curing life-threatening and seriously weakening diseases and fell as conditions became milder or later in onset.

Editing embryos drew less support than editing a patient's own body cells, and almost nobody endorsed editing to boost physical or mental abilities. Attitudes clustered into broad support and caution camps shaped by age, gender, religion, and knowledge. Switzerland may one day vote on such medicine, so a careful national snapshot shows where public consent actually stands.
plos-pone-0335005:
Sławomir Grzegorczyn, Paweł Dolibog, Iwona Dylong, and Andrzej Ślęzak studied flickers in electric current passing through bacterial cellulose membranes bathed in salt solutions. When the stronger solution sits above the membrane, the current pulses instead of flowing steadily, betraying swirling instabilities in the thin layers near the surface. The team analysed these pulses with Fourier techniques that separate rhythms over time.

Raising the concentration contrast increased the pulses' frequency and changed their strength, with signal power peaking at an intermediate contrast. A difference-signal method sharpened the picture further. Strong instability flared in the first fifty minutes at high contrasts, then faded. The work aids understanding of transport in membrane systems used in medicine and industry.
plos-pone-0336005:
Hilary Stewart and co-workers survey the United Kingdom's health service to map exercise and nutrition programs that prepare patients for cancer surgery. Such preparation, called prehabilitation, can speed recovery, but provision may be patchy and unfair. Their 2026 study asks every surgical organization whether it runs a service and gathers detail from those that do.

About two-thirds of responding organizations had a service, and those varied in nearly every way. Physiotherapists and dietitians staffed most teams. Roughly half tailored first assessments to patient traits that affect access, such as language or income. The map exposes a postcode lottery and gives commissioners a baseline for leveling up cancer surgery preparation.
plos-pone-0344505:
Yulei Wang and colleagues tested engineered bone grafts for large gaps in rabbit leg bones in 2026. Big missing bone sections do not heal alone, and grafts from a patient's own body are limited and costly to harvest.

Their graft used a mineral scaffold seeded with vessel forming cells, with an artery threaded through a channel in the middle. Rabbits were split among scaffold types, and scans and tissue checks ran for three months. The graft with both cells and artery grew the most new bone and vessels. Feeding a graft its own blood supply looks key to rebuilding long bones.
plos-pone-0347105:
Richard Spacek and colleagues tested whether freezing fluid from the womb changes a key test result. When waters break early before labour, doctors check the fluid for signs of swelling inside the womb. One marker, called IL-6, guides that call, but most cut points came from stored, frozen samples rather than fresh ones.

Records covered one hundred and fifty two women with early broken waters. Fresh and once frozen results tracked each other very closely, yet frozen samples read about one fifth higher on average. Using the frozen sample cut point on fresh fluid missed three cases. Care teams should treat fresh and stored values as close but not equal when they judge risk.
plos-pone-0347305:
Note on status: this text sets out a study plan, not finished results. Juliana Magalhães Chaves Barbosa and colleagues wrote the protocol. It appeared in PLOS ONE in 2026. The topic is Chagas cardiomyopathy, heart damage from long-term Chagas disease. The drug in focus is amiodarone. Doctors use it to steady the heart's rhythm in this disease.

The AMIO-CHAGAS study will track patients two ways. It will look back through past records. It will also follow patients forward over time. The team wants to know if the drug does more than calm rhythm. It may also cool immune activity. It may even act on the parasite itself. Proof of extra effects would boost a cheap, common drug.
plos-pone-0347605:
Nagendra P. Luitel and co-workers interview Nepali adults receiving care for depression or anxiety about how their illness feels and where they turned for help. Fewer than one in five people with such conditions in poorer countries get proper care, and culture shapes the path. Their 2026 study speaks with twenty-four patients across three districts using a guided illness-story interview.

People described fear, restlessness, sadness, and body complaints such as headaches and stomach trouble, often read as stress damage. Some told of detachment or memory gaps that led to panic or self-harm. Most went first to clinics or hospitals, some also to traditional healers. Schooling and caste steered choices. Care that hears the patient's own story may reach people sooner.
plos-pone-0348005:
Laouen Belloli and co-workers release a software library that measures how groups of three or more things interact, not just pairs. Many fields, from brain science to climate study, miss key behavior when they only look at pairs. Their 2026 paper tackles the twin problems of estimating shared randomness well and handling the huge number of group combinations.

Built on a popular computing toolkit, the library runs batches in parallel on standard or graphics hardware. Benchmarks show it outruns existing tools, and its shortcuts make large systems workable. Tests on brain scans from awake and deeply sleeping subjects showed it can capture real shifts in brain teamwork. The open tool puts group-level analysis within reach of smaller labs.
plos-pone-0348205:
Yahong Cai, Nalini Arumugam, and Yukai Chen tested a hands-on way of teaching career planning to college students. Instead of lectures, one group of students in their 2026 study worked through design thinking: empathising, experimenting, and prototyping their way toward career choices. A matched group of one hundred forty students in total received ordinary teacher-led guidance, and both groups were compared on confidence about career decisions.

Students in the design thinking group ended up clearly more confident and rated the course more valuable. Interviews traced the gain to practical skills practice, feeling emotionally empowered, and a stronger sense of identity. The authors recommend design thinking as a working model for career education in universities.
plos-pone-0348505:
Ya-En Catherine Lin and Fong-Ching Chang led a test of ad labels on social media. Teens are prime targets for stealth ads. The team split more than three thousand Taiwan high school students into three groups. Each group saw posts with a full sponsor label, a weak one, or none. Then the team gauged ad smarts and buying plans.

The full label group spotted the ads far more. They also grasped how ads work at a deeper level. Students who spotted ads held a more wary stance. That stance went with weaker plans to buy. The team says clear labels arm teens against hidden sales pitches.
plos-pone-0348605:
Gloria Guht and colleagues asked whether people born without wisdom teeth also grow slightly smaller other teeth. They measured the crown widths of every permanent tooth in three hundred and fourteen German orthodontic patients, eighty-nine of whom lacked at least one wisdom tooth from birth. They compared them with patients holding a full set of thirty-two teeth.

Patients missing wisdom teeth had measurably narrower crowns across the mouth, with the biggest gaps in second molars and the upper side incisors. In men every tooth ran smaller; in women most did. Missing wisdom teeth was equally common in both sexes. The pattern suggests the same developmental programme sizes the whole dentition, so a missing wisdom tooth may be one visible sign of a generally more delicate tooth-building plan.
plos-pone-0348705:
Madhu Golla and a large team built a capsule network, a vision architecture that tracks parts and wholes, to diagnose gallbladder disease from ultrasound images automatically. Reading these scans by hand is slow and varies between operators. Their tailored model, GBCapsNet, adds a custom routing method for sharper class separation and a calibration step that aligns the model's confidence with reality.

Scores under favourable splitting reached near perfection, but the authors flag the catch themselves: images from the same patient could sit on both sides of the split, inflating results. True patient-level separation and outside datasets are still needed before any clinical claim. Calibration did improve the honesty of the model's probabilities. The work stands as an early, carefully hedged exploration of capsule networks for this organ.
plos-pone-0348805:
Amlakie Aschale Alemu and colleagues taught deep learning models to sort Ethiopian legal documents into categories automatically, a pressing need as the country's digital legal records multiply. Legal language is dense and context-heavy, so the team layered attention mechanisms, which let a model focus on the words that matter most. These sat on several network designs that read text both as patterns and as sequences.

The strongest design, combining a pattern-reading network with a two-direction sequence reader plus self-attention, classified documents with accuracy above ninety-nine percent under two different testing schemes. The authors report consistent gains from adding attention across all the designs tried. They present the system as a step toward searchable, well-organised digital law for a legal system whose documents are rapidly moving online.
plos-pone-0348905:
Kristýna Krejčová and Fabio Ibrahim led a survey of Czech students. The topic was the impostor feeling: the fear of being a fraud despite real success. The team asked how that feeling links to self-compassion. Six hundred students filled in two standard surveys. The team then mapped how the parts of each trait connect.

Doubt about one's own skill tied most to two dark habits of mind. One is feeling alone in one's struggles. The other is drowning in bad feelings. These habits explained about a quarter of the doubt scores. The bright side of self-compassion mattered far less here. The team says aid should target the sense of being alone with one's flaws.
plos-pone-0349105:
Anna L Valentine and colleagues explored a puzzle in cancer genetics known as the RAD51 paradox. The protein RAD51 repairs broken DNA, and its loss should spell disaster, yet tumours show rampant chromosome chaos while almost never mutating RAD51 itself. The team suspected the protein's backup crew, its paralogues, spare copies that took over some of its jobs during evolution, and searched a large cancer mutation database for damage there instead.

Mutations in three paralogues did run high in human cancers. Few looked like classic cancer drivers, but many were predicted to damage or destabilise the enzymes, and three-dimensional modelling showed how some would warp the protein's structure. The authors argue the paradox eases if the repair crew, rather than its captain, is what cancer quietly breaks.
plos-pone-0349205:
Yuansheng Jiang and co-authors built an automatic grader for chrysoprase, a green gemstone whose price depends heavily on colour judged by eye. Human grading varies from person to person, so the team measured colour precisely for fifty-one stones with a light instrument. They generated hundreds of reference greens and taught several computer methods to sort stones into colour groups.

A simple statistical method and a neural network both scored near the top, and the team chose the simpler one because its reasoning is easy to follow and it runs fast. On a fresh set of real stones it sorted every stone correctly within this dataset. The authors offer the framework as a path toward fairer, repeatable grading for a trade built on subjective judgement.
plos-pone-0349305:
Yuan Sun and Bin Wen studied how government culture and tourism accounts on TikTok turn viewers into travelers. Surveying four hundred six followers, they modeled a chain from the account's content to the viewer's feelings to the intention to visit. Information quality and service quality were the starting points; the image of the destination and positive emotions carried the effect forward.

Good information raised travel intention directly and also indirectly, by improving the destination's image and warming emotions. Service quality had no direct effect but worked entirely through image and emotion, and the two-step chain through both was significant as well. The practical lesson for official accounts is sharp: polish information first, and treat service interactions as image building, not clerical replies.
plos-pone-0349405:
Isabel Vigmo and colleagues measured antibody levels in the blood of seven hundred fifty people with HIV, comparing those on effective treatment with those not yet treated. HIV often pushes the immune system to overproduce antibodies, a state called hypergammaglobulinemia, alongside chronic inflammation. Blood samples were checked for these antibodies and several inflammation markers.

Nearly every untreated group showed the excess, except people in the very earliest infection stage, and levels peaked in those with mid-range immune cell counts. Even among people whose virus was fully suppressed by treatment, about a quarter still had raised antibody levels. The persistence suggests treatment quiets the virus more completely than it calms the immune system.
plos-pone-0349505:
Guansheng Chen and co-authors investigated a protein called decorin in endometriosis, a painful condition where tissue like the womb lining grows outside the womb. A link between decorin and the condition was known, but its role was murky. The team mined single-cell and bulk gene data from patient tissue, then confirmed their findings with lab tests on cells.

Stromal cells, the supporting cells of the tissue, carried most of the decorin, and several stromal subtypes shifted in share within diseased tissue. Decorin levels ran clearly higher in endometriosis, high enough that the protein separated patients from controls well in two datasets. The protein also tracked with immune and scarring pathways. The authors propose decorin as a possible diagnostic marker and a handle for future drugs.
plos-pone-0349605:
Zhengda Yao, Juanjuan Zhang, and Dejun Kang surveyed more than five hundred teachers and school staff in Guangdong, China, to learn what keeps educators in their jobs. Their study sorts the forces into pulls that attract people to stay, such as training, pay, and having a real say. Pushes that drive people away include burnout and unhappy work.

Pulls raised the wish to stay, while pushes lowered it, just as the framework predicts. Feeling engaged at work strengthened the effect of training in particular. Only burnout behaved differently between public and private schools. The authors urge school leaders to pair fair material rewards with real attention to how engaged and supported teachers feel.
plos-pone-0349705:
Guangyu Zhang and colleagues measured how much fresh plant growth Tibetan grasslands produced each year from 2000 to 2022. Growth was split among the whole plant community and three plant types: sedges, grasses, and broad leaf herbs. Models separated the push of a changing climate from the push of human use like grazing and restoration.

Whole community growth dipped slightly overall, while sedges grew more and grasses and herbs fell back. Human action shaped more than half the plateau, climate about a fifth, and both together the rest. Maps varied sharply by place. Care for these high pastures must fit local plant mixes, since one rule for the whole plateau will miss what each patch needs.
plos-pone-0349805:
Mekuriaw Dereje Tekele and five colleagues publish a protocol in PLOS ONE in 2026 for a trial testing whether pharmacists can teach asthma patients their way to better control, in Ethiopia. The trial will run at a large specialised hospital's chest clinic. Patients will be assigned at random to usual care or to a structured education package: teach-back conversations, illustrated leaflets, and follow-up by phone and text message.

After three months, assessors who do not know the assignments will measure medication knowledge, inhaler technique, adherence, and asthma control. The design uses intention-to-treat analysis and explores whether some patient groups benefit more. Pharmacists are an underused teaching force in asthma care, and this trial tests their value rigorously.
plos-pone-0350005:
Jolien Arendsen, Guido M van Koningsbruggen, and Marieke L Fransen tested a popular claim from psychology: that reminders of death push people toward status purchases like luxury brands. Earlier work suggested the effect, but the mental route was unmapped. Their 2026 pair of studies first catalogued the beliefs people hold about status consumption, then exposed participants to a mortality reminder and measured how those beliefs and intentions shifted.

The reminder moved only two of twenty-nine beliefs, and it weakened the link between enjoying the experience and intending to buy. Crucially, buying intentions themselves did not budge at all. The authors conclude that whatever death reminders do to status thinking is too faint to change behavior, and that the effect may be far more limited than earlier research assumed.
plos-pone-0350105:
Tamara J Huizer and co-authors reviewed follow-up scanning for oesophageal cancer patients on nivolumab after surgery in 2026. The drug lowers relapse risk after chemotherapy, radiation, and surgery, yet relapse stays common and the best scan schedule was unknown.

Records from three Dutch hospitals covered one hundred fifty-one treated patients. About one in five relapsed during treatment, and routine scans caught two thirds of those relapses, most already spread. Survival free of disease fell steadily over the first year. The figures give teams a realistic picture of what scheduled scanning finds, and when, during this treatment.
plos-pone-0350505:
Byron Hernández-Ortiz and three colleagues hunt for bird species linked to avian influenza outbreaks in Brazil. Their 2026 study uses nationwide surveillance records gathered up to July 2025. The data cover more than eleven hundred records, one hundred twenty-seven species, and hundreds of municipalities. Finding the riskiest species helps officials aim limited monitoring effort.

Terns stood out sharply. Four tern species showed strong positive links with the highly pathogenic H5N1 virus. One, the Cabot's tern, was the single strongest predictor in the team's models. Adding location improved prediction further. Outbreaks clustered along Brazil's southeastern coast, exactly where dense poultry farming sits. Inland cases stayed scattered. Surveillance should therefore watch coastal tern colonies closely, since they appear to flag where spillover danger is highest.
plos-pone-0350805:
Tran Tuan Nguyen compared how three capital cities in Southeast Asia used their land between 2017 and 2024, in work published in 2026. Hanoi, Vientiane, and Phnom Penh are all growing fast, and the question was whether growth stayed compact or sprawled.

Land grew faster than population in all three cities. Phnom Penh spread the most yet stayed the most compact in shape, while Hanoi grew more loosely and Vientiane's growth looked scattered and random. The author links the contrasts to planning rules and investment choices. The method, built on a global city goal, can be reused in other fast-growing cities of the developing world.
plos-pone-0350905:
Ye and colleagues tested a skin cream made from DNA fragments on sun-damaged skin in a 2026 study. Sunlight breaks down the skin's support network, causing wrinkles and sagging. The team traced how the cream enters skin, which cell pathways it switches on, and how it performed against a standard retinol cream in a split-face trial.

Treated skin samples grew thicker surface layers and more collagen and elastic proteins. In the face trial, the new cream improved wrinkles, thickness, and eye bags about twice as much as retinol, with good tolerance. The results support the cream as a repair option for sun-aged skin, pending larger trials.
plos-pone-0351005:
Abuse of older people by the very relatives and helpers who care for them often stays hidden. Oludoyinmola Omobolade Ojifinni and Obioma C Uchendu built a short screening questionnaire for this problem in southwest Nigeria, reported in PLOS One in 2026, because existing tools were designed for other cultures.

They drafted questions from past research and talks with caregivers, covering neglect plus physical, emotional, money-related, and sexual harm. After expert review, more than eleven hundred caregivers answered the ten-item tool. Scores hung together well and matched related measures of caregiver strain and health. One weak spot was the sexual harm section, which the authors flag honestly.
plos-pone-0351305:
Jauharah Khudzari and colleagues compare in 2026 the fire risk of heated tobacco devices and lit cigarettes in Malaysia. A heat camera recorded surface warmth while products ran alone and while resting on common burnable materials. Tests took place under normal room conditions, with and without simulated puffing.

Lit cigarettes grew extremely hot and left burn marks on fabrics and dry matter. Heated devices stayed far cooler, well below the point where the tested materials would catch fire, and left no visible damage. Puffing raised cigarette heat but barely changed device heat. The authors still limit their claim to the products and conditions they tested.
plos-pone-0351405:
A gene switch helps doctors predict chemotherapy success in glioblastoma. Testing that switch today requires tumor tissue. Freddy Oulia and colleagues asked whether MRI scans could replace the biopsy. They used a public dataset of about five hundred eighty patients. Deep learning models read the scans. The study appeared in PLOS One in 2026.

The team ran nearly fourteen hundred model configurations. Single scan types competed against combined scans. Viewing planes, slice counts, and merge styles all varied. The best single-scan model reached only about sixty-five percent accuracy. Results stayed modest across the whole sweep. The authors conclude scan-based prediction is not clinic-ready. A needle-free test remains a hope, not a tool.
plos-pone-0351505:
Sian Calvert and a large team set out the plan for an updated review of what helps adults actually wear their hearing aids. Hearing loss is common, aids are the main treatment, and yet many fitted aids sit in drawers. This protocol describes, before the work begins, how the reviewers will search, judge, and pool trials of programs meant to raise regular use.

The review is framed by a behavior model that splits action into capability, opportunity, and motivation. Sorting past programs by which of those levers they pull should show which levers work. Because it is a protocol, no findings appear here. Its value is discipline: fixing the questions and methods in advance keeps the later review honest and lets clinics see which support styles deserve their money.
plos-pone-0352705:
Amy Palmer and seven colleagues check whether a widely used child mental health questionnaire makes sense to Indian teenagers, in this 2026 study from Karnataka. India urgently needs trustworthy youth mental health data, but the anxiety and depression scale in question was written for other cultures and had never been culturally validated there. Twelve adolescents aged thirteen to seventeen thought aloud as they answered each item, revealing where the wording stumbled.

Fourteen of the forty-seven items caused problems for at least three teenagers, with the obsessive-compulsive section faring worst. The authors discuss why particular phrases misfire, covering unfamiliar concepts and awkward phrasing, and propose reworded versions. This think-aloud step is the first stage of full validation, and the authors frame it as essential groundwork before the scale's scores can be trusted in Indian prevention programs.
plos-pone-0352905:
Amadeusz Jacek Miązek and Justyna Światowiec-Szczepańska published this 2026 study of how chief executives take risks. They measured whether bosses focus on gains or on avoiding losses by analyzing the language of shareholder letters from Warsaw-listed firms over a decade. They then matched that mindset to company risk choices and pay structures.

Gain-focused chief executives steered their firms into bolder risks, while loss-focused ones played safer. Pay design shifted both tendencies: steady salary cooled the bold, and bonuses pushed the cautious. The pair suggest boards tune pay packages to the individual chief executive's mindset.
plos-pone-0353105:
Zhai and colleagues, in a 2026 study, link exercise to the wish for children in China, where birth rates have fallen below replacement level. Money worries get most attention, but anxious minds may also hold people back. Drawing on a large national social survey from 2021, the team asked whether people who exercise more also want more children, and why.

More exercise went with stronger fertility intentions. Tracing the paths, exercise was tied to better mental well-being and to more social engagement, and both of those were tied to wanting children. The link was strongest among single people and among those with more education and income. The authors are careful to speak of association, not proof of cause, since the data are a one-time snapshot. Still, they suggest that public health support for body and mind belongs in any serious answer to low fertility.
plos-pone-0353205:
Wenfang Li, Xingchen Zhang, and Sen Cao present this 2026 PLOS One study on what makes a traffic crash in Changsha, China, likely to injure someone. Using nearly ten thousand crash records from 2017 to 2019, they combined built-environment features, grouped into five dimensions such as density and transit access, with crash-context factors like lighting. Three machine learning models were trained and the best was pried open to rank its influences.

Models using both kinds of information beat models using either alone, with the combined approach discriminating best. Distance to the nearest metro station, lighting, road density, and land-use mix ranked among the strongest factors. Farther metro access generally raised injury risk, while denser, more mixed neighborhoods lowered it. The authors frame built environment and crash circumstances as partners, not rivals, in explaining injury risk.
plos-pone-0353505:
Zhang, in a 2026 paper, designs a search engine for archive images that contain text, such as stamped official documents. Archives hold mountains of such pages, and finding one page by its content is hard when seals cover text, print blocks are tiny, and scans are noisy. Plain text reading misses how words and pictures relate.

The proposed system has five layers, from cleaning the image to matching a query. A scene graph step maps the elements on the page and how they relate. An attention step then fuses three kinds of features: the graph, the text, and links between image and text. On test data, the first returned result was right far more often than with a classic text-only method, including on pages with seal cover and tiny print. Each search answered in a small fraction of a second. Zhang presents the design as support for archives going online.
plos-pone-0353605:
C. K. Revathi and H. Santhi combine several layers of computer optimisation to sharpen heart-disease prediction, in this 2026 PLOS ONE study. Coronary artery disease, the narrowing of the heart's own arteries, is a leading killer, and deep-learning image models can spot it — if their settings are tuned well. The authors hybridised an optimiser inspired by hunting hawks with an automated tuning library, and adjusted the settings dynamically during training.

Applied to four image networks, the framework lifted accuracy sharply over the conventional version of the optimiser. One network reached the highest score, near ninety-eight percent, on their artery-narrowing dataset. Better-tuned models could one day support faster, more reliable screening of heart scans.
plos-pone-0354205:
Yang and Feng, in a 2026 study, use tracking data from four men's World Cups to see how the physical demands on footballers changed from 2010 to 2022. Two hundred twenty-five matches were analyzed, covering players from the five world confederations. Measures included total distance, top speed, sprinting, and low- and high-intensity running.

Top speed, sprint distance, and low-intensity running all rose across the period in every confederation, a shared global shift toward a faster game. Total distance and high-intensity running told regional stories instead. Total distance rose late in the period in Asia, Europe, and the Americas, but not in South America. High-intensity running fell in several confederations while barely changing in Africa. The authors conclude the modern World Cup asks more speed of everyone, while how much ground players cover still depends on regional styles of play.
plos-pone-0354305:
Reema Al-Daraiseh led a team of six authors on this 2026 study building a questionnaire about how mental health service users view artificial intelligence. More than four hundred people attending clinics in Jordan answered structured interviews while the team developed the tool and checked its consistency.

The result is a twenty-item questionnaire that measures perception of artificial intelligence reliably. Al-Daraiseh intends it for finding what shapes readiness to accept AI tools, so policymakers can see adoption barriers through patients' eyes. The team notes the same tool can now be tested in other populations and health systems.
plos-pone-0354605:
Ghalia Khoder led a team of eight authors on this 2026 laboratory study of a possible stomach cancer drug. The compound, NSC 57774, blocks SHP2, a signaling switch that stomach tumors often run at high levels. Using a stomach cancer cell line, the team tracked growth, movement, and several cancer signaling pathways after treatment.

The drug slowed cell growth and migration while sparing ordinary fibroblast cells, and it outperformed a commercial blocker and a standard chemotherapy drug in these dish tests. Khoder calls it a promising candidate that still needs animal and clinical testing.
plos-pone-0354705:
Guanglong Bao and six colleagues published this 2026 study of level design in Metroidvania games, where players explore large maps and unlock new routes. They turned the maps of three well-known games into networks, then measured where save points, teleport points, and boss encounters sit and how central those spots are.

The three games used their special points very differently. Save and travel points shifted from spread-out support toward late-game travel efficiency, while bosses stayed off to the side everywhere. Bao suggests network measures give designers a concrete way to judge and tune map layouts.
plos-pone-0354805:
Usama and colleagues, in a 2026 computer study, test whether chemicals made by a salt-loving bacterium could help maize grow under drought. Maize feeds much of the world, and dry spells cut its growth badly. Some soil bacteria help plants cope, but how their chemicals act inside the plant is poorly mapped.

The team docked bacterial chemicals, in simulation, into a maize enzyme that helps manage plant growth signals. Two bacterial compounds gripped the enzyme more tightly than two well-known plant hormones used as yardsticks. A long motion simulation, lasting two hundred nanoseconds of model time, showed the pairings stayed stable, held together by steady bonds. The authors are clear that this is all in silico, meaning done on a computer. The results nominate these bacterial chemicals for greenhouse and field tests, which alone can show whether they truly help crops in dry soil.
plos-pone-0354905:
Kyla Lee, Anna Gagliardi, and colleagues present in 2026 a study plan on how Korean immigrants in Canada share health decisions with family doctors. Earlier work on East Asian patients gave mixed results and rarely sampled with this group in mind. The planned interviews will be held in Korean or English, as each person prefers.

Twelve adults who moved under the economic stream and who see one doctor regularly will take part. Analysis will look for shared themes about care and about sharing choices, reported only in grouped, unnamed form. Recruitment was still open, so the document describes aims and methods rather than findings.
plos-pone-0355105:
Duyen Nguyen, Taehyeong Kim, and Junyoung Park combine in 2026 live experiments and computer simulation on how groups of mice escape under stress. Electric stimulus strength, an obstacle near the exit, guide walls at several angles, and group size were all varied. Escape time, speed, and spacing between mice were measured, and a validated agent model replayed and widened the conditions.

Obstacles and walls helped when groups were dense and stimulus was moderate, smoothing flow and cutting escape time, but hindered when groups were sparse or stimulus was extreme. Wide enough spacing between mice kept flow stable and prevented clogging at the narrow exit. The joined method validates well.
plos-pone-0355205:
Zhoujun Zhu and co-authors study in 2026 the pollen of a woody oil tree valued in Guizhou, China, building reliable tests for whether its pollen is alive and can sprout. Fruit yield and oil quality depend on good pollination, yet pollen testing for this tree lagged. Microscope work described pollen shape across family lines, and nine staining methods plus sprouting recipes were compared across two breeding lines.

Pollen kept a shared genus shape with clear variety between lines. Two stains separated living from dead grains best, and each line had its own best sprouting recipe in a growth mix. A two tier plan is proposed: one stain for precise lab work, another for quick field checks.
plos-pone-0355305:
Yinda Long and co-authors build in 2026 a physics based model that forecasts how long a phone battery will last. They used an open source phone as their test case and built the model in parts, covering the screen, chip, radio, and other uses. Heat effects on the battery were built in as well.

Across six common patterns of use, predicted run time ranged from about an hour under heavy load to more than a day when light. Chip use and room temperature drove fast drain most. Simple steps such as easing workload and screen use stretched heavy use time a lot in the model.
plos-pone-0355405:
Emily Zabor, Yağmur Seda Yeşiltaş, and Arun Singh ask how often doctors should scan the livers of patients treated for melanoma inside the eye, in this 2026 study. This cancer, uveal melanoma, tends to spread first to the liver, and catching spread early matters. At their center, a gene test sorts patients into low and high risk, with higher-risk patients scanned more often or with stronger imaging. The team modeled schedules from monthly to yearly against real outcomes.

Among roughly three hundred fifty patients, about one in five developed spread during follow-up. The analysis found yearly scans optimal for low-risk patients and scans every nine months optimal for high-risk patients, balancing detection delay against scan burden. Longer gaps were tied to larger lesions at detection. The authors offer the risk-tailored schedule as a framework for designing surveillance that is neither lax nor wasteful.
plos-pone-0355505:
Tahir Hussain and colleagues derive new exact solutions of Einstein's equations for cylinder-shaped universes filled with an imperfect, uneven fluid. Exact solutions are rare treasures in relativity because the equations resist direct solving. The team uses scaling symmetries of different sizes to organize the search. Then it reads off the matter content each geometry demands. It checks which solutions are empty. It checks which carry flowing matter, and which ripple like waves.

The family they build connects to classic models, including cylindrical waves, older static cylinders, and expanding models of Kasner type. Hussain and colleagues present the catalog as raw material for testing ideas about cosmic strings, gravitational waves, and how lopsided matter shapes spacetime over time.
plos-pone-0355605:
Ali Yalçın and co-authors address in 2026 how shoulder motion should be reported for children born with brachial plexus injury. Clinicians use a set of standard arm movements, yet labs describe the joint angles in different ways. The team rechecked motion sensor data from the uninjured arms of ten children.

Three common ways of ordering angle calculations were compared for jumps and for match with expected clinical values. One order caused locking problems in several movements, and no single order suited every movement best. The authors argue for movement specific reporting rules, so results from different studies can be compared with more trust.
plos-pone-0356005:
Yi Li and colleagues tested a simple blood-count score for predicting outcomes in advanced throat cancer behind the nose. Chemoradiation often suppresses blood cell production, but the combined effect across cell types was unclear. Their 2026 study scored several hundred patients by how many of three blood lines fell below normal.

Higher scores tracked with clearly worse survival and more spread of disease during about six years of follow-up. Patients with all three lines low faced far higher risks of death and distant spread than those with none low. The score added modest sorting power on its own. Li and colleagues suggest it can sit beside standard staging when judging a patient's risk.
plos-pone-0356105:
Saba Desta Tessema and six colleagues test a color-coded early warning chart for mothers in Ethiopian hospitals, in this 2026 quasi-experimental study. Most maternal deaths in Ethiopia are preventable if deterioration is caught early, yet warning charts are used inconsistently. More than eleven hundred obstetric inpatients at four public hospitals were split between two kinds of monitoring. One group used the chart, which grades vital signs, consciousness, bleeding, and other signs green, yellow, or red. The other received standard monitoring.

Charted patients triggered alerts nearly five hours sooner on average, were seen by a physician faster, and received interventions faster. They needed fewer ultrasound scans, left hospital about half a day earlier, and faced a meaningfully lower risk of severe maternal outcomes. The authors support wider use while calling for larger multi-cluster trials to confirm the effect across settings and risk groups.
plos-pone-0356205:
Ai Cui and colleagues lay out a trial plan, published in 2026, for testing whether a lung-scarring drug can prevent radiation harm in lung cancer care. Patients with advanced lung tumors that cannot be removed often receive combined drug treatment and radiation, and the radiation itself can inflame and scar the lungs. The drug nintedanib already treats one scarring lung disease, so the team asks whether it can also protect these patients.

Under the plan, a small group of patients at three centers in China will be split by chance. Half will take the drug around their radiation course. Half will receive standard care alone. Doctors will track lung injury, safety, and quality of life. Because no results exist yet, the value here is the careful design future findings will rest on.
plos-pone-0356305: Fielder and six co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE review on vaping during pregnancy. As a scoping review, it maps studies in both people and animals. The outcomes cover the mother, the unborn child, and the infant after birth. Pregnant people get mixed messages about vaping, so a clear map of what is known and unknown can guide honest advice.
plos-pone-0356505:
Likai Wu, Meina Zhang, and Wenzhe Wang combined two control ideas to make a cheap four-legged robot walk well. The first idea is biological rhythm generators that set each leg's beat. The second is a team of learning agents, one per leg, that nudge the rhythm to fit the ground. Their 2026 framework deliberately keeps the robot's onboard brain tiny. All four legs share one small policy network, run from simple body sensors.

In simulation and on a real low-cost robot, the system crossed obstacles, ramps, stairs, and rough ground. It did so more stably and efficiently than baseline controllers. Cameras, torque sensors, and motion capture stayed in the lab, not on the robot. The design points toward inspection and rescue robots that schools and small firms can actually afford.
plos-pone-0356605:
