Jason Johnson-Peretz and a large team report what patients and clinic staff thought of a flexible HIV care model in rural Kenya and Uganda. Their 2026 paper draws on the SEARCH trial, which served people whose work and travel make regular clinic visits hard to keep. The model let patients choose longer refill gaps, community pickup, and help when moving between clinics.

Interviews with patients and providers found every option welcome, with a discreet travel pack of medicine and supplies liked most. Longer gaps freed patients to focus on taking doses rather than chasing appointments. Poverty and hunger still blocked steady treatment, so participants asked for wider services, food or job help, and stronger supply chains.
plos-pone-0356905:
You Tang and coauthors published a 2026 proteomics study in PLOS ONE on a tobacco relative used to manufacture proteins in leaves, called plant molecular farming. Yields often disappoint because the plant's own protein-cutting enzymes chew up the product. Using deep protein measurement, they separated three stresses leaves face: infiltration, the bacteria delivering genes, and the burden of making a foreign protein.

Even plain buffer infiltration, usually treated as a neutral control, triggered cell-wall remodeling and oxidative stress on its own. Filtering that background out revealed a core bacterial response marked by a growth-versus-defense trade-off. Making a virus capsid precursor provoked a stronger, distinct wave of protein-cutting enzymes than making a simple glowing marker protein did. They also expanded the plant's known enzyme catalog to about fifteen hundred entries The cargo itself shapes the plant's defenses, they conclude, so strategies should be tuned per product.
plos-pone-0357005:
Md Ahosanul Haque Shahid and colleagues isolate and sequence the bacterium behind fowl cholera, a major killer of poultry, from layer birds. Knowing the local strain's resistance pattern and danger genes guides control. From dozens of suspect field samples the team confirmed a small set of type A isolates. Culture and gene tests did the confirming. The isolates then faced a panel of common antibiotics. One representative genome was sequenced in full.

The sequenced genome held the usual two thousand or so genes. It also held a set tied to sticking to hosts and dodging immunity. A predictor flagged possible risk to people. Isolates resisted several front-line drugs yet stayed sensitive to a handful of others, including common fluoroquinolones. Shahid and colleagues offer the profile for surveillance and vaccine planning.
plos-pone-0357205:
Irtaza Tahir and colleagues publish the plan for a systematic review asking whether adding immune therapy to radiation before surgery raises danger for patients with removable solid tumors. The combination is spreading fast in cancer care, and harm data are scattered across small studies. Their protocol searches major databases, trial registries, and conference records from the past decade for studies reporting severe side effects, treatment stops, deaths, and surgical complications.

Where studies allow, results will be pooled with random-effects models and split by tumor site and radiation style. The entry here is the protocol itself: no results yet, but a fixed, public recipe meant to keep the later review honest. Tahir and colleagues aim to give surgical teams a clear harm ledger for a popular new combination.
plos-pone-0357405:
Md Sadiq Iqbal and Mohammod Abul Kashem published a 2026 paper in PLOS ONE arguing that asking whether a text is human or machine-written is the wrong question. Forensics wants to know which model wrote it; universities want to know whether a human collaborated. Their system, SiBot, treats detection as source attribution across many classes. They built and released two benchmark corpora. One spans more than twenty AI sources; another models pure and human-AI hybrid writing.

On the harder many-source corpus, the best classical combination reached only middling accuracy, showing how tough attribution is. On the ten-class corpus, their hybrid design, blending word-frequency features with a transformer's contextual embeddings, scored above ninety percent, beating the strongest transformer alone by a wide margin. The framework is publicly deployed. Detectors, they say, must move from binary verdicts to graded, source-aware answers among hybrid drafts.
plos-pone-0357605: Danilovich and six co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE trial on walking as a cure for frailty in older adults. One group walked at a brisk pace; the other walked at a casual pace. Whole clusters of people were assigned together in this randomized trial. If brisk walking reverses frailty better, a cheap daily habit could help older adults stay strong and independent longer.
plos-pone-0357805:
Jessica Chen and colleagues published a 2026 qualitative study in PLOS ONE on what happened to people displaced by the huge 2022 floods in Lismore, in regional Australia. The study draws on online news coverage over the following two years. Rather than interviewing survivors, the team analyzed seventy-one news articles and then checked how closely the coverage matched the wider research literature on flood displacement and health.

The reporting tied displacement to trauma, distress, and a gnawing feeling of being in limbo while housing stayed unresolved. Articles traced families through emergency shelters, short-term fixes, and the hunt for long-term homes, including informal arrangements that official systems never record, and showed how each stage shaped health. Yet the most severely affected groups received little attention. The authors conclude the media captured the broad harm accurately but underplayed the worst cases, which matters because coverage steers where help and sympathy flow.
plos-pone-0357905:
Vigneswaran Ravi and three colleagues describe a computer model of the Hall effect in a 2026 PLOS ONE article. The Hall effect is the small voltage that appears across a conductor in a magnetic field, and it sits at the heart of many magnetic sensors. Exact formulas struggle once a device's shape, material, and metal contacts all matter at once, which is where their model comes in.

Working in the free program FreeFEM++, they simulate the effect with the finite element method and check the output against known analytical solutions. They then show how physical defects, which formulas cannot handle, change the readings, using a cross shaped graphene sensor as the worked example. The shared script doubles as a teaching aid and a research tool.
plos-pone-0358705:
Tekle Gebremeskel Ygzaw leads a team of eight following children treated for severe pneumonia in Tigray, Ethiopia, reported in PLOS ONE in 2026. Pneumonia remains one of the biggest killers of young children, and Ethiopia carries a heavy share of that burden. Knowing how long recovery takes, and what slows it, helps hospitals plan beds and follow up care. Prospective local data from Tigray's public hospitals were lacking.

The team tracked just over three hundred admitted children across two months, recording when each recovered. About eighty-five percent recovered, with the typical child well again in five days. Statistical models then separated the factors tied to faster or slower recovery from background noise. Findings like these let regional clinicians counsel families realistically and flag the children who need closer watching during admission.
plos-pone-0359105: Heron and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on a urine test tied to a risky pregnancy condition. Preeclampsia raises blood pressure and can harm mother and baby. The team analyzed bits of DNA in urine that come from kidney cells. If kidney DNA in urine flags the condition early, a simple sample could help doctors watch high-risk pregnancies more closely.
plos-pone-0359205: Islam and six co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on what people eat in Bangladesh at each stage of life. They mapped food consumption patterns from childhood to old age. They also checked whether diets at each stage supply enough nutrients. Gaps found at a given age can guide food aid and advice aimed at that stage rather than at everyone at once.
plos-pone-0359405:
Zihui Liu and eight colleagues wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on esophageal cancer. The cancer studied is squamous cell carcinoma of the food pipe, tested in cell cultures and in TE-1 xenografts, tumors grown in animals. The treatment under study is Shenling Qige Granules, a traditional Chinese medicine preparation.

As the title states, the granules inhibit the cancer's progression in these models by acting on a chain of molecular signals that runs from DCN through TGF-β to Smad. Showing a mechanism, not just an effect, helps judge whether a traditional remedy deserves clinical testing. Researchers working where traditional and modern cancer medicine meet are the audience.
plos-pone-0360005:
Tharun Tom Oommen and a large clinical team studied in 2026 a blood signal that may help predict outcomes for patients hospitalized with cirrhosis, advanced scarring of the liver. The signal is interleukin-6, a messenger of inflammation, measured on admission. The authors describe it as a time limited and cause dependent prognostic signal: it carries information about the near future, and its meaning shifts with what caused the liver disease.

Their cohort study analyzes the data two ways, with standard frequentist statistics and with Bayesian methods that weigh prior knowledge openly. A cheap admission blood test that sharpens prognosis could help doctors triage scarce intensive care and speak more honestly with families about what lies ahead.
pmc-13195405:
Mayasah Al-Nema is first author on a 2026 review of computer methods for finding drugs against flaviviruses. This virus family includes Zika, dengue, West Nile, and yellow fever. These viruses infect millions yearly, mostly in tropical regions. Good antiviral treatments remain limited despite vaccine and therapy progress.

The review maps the viruses' protein targets. Some are outer structural proteins, and seven are inner working proteins. It then surveys computer methods that predict a candidate's activity and toxicity from its chemical structure. Recent examples and new trends are highlighted. Frequent mutation breeds resistance, the authors note, so robust strategies matter. Challenges and future directions for faster, computer-guided drug discovery close the review.
pmc-13202205:
Sows pass protection against a deadly piglet diarrhea virus through colostrum, and a 2026 study from Ping Chen tracks those antibodies across many sample types. The research article follows responses to porcine epidemic diarrhea virus in infected pigs and in pregnant sows under different immunization strategies on commercial farms.

Antibody tests showed piglets seroconverted one week after infection, peaked within three weeks, and stayed detectable for up to thirty-one weeks afterward. In more than a thousand sow samples, blood antibody levels correlated strongly with colostrum levels, most tightly on the day of farrowing. Mouth and rectal swabs also tracked colostral antibody of one class, offering easier ways to judge maternal immunity.
pmc-13202305:
A childhood lung infection that destroys tissue nearly killed a five-year-old in a 2026 case report by Hani Abu-Hijleh from Palestine. The article describes a previously healthy girl whose illness first looked gastrointestinal before becoming necrotizing pneumonia linked to influenza, then sudden bleeding into the chest cavity.

Her course grew harder with drug-related kidney injury that required temporary dialysis, while bacterial cultures stayed puzzlingly negative throughout. Surgeons performed an urgent chest operation and removed the destroyed lung tissue, after which she recovered fully. The authors highlight how quickly this infection can escalate, and how timely surgery within multidisciplinary care can save a child's life.
pmc-13206905:
Allergy may shape how children fare long after COVID, and a 2026 questionnaire study by Giulia Brindisi explores that question in Rome. Families attending a pediatric allergy clinic at Umberto I Hospital noted infections, vaccination, lingering symptoms, and how allergic diseases changed once pandemic restrictions ended.

Two hundred fourteen surveys were analyzed for the study's comparisons. Allergy itself was not tied to catching the virus, but among infected children it came with clearly higher odds of Long COVID symptoms. Severe initial illness raised those odds further, while full vaccination lowered the odds of infection overall. After restrictions lifted, most allergic children reportedly had worse hay fever.
pmc-13212405:
Taiane Campos Braga de Assis and co-authors address, in 2026, gaps in hourly carbon monoxide readings from an air monitor in Salvador, Brazil. Missing stretches arise from power cuts, calibration, and transmission faults, and they weaken pollution records used for policy.

The team hid real data in artificial gaps lasting one to three days, then tested three models at filling them in. A boosted-tree model scored slightly best on error measures, though recurrent neural networks described more gaps consistently, and neither lead was statistically firm. Filled values showed no systematic bias and kept the series' daily and seasonal patterns, supporting model-based repair of monitoring records.
pmc-13212705:
Hongzhi Xiong and colleagues demonstrate in 2026 a chip that stretches a pulse of light into a rainbow spanning ultraviolet-C to mid-infrared wavelengths. Such broad spectra help probe molecules directly, but chip devices had never reached so deep into the ultraviolet.

The team built waveguides from lithium tantalate, a crystal prized for transparency and strong nonlinear response, with finely patterned domains that vary along their length. Their device reached below 270 nanometres at one end and 2400 nanometres at the other, using very low pulse energy. Covering more than three octaves on one chip opens paths toward compact ultraviolet light sources for spectroscopy and precision measurement.
pmc-13213105:
Bushra Elhusein and co-authors present in 2026 a woman in her fifties who heard voices for more than three years despite having no psychotic illness. Her hearing loss in both ears, from damaged inner-ear nerves, starved her brain of sound and likely generated the experiences.

Brain scans looked normal, she kept clear insight and functioned well, and several antipsychotic medicines barely helped. Hearing aids improved her sound input, yet the hallucinations continued, showing that such symptoms may not switch off once hearing is corrected. The authors warn that sensory causes are often missed, leading to needless psychiatric treatment, and they call for early hearing checks plus teamwork across specialties.
pmc-13213605:
Mohannad N. AbuHaweeleh and co-authors present in 2026 a case of brucellosis, an animal-borne infection, settling in one testicle of a camel and goat handler. The disease mimics many others, so genital involvement is easily missed or misread.

The 32-year-old man arrived with fever, aches, fatigue, and a lip ulcer, while early examination found little. Blood tests showed anaemia and inflammation, antibody tests pointed to brucella, and cultures confirmed the species. A scrotal scan showed an enlarged, overactive testicle and cord structures. Side effects first undermined his antibiotic course, yet after completing treatment his symptoms and laboratory values improved. He left hospital on two antibiotics with close follow-up planned.
pmc-13215205:
Jianyu Zhou and co-authors borrow in 2026 the armadillo's party trick for soft machines: a skeleton that curls into a protective ball when danger appears. Soft robots deform beautifully but usually stay fragile, the very softness that helps them move leaving them exposed.

Their module layers a segmented outer shell over an interlocking inner frame, echoing the animal's double skeleton. A muscle-like polymer skin drives curling, rolling, and grasping when a sensing layer detects a threat and heats it locally. The structure shrugs off impacts, punctures, and concentrated loads while carrying fragile cargo. Wireless control frees it for hazardous places. Morphing and armour, usually traded against each other, arrive together here.
pmc-13216105:
Hannah S Jesani and co-authors present a 2026 national survey of robotic chest surgery training across the United Kingdom and Republic of Ireland. Robotic operating is spreading fast, but nobody had mapped what trainees actually get to do.

Eighty-two trainees from all 14 training regions answered. Robotic surgery ran in 71 percent of their units, yet only 16 percent of those units had a structured training program. Over half of respondents had never fully performed a robotic procedure themselves. Most wanted more robotic training before finishing. Barriers included idle dual consoles, exposure limited to bedside assisting, and scarce simulator access. The authors call for national standards with staged, competency-based progression.
pmc-13216305:
Markus Mergen and co-authors present a 2026 study testing whether a general-purpose language model can sort cancer scan reports into standard tumour response categories by itself. The model ran entirely offline inside hospital infrastructure, which keeps patient data private.

The team fed 142 real CT reports, with their expert labels hidden, to a locally hosted LLaMA-3.3 model using three prompting styles. Simple zero-shot and example-based prompts already performed strongly. Asking the model to reason step by step worked best, reaching a micro F1 score of 0.81 against expert labels across the five RECIST categories. The authors see prompt-guided offline models as a scalable way to standardize response assessment without sending data outside the hospital.
pmc-13218105:
Emma Huijs and co-authors present the PEARL study in a 2026 protocol, a randomized trial of lifestyle treatment for endometriosis pain. Hormonal drugs for this condition often work only partly, cause burdensome side effects, and interfere with fertility, while surgery carries a real risk of complications. Many women are turning to lifestyle approaches, but solid evidence for them is thin.

The five-arm Dutch trial will enroll 250 premenopausal women, 200 with endometriosis and pain plus 50 healthy controls. Women with endometriosis are assigned to standard care alone, standard care with an anti-inflammatory diet, standard care with cognitive behavioral therapy, or both additions together. The diet is expected to calm immune activity and inflammation, while the therapy targets pain mechanisms and coping and should help dietary changes stick. Outcomes center on pain and health-related quality of life, measured around hospital visits at the start and end of the intervention period.
pmc-13220905:
Mayank S. Kotadia and co-authors recount a 2026 case in which glue used to treat stomach varices later complicated a liver transplant. Their 62-year-old patient had cirrhosis, a shunt inside the liver, and clots spreading from that shunt toward the heart and into the splenic vein. Such clots once ruled out transplantation for many patients.

Surgeons removed the shunt, cleared the clots mechanically, and completed the transplant successfully. The report walks through the planning that balanced bleeding risk against clotting risk in a patient whose blood system was unstable. It shows that even extensive clots in this setting need not end transplant hopes when specialist teams coordinate care.
pmc-13221905:
Bijaya K Behera and co-authors study heart dysfunction in liver cirrhosis and its link to disease severity, in a 2026 hospital study from Cuttack, India. Between April 2023 and June 2024, 103 patients received heart ultrasounds, electrocardiograms, and laboratory tests. Cirrhosis severity was graded with the Child-Turcotte-Pugh scale, and alcohol caused most cases.

Diastolic dysfunction, a stiffening of the heart's filling phase, was the commonest abnormality and grew more frequent as liver severity worsened. Pumping function stayed preserved in most patients. Electrical changes such as a lengthened QT interval appeared in a subset. The authors note alcohol itself may contribute to the heart findings, so severity links need cautious reading.
pmc-13222605:
Dayong Xia and co-authors test a blended teaching method for neurosurgery residents, in a 2026 education study at Wannan Medical College. Sixty trainees in formal residency training were split evenly: one group learned through case-based lessons, scenario simulation, and flipped classrooms combined, while the other received traditional teaching. A varied scoring system compared the two.

The blended group reported higher approval of teaching arrangements. Their scores ran higher in surgical skills, theory examinations, and case analysis pass rates. Self-rated benefit also favored the blended group across all three measured dimensions. Given the field's speed and risk, the authors recommend wider adoption of the integrated approach in clinical teaching.
pmc-13223805:
Yukun Li and co-authors pair a KRAS-blocking drug with an autophagy inhibitor against pancreatic cancer carrying the G12C mutation, in a 2026 study spanning cell and animal experiments. Sotorasib was developed for this exact mutation, yet pancreatic tumors have rarely been its target. Pancreatic cancer still kills most patients within years, with five-year survival near ten percent.

The team reports that sotorasib switches on a protective self-eating process, autophagy, early in treatment, which blunts its killing power. Adding 3-methyladenine, a blocker of that early autophagy step, strengthened the antitumor effect in their models. The combination, they argue, deserves development as a strategy for this hard-to-treat mutation group.
pmc-13224005:
Shiyao Han and colleagues build a 2026 single-cell atlas of early ovary development in female cattle, then compare it with goats and pigs. Gene activity was measured cell by cell from the stage when sex is determined through the first formation of follicles. The comparison aims to separate shared mammalian programmes from traits specific to each livestock species.

Major germ cell and supporting cell groups emerged, and germ cells followed conserved stages involving retinoic acid response and the start of meiosis. Goats progressed through meiosis more slowly than cattle or pigs. Signalling between cells also differed, with certain retinoic-acid-linked pathways active in cattle and pigs but absent in pre-meiotic goat tissue.
pmc-13224705:
Shuaijie Pei and colleagues apply a 2026 data-mining approach to sepsis, hunting for genes tied to cellular senescence, the worn-out state cells enter under stress. Sepsis can push cells into that state and worsen organ damage, yet marker genes and matching drugs were unknown. Bioinformatics screening and machine learning narrowed the field to eight standout genes.

Those genes separated septic from healthy samples well, and six behaved consistently in validation data and laboratory samples. Immune-cell patterns tracked closely with the gene set. A drug database pointed to compounds acting on three of the genes, and one candidate, fenofibrate, reduced senescence and inflammation in cell and animal models of sepsis-related kidney injury.
pmc-13227005:
Rola Kwayess and co-authors compare a 2026 set of choices for hormone monitoring during parathyroid surgery at a Beirut hospital. Removing an overactive parathyroid gland cures the common disorder behind high blood calcium, and surgeons check hormone levels mid-operation to confirm success. Sixty-eight cured patients had samples drawn from both a central and a peripheral vein, each tested with two generations of assay.

Newer third-generation assays and central sampling each gave higher readings than their counterparts. Even so, the share of patients meeting the standard success rule, a hormone drop of at least half, did not differ by assay or sampling site. The newer assay fell more steeply and consistently, leading the authors to suggest assay-specific thresholds could sharpen decisions.
pmc-13227205:
Alejandro J Friedman and co-authors report a 2026 first published case of a finger pulley tearing without any injury, in a 27-year-old woman with ulcerative colitis. Pulleys are small bands that hold finger tendons against the bone, and climbers usually tear them through force. She presented with pain, loss of function, and a finger stuck bent at ninety degrees at the middle joint.

Imaging showed the A3 pulley of her right index finger had ruptured, letting the deep flexor tendon bowstring away from the bone. No trauma preceded it, implicating her inflammatory bowel disease, which is known to attack joints and tendons. Coordinated conservative care plus adjustment of her anti-rheumatic medication partly straightened the finger and restored pain-free use.
pmc-13229305:
Rodney N. Nagoshi, Ashley E. Tessnow, and Robert L. Meagher describe a 2026 pair of new genetic markers for telling apart the two host strains of the fall armyworm. This moth's caterpillars devastate corn and other crops across the Americas and, since 2016, Africa and beyond. The corn and rice strains look identical, and strain identification has rested on variants in a single gene, leaving population studies on shaky ground.

Two additional markers now back up that lone test. Their data support earlier conclusions that strain identity is anchored in the sex chromosome, which diverges as one unit, and they quantify how differently the two strains are evolving. Better strain tracking sharpens forecasts of this pest's global movements and host choices.
pmc-13233205:
Danilo Češljarac and colleagues published a 2026 narrative review of short screening tools that flag vulnerable older adults in emergency and acute hospital care. Older patients face higher risks of functional decline, delirium, falls, and early death, yet full geriatric assessment rarely happens at admission because time is short. The review gathers instruments that take only minutes to complete.

Tools such as ISAR, TRST, PRISMA-7, and APOP predict decline, readmission, or short-term mortality with moderate accuracy. Wider instruments add prognostic detail that helps discharge planning. The authors favor a two-step model: quick screening at the door, then a fuller assessment on the ward, with results tied to actions like early mobilization and medication review.
pmc-13233905:
Chan-in Sio and colleagues published a 2026 study of MetaCourt, a virtual reality courtroom for training court interpreters. Fair trials depend on them, yet traditional training is passive and short on live practice. The team designed the immersive environment with trainee input, framing the design around self-determination theory and a player-experience model of needs satisfaction. Twenty-one undergraduates in the field then tested it against conventional digital methods.

Students interpreting in virtual reality spoke more fluently, while accuracy stayed level with the traditional approach. Users reported strong feelings of autonomy, intuitive controls, and presence in the scene, plus lower mental workload than expected. The authors present MetaCourt as the first court interpreting trainer built on this motivation framework and a promising route to more engaging practice.
pmc-13234205:
Dhika Dharmansyah and colleagues published a 2026 mixed-methods systematic review on why older adults in Asian low- and middle-income countries accept or reject assistive health technology. Devices and apps for ageing at home are spreading, yet uptake stays low, and standard acceptance models were built in Western settings. Following a pre-registered protocol, the team searched four databases and kept only studies that examined culture directly; six qualified.

Five cultural themes organized the evidence. Family duty and filial piety could enable adoption or block it, stigma and concern for face discouraged use, and collectivist norms shaped choices. Trust in traditional health beliefs mattered, and digital literacy gaps were themselves cultural. Study quality was good across designs. The authors conclude that technology programs ignoring these forces will keep missing older Asian users.
pmc-13234405:
Isaac Allen and a large group of collaborators estimated in 2026 the risk of a second cancer in the opposite breast for women carrying inherited gene variants. They combined data from two large cohort projects on breast cancer genetics. Genes covered were BRCA1, BRCA2, PALB2, CHEK2, and ATM. Dutch population risks helped convert relative effects into ten-year cumulative risks.

Ten-year risks for cancer in the other breast reached roughly ten percent for BRCA1 and BRCA2 carriers. Estimates were lower for the other genes, with ATM carriers near four to five percent. Hazard ratios were clearly raised for BRCA1, BRCA2, and CHEK2 carriers in the pooled analysis. No clear rise appeared for PALB2 or ATM overall, though hormone receptor status of the first cancer changed the picture. The numbers can support counselling about preventive surgery and follow-up.
pmc-13235005:
Michael Peddle and a large expert panel set out in 2026 agreed best practices for giving blood before hospital arrival in Canada. A national summit in 2025 gathered more than fifty specialists from eight provinces and several transport services. Canada's huge distances, harsh weather, and varied regional systems complicate any single method. Talks covered when to start transfusion, which products to prioritize, logistics, and remote care.

Red blood cells and a clot-supporting drug called tranexamic acid formed the foundation in the consensus. Freeze-dried plasma and whole blood offered useful advantages, mainly far from hospitals. Other concentrates can substitute when plasma is unavailable in the panel's view. Calcium replacement and preventing body cooling were stressed as vital companions. Twelve consensus statements resulted, plus a call for a standard national dataset and registry.
pmc-13235505:
Md Zainul Ali, Manjari Kiran, and Pankaj Singh Dholaniya searched in 2026 for genes tied to loss of smell in Parkinson's disease. Smell problems often appear years before movement symptoms in this brain disorder, making them attractive early signals. Machine learning first ranked non-motor symptoms for separating patients from healthy people. Blood gene activity data were then mined for patterns linked to smell dysfunction.

Smell dysfunction emerged as the most discriminatory non-motor feature in the classification work. Nine non-motor symptoms carried the greatest weight for disease prediction overall. Thirty-two genes linked to both smell status and disease status in the blood data. Groups of those genes overlapped with pathways central to Parkinson's biology in the analysis. Changes specific to monocytes, a blood immune cell type, added another link between smell loss and disease.
pmc-13237305:
Tiffany Tavares and co-authors argued in 2026 that training for head and neck pathologists must change now that artificial intelligence shares diagnostic decisions. AI tools promise accuracy and speed in tissue, imaging, and molecular work-ups, yet they can amplify human biases and invent new error types. The authors build their framework on national pathology training milestones and on decision science.

Their central claim is that AI moves uncertainty around rather than removing it. Automation bias, overconfidence, and anchoring can bend judgment when clinicians accept machine output uncritically. Training should therefore rest on three skills: AI literacy, diagnostic skepticism, and ethical transparency. The goal is doctors who use the tools hard while keeping final judgment unmistakably human.
pmc-13238505:
Thakore and colleagues watch two notorious proteins misbehave together in a new mouse model of brain disease. Clumping of alpha-synuclein and amyloid-beta proteins marks Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, and Lewy body dementia. Each protein twists into amyloid fibres that upset the cell's balance, yet in real patients they often appear together, possibly feeding each other's damage.

The team built mice carrying the human forms of both proteins. They then tracked the earliest amyloid formation and the brain's inflammatory response that follows. Catching the partnership at its start could reveal which protein moves first, and where a future drug might break the chain before symptoms begin.
pmc-13239805:
Subadra Wanninayake and co-authors examine diagnostic delay in a rare inherited metabolic disorder in a 2026 British study. Classical homocystinuria, caused by a faulty enzyme in methionine processing, can damage eyes, bones, blood vessels, and the brain, and early treatment prevents much of that harm.

Two specialist centres reviewed fifty-nine adults with enough records for detailed analysis. Thirteen were found through newborn or family screening, while others presented with symptoms first. In a delayed subgroup the wait between first signs and diagnosis stretched to a median of seven years. A dislocated eye lens was the commonest first clue, and a third of symptomatic patients already had two or more complications.
pmc-13240005:
Julia Marchenko and colleagues ask why subarctic blue mussels remain scarce despite warming seas in a 2026 long-term study. Mussels returned to Spitsbergen after a thousand-year absence, heralding Arctic warming, so the team expected thriving populations along Russia's Murman Coast as well.

One monitored population showed warmth helping young mussels recruit and survive. Historical biomass records from sixty-two sites told another story, with abundance high until the 1960s, then collapsing tenfold during a cold spell. Recovery since has been partial and unrelated to temperature. The authors blame lasting effects of the crash, including sparse populations struggling to reproduce and competition with an invading sister species.
pmc-13240905:
Jo and Ahn in Seoul modeled what shapes job satisfaction and well-being among solo workers. Their data came from the Sixth Korean Working Life Survey of 2020. 12,703 people fed a path model. Digitalization, autonomy, work-life balance, engagement, and burnout were the five moving parts.

New tech and automation raised tech anxiety sharply. Leadership freedom lifted job satisfaction yet eroded well-being. Work bleeding into life hurt both outcomes and tracked with burnout, while engagement and contentment supported well-being. Surprisingly, overtime work tracked with higher contentment and well-being in this group.
pmc-13241005:
Qiuju Yang and co-authors present a 2026 retrospective study of brucellosis in southwestern China across two decades. This bacterial disease spreads between animals and people and has been returning to the region. The team combined case records, trend analysis, mapping, and blood surveys of people and livestock.

Cases rose steadily over the period, with most reported in Yunnan. Blood testing of tens of thousands of people found a notable share with signs of past or current infection. Sheep and goat results tracked the human pattern closely. Cases shifted from scattered to clustered, forming clear hot spots. One bacterial type dominated, carried by two widespread genetic lines. Coordinated regional control is the authors recommendation.
pmc-13241505:
Vulinovic's team at Lübeck probed why dopamine neurons die first in Parkinson's disease. Lab-grown cultures were sorted into pure dopamine-making and other neurons using a glowing tag. Cells came from healthy controls and Parkin variant carriers. Mitochondrial function and gene activity were compared across all groups.

Dopamine neurons ran lower mitochondrial voltage than their neighbors. In Parkin carriers, their mitochondria shrank and energy output fell while dopamine itself built up to toxic levels. Two other Parkinson's genes shifted activity just in these neurons. The trio's interplay under stress may explain the selective death.
pmc-13241805:
Jiao Wang and Chunyu Zhou report a 2026 study of digital technology in teaching surgical procedures to medical students. Digital change has reshaped medical education, yet surgical teaching still struggles to join theory with hands-on skill. The authors surveyed students after a digitized surgical course.

Nearly three hundred students answered the questionnaire. Large shares reported clear gains in surgical theory mastery. Skill scores for laparoscopic technique and anatomy recognition were both high on a five-point scale. Most students said they were satisfied or strongly satisfied with the digital methods. The authors conclude that digital tools raised teaching efficiency and skill levels in their course. They propose the model as a path for practice-focused medical training.
pmc-13242105: Mohan and colleagues, writing across London, Karachi, Brazil, Calgary, and Boston, argue in an editorial that child and adolescent mental health training needs a shared global curriculum. Their proposed GC-CAMH framework answers a worldwide shortage of specialists equipped for young people's mental health. The piece contends the world cannot wait for piecemeal national efforts. It appears in Child and Adolescent Psychiatry and Mental Health in 2026.
pmc-13242205:
Amornrat Deeboonno and co-authors present a 2026 qualitative study of how pregnant women in Thailand use online health information. Digital literacy shapes whether mothers-to-be benefit from internet resources or fall for misinformation. Interviews explored searching, judging, and applying pregnancy information in daily life.

Twenty women, pregnant or recently delivered, from urban and suburban hospitals took part. Most searched through Google, YouTube, and Facebook. Participants could find information readily, yet they worried about source credibility, privacy, and hard medical wording. They asked for Thai-language resources that are simple to use and endorsed by trusted national health bodies. The authors urge providers and institutions to build and promote reliable digital materials rather than leaving women to navigate alone.
pmc-13242405:
Koray Özşeker and colleagues at Karadeniz Technical University studied toxic metals in reservoir sediments in northeastern Türkiye, publishing their findings in Environmental Geochemistry and Health in 2026. They took samples of the top sediment layer in three dam reservoirs: Borçka, Deriner, and Torul. Rather than testing each sample as one bulk mix, they split it into four grain-size fractions and measured five metals in each.

The finest particles held by far the most metal, with copper, lead, and zinc passing sediment safety thresholds in several cases. Levels fell steadily as grain size grew, and autumn samples ran higher than spring ones. Borçka was the most contaminated reservoir, a pattern the authors link to mining inputs nearby. They argue that bulk testing can miss these fine-grain hotspots, so risk checks should treat each fraction separately.
pmc-13242505:
A. M. Al Sabagh and colleagues turned waste cooking oil into cleaning agents that help squeeze extra crude from rock. Their study appeared in Scientific Reports in 2026. Used cooking oil is both a disposal problem and a cheap renewable raw material. The team synthesized two surfactants from it, one aromatic and one oily in character, and blended them with a helper alcohol for tests in a sand-pack model of a reservoir.

The blends sharply lowered the tension between oil and water and turned rock surfaces from oil-loving to water-loving, as shown by contact angle drops. Flooding tests recovered the most oil at a mid-range salt level and moderate heat. The best blend, combining both surfactants with the co-surfactant, recovered close to four-fifths of the oil in place. The results tie the molecules' structure to their performance underground.
pmc-13242805:
Ruofan Wang and co-authors report a 2026 case of a severe burn wound infection caused by an uncommon environmental bacterium. A 71-year-old farmer with diabetes burned her lower leg badly with a home moxibustion patch, then treated the wound herself. Such patches are popular for home pain care, yet reduced feeling in diabetic legs makes deep burns easy to miss.

Culture of wound fluid identified Pseudomonas oryzihabitans, an opportunist common in soil and water. Antibiotics were chosen to match the laboratory sensitivity results. Surgery cleaned the wound, suction therapy prepared it, and a skin graft closed it. Infection markers fell sharply, healing was good, and no recurrence followed. The authors credit the combined microbe-guided and surgical approach.
pmc-13243205:
Ilaria Righi and co-authors compare three ways to remove the thymus gland in a 2026 surgical study. The gland sits in the chest, and surgeons now reach it through small cuts rather than opening the breastbone. Care can use a camera alone or one of two robot systems.

The study covers 90 patients treated at one large center between 2016 and 2025. Thirty had camera surgery, and sixty had robot help split across the Da Vinci and Versius systems. Robot patients left the hospital about a day sooner, while pain, tube time, and complications stayed similar. Surgeons also settled into the robot methods faster, though Versius felt more demanding to use.
pmc-13243505:
Jinyoung Jeong and co-authors weigh published findings on low-calorie sweeteners and health in a 2026 umbrella review. Sweeteners replace sugar in many drinks and foods, yet their long-term effects remain disputed. The review pools prior meta-analyses rather than single studies to see the whole field at once.

The team reanalyzed 29 meta-analyses covering more than 50 million people in total. In observational data, higher intake of non-sugar sweeteners tracked with more weight gain, diabetes, and high blood pressure. Trial data told a softer story and at times pointed the other way. Quality ratings varied widely across the pooled reviews. The authors urge care in reading pooled claims about sweeteners.
pmc-13243705:
Yiyang Shen, Xiaofei Jiao, and Yuanjia Wen reviewed how recent clinical trials are changing the treatment of gynecologic cancers. Their review appeared in Cancer Innovation in 2026. Care has shifted toward specialist-led combinations of surgery, drugs, and radiation, yet surgeons still face hard calls in the operating room, and drug resistance and toxicity limit medical therapy. The authors sort the newest trial evidence by cancer site and strategy.

In early cervical cancer, sentinel node biopsy now looks like a safe stand-in for full lymph node removal, sparing patients much harm. In advanced ovarian cancer, upfront debulking surgery beat chemotherapy-first approaches in fit patients at expert centers. Immune therapy gains ground through paired checkpoint drugs and triple regimens, while antibody-drug conjugates aimed at two tissue targets produced lasting responses in selected patients. The review maps where precision is genuinely replacing routine.
pmc-13244505:
Ayuko Yamashita and colleagues checked whether two kidney risk scores, built in Europe, predict outcomes for Japanese patients with ANCA-associated kidney inflammation. Their validation study appeared in Renal Failure in 2026. They gathered 109 biopsy-proven patients from thirteen institutions in Nagasaki Prefecture, treated between 1995 and 2019. Both the original 2018 score and its 2024 revision sorted patients into risk bands, which were then tested against who reached end-stage kidney disease.

Both scores worked: renal survival worsened step by step as risk band rose, with highly significant separation. The revised score discriminated slightly better, with an area under the curve of 0.82 against 0.76 for the original. Nine in ten patients carried the MPO form of the antibody, the dominant pattern in Japan. The authors conclude the newer score is a useful prognostic tool for Japanese practice. It gives doctors an evidence-based way to counsel patients and plan follow-up intensity.
pmc-13246005:
Biswas, Moore, and Rogers showed that a worm's nervous system must give permission before its body mounts antioxidant defenses, in this 2026 eLife study. Using the nematode C. elegans under chronic oxidative stress, they found mutants unable to make the neurotransmitter acetylcholine were strikingly vulnerable. The broad gene program that healthy worms switch on against the stress depended heavily on cholinergic signaling through one muscarinic receptor, GAR-3.

Without that signal, worms failed to ramp up their proteasome, the machinery shredding damaged proteins. Extra copies of the receptor in motor neurons, conversely, prolonged survival under stress. The authors frame antioxidant defense as neuronally coordinated, not merely cell-autonomous, and point to fresh links between cholinergic signaling, oxidative damage, and neurodegenerative disease worth exploring in larger animals.
pmc-13246805:
Borlepawar, Neu, Ma, and co-authors review proteostasis, the cell's system for keeping its proteins correctly made, folded, moved, and destroyed, in this 2026 Signal Transduction and Targeted Therapy article. Chaperone proteins, the proteasome shredder, autophagy, and organelle quality-control programs all cooperate in that balance. When it collapses, misshapen proteins pile up and drive disease.

The authors link proteostasis failure across Alzheimer's-type neurodegeneration, cancer, heart and metabolic disease, and autoimmunity, hitting hardest in heart and brain tissue that barely regenerates. They frame the system's strength as proteostasis resilience, its capacity to absorb stress and restore balance. The review closes with emerging drug platforms that aim to restore that resilience rather than fix single broken parts.
pmc-13247105:
Romero-García and co-authors used machine learning to sort intensive-care patients with brain dysfunction in this 2026 Intensive Care Medicine Experimental pilot study. Delirium and coma in critically ill COVID-19 patients vary widely, making prognosis hard. Working from an international database of the pandemic's first wave, the team clustered more than sixteen hundred patients using only data from their first ICU day.

Four reproducible groups emerged with distinct profiles. One with mild respiratory failure woke fastest and spent the least time on ventilators; others, defined by moderate or early severe lung failure, endured longer delirium. Intriguingly, the clusters did not differ in twenty-eight-day survival. The authors offer the grouping as a pilot step toward tailoring delirium prevention, needing prospective testing in today's ICUs.
pmc-13247305:
Hammad and co-authors present a rare birth defect of the thigh bone, with a literature review, in this 2026 Case Reports in Pediatrics article. Proximal femoral focal deficiency means the upper femur fails to form properly, shortening the leg. It occurs in about one in one hundred thousand births and affects both sides in only a small minority. Their patient was a two-year-old girl with odd crawling and walking, short bulky thighs, and tight, bent knees.

Imaging told two different stories: the right hip lacked a femoral head entirely, while the left had a head detached from its shaft. Both sockets were severely malformed with dislocations. Because the two sides differed, the authors stress imaging-led, individualized planning and a multidisciplinary team, weighing options from conservative care to reconstruction.
pmc-13248905:
Akingbola and co-authors charted forty years of childhood vaccination in Nigeria, in a 2026 study. Using Global Burden of Disease estimates, they tracked five routine vaccines from 1980 to 2023, including BCG, the triple DTP shot, polio, measles, and hepatitis B. Nigeria's program is one of Africa's largest, and its progress has been uneven.

Coverage sat lowest in 1980, rose through the early nineteen nineties, stalled for a decade, then improved again after 2005. The best years came around 2019 to 2021, with BCG peaking near three quarters of children. No vaccine ever reached the World Health Organization's ninety percent goal, so the authors urge fairer, targeted delivery.
pmc-13249705:
Creangă-Murariu and co-authors pooled the evidence on cannabis compounds for cancer pain, in a 2026 meta-analysis. Fifteen studies asked whether adding cannabinoids lets patients cut their opioid doses, a hoped-for benefit given opioid side effects. The reviewers separated fair comparisons against placebo from weaker before-and-after reports, and graded the certainty of everything they found.

Against placebo, cannabinoids changed nothing: total, background, and rescue opioid use all stayed put. Before-and-after analyses hinted at modest savings with THC-heavy preparations, but single studies drove those hints and results clashed. With certainty rated low, the authors conclude cannabinoids cannot be relied on as an opioid-sparing strategy in cancer pain.
pmc-13249805:
Giannini and colleagues ask whether the Mediterranean will trap its own sea snails as the climate warms, in a 2026 Ecology and Evolution study. Four collectible species, three cowries and a frog shell, were modeled using more than a century of occurrence records. The team projected past, present, and future ranges for the northeastern Atlantic and Mediterranean under two climate paths.

Mid-century decades look like a squeeze point, with habitat shrinking and no new ground opening in compensation. The Mediterranean's circulation works against escape toward cooler water, especially for species whose young drift as larvae. Adding larval sensitivity to more acidic water erased still more Atlantic habitat. The authors urge range forecasts that include life history, not just adult tolerance.
pmc-13251205:
Wafaa Yahia Alghonemy and co-authors tested injectable treatments for gum disease in rats, reporting in 2026. Periodontitis destroys the tissues and bone that hold teeth, driven by bacteria and the body's inflammatory response. The team compared hyaluronic acid gel, platelet-rich plasma from the animals' own blood, and the two combined.

Forty male rats with wire-induced gum disease were divided into five groups, including healthy and untreated controls. After two weeks, treated animals showed less tissue damage under the microscope than untreated ones. Blood markers of inflammation, two signals known as TNF-alpha and IL-1beta, also fell with treatment. The combined gel and plasma group healed best, while each treatment alone gave partial recovery. The authors suggest the pairing strengthens both the calming of inflammation and the rebuilding of tissue, though they call for further study.
pmc-13252705:
Sheng Soh and colleagues count hidden COVID-19 infections in Singapore in this 2026 study. Official case counts miss people who never seek care, yet planners need the true spread of an epidemic in near real time.

A community cohort of 1,899 people answered eleven survey rounds from September 2021 to November 2022, across two variant waves. Of 2,284 illness episodes, 756 were COVID-19, and only about six in ten of those saw a doctor, a share that fell over time. By modelling symptoms plus wastewater and staff testing signals, the team estimated total infections at one to nearly three times the reported numbers, matching blood-test surveys.
pmc-13252805:
Katherine Tezanos and colleagues pilot a positivity skills group for young adults with depression in this 2026 trial. The programme, called STEP, trains people to build positive emotions, aiming to cut suicide risk alongside standard care.

Fifty-two adults aged 18 to 26 at a community mental health service were split by chance between group STEP and enhanced usual care. Attendance was high and feedback positive, so the group format passed its feasibility test. The small trial could not prove group differences, yet STEP members showed larger rises in positive emotions and larger drops in depression and suicidal thoughts by follow-up. The authors call for a bigger trial.
pmc-13252905:
Fazeela Bibi and a large team report removing a giant nerve tumour in this 2026 case report. A 44-year-old labourer had a swelling in his neck for four years, and over the last year it brought arm pain, hand weakness, and wasting of the thumb-side muscles.

Scans showed a dumbbell-shaped tumour about eleven centimetres long threading from his neck into his upper chest, without invading nearby parts. In one operation through the back of the neck, surgeons removed it fully, using an ultrasonic tool to hollow it out safely. His pain vanished and nerve function recovered markedly. Lab tests confirmed a benign nerve sheath tumour. Careful planning, the authors say, made a giant case manageable.
pmc-13253205:
Justin A Kaskow and colleagues deliver a piece of the STING protein directly into ovarian cancer cells using nanoparticles in a 2026 study. STING is an internal alarm that, when triggered, floods a tumor with immune-stimulating signals. Many cancers silence STING itself, which defeats drugs that work by switching it on, so the team delivered a working fragment of the protein instead.

Their carrier is a degradable polymer nanoparticle tuned to slip into cells and release its cargo in the cytosol, the cell's interior fluid. A pH-shift assembly method then produced smaller, negatively charged particles, and the choice of partner polymer steered activation toward ovarian cancer cells over other types. In a mouse model, particles gathered in tumors across the abdomen, slowed their growth, and extended survival. The authors see protein-fragment delivery as a route to immunotherapy for cancers that have disabled this alarm.
pmc-13253905:
Yaying Song and colleagues propose a new field name, onco-neurology, in a 2026 article. Cancer care now keeps more people alive longer, yet nerve problems in cancer patients are rising in importance. Many are not caused by tumors pressing on nerves, but by immune reactions, treatments, or body-wide effects of the disease.

Old labels for these problems overlap and split care between cancer and nerve specialists. The authors argue a shared name would cut that fragmentation and push joint review of patients. pmc-13255205:

pmc-13255705:

pmc-13256305:

pmc-13256805:

pmc-13257205:

pmc-13257705:

pmc-13258005:

pmc-13258105:

pmc-13258505:

pmc-13258805:

pmc-13259205:

pmc-13259305:

pmc-13259505:

pmc-13260205:

pmc-13262105:

pmc-13262805:

pmc-13263105:

pmc-13263305:

pmc-13264105:

pmc-13264205:

pmc-13264305:

pmc-13264405:

pmc-13264605:

pmc-13265005:

pmc-13265305:

pmc-13265405:

pmc-13266705:

pmc-13266905:

pmc-13267505:

pmc-13267705:

pmc-13267805:

pmc-13269305:

pmc-13269705:

pmc-13270405:

pmc-13271005:

pmc-13271905:

pmc-13272405:

pmc-13272505:

pmc-13272905:

pmc-13273205:

pmc-13274005:

pmc-13274105:

Children with type 1 diabetes carry lower levels of vitamins A and D than healthy peers, Shuhan Rao and colleagues found in a 2026 retrospective study at a children's hospital in Zhengzhou. Both vitamins help regulate the immune system, yet their status in this disease is little studied.

The study compared 31 children diagnosed with type 1 diabetes who had vitamin tests from January 2022 through October 2025 with 31 children seen for health checks. The diabetes group showed significantly lower levels of both vitamins and higher deficiency rates, and both levels fell as fasting blood sugar rose. Adjusted analysis kept each vitamin independently tied to the disease. Rao and colleagues suggest watching vitamin status in care, while noting that longitudinal and intervention studies must confirm any benefit.
pmc-13290605:
Umbilical cord stem cells proved safe in a first human trial for acute respiratory distress syndrome, Qinggang Ge and colleagues report in 2026. ARDS kills heavily and has few specific treatments, so the team ran an open-label, multicenter phase 1 study of an intravenous cell product called BC-U001.

Twelve patients with mild-to-moderate ARDS entered a 3+3 dose-escalation scheme run from 2019 to 2024 and got one infusion on top of standard care. No dose-limiting toxicity or treatment-related severe events appeared, and 28-day mortality was 8.3%, one patient of twelve in the trial. The middle dose group improved most on oxygen measures and organ-failure scores, though gains did not rise with dose. Ge and colleagues say the safety readout justifies large randomized trials.
pmc-13290805:
A nine-feature model can flag early which breast cancers will shrug off pre-surgery drug therapy, Xiangyuan Zhou and colleagues report in a study from 2026. Spotting non-responders to neoadjuvant therapy early would spare patients ineffective treatment, yet single markers have not sufficed.

The retrospective study followed 112 patients through baseline MRI, a second scan after two therapy cycles, and surgery; about a third were non-responders. Features came from four domains: tumor traits, MRI dynamics, the tumor microenvironment, and blood inflammation markers. Combined after statistical selection, the nine features discriminated far better than any single domain, and validation held up well after optimism correction. Zhou and colleagues caution the model is exploratory and single-center, so outside testing must come before clinical use.
pmc-13291105:
Min Wu and co-authors describe a 2026 case where two heart rhythm drugs turned dangerous in a man whose heart muscle had been weakened by sepsis. The 89-year-old patient arrived in septic shock from a gut source, with a long electrical recovery interval in the heart and poor pumping function before any new drug was given.

After moxifloxacin and amiodarone were added, that interval stretched further and repeated abnormal beats spiraled into torsades and ventricular fibrillation that shocks and resuscitation could not stop. A steady infusion pairing lidocaine with anisodamine finally calmed the rhythm, and no further storm episodes followed. Heart function returned to its prior level within two weeks, and a check nine months later showed near-complete recovery.
pmc-13291305:
A cell energy protein may serve as a drug target in chest cancer. Cormac J. Jennings leads a 2026 study of pleural mesothelioma. This cancer wraps the lung lining and resists most care. The protein SDHB sits in a key energy complex.

Gene tests found SDHB in all cell lines checked. Tumor samples showed far higher gene levels than normal tissue. Protein staining on tissue grids told a split story. High protein did not link to longer survival. A drug blocking the energy complex was then tried. Cell growth effects were tested in dishes. The split results warn that gene level alone misleads.
pmc-13292305:
Xinyi Fang and colleagues review a 2026 topic linking the mouth's microbes to chronic kidney disease. The oral cavity is the body's second most densely colonized site, and gum disease bacteria show up more often in kidney patients than in the general population. The review gathers evidence on how oral imbalance might feed several forms of kidney damage.

Proposed routes include body-wide inflammation, vessel lining dysfunction, and oxidative stress. In IgA nephropathy, mouth microbes may distort IgA1 sugar coating, and in glomerulonephritis they may stoke immune misregulation. The authors are candid that trial proof is thin: small studies, short follow-up, mixed dental treatments, and weak confounder control. They call for better trials before anyone claims that fixing oral health slows kidney decline.
pmc-13293305:
Fiona Douglas reviews, in a 2026 evidence summary, whether cuff-style blood pressure checks in cats match direct artery readings. Vets need reliable pressure values in sick, older, or anesthetized cats, where low or high pressure can change care.

Fourteen studies were reviewed, covering two cuff methods: Doppler and oscillometric. For Doppler, no study found full agreement with the direct method, and most found poor agreement. Oscillometry fared better, with some studies finding agreement, often only in set conditions or for mean pressure. Overall proof was rated moderate. Clinicians should read cuff values with caution and note the setting.
pmc-13293405:
Xia Li examines, in a 2026 policy study, how government attention is shared out for new strategic industries in Shanxi province, a less-developed region of central China. Official focus can shape whether such regions catch up or fall further behind.

Sixty policy documents from 2010 to 2025 were coded by actor, tool, and theme, using topic and network methods. Teamwork among policy actors was weak, and tools leaned hard on supply-side and setting measures. Themes formed a pyramid that puts groundwork first, which may aid early takeoff. The author warns of crowding out fresh ideas and locking in old paths, and urges better coordination.
pmc-13293905:
Simone Sarti, Marco Terraneo, and David Consolazio describe a 2026 whole-network dataset from a small municipality in Lombardy, Italy. Every resident aged 18 to 75 was invited to answer questions on background, health-risk behaviors, and social ties inside and outside town. Face-to-face interviews, careful ethics steps, and incentives supported participation.

Altogether 578 interviews were completed, a 66.3% response rate, and results matched official ISTAT figures well. Full network maps of a real community are rare, so the data can show how risky habits cluster and spread. The authors also see uses for fairer, targeted public health action.
pmc-13294205:
Donghai Lu and a large team build separate prediction models for tumor shrinkage versus survival in liver cancer in a 2026 multicenter study. Shrinkage after combined local therapy plus targeted immunotherapy does not guarantee longer life, a gap the authors call the responder paradox. Data from 246 patients mixed clinic details with dual-phase CT image features.

Two PRIME models were trained, one for response at 3 months and one for survival. Outside validation gave an area of 0.85 for response and a concordance index of 0.72 for survival, with strong risk splitting. Drivers diverged: response leaned on tumor shape, while survival leaned on different clinical and molecular signals. One score cannot serve both goals.
pmc-13294305:
Haruna Takahashi and colleagues probe false fear memories in mice for a 2026 brain study. Over time, context memories blur, and animals freeze in safe places that merely resemble a shock setting. The memory-keeping enzyme PKMζ was lowered or boosted in upper or lower hippocampus with viral tools two weeks before testing in young adult male mice.

False freezing appeared by 3 hours and grew by 24 hours. Lowering the enzyme in the upper hippocampus sharply boosted false freezing at 24 hours, while adding active enzyme blocked the rise and an inactive version mimicked loss. Upper hippocampus loss also hurt spatial recognition. Enzyme upkeep guards memory precision.
pmc-13294705:
Roshini Thangaraj and Venkatesh Selvaraj describe anesthesia for neck artery surgery without putting the patient fully to sleep, in a 2026 case report. Carotid endarterectomy scrapes plaque from the carotid artery to prevent stroke, and keeping the patient awake lets the team watch brain function directly while the artery is clamped. Their patient was a sixty-nine-year-old man with repeated strokes, hypertension, and diabetes, whose right carotid artery had narrowed by up to eighty percent.

The anesthetic combined two layers of neck nerve block, superficial and intermediate cervical plexus blocks, placed under ultrasound guidance. With the region numbed, surgeons removed the plaque while the man stayed responsive, allowing continuous checks of his neurological state and early warning of any loss of blood flow to the brain. The operation succeeded, and the authors present the technique as a sound option for carefully chosen patients.
pmc-13294805:
Sibei Qin and colleagues weigh one against two stem cell transplants for multiple myeloma in a 2026 review and combined analysis. Double high-dose treatment followed by transplant is costly and demanding, so its added value, especially for high-risk patients, needed weighing. The team searched major databases for trials that directly compared the two strategies.

Eight randomised trials were pooled, covering treatment given up to April 2023. Double transplant improved both progression-free and overall survival for patients with at least one poor-risk feature. Response depth was also greater, with more patients reaching at least a very good partial response, while deaths linked to treatment stayed similar between strategies.
pmc-13294905:
Changzhong Zhao and colleagues watch carbon dioxide push salt water through rock at microscopic scale, in a 2026 study of underground carbon storage. Storing carbon dioxide in deep salty aquifers is a leading climate strategy, and how much gas the rock holds depends on the pattern the two fluids form in the pore space. The team etched two glass micromodels from real Berea sandstone cores and filmed the displacement under varied conditions.

Three patterns appeared. When the gas advanced in bold viscous fingers, it filled the most space, flowed most easily, and traced the most complex shapes. When capillary forces ruled, the gas broke into many small clusters and filled the least. A crossover state, pulled by both forces, behaved in between but with extra complexity. Gas state and temperature, working through viscosity, strongly shaped pressure and progress, while the rock pattern altered local details rather than the overall trend.
pmc-13295005:
Maria Natalia Calienni and colleagues wrap a skin cancer drug in squishy carriers to change how it behaves, in a 2026 study. Vismodegib blocks the Hedgehog signaling pathway and is approved for basal cell carcinoma, but swallowing it brings real side effects and getting it into skin tumors is hard. The team first screened the free drug on four mouse tumor cell lines, then loaded it into ultradeformable liposomes, flexible fat bubbles designed for topical use, and tested them on melanoma cells.

Melanoma cells answered the free drug most strongly among the lines screened. Once wrapped, the drug killed more melanoma cells and slowed their expansion more than the free form at matched doses, beyond what pathway blocking alone explains. A tree-like dendrimer carrier, tried for comparison, showed no detectable effect at safe levels. The authors back skin-applied nanocarriers as a repurposing route for early melanoma.
pmc-13295105:
Lweendo Hachamba and co-authors survey smallholder dairy farmers on antibiotic use in Zambia in a 2026 study. Careless antibiotic use on farms feeds drug resistance that threatens human health. What these farmers know, believe, and actually do had to be measured before stewardship work could be aimed well.

Structured questions reached 360 farmers at milk collection centres across six districts in two provinces. Three quarters scored poorly overall, even though almost all agreed a vet should be consulted. Many still dosed animals themselves, ignored milk withdrawal times, or sold milk from treated animals. Schooling level, district, and earlier training all shaped scores, pointing to education as the main lever.
pmc-13295405:
Rama Krishna Thelagathoti and colleagues use unsupervised machine learning to find ovarian cancer signals in the parcels tumors shed into body fluids, in a 2026 study. Those parcels, extracellular vesicles, carry messenger RNA from their parent cells, giving a blood-based window on cancer. The data are noisy and the sample sizes small, so group contrasts can miss hidden structure.

The team applied non-negative matrix factorization, which splits expression data into a few gene programs and shows how strongly each sample uses them. A strict cleaning pipeline came first. Judged by rebuilding error and steadiness across runs, the model settled on a compact picture and a shortlist of telling genes. The authors present the method as a low-bias way to rank features in small, wide datasets.
pmc-13295505:
Wanqi Ma and colleagues catalogue a lipid-cutting gene family in mulberry in a 2026 study. Mulberry feeds silkworms, serves traditional medicine, and restores worn land, yet its drought and salt defences are little mapped. The PLA family helps plants answer stress by releasing signal molecules from membranes.

Fifty family members were found in the genome and sorted into three subfamilies by shared ancestry. Most genes read quietly in leaves and more strongly in roots across tissues tested. Ten genes rose sharply under drought and twelve under salt, marking them as candidates for breeding or engineering hardier mulberry for dry, salty ground.
pmc-13295605:
Deurimar Herênio Gonçalves Júnior and colleagues measure how efficiently coffee cherries become saleable beans, in a 2026 breeding study from northern Espírito Santo, Brazil. Farmers are paid on processed coffee, so a variety needing less fruit per bag quietly cuts harvest and processing costs, yet breeders rarely select for that trait. Rankings shuffled considerably between years, warning that one-season selection misleads. Two varieties, Z21 and VR3, stayed on top in both seasons and graduate to wider trials. A cheap shortcut emerged as well: the simple share of grain inside the fruit predicted processing efficiency, which could speed screening of large collections. The authors press for multi-year testing as the price of trustworthy variety advice.
pmc-13295705:
Mireia Mestre and colleagues show that water masses carry their own microbial marks in a strait near Antarctica, in a 2026 study. The Gerlache-Bismarck Strait mixes waters of unlike origin, and how that mixing shapes microbes was little known. The team sampled from the surface down to four hundred meters, sorting microbes into three size bands, and logged water chemistry alongside.

Which water mass a sample came from proved a prime driver of which microbes lived there. Surface layers held Antarctic and glacially shaped waters, while deep layers held circumpolar deep water. Known guests matched their waters, among them ammonia-eating archaea in the deep layer and a light-loving alga in glacial water. The authors offer microbial marks as a way to read water movement and food web shifts.
pmc-13296005:
Roy Fleischmann and co-authors report seven-year results in 2026 from SELECT-COMPARE, a large rheumatoid arthritis trial pitting daily upadacitinib tablets against adalimumab injections. Patients who had not responded enough to methotrexate could switch to the other drug if their first choice fell short.

Both drugs held their gains through seven years, with upadacitinib slightly ahead on remission rates among those staying on treatment. Its side-effect pattern matched earlier reports, with somewhat more shingles, skin cancers and liver issues noted. Switching helped initial non-responders too. The authors judge the long-term balance of benefit and risk acceptable.
pmc-13296105:
Zexu Li and colleagues compare, in 2026, back muscle from stallions and castrated Kazakh horses to see how castration changes meat. Samples from three-year-old animals were checked for eating quality, fibre structure and gene activity.

Gene reading found 848 genes differing between groups, centred on the cell scaffolding system, with eleven core genes flagged. The authors say the results explain the tenderness gain and can guide breeding for better horse meat.
pmc-13296305:
Sofya Mishina and co-authors propose, in 2026, that pollution rather than infection may increasingly explain rising autoimmune disease. Infections are falling, yet autoimmunity climbs, and the classic trigger story relies on germs whose shapes resemble body proteins, fooling defences into attacking self tissue.

The authors suggest pollutants could mimic that invasion signal in people prone to autoimmunity. Their hypothesis paper lays out the mimicry idea, its history since the 1960s and why a non-infectious stand-in deserves study. If right, the account would redirect attention toward chemical exposures in prevention research.
pmc-13296505:
Yue Yu, Shuntian Wang, Livia Cabernard, and Stephan Pfister trace biodiversity damage hidden inside global mining supply chains in a 2026 study. Mining land destroys habitat where it sits, but the goods are usually consumed elsewhere. Their framework links local species loss at mine sites to a global trade model of who ultimately buys the output.

Estimated impacts came out nearly twice as high as earlier global figures. Five hotspot regions, led by Indonesia and Australia, accounted for well over half of the total. Most of the footprint fell outside the consuming country, with demand from China, Europe, Japan, and the United States driving much of it. The maps give conservation planners clearer targets along supply chains.
pmc-13296605:
Dong-Ho Shin and co-authors grow, in 2026, stacked layers of lead sulphide and tin disulphide one atomic layer at a time and show the stack squeezes charge carriers into quantum confinement. Thinning the lead sulphide layer below a key size widened its energy gap in steps the team could dial in.

Vibration tests showed the layers coupled strongly despite clean, strain-free boundaries, and computer models confirmed squeezing in both directions. An individually grown film sat far below the stack's tuned range. The authors say the method opens precise quantum engineering of layered materials for light-based devices.
pmc-13296705:
Frédéric Millot and co-authors report, in 2026, registry outcomes for adolescents with chronic myeloid leukaemia, a rare blood cancer in the young. Data on 132 patients aged fifteen to eighteen in the early phase are compared with younger children treated in the same era.

Adolescents showed enlarged spleens less often and lower white cell counts at diagnosis than younger children. Among those starting on imatinib, response depth, freedom from progression and survival matched the younger group. Five-year survival compared well with adult figures. The authors say teenagers fare like children on modern targeted pills.
pmc-13296905:
Neha Chaudhary and colleagues uncover how a signalling protein protects pancreatic cancer cells from radiation in a 2026 study. The protein Rac1 sits downstream of the KRAS signal that drives most pancreatic tumours. Blocking Rac1 weakened the cells' DNA-damage alarm system, the team found.

The reason was loss of claspin, a protein needed to activate the damage checkpoint. Rac1 blockade sped claspin's destruction through a named degradation route, without changing its gene message. Normal pancreatic cells lost claspin too, yet only the cancer cells were pushed into death by radiation. Exploiting that difference could make radiotherapy work harder against this resistant cancer, the authors propose.
pmc-13297205:
Xingyu Hou and co-authors probe, in 2026, how xylazole, a sedative used in Chinese veterinary practice, shifts brain chemistry in rats. Young cortical cells in dishes and adult brains sampled by microdialysis were exposed, tracking the messenger cAMP and mood-related chemicals.

In young cells the drug raised cAMP through a known receptor, briefly lifted dopamine and steadily raised serotonin and its breakdown product. In adult brains it mostly lowered cAMP, dopamine and noradrenaline while raising serotonin, with one region rebounding late. The authors caution the high test dose makes the brain patterns exploratory, not proof of one receptor route.
pmc-13298005:
After BCMA-targeted therapy stops working in multiple myeloma, what helps next? Nagham Youssef and a large multicenter team examined real-world records from US academic centers in a 2026 study to compare salvage strategies.

BCMA-directed CAR T-cell therapy gave responses that ran deeper, and survival that ran longer, than BCMA T-cell engagers given after earlier BCMA treatment. Teclistamab lost potency when it followed prior BCMA therapy, especially within six months. Talquetamab, which aims at a different target called GPRC5D, stayed active in many patients, supporting a switch of target after BCMA failure. The authors argue that timing and antigen choice should guide the next trials and guidelines.
pmc-13298505:
Plain clinical tables beat endoscopy images for predicting a painful ERCP complication, found Anum Jamil and colleagues in a 2026 single-center study. They compared machine learning on tabular data, deep learning on procedure images, and a fused multimodal system for forecasting pancreatitis after the bile duct procedure.

The gradient-boosted tabular model reached an AUC of 0.95, though it caught only half the cases, and cross-validation lowered that to 0.79. The best image model scored 0.76, and the combined system trailed at 0.57. Explanation analysis highlighted cannulation time, ampulla type, and age. The authors blame the rare outcome and small image supply, urging multicenter data collection.
pmc-13298605:
Garrison Thornton and a large team review whether ultrasound elastography stiffness reflects force and activation in foot and ankle muscles, in a 2026 systematic review. Shear wave elastography measures muscle stiffness inside the living body, yet its meaning for strength was untested as a body of evidence. Twenty studies covering 637 participants met their criteria.

Most studies found at least one significant link between stiffness and a force or activation outcome. Resting stiffness related weakly to maximal strength yet consistently to rapid torque development at stretched lengths. Stiffness during contraction tracked effort within a person. Joint angle, contraction state, and the specific muscle all shaped the relationship.
pmc-13300305:
N M A S Atan and co-authors report a 2026 ten-year comparison of pacing-induced cardiomyopathy between leadless and transvenous pacemakers at Malaysia's National Heart Institute. Frequent right ventricular pacing can weaken the heart over time, and this study asked whether the leadless design changes that risk in a Southeast Asian population. Records covered implants from 2013 to 2023, with cardiomyopathy defined by a clear drop in pumping function and no other cause.

Of 1,053 patients meeting the study criteria, 244 developed the condition. Rates were 22 percent with transvenous devices and 32 percent with leadless devices, and one leadless model fared worse than its sibling version. Male sex, a wide paced QRS pattern, and high pacing burden were the dominant predictors. The authors urge structured follow-up after implant and favor pacing strategies that keep the ventricles in sync.
pmc-13301005:
Masahiro Shirata and Michiko Tsuchiya report the first known case of pleural empyema caused by the gut bacterium Mediterraneibacter gnavus, in a 2026 case report. The patient was a seventy-eight-year-old Japanese man with diabetes, severe malnutrition, and kidney disease from his diabetes. He also had a pre-existing pocketed pleural effusion, and he arrived with fever after days of fatigue and appetite loss. Standard aerobic cultures of blood and pleural fluid grew nothing.

Only anaerobic culture of the pleural fluid yielded growth. The authors warn that lung infections from such organisms will be missed unless laboratories run oxygen-free cultures and reach for advanced testing when routine cultures stay silent.
pmc-13301405:
