Younger players showed a web of links: height and lean mass helped jumping and sprinting, while fat held most scores back. Models explained up to forty-four percent of sprint variation in that group. Older boys showed fewer ties, though body fat still dragged on jumps and agility and mass aided sprinting. No body measure predicted reactive agility at either age.
pmc-13301505:

Large structural rearrangements and copy number changes were resolved and phased alongside the small variants, and nearly every known cancer pathway in the samples carried at least some of the cataloged mutations. The authors present linked read barcoding as a workable route to haplotype aware tumor profiles, information they argue personalized treatment planning will need.
pmc-13301805:
M Macgillivray and colleagues present a 2026 systematic review on how extra heartbeats arising in the lower chambers affect daily life and mental state. These early beats are common, and even people with few of them sometimes report strong symptoms. The review centres on psychological factors that shape how symptoms are noticed and felt.

Six studies with 408 patients met the criteria, most involving structurally normal hearts checked by ultrasound. Treatments across the studies included beta-blockers, other rhythm medicines, and a targeted ablation procedure for many patients. After treatment, depression, anxiety, and fear of bodily sensations generally eased, while activity levels and social functioning improved. The authors argue that care should address mood and lifestyle alongside the rhythm itself.
pmc-13301905:
P Jurak and colleagues examine, in a 2026 study, whether ultra-high-frequency ECG measures of left-heart timing match real gains in pumping pressure during resynchronization therapy. This treatment paces both sides of a failing heart to restore coordinated contraction. Standard trace width is a crude guide, so finer frequency-based measures might track benefit better.

Pressure rose under both biventricular pacing and left bundle branch area pacing compared with single-site pacing. Two measures of timing spread within the left wall matched pressure change perfectly across 46 paired comparisons. Ordinary trace width and between-chamber timing matched less well, supporting the finer measures for tuning therapy.
pmc-13302005:
Metal sheets that dissolve as bone regrows tempt dental surgeons, and Dragana Gabrić with colleagues map the evidence in a 2026 scoping review of magnesium-based membranes. Thirty-nine studies, from bench tests to small case series, covered membranes and screws used in ridge regeneration and guided bone growth. The search followed scoping review guidelines across several databases.

Cells tolerated the material and stuck to it, and moderate magnesium levels nudged bone-forming markers upward in the lab. Animal work showed orderly breakdown with the barrier intact through early healing. Human reports describe mostly smooth healing and kept bone volume, with minor troubles such as membrane exposure and small gas pockets. Controlled trials are still missing.
pmc-13303205:
Iron stores relate to anemia in Chinese schoolchildren through a curve, not a straight line, Yan Sun and colleagues show in a 2026 matched case-control study. National surveillance supplied 175 anemic children and adolescents plus 525 matched controls. Serum ferritin was modeled in quartiles and with flexible splines, adjusting for age, body mass, sex, and inflammation.

Children in the second and fourth ferritin quartiles carried about half or less the anemia risk of the lowest group, and the spline confirmed significant non-linearity. The protective pattern belonged to girls alone; boys showed no association. The authors urge sex-aware, non-linear thinking when ferritin guides anemia assessment in pediatric practice.
pmc-13303305:

Patients admitted with non-aneurysmal, non-traumatic subarachnoid hemorrhage between 2015 and 2021 answered questionnaires and interviews at a median of nearly five years afterward. One hundred eleven responded, split between perimesencephalic and other patterns.

Forty percent scored at least two on the disability scale, a worse picture than earlier reports suggested. Seventy percent of previously employed patients had fully returned to work, but fifteen percent had not returned at all. Only about a quarter reported no complaints; tiredness and trouble remembering new information led the residual list.
pmc-13303605:
Hannes Vermue and colleagues present a 2026 review asking whether knee looseness after total knee replacement should be measured with tools rather than surgeon feel. Robot help has grown in knee surgery, yet soft tissue balance is still often judged by hand.

Searches of two databases found 34 studies linking measured looseness in two planes to patient-reported outcomes, with follow-up from one month to over eight years. A middle range of front-to-back looseness tied to better function, while too much or too little did worse. Side-to-side looseness on the inner side mattered most. Routine objective checks may lift results for patients.
pmc-13304105:
Fahri Akgül and co-authors test, in a 2026 multicentre study, a combined blood index as a survival marker in stomach cancer that has already spread at diagnosis. The CALLY index blends an inflammation protein, a nutrition protein, and immune cell counts into one number. Its value in this specific, poor-prognosis group was undefined.

The study covered 234 patients treated between 2015 and 2025, split at a data-derived threshold into low and high index groups. Patients with high scores lived a median of nearly fourteen months against under nine months for the low group. The disadvantage of a low score persisted after adjustment for tumour features, treatment type, and diagnosis era. Time to progression, by contrast, showed no significant split.
pmc-13304305:
Aleksandra Arsić and co-authors compare, in a 2026 case-control study, chemical signs of oxidative damage across heart failure severity grades. Eighty-five patients and thirty-three healthy controls gave blood for a panel covering damage products, nitrogen-based stress markers, and antioxidant defences, plus the standard heart hormone.

Every marker differed clearly between patients and controls, and the pattern worsened with symptom class and weaker pumping. In combined models, a nitrogen marker stayed tied to symptom severity while a fat-damage marker stayed tied to pumping weakness. The heart hormone still separated severe from mild symptoms best of all. The authors propose the two oxidative markers as complementary windows onto different faces of the disease.
pmc-13305305:
Dmitry Medvedev and colleagues develop a way to pull hypericin, a light-activated red pigment, from St. John's wort and package it for medicine in a 2026 study. The compound fights disease under light but barely dissolves in water.

Fat was stripped first with a Soxhlet setup, then sound-assisted acetone extraction freed the pigment from plant tops. A thin-film method packed it into soap-like bubbles of a common polymer, giving steady particles about 30 nanometers wide with very high loading. Mouse brain tumor cells soaked up the bubbles over time and died under light, with no dark harm.
pmc-13306005:
Daniela Mirela Vîrtosu used a coronary care example in 2026 to question standard risk modelling when outcomes are rare. Infections picked up in hospital affected only 16 of 870 unit patients, a rate of 1.8% in the reported cohort.

With four candidate predictors, events per variable came to about four, a level the authors link to unstable coefficients and overfitted models. As an alternative, they explore a preset adding-up framework that combines baseline frailty and exposure factors without heavy fitting. The case argues for simpler, pre-planned scoring when rare events make complex models unreliable.
pmc-13306105:
Claude Lambré chaired an EFSA panel that judged a plastic recycling method for food packaging in a 2026 safety opinion. The Bandera Twin process, listed as RECYC341, starts with washed flakes from used PET bottles, with at most 5% from non-food uses.

Flakes pass through hot extrusion under vacuum, named as the key cleaning step in the assessment. Challenge testing checked temperature, pressure and one further controlled factor against movement of unknown contaminants into food. The panel found the output acceptable for stated uses, including a capped share for drinking water containers stored at room temperature.
pmc-13306205:
Olga Felip reviewed evidence on the edible green alga Chlorella for gut microbes and brain health in a 2026 systematic review. Searches covered three databases for English work from 2009 to 2026 under a registered protocol.

From 1333 records found, 47 passed first checks and 21 met full criteria for the final synthesis. Outcomes covered microbe mix, short-chain fatty acids, a brain growth factor, hippocampal cell counts, behaviour tests and mood questionnaires. The authors weigh whether nutrient-rich Chlorella can link bowel change to brain benefit, while noting uneven study quality across the field. The review asks for more work on dose, safety and long term brain gain.
pmc-13307205:
Daniel Vélez-Díaz and colleagues describe a surgical technique in 2026 for rebuilding a long-ruptured patellar tendon using the patient's own peroneus longus tendon. The graft offers consistent size and low harm at the donor site in the lower leg. Planning relied on X-ray measures of kneecap height and magnetic resonance confirmation of complete rupture. The authors report satisfactory short and mid-term results. Restoring the knee's extension mechanism with strong, simple fixation is the goal of the design.
pmc-13307405:
Fatemeh Sadat Gheibi and co-authors review in 2026 animal studies of AdipoRon, a drug that acts on adiponectin receptors, for memory loss, low mood, and anxiety. Their search covered four databases up to August 30, 2025, and they rated study quality with animal research checklists and bias tools.

Treated rodents spent less time still in a forced swim test and showed calmer behaviour in an open field, most clearly under long term stress. Memory of new objects also improved in models of Alzheimer and Parkinson disease, and levels of two synaptic proteins rose. Gains varied a lot between studies, so careful human trials must come first.
pmc-13307505:
Padmasri Sridharan and Mini Ghosh build in 2026 a shared digital twin to test why cytomegalovirus flare ups weaken CAR-T cell therapy for B-cell lymphoma. Their model frames the clash as a contest for IL-15, a scarce growth signal, between virus specific T cells and the engineered cells.

Training drew on 414 patients from five cancer centres without pooling raw records, and a sixth centre with 89 patients served for checks. The twin foresaw major flare ups well, and its runs linked flare ups to a 41.8 percent cut in peak CAR-T growth under the model rules. Guided virus prevention in the model cut projected disease advance while using less drug overall.
pmc-13307605:
Hao Zhang and co-authors test a plant saponin in 2026 as a possible antibiotic-free treatment for cow udder infection. Pulsatilla saponin B4 was applied to bovine mammary cells inflamed by bacterial toxin and to mice with mastitis. Inflammation signals, tissue damage, and pathway activity were measured in both settings.

The compound reduced the inflammatory response in cells and eased signs and tissue injury in the mouse model. Blocking experiments pointed to the IL-17RA receptor switch as its main route, feeding into MAPK and NF-kappa B signalling. When that route was blocked first, the compound lost its effect, which supports the proposed mechanism. Mastitis costs dairy farmers heavily and drives antibiotic use, so alternatives matter. The authors present the saponin as a candidate worth developing toward farm use.
pmc-13307905:
Priscila Guerra and colleagues field-test in 2026 a sow vaccine built from virus-like particles against a toxin-producing E. coli that causes post-weaning diarrhoea in piglets. Thirty-five sows received the new vaccine twice before farrowing, and thirty-five received the herd's usual commercial products. Piglets were followed to eight weeks after weaning.

Piglets from vaccinated sows carried higher antibody levels against the bacterial attachment factor throughout the post-weaning weeks. Pathogen detection rates were similar between groups, yet diarrhoea scores at week six were lower in the vaccine group. Those piglets also gained weight faster and finished significantly heavier, with a trend toward fewer treatments. Antibodies passed through colostrum and milk did the protective work, since piglets were never vaccinated themselves. The authors present sow immunisation as a practical lever on a stubborn production disease.
pmc-13308105:
Sanne Boetzkes, Leontine van Balveren, and Florence van Hunsel review in 2026 reports of floppy, unresponsive spells in infants after vaccination, logged at the Dutch centre Lareb from 2012 to 2025. Only cases that met the strict top level rule, with all three core signs clear, entered the count.

In all, 294 cases met that bar, most after combined six in one plus pneumococcal shots in young infants. Median onset age was 9 weeks, spells began about five hours after the shot, and most lasted near ten minutes. Every child recovered fully, yet more than a quarter of cases counted as serious due to hospital stays. Wider staff awareness could cut needless urgent care.
pmc-13308705:
Dazhen Liu and co-authors uncover in 2026 a damage-response job for Orc6, a DNA replication starter protein, at the sites where chromosomes are copied and repaired. Mapping showed Orc6 sitting at replication origins and at damage sites during the copying phase. Its partner there is SMARCA1, a chromatin remodeller that slides DNA packaging proteins.

When Orc6 is missing, the remodeller binds more widely and reshapes packaging at those sites. After oxidative damage, Orc6 instead grips the remodeller and blocks its activity, which halts copying progress near the injury. The authors cast Orc6 as a barrier factor that rations remodeller access during normal copying. Upon damage, the same grip becomes a brake that protects the genome. Their model links replication licensing proteins to repair decisions far beyond their textbook starting role.
pmc-13309605:
Maryam Saba models heat flow in a tiny channel filled with a three-metal nanofluid in a 2026 study. Small channels cool electronics, medical tools, and compact heat units. The fluid here is water carrying gold, copper, and silver particles, with a thick, memory-like flow under magnetic forces.

Equations using a fractional derivative capture the flow memory, and a grid-based computer scheme solves them. Results were checked against earlier published profiles and matched closely. A sensitivity scan ranks which factors move speed and heat profiles most, covering magnet strength and particle traits. The author aims to guide cooler design where space is tight and heat loads keep rising.
pmc-13310405:
Hongzhu Bao and co-authors build a prediction chart for breathing machine weaning in lung disease in a 2026 study. Patients with COPD and carbon dioxide buildup often need a breathing machine, and judging when to remove it is hard. A simple chart that sums risk points could guide that call at the bedside.

Records for 159 patients admitted between 2020 and 2024 were split into building and check groups. Screening methods narrowed predictors to anxiety, collapsed lung, blood-pressure drug use, and a heart strain marker as independent risks for weaning failure. The chart scored very high accuracy in the building group, near 0.942 on the standard curve measure reported. The authors propose the chart for everyday weaning rounds.
pmc-13310705:
Alessio Falasca Zamponi and colleagues compare two ways to confirm heart vein isolation during ablation for atrial fibrillation in a 2026 study. Standard care adds a round mapping catheter to check the result. The team asked whether the ablation catheter alone could do that check in first time cases done point by point.

One group of 81 people had the extra catheter, while a later group of 245 people did not. Cases without the extra tool were shorter and used less radiation, with no clear gap in rhythm control after 12 months of follow up. Extra checks found missed conduction in a small share of veins, so gains need care.
pmc-13310905:
Qionglan Li and colleagues survey knowledge of scar pregnancy among women who had cesarean births in a 2026 study. A pregnancy that implants in a cesarean scar is rare but dangerous, and rates rise as cesarean births grow. What women know after surgery shapes early care seeking.

A poll covered 325 women at two Fujian hospitals in late 2023. Knowledge scores sat near half of the top score, while attitude scores were more positive. Higher schooling linked strongly to both better knowledge and more positive views. Tailored teaching after surgery, with focus on women with less schooling, could close the gap.
pmc-13311005:
Dan Zhou and a large team arm a cancer killing virus with a cell cycle blocker for bowel cancer in a 2026 study. Virus care needs high repeat doses, which can tire killer immune cells through constant antigen contact. The team built a virus that makes the blocker inside the tumor to limit body wide exposure.

In mouse models the armed virus curbed tumors better, built strong immune memory, and depended mostly on killer T cells. Blocking the cycle freed a signal part that raised a T cell luring factor, which drew cells in and reversed their tired state. Pairing with other immune drugs boosted gains.
pmc-13311105:
Hongxun Ruan and co-authors trace a low oxygen gene chain that drives liver cancer growth in a 2026 study. In oxygen poor tumor zones, a methyl adding gene rises while a muscle protein gene fades. Data from three large cohorts plus mouse tests were used to map the chain and its value for outlook.

High chain scores marked far shorter survival and stood as a solo risk factor. A fusion protein that restores the faded gene shrank tumors in mice, cut vessel growth, and slowed invasion and spread. Blocking a mid chain step raised protective proteins further under low oxygen. The chain may guide drug picks.
pmc-13311305:
Bing Wang and colleagues, in 2026, share a study on heart strain measures taken soon after a heart attack and later heart shape change. Global longitudinal strain, a measure of heart squeeze, is the test under study.

The study followed 131 patients who had artery-opening treatment at one hospital from March 2023 to October 2024. Strain was measured within seven days, and heart shape and thickening were checked at six to twelve months. Weaker strain on its own tied to higher odds of later shape change. Patients in the weakest strain third faced far higher odds than those in the strongest third.
pmc-13312005:
Claudia Montoya and co-authors offer a 2026 multi-center study of a patch-free form of lichen planopilaris, a scarring hair loss disease. The classic form shows clear bald patches with red, scaly edges; this form stays local without patches.

The study pooled 74 patients from 20 trichology centers, all confirmed by scalp viewing and tissue study. Patients with other hair loss types were excluded to keep the picture clean. The team describes the group's age and sex pattern, clinical signs, scope findings, and tissue features. Naming this variant helps doctors spot scarring loss early, before follicles are destroyed for good.
pmc-13312105:
Ruan Spies and colleagues report a 2026 genomic study of rifampicin-resistant tuberculosis in Ho Chi Minh City, Viet Nam. The country sees nearly 10,000 new cases of this drug-resistant form each year. It was unclear how many come from spread of resistant strains versus resistance arising during a patient's own treatment.

The team sampled adults newly diagnosed across the city from March 2020 to April 2024 and sequenced isolates from 1,491 of the 2,319 cases found. Most isolates belonged to Lineage 2. After correcting for sampling gaps, the authors estimate that between 72 and 87 percent of cases came from transmission of already resistant strains. Dating analyses traced repeated emergence of resistance from the 1980s onward, feeding long-lived spread across the city.
pmc-13313205:
Ying Hei Kan, Lin Gao, and Danny Leung review, in a 2026 article, how epigenetic control of non-coding DNA shapes the placenta. The placenta grows fast, invades in a controlled way, and tolerates the mother's immune system, all under an unusual epigenetic regime of widespread low methylation that resembles a managed, cancer-like state. That flexibility helps trophoblast cells switch programs across pregnancy, but it also leaves the organ sensitive to maternal inflammation, low oxygen, toxins, and stress.

The review explains how promoters, enhancers, their looping networks, and non-coding RNAs are rewired in the placenta, with ancient retrotransposons supplying much of the regulatory novelty. Disturbing any layer can derail cell differentiation, invasion, hormone signaling, or immune balance, feeding growth restriction, preeclampsia, preterm birth, and pregnancy loss. The authors see non-coding epigenetic signatures as promising early biomarkers, while noting how hard cell-specific mapping remains.
pmc-13313705:
Jianqiao He and colleagues pool, in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis, the search for markers that predict benefit from immune therapy given before surgery. The setting is locally advanced head and neck cancer. Many patients gain little from this neoadjuvant treatment, and no validated predictor existed. Searching four databases through June 2024, the team gathered 26 studies covering 980 patients. They compared tissue response rates across candidate markers.

The combined positive score, a measure of PD-L1 staining, tracked response consistently. Patients above a cutoff of 5 responded at notably higher rates, with a relative risk of 1.852 in the pooled comparison. Higher cutoffs pointed the same way. Tumors positive for HPV achieved complete tissue responses more than twice as often. Counts of tumor-infiltrating CD4 T cells also correlated with response. The authors nominate all three as candidate predictors, while asking for prospective validation before clinical use.
pmc-13314505:
Anouk Geraets, Artur Rydosz, and Frank Snoek introduce a journal research topic on digital health tools for diabetes in an editorial published in 2026. Apps, glucose sensors worn on the body, and AI tools are reshaping diabetes care with live tracking and tailored advice.

Proof grows that such tools improve sugar control and patient engagement, at least in the short term, as the editors note. Open questions hang on long-term success, which needs tools woven into steady, patient-led, clinic-based care paths. The topic gathers eleven pieces: three reviews, four studies, a trial, a methods piece, an opinion, and a brief report, spread across four Frontiers journals, as counted in the editorial. The set weighs promise against the work of making digital care last.
pmc-13314605:
Fan Zhang and colleagues study how parks, water, and heat shape jogging in a dense Chinese city in a paper dated 2026. Blue-green spaces are praised in health-led city planning, but proof on how they steer daily use of public space under heat stress was thin.

Taking Fuzhou as the case, the team blended crowd-sourced jogging data with maps of green and water features, land surface heat, and built form. Nine machine learning models were run side by side, and a method called SHAP ranked which factors mattered and how. Distance to vegetation, the green view index, sky view, and surface heat stood out as key factors, as the authors report. Path models then traced direct and indirect routes. The work gives planners hard signs for making hot cities more run-friendly.
pmc-13314805:
Folkert H van Bruggen and Roger S McIntyre review PCSK9, a cholesterol-control protein, at the crossroads of metabolism and mental illness, in their 2026 paper. The protein is a proven heart risk factor, yet it also touches immune and metabolic paths that go awry in psychiatric disease.

The review pulls lab, gene, and clinical proof on fat handling and PCSK9 paths in mental disorders. It maps disorder-by-disorder patterns of blood fat quirks and shifts in brain fat makeup and turnover. Data on the protein inside the brain and on its blood levels against metabolic load, inflammation, and symptoms are summed up. The authors argue that a heart drug target may also matter for the body-wide metabolic strain that shadows severe mental illness.
pmc-13315105:
Viviane Fahrni leads a large team that shares survey data on what farmers would accept to join group nature schemes, in a paper from 2026. The data cover grassland farmers in six European case studies: Austria, Switzerland, Germany, Estonia, Ireland, and Norway, as listed in the report.

The survey ran from spring 2024 into 2025 in two parts. A choice experiment gave each farmer 10 tasks in a row. Each task held two draft designs for a collective biodiversity scheme plus an opt-out that kept the status quo, as the design states. The second part logged farm and farmer traits, attitudes, and likes. Because the schemes pay groups of farmers to guard nature at landscape scale, knowing the price and terms farmers accept can make or break such programs. The open data set lets others retest the drivers.
pmc-13315605:
Paula Freixeiro and colleagues report, in a 2026 pre-clinical study, a built vaccine candidate against gonorrhoea, a sexual infection causing some 82 million cases a year and outrunning antibiotics. Meningitis B vaccines made from the cousin germ's membrane vesicles already cross-protect at 31 to 59 percent shield, suggesting the approach works. The team reasoned a vaccine from the gonococcus itself should do better. They built outer membrane vesicles from gonococcal strains, deleting two genes to soften immune side effects and remove a protein that elicits blocking antibodies.

Mixed with alum, the germ's vesicles raised stronger germ-specific antibody levels than the comparator. They cleared an infection from treated mice much faster, with the difference reaching a strong level. Removing one gene also reduced the immune signal the vesicles triggered in blood cells. The authors advance the candidates as prototypes for a disease where drug resistance has made a vaccine a health priority.
pmc-13315805:
Konstantina Tzimou and colleagues investigate, in a 2026 study, why Chinese hamster ovary cells struggle to produce AAV vectors for gene therapy. Scalable vector production remains a manufacturing bottleneck. HEK293 and insect cell systems dominate but carry cost, scalability, and quality limits, while ovary cells, established in drug manufacturing, assemble vectors poorly. The team expressed individual AAV and adenoviral helper proteins in ovary cells and characterized responses with integrated gene and protein analyses.

Energy building was broadly suppressed across conditions, alongside a drop in antiviral nuclear regulation and signaling networks including JAK-STAT and immune gene pathways. Testing host proteins from the analyses, extra copies of nuclear components Mx2 and Rad23A supported vector production, reaching a yield of 10 to the power of 5 vector genomes per milliliter. The authors map ovary cell responses to helper elements and flag both the promise and remaining barriers to a viable ovary-cell platform.
pmc-13316205:
Tamjid Imtiaz and colleagues used task-based brain scans in 2026 to map how the language network reorganizes in temporal lobe epilepsy. Repeated seizures can disrupt temporal lobe tissue and nearby language areas, and 84 patients with drug-resistant disease completed a sentence completion task during imaging.

Left-sided epilepsy showed clearly more whole-brain language reorganization than right-sided disease, with regional patterns also differing. Age at seizure onset and years lived with epilepsy further shaped how far language had shifted. Knowing each patient's new language layout matters before surgery near language cortex. Regional checks inside standard language areas of interest completed the analysis.
pmc-13316305:
Tyler M Cook and co-authors report 2026 mouse work on low blood sugar attacks that can follow sleeve surgery for weight loss. Their question centers on glucagon, the hormone that should raise blood sugar, and whether its release and effect go wrong after the operation.

Sleeved mice showed high glucagon after meals yet weak sugar gains from small glucagon doses, whether fed or fasted. In the fed state, a small dose even triggered insulin release and low sugar in some mice, an effect partly blocked by a drug that stops GLP-1 signaling. Islet cells taken out alone behaved mostly normally, which points to gut signals as the driver. The results reshape how doctors may think about treating these attacks.
pmc-13316405:
Sarbjit Clare, Jane Ho, and Rachel Barlow describe a 2026 blueprint article on the Midland Metropolitan University Hospital. It opened in October 2024 as one of the first big British hospitals designed around acute internal medicine. Two older sites merged into one building with 100 fewer acute beds.

Even with fewer beds, early results showed better patient flow, lower occupancy strain, faster emergency access, a steadier workforce, and gains in death rates and infection control. The design put senior acute doctors at the working core, with fast tests, quick sorting of risk, and clear leadership for walk-in demand. The authors offer the model to the national hospital building program, while noting longer follow-up must prove the gains last.
pmc-13316605:
Ellen C. Francis and colleagues, in a 2026 cohort study, link heart health during pregnancy with later metabolic disease. Pregnancy strains the body and can reveal hidden risk. The team used a modified Life's Essential 8 score, a measure that combines behaviour and clinical factors, for 1,225 pregnancies.

Healthier scores during pregnancy were tied to a significantly longer time before chronic high blood pressure or metabolic conditions were diagnosed. The pattern held even after people with diabetes or blood pressure disorders of pregnancy were removed. Follow-up lasted seven years. The authors argue that scoring heart health in pregnancy may flag latent vulnerability early, when prevention could still change long-term outcomes for mothers.
pmc-13316705:
Sydney T Puda and co-authors developed, in a 2026 methods study, silicone implants that release testosterone steadily in young castrated male pigs, a model for studying hormone action during early development. Swine work lacked a proven way to replace androgens at controlled levels.

Pigs received implants holding low, medium, or high doses of testosterone propionate, alongside castrated controls and intact males for comparison. Blood hormone levels peaked one to two weeks after surgery, matched or beat intact levels, then eased down yet stayed above controls through all 49 days of checks. Growth ran evenly across groups, so the implants did not distort body gain. The setup gives researchers a reliable dial for hormone exposure.
pmc-13317605:
Qun Ma and Yan Xu review, in 2026, biosensing built on nanofluidics, the control of fluids inside channels and pores only nanometres wide. Confined fluids behave in odd ways, flowing faster than standard theory predicts and showing distinct electrical effects. Turning biomolecular events into such fluid signals could reshape testing.

The review sorts devices into in-plane, out-of-plane and free-plane structures, covering both nanochannels and nanopores. Uses range from DNA and protein sequencing to single-molecule analysis, disease diagnosis and tailored care. The authors weigh current limits, including fabrication cost and reliability problems, and suggest routes forward. Their aim is to guide teams building sensors that read biology through fluid behaviour at tiny scales rather than bulk chemistry alone.
pmc-13318705:
James Florin Petri and Gerard Lacey survey, in 2026, legged robots fitted with passive wheels. Legs handle rough, human-built spaces well but waste energy. Wheels roll fast and cheaply on flat ground. Hybrids promise both strengths, yet most research uses powered wheels.

Unpowered wheels are simpler, lighter, and more efficient. New control methods and faster onboard computing now make them workable. The survey gathers designs that place skates or free wheels on robot feet. It compares implementations and the control problems they raise. Key factors deciding whether such systems are viable are laid out. The authors close with directions for future research in this niche.
pmc-13318805:
Ehsan Alam and colleagues present, in 2026, a planning approach for nature-based flood solutions in urban coastal areas of the Great Lakes. Changing rainfall is worsening flood risk across the basin. Green infrastructure can ease pressure on grey drainage systems and support wildlife, yet projects remain fragmented and hard to coordinate across a whole watershed.

Working in deindustrialising southeast Michigan, the team used research through design to build shared planning tools. The tools translate engineering models, historical records and ecological knowledge into objects that utilities, municipalities, watershed groups and communities can use together. They reveal links between surface flooding, buried water paths and storm sewers, and clarify who holds authority and resources. Fish and wildlife habitat is treated as a core aim, not an afterthought.
pmc-13318905:
Génesis Carolina Arévalo-Guadalupe and co-authors offer a 2026 scientometric map of digital epidemiology from 2000 to 2025. The field uses artificial intelligence, big data, connected devices, and social media mining for disease surveillance. The team analysed records in Scopus and Web of Science. They also read the fifty most cited studies closely.

Publication output grew exponentially from 2010 onwards. The COVID-19 pandemic marked a sharp turning point in volume. The United States, United Kingdom, and China led production and collaboration. Big gaps remain in digital fairness, system compatibility, and ethical oversight. Those gaps bite hardest where technology infrastructure is weak. The authors propose a future agenda centred on algorithm ethics, transparency, cooperation, and inclusion.
pmc-13319705:
Alessandro Villaschi and co-authors report a registry study from 2026 on drug care for heart failure in rehab wards across Italy. People sent to live in rehab after a hospital stay for sudden heart failure often carry many other illnesses and complex drug lists. Whether wards use that stay to tune proven drug sets was the main question.

Among 263 people with a known pump score, three in four had a weak heart pump and most were men. At intake most already took core drug types, and by discharge use of one key type rose and overall drug scores improved. Kidney illness made tuning harder, while higher body weight linked to more tuning. Rehab stays offer a real chance to lift drug care.
pmc-13320105:
Jie Lan and co-authors issue expert agreement in 2026 on pairing beam care with new drug care for breast cancer in China. Beam tools and drug types have both leapt ahead, which opens gains but also raises safety and timing puzzles when they are used together. Two national cancer groups called the panel, which weighed past proof through late 2025 and voted in rounds to settle shared advice.

Advice covers pairings with immune drugs, aimed drugs, drug linked antibodies, and hormone drugs across all stages of the illness. The aim is safer, more even care in daily clinics and a clear map of what to test next. Breast cancer is among the most common cancers in women in China, so shared rules carry wide weight.
pmc-13320405:
Sidar Copur and colleagues pool, in 2026, five randomised trials of a once-weekly insulin for diabetes. Daily injections burden patients and hurt adherence, so a weekly basal insulin, efsitora, has been developed and tested against the daily drug degludec. The review covered 2,562 patients with type 1 or type 2 diabetes.

Overall blood sugar control, measured by HbA1c reduction, was similar between weekly and daily treatment. Separate analyses for each diabetes type also showed no significant difference. Rates of low blood sugar events, including severe episodes and night-time episodes, did not differ significantly either. The authors conclude that weekly efsitora matches daily degludec on both control and hypoglycaemia in the trials reviewed, easing injection burden without obvious penalty.
pmc-13320505:
Nina Yu, Scott Levin and Granger Wong review, in 2026, patients who arrived at their institution with complications after cosmetic surgery in private settings. Such complications burden patients and the hospitals that rescue them, yet this population is poorly understood. Records covered cases from 2020 to 2023.

Thirty-six patients were included, averaging about 38 years old. Nearly half had their original procedure abroad, most often in Mexico or the Dominican Republic. Tobacco or cannabis use and obesity were common in the group. Hospital charges were large while insurance payments covered only a fraction, and costs rose sharply when another operation was needed. Smokers presented more often with infection. The authors call for measures that give patients safer, fairer access to aesthetic procedures.
pmc-13321205:
Olga Maria de Silvério Carvalho and co-authors write a 2026 letter welcoming a dog ageing project as a model for human ageing research. The OLD-DOG Project follows companion dogs for 30 months to find and validate markers of ageing. Dogs age in shared human homes yet live short enough lives for full ageing paths to be tracked.

Calendar age is a weak stand-in for biological age, a core flaw the project targets. Its mix of clinical checks, physical and thinking tests, inflammation markers, microbiome study, and stored samples is praised as a step forward. Within a One Health frame, such dog data could bridge lab animal work and human ageing science.
pmc-13321305:
Dominic Shiels, William W. Brennessel, and Ellen M. Matson report new uranium complexes in a 2026 chemistry study. The team built asymmetric sandwich type polyoxometalate complexes holding uranium in the IV state, with either phosphorus or silicon at the centre. Such actinide assemblies with lopsided builds are rare and hard to make cleanly.

Oxidised U(V) versions of both complexes proved stable and were isolated. Pushing to U(VI) worked poorly: the phosphorus version fell apart, while the silicon version formed only briefly in solution during electrical oxidation tests before decaying. Stability at high charge states thus depends on the overall charge of the assembly, a design rule for future actinide chemistry.
pmc-13321805:
Naibijiang Abuliezi and co-authors reframe immunotherapy for glioblastoma in a 2026 review. This brain cancer resists immune treatment through a suppressive setting, few mutations, wide variety, weak antigen display, and the blood-brain barrier. Successes in other solid tumours have not carried over, and gains stay modest.

Rather than sorting treatments by type, the authors build four pillars: raising antigen display, reversing T cell failure, reprogramming the suppressive setting, and engineering delivery into the brain. Checkpoint drugs, vaccines, virus therapy, and cell therapies are all mapped onto those pillars. Recent designs, including bispecific engagers and new CAR T forms from 2024 and 2025, are highlighted as convergence points.
pmc-13322505:
Scott L Nuismer and co-authors assess a self spreading vaccine idea against Lassa fever in a 2026 study. Lassa virus spills from rodents to people across West Africa each year, sickening tens of thousands, and blocking spillover has resisted decades of effort. A vaccine that spreads through the rodent reservoir itself could give wide immune cover.

Candidate carriers were native cytomegaloviruses taken from the reservoir rat Mastomys natalensis in northern Sierra Leone. Field sampling, genome work, and Bayesian models measured spread rates and virus interactions. Two of three viruses infected freely alongside each other and showed spread rates fit for wiping out Lassa in the reservoir, which sets up vaccine development.
pmc-13322805:
Young-Hyo Jeon and co-authors review ginkgo extract for dizziness from brain disorders in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Dizziness tied to central nervous disease, from stroke related damage to degeneration, has few proven treatments. Nine databases were searched for randomised trials in adults, and study quality and proof certainty were rated with standard tools.

Nine trials with 2394 people were included, drawn mostly from dementia groups at 71.6 percent of participants in the review. Smaller shares came from cerebral arteriosclerosis and rear circulation disorders. Planned subgroup and sensitivity checks probed differences by cause and treatment type. The review weighs whether ginkgo's blood flow and protective actions translate into real relief.
pmc-13323305:
Vivek Mahapatra and co-authors pool how well artificial intelligence reads baby X-rays for necrotising enterocolitis, in a 2026 meta-analysis drawing on a systematic search. This bowel disease is a leading threat to premature and very low birth weight babies, and early signs are vague.

Searching five databases for work from 2015 to July 2025, they kept ten retrospective studies, pooling six. Most used convolutional neural networks, with little testing outside home data. Pooled sensitivity sat near 0.78 and specificity near 0.84 in their hierarchical model, giving moderate diagnostic value with wide variation between studies. The authors back wider external validation before such tools steer care for fragile newborns.
pmc-13323405:
Thomas E Wessendorf reviews doping in chess in a 2026 article written in German, asking whether performance drugs matter in a mental sport. Stimulants such as amphetamines, methylphenidate, modafinil and ephedrine show signs of modest cognitive gain, yet can also harm decisions under time pressure.

Health risks include strain on the heart and circulation, psychotic symptoms at high doses and a path toward dependence. Chess counts as an organised sport, so doping controls exist, but they cover only elite play and stay rare, with no major cases known so far. The author judges electronic cheating the larger threat to fair play, while suspecting higher hidden use among professionals and amateurs alike.
pmc-13324305:
Jiyoung Lee and co-authors grow human heart organoids with working electrical currents, in a 2026 stem cell study. Their culture recipe for embryonic stem cell derived organoids used concentrated laminin-entactin and growth factor FGF4, plus BMP4, BMP10 and a ROCK blocker to steer heart formation.

The organoids formed atrium-like and ventricle-like chambers holding heart muscle, smooth muscle and vessel lining cells. They carried gap junction proteins and the main cardiac ion channel proteins, and they contracted as whole structures. Single heart cells taken from them showed sodium and calcium currents under patch clamp testing, matching living heart behaviour in part. The authors offer the system for development studies and drug safety testing.
pmc-13326005:
Tian Zhou and co-authors study how spare walking capacity cushions the cost of thinking while walking in older adults in a 2026 study. Doing two things at once strains gait and raises fall risk as people age.

A sample of 4,443 healthy adults with a mean age of 74.8 years walked alone and while naming animals or counting backward. Costs on both walking and thinking were clear, and the memory task tangled with walking in an uneven way. Higher functional reserve, the gap between normal and fast walking speed, predicted smaller costs. Stopping to talk was rare, at 2.8 percent of participants, and marked a coping style rather than fall history.
pmc-13327105:
Haruka Harata and colleagues report a 2026 heart case tracked with repeated ultrasound scans from inside the food pipe. A 79-year-old woman with an irregular heartbeat arrived after a brief loss of memory. Brain scans showed several small strokes on both sides despite blood-thinning medicine, so doctors looked for a heart source.

Imaging found a round, mobile mass measuring 11.8 by 8.3 mm sitting on heavy calcium at the mitral valve, with a pale core and a bright thin shell. During surgery the mass flattened, and lab study of the removed tissue confirmed a calcified amorphous tumor with a soft, caseous form. Her memory problem cleared and no new clots appeared over one year, favoring early surgery once such a mass is spotted.
pmc-13327805:
Hung-Ruei Liao and co-authors report the first use of boron neutron capture therapy for a child's returning salivary gland tumor in a 2026 case report. Sialoblastoma is rare and aggressive, and standard radiation threatens a young child's growing jaw and face. A six-year-old girl received two sessions of the boron-based treatment, which targets tumor cells selectively.

Her cancer vanished for 23 months after the first session, and a lasting partial response followed the second, with follow-up reaching 52 months in total. Dose checks put the jaw exposure near 4.3 Gy-Eq on their scale, well under the 15 Gy level linked to skeletal harm. The case frames the method as a salvage option that spares facial growth.
pmc-13328005:
Diogo Fonseca da Cunha and colleagues compare two nerve block plans for hip surgery pain in a 2026 meta-analysis. A combined pericapsular and skin nerve block promises pain relief that spares leg strength, unlike the wider fascia iliaca block. Six randomized trials with 442 patients were pooled under standard bias checks.

The combined block cut resting pain at six and twenty-four hours, by mean differences of 0.72 and 0.91 points against the rival on their scales, and quadriceps strength grades stayed higher, with far less weakness at six hours. Patients also walked sooner, while opioid use and nausea did not differ clearly. Sparing muscle strength matters because early walking speeds hip recovery.
pmc-13328505:
Dengling Huang and colleagues report in 2026 on a new blood test for tuberculosis in captive cynomolgus monkeys. Older tests often miss cases or give false results, which makes screening whole colonies hard. The team used computer methods to search bacterial proteins for short pieces that trigger immune responses.

Their search found a peptide called MP71, taken from the MPT64 protein. They linked it to a carrier and built an indirect ELISA test around it. The test was checked in a learning group of 19 animals and a separate group of 21 animals. In the second group it found over 92 percent of cases with no false positives. The authors present it as a fast tool for routine colony checks.
pmc-13329905:
Weijia Shen and team built a ruthenium catalyst for highly enantioselective alkynylation of fluoral. Their 2026 paper tells of an iodide-bound catalyst made from a hydride precursor and a chiral Ph-BPE ligand, driving additions of terminal alkynes with fluoral hydrate and related difluoro-aldehydes. It tolerates air and water, works without added base, and picks fluorinated aldehydes over aromatic ones.

Math across twelve possible stereogenic-at-metal acetylide complexes showed two octahedral forms make up 99.9% of the Boltzmann population, yet in one Curtin-Hammett-type case the less stable of the two drives carbonyl addition rates. Fuzzy bond order math showed formyl-hydrogen bonds to iodide are stronger than to chloride in transition states, since iodide's greater size and polarizability partly explain why the iodide version wins out. The work explains how a minor diastereomer can govern selectivity in asymmetric catalysis.
pmc-13330605:
Elias Guillén-Guzmán and a large team study relatives who support people with gambling disorder in a 2026 report. Harm spreads beyond the gambler to partners and parents, yet their burden is little mapped. In total, 184 patients in treatment and their affected relatives took part in interviews and standard mental health checks.

Relatives were mostly women in partner or parent roles and reported high distress in the reported profiles. Partners fared worst, while fathers tended to be older and more often jobless. Self-blame and withdrawal coping tied strongly to higher distress, while problem-solving tied to better wellbeing. Coping style, patient impulsivity, and patient traits together explained about 30 percent of distress spread. Support for relatives matters, the authors argue.
pmc-13330805:
Aziz Atashov and team present the making and structure of a trisulfane-bridged bis-thiadiazole. Their 2026 structure paper covers 5,5'-(trisulfane-1,3-diyl)bis(1,3,4-thiadiazol-2-amine), with two thiadiazol-2-amine moieties bridged by a trisulfanediyl group. The 1,3,4-thiadiazole ring has five members, with two nitrogen atoms and one sulfur atom, valued as a stable, electron-poor scaffold for diverse bioactive compounds.

In the crystal, N-H···N bonds form endless chains along [010]. Groups at the 2- and 5-positions of these rings enable creation of germ-fighting and cancer-fighting leads. Common routes include ring-closing of thiosemicarbazides or diacylhydrazines, substitution, and C-H activation. The paper covers the new compound by spectroscopy and refinement, with hydrogen spots set by a riding model. The report adds a trisulfane-bridged example to this ring family, backing further work on sulfur-bridged rings in bioactive design.
pmc-13332505:
Adriana Vazão and co-authors pose a 2026 ECG challenge from an out-of-hospital emergency call. An 81-year-old woman had taken multiple tablets of alprazolam, lorazepam, and dosulepin in a suicide attempt, and monitoring during gastric lavage showed a strange tracing.

Her first ECG showed sinus rhythm with first-degree AV block and left axis shift. It also showed a right bundle branch block pattern with ST elevation across V1 to V3, I, and aVL, which would normally suggest a heart attack. She denied chest pain, her creatine kinase was normal at 93 U/L, and ultrasound showed a thickened left ventricle with no wall motion problems. The walkthrough reveals the culprit as swapped right and left arm electrodes, which reshuffles the limb leads into exactly this confusing picture. The case then asks about next management, favoring monitoring and firm blood pressure control over rushed angiography.
pmc-13332705:
Khaled M Malkawi and colleagues report a 2026 case of ANCA-positive eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis presenting as stubborn asthma plus nerve and skin disease. This rare small-vessel inflammation features asthma, high counts of a white cell type, and tissue inflammation rich in those cells. Early diagnosis is often hard because first signs mimic uncontrolled asthma or other eosinophilic lung diseases. The patient was a 66-year-old man with adult-onset asthma and four months of worsening breathlessness, general symptoms, nerve damage, and skin inflammation.

Tests showed markedly high eosinophil counts, raised inflammation markers, and high creatine kinase, lactate dehydrogenase, and IgG4. Imaging showed calcified chest lymph nodes without lung infiltrates. A key antibody test was positive, and skin biopsy confirmed small-vessel inflammation with eosinophil buildup. The case urges clinicians to weigh this disease when asthma resists care and nerve or skin signs join the picture.
pmc-13333405:
Ryuk Jun Kwon and Yohwan Lim followed fatty liver trajectories in the UK Biobank in a 2026 cohort study. They asked whether a single snapshot of metabolic fatty liver disease tells the whole cancer story. The condition can appear, persist, or fade between check-ups, and earlier work hinted that even past exposure leaves a mark.

The study included 12,111 people screened twice. Fatty liver disease was defined by a fatty liver index of at least 60 plus a metabolic risk factor, and 33.1 percent had it at baseline. Having the condition at either visit roughly tripled later liver cancer risk, with adjusted hazard ratios of 2.81 and 2.61. Sorting people into four paths, those whose disease cleared still carried a hazard ratio of 4.00, and those with it at both visits 3.51, each against the never-diseased group. The authors argue both lasting and past fatty liver exposure deserve weight in cancer risk thinking.
pmc-13333505:
Aikaterini Skeva and a Greek team report in 2026 that a fragment of hepatitis B virus genetic material circulating in blood does more than mark viral activity: it stirs inflammation. Pregenomic RNA can be detected in patients on treatment, and the study asked what immune machinery its presence switches on.

Among 88 chronic hepatitis B patients, 18.1 percent carried pregenomic RNA. Gene profiling of eight patients, half positive and half negative, converged on platelet activation and neutrophil granule-release pathways. Lab work showed platelets exposed to positive serum switched on self-digesting autophagy and freshly made the germ-fighting peptide LL-37. When platelets met neutrophils, the pair adopted an inflammatory stance heavy on IL-1β with little net formation. The same IL-1β and LL-37 excess showed up in patient liver tissue. The authors conclude the viral RNA drives a platelet-neutrophil inflammatory axis, offering an angle on why hepatitis B smoulders even under therapy.
pmc-13335805:
Yang Chen and co-authors ran a fully automated randomized trial inside a hospital's electronic record system in a 2026 feasibility study called THIRST Alert. Many everyday treatments lack trial evidence because conventional trials are slow and costly, and randomization rarely lives inside routine care.

At one center between May and November 2023, an interruptive alert fired when doctors opened a patient's drug chart. The patient had acute heart failure and had received more than one intravenous furosemide dose within 48 hours. Consenting patients were randomized to a one-liter daily oral fluid restriction or no restriction. Identification, allocation, and outcome capture all ran through the record system. The study tests whether embedded alerts can make pragmatic trials nearly automatic.
pmc-13336405:
Mingxu Song and co-authors built radiation-hard neuromorphic hardware to reconstruct sea surface temperature in a 2026 device study. Ocean monitoring electronics face memory bottlenecks and radiation damage that conventional CMOS handles poorly.

Their synapses use synthetic antiferromagnetic stacks that switch magnetization without external fields through spin-orbit torque and hold many conductance levels, mimicking synapses and neurons. After a hefty gamma dose of 1 Mrad, the devices kept over 92 percent of their performance, thanks to strong antiferromagnetic coupling. Mapping the devices' nonlinear response onto a Perceiver IO cross-attention model let the system rebuild full temperature fields from sparse sensors. On a NOAA dataset it reached root-mean-square error below 2 degrees Celsius, rivaling deep learning on ordinary hardware.
pmc-13336605:
Amelie H Ohlrogge and colleagues published a 2026 update on high blood pressure across Australia. Drawing on the National Health Survey, the update tracks how common the condition is, how often it is treated, and how often it is brought under control between 2022 and 2024. High blood pressure remains the leading risk factor for heart disease and early death in the country.

Control improved to 39.6 percent in 2022 to 2023, up from 32 percent in 2017 to 2018, while overall prevalence rose from 33.7 to 39.4 percent. Rates were worse for First Nations peoples, younger people, and people in poorer areas. The authors argue that fairer care is essential if Australia is to reach its goal of 70 percent control by 2030.
pmc-13336905:
Jaeyong Ahn and co-authors use heat to flip and strengthen twisted light sensing in a 2026 optoelectronics study. Detecting circularly polarized near-infrared light serves imaging, health wearables, and optical links. Their chiral fused-ring molecules self-organize into twisted assemblies whose handedness changes with halogen choice and baking temperature.

Fluorine versions grew ordered domains step by step as heat rose, while chlorine versions stalled above 150°C in the comparison runs. The fluorine films reached a top absorption dissymmetry factor near 0.1 in optical tests. Built into vertical transistors, they gave fast, record-level polarized detection at 850 nm with strong sensitivity in the reported devices. Heat-tuned twist offers a dial for chiral light sensors.
pmc-13337005:
Yang Yang and co-authors strap nano backpacks onto probiotic bacteria to treat inflamed bowels in a 2026 study. Inflammatory bowel disease mixes microbe imbalance with overload of harmful oxygen species, and loose drug mixtures often miss the inflamed spot in time and place. Their Bacillus subtilis spores wear chitosan coats plus tungsten oxide particles wrapped in polydopamine.

At inflamed sites the shell mops up oxygen species, then breaks down and slowly releases tungsten ions. Those ions block a nitrate-using enzyme in harmful Enterobacteriaceae, clearing space for friendly microbes. The settled probiotics restored microbe balance, fixed metabolic disorder, and repaired the gut barrier in models. Timed cascade control beats simply mixing therapies.
pmc-13337205:
Duuamene Nyimanu and Alan S.L Yu comment on timing in polycystic kidney disease in a 2026 editorial titled Timing Matters. The disease, among the most common inherited disorders, affects nearly 12.5 million people worldwide and ranks fourth among causes of adult kidney failure. The editorial discusses a study by Sharma and co-authors in the same journal issue.

That study charted kidney microRNAs, tiny gene regulators, across the whole course of disease in a mouse model. Earlier work showed removing the microRNA-making enzyme Dicer causes cysts, and clusters such as miR-17 drive cyst growth and metabolic rewiring. A time-ordered map could show when each regulator acts, helping match future treatments to disease stage rather than giving one therapy for all stages.
pmc-13337705:
Müzeyyen Soyer and Seçil Ömür Sünbül examine partner phubbing in a 2026 survey of adults in romantic relationships. Phubbing means ignoring a partner to look at a phone during face-to-face time. The study asks how that experience differs by gender, marital status, age, and time together.

A total of 446 adults completed the Partner Phubbing Scale. Women reported higher levels than men, and married respondents scored higher than single ones. Reports rose with age, and couples together 5 to 10 years scored highest. Statistical models flagged gender and that mid-length duration as predictors, suggesting daily phone habits weigh differently across stages of a relationship.
pmc-13337905:
Alex Zaharakis and Christian Bogner report a 2026 single case of light therapy and urine metals in a young child. A 5-year-old boy with autism spectrum disorder had earlier shown high urinary aluminum. Pulsed red light at 660 nm, which acts on cell energy systems, was tested without chelation drugs.

Eight urine samples from November 2025 were measured, with two taken before light sessions began. Baseline aluminum sat near 10 units, then rose to 58 on day 3 and peaked at 98 on day 7 in the reported values. Levels stayed above the reference range at two-month follow-up. Mercury also ran high throughout, so results need cautious reading.
pmc-13340305:
Yani Hao and colleagues hunted root microbes in 2026 that free phosphorus in chalky soils, where locked phosphorus wastes plant food. Rapeseed roots give off organic matter that can free bound phosphorus, yet the microbe route in chalky soils was unclear. The team screened root zone soil for microbes that dissolve phosphate and mapped their key chemical routes.

Fourteen main phosphate freeing strains were found, and Advenella alkanexedens was proved a strong activator of bound phosphorus. Such microbes could cut plant food waste and lift crop phosphorus uptake. Field tests must now check whether lab promise holds in real chalky soils.
pmc-13341005:
Umesh Pandwar and colleagues tested the Renal Angina Index in 2026 for predicting acute kidney injury in paediatric intensive care. The prospective study included 300 children aged one month to 13 years, treated at Gandhi Medical College in Bhopal between September 2022 and February 2024. The index was calculated 24 hours after admission and correlated with kidney injury after that point.

Mean age was 36.16 months and 50.7 percent were male, while acute kidney injury occurred in 5 percent. Death rates rose sharply across risk groups: 0 percent low risk, 7.5 percent moderate risk, and 68.8 percent high risk. The index offers an early warning tool to target monitoring and preventive care in critically ill children.
pmc-13341305:
Forecasting a hard airway view in babies with Pierre Robin sequence is tackled by Danling Hu and colleagues in the 2026 machine learning study. These infants often have small jaws and displaced tongues, so laryngoscopy can be unexpectedly difficult during surgery.

Records covered 214 infants treated in 2023 and 2024, with airway anatomy measured from three-dimensional CT scans. Seven learning models were built and checked in a separate group of 80 infants from a later period. Tongue length emerged as one independent predictor among the scan measures. Objective imaging-based forecasts could help anesthesia teams prepare equipment and plans before the first attempt.
pmc-13341505:
A hybrid neural network sorts nine retinal diseases from fundus photos, in a 2026 study by Yaoyang Cheng and colleagues. RHT-Net fuses residual convolutional layers for local detail with transformer encoders that catch long-range patterns across the image.

Training used 5,318 real fundus images from Bengali patients, expanded by rotation, flipping, and noise to 21,272 images, then contrast-enhanced and resized. The model hit 97.93% training accuracy and 96.12% on held-out tests, with an overall F1-score of 95.31%. Heat map visualizations supported its decisions. Scalable screening like this could ease specialist shortages in eye care.
pmc-13341605:
Banana varieties host partly distinct inner microbes, in a 2026 study by Shiva A. Aghdam and Amanda M. V. Brown. Six cultivars, three wild diploids and three domesticated triploids, grew side by side while their above- and below-ground endophytes were deep-sequenced.

Pseudomonas, Acinetobacter, and Enterobacter were among the common genera, along with Devosia and Rhizobium, though 27.4% of sequence variants defied classification. Cultivar explained a small but real share of community differences, about 2.7% by one measure, with tissue type and domestication status adding less. Guessed functions differed too, with 49 pathways separating wild from domesticated plants. Genotype shapes the microbiome, but only a little.
pmc-13342205:
Qiuyu Mo and co-authors present a 2026 laboratory study of signaling proteins in bone marrow fluid from people with acute myeloid leukemia. The group measured a broad panel of interleukins and related immune signals and asked whether the mix shifts as the disease starts, clears, or returns.

Marrow samples came from 75 patients: 41 newly diagnosed, 19 in complete remission, and 15 with relapsed or stubborn disease. Several signals differed across the groups, and levels of IL-17 and TGF-β rose at diagnosis, fell in remission, and rose again at relapse. Tracking these proteins over time could help doctors judge disease activity and adjust treatment.
pmc-13343005:
Ulrike Grote, Trung Thanh Nguyen, and Manh Hung Do describe the Thailand Vietnam Socio-Economic Panel in 2026, a long-running household dataset from rural Thailand and Vietnam. Farm families there face droughts, floods, price swings, and health shocks, and the panel tracks how welfare and coping change over many years.

Ten survey waves from 2007 to 2024 cover 2,200 households in 220 villages across three provinces in each country. Topics span income from land, crops, and livestock, spending, assets, housing, well-being, and personal traits, with a migrant tracking arm linking city workers to remittances sent home. The data let researchers and policymakers study long-term rural change with real household histories.
pmc-13344205:
Carrie J Ngongo and colleagues reviewed heat risks in pregnancy in 2026, urging clearer public messages to help mothers and babies in a warming climate. Extreme heat exposure raises pregnancy risks, and exposure is increasing worldwide, with low income countries hit hardest by high maternal and neonatal death plus marked climate vulnerability. Despite proof on heat linked risks, clear messages have not reached the public in usable form.

Heat exposure links to obstetric harms affecting mother and offspring, yet risk communication stays weak. Strengthening proof and improving messages are urgent needs to prevent heat linked deaths and illnesses. The review calls for heat guidance that pregnant people can actually act on during heatwaves.
pmc-13346005:
Agasthian Thirugnanam reported in 2026 the first known case of an isolated jugular vein clot caused by an abnormal thymoma pressing on the vein. Tumours of the thymus can invade nearby veins and cause superior vena cava syndrome, but blockage limited to one internal jugular vein had not been described.

A 51-year-old man noticed prominent left neck veins for a month, and ultrasound confirmed a clot in the left internal jugular vein. Scans found a five-centimetre thymoma growing from an anomalous thymus lobe behind the left innominate vein, compressing the junction with the subclavian vein. The clot cleared within a week of treatment, and the tumour was removed by keyhole chest surgery. The case widens the differential diagnosis for unexplained neck vein clots.
pmc-13347705:
Witness Mapanga, Chenai Mlandu, and Khuthala Mabetha map child health policy and its weak spots in South Africa, in a scoping review published in 2026. Sources from 2008 to 2023 spanned journals, health ministry reports, planning bodies. Grey material, charted by a standard scoping method to show where policy effort clusters and where delivery lags over fifteen years.

Effort clustered on food provision, mother and child health, growth, income support, and access to resources. Yet wording and delivery in those areas still rated poor to moderate in the synthesis. Caregiver support and related areas drew weak priority and vague plans, leaving uneven care despite a wide policy shelf, a gap the review urges planners to close.
pmc-13349905:
Wenbo Lv and co-authors reviewed lactylation, a newer chemical tagging of proteins, in atherosclerosis in 2026. Atherosclerosis narrows large and medium arteries and underlies much heart disease and stroke.

Lactylation attaches lactate-derived groups to proteins, changing how they behave. The review gathers evidence tying this process to inflammation, vessel wall cell ageing and identity shifts, new vessel growth, and disturbed metabolism inside plaques. Lactate was once seen as mere waste from oxygen-starved cells. Showing it actively rewrites protein function opens fresh drug targets, and the authors argue that blocking harmful lactylation might slow plaque growth and cut cardiovascular events.
pmc-13350005:
Chun-Rui Liu and co-authors weighed in 2026 deep learning, radiomics, and fusion models for telling parathyroid adenoma from carcinoma or atypical tumours on ultrasound. This split is vital for surgery planning. Yet ultrasound accuracy still leans heavily on the operator.

Looking back at 1,122 patients from two Chinese hospitals from 2016 to 2025, the team pooled multi-centre data to tackle the rarity of carcinoma and atypical cases, only 74 in total. Cases were split into training and validation sets by pathology. Radiomics, deep learning, and joined models were weighed head to head. The fusion path promises more steady, less operator-bound sorting, helping surgeons plan the right operation first time.
pmc-13350605:
Jakub Śmiechowicz and co-authors audited sepsis care in 55 Polish hospitals in a 2026 analysis drawn from a European survey. Sepsis kills quickly when missed, so hospitals are urged to screen and treat it in a standard way.

Only 44 percent of hospitals applied the current Sepsis-3 definition. Screening ran in just 27 percent, and standardised management in 38.2 percent, across emergency departments, wards, and intensive care. Quality improvement programmes were also patchy. A national baseline like this turns vague concern into specific gaps that training, staffing, and protocols can be aimed at closing.
pmc-13352505:
Yang Ma and co-authors build a layered graphene and MXene material for charge storage in 2026. MXene sheets tend to restack during use, which blocks electrolyte access and caps storage. Vertical graphene nanowalls were grown on Ti3C2Tx MXene films to hold the layers apart, using acid etching, filtration assembly, and plasma vapour growth.

The upright walls widen sheet gaps and open multi-direction paths for ions, exposing more active sites. In sulphuric acid within a 0.7 V window, the hybrid reached an areal capacitance of 163.17 mF per square centimetre at a slow scan rate. That value is a 1.2-fold gain over the base material. The design offers a route to stronger supercapacitor electrodes.
pmc-13352605:
Noah Richter and co-authors report a nickel-catalysed route to fluorinated alcohol building blocks in 2026. Their catalyst forms in place from a stable nickel stilbene complex and a chiral VAPOL-based ligand, with triethylborane as promoter. Fluorinated sorbamides were coupled with aldehydes in a handedness-controlled way.

The ligand steered where the new bond formed and set excellent handedness control, creating a fluorinated carbon centre beside a fresh alcohol group. The motif mimics a common anti-configured unit in natural products with fluorine swapped in, enabling a fluorine scan of known active compounds. Mechanism checks showed the only visible nickel complex sits off the working cycle as a reservoir, backed by a negative nonlinear effect and computer modelling.
pmc-13355005:
Naima Parveen and co-authors review in 2026 how the thyroid gland and the liver affect each other. Thyroid hormones steer how the liver handles fat, sugar, and energy, while the liver moves, activates, and clears those hormones. The review pulls together work on body processes, clinic care, and new drugs.

Thyroid problems link to fatty liver disease, poor blood fats, and liver harm, while liver disease can skew thyroid tests and cause misleading results. A new liver-focused drug, resmetirom, marks a major step for fatty liver care. The authors flag open questions on hormone measures, long-term drug safety, and when hormone replacement helps the liver.
pmc-13355405:
R van Pel and co-authors report a 2026 case series on using guided bronchoscopy to check lung spots in people being assessed for lung transplant. Such spots raise fears of cancer, which can bar transplant, yet biopsy answers are slow to get. Of 173 patients assessed at one center, twelve had suspect spots and eight had the guided scope test.

The scope reached the spot in every case, with no complications, and results changed transplant or care decisions in most cases. Most patients had severe COPD, and spots were small, at a median of twelve millimeters. The authors say the method can speed clear decisions on who can proceed to transplant.
pmc-13355805:
Emil Espinal and co-authors compared two repair methods in 2026 for a bone cut used in stemless shoulder replacement surgery. During the operation, a small bone piece with tendon attached is cut and must be fixed back. Ten cadaver shoulders were repaired either by bone tunnels or by suture anchors, then loaded again and again until failure.

Both methods failed at much the same load and after much the same number of cycles, and gapping during loading did not differ. The tunnel method trended stiffer but also shifted more, though neither trend reached significance. The authors call this pilot work a base for larger studies of repair choice.
pmc-13356505:
Andrea Mazzoleni and co-authors built a fully human 3D bone niche model in 2026 to study how prostate cancer interacts with bone, its most common spread site. Animal models differ from humans, and the role of bone-eating cells called osteoclasts was murky. Their model grows bone-forming and bone-eating cells together on a mineral scaffold, and hosts cancer cells and patient tumor organoids.

Cancer cells quieted bone cell genes, hinting they suppress bone renewal. In return, cancer cells began to copy bone cell traits, a shift strongly shaped by the bone-eating cells. Patient organoids grew in the niche without added cancer growth factors, which supports the model's clinic relevance.
pmc-13358505:
Abisiniya Kabtimer and co-authors tell the story of a tricky case in a 2026 report. A 21-year-old woman had a thigh lump that looked like a stubborn infection. It did not heal with antibiotics or drainage, a strange course for a simple abscess. Tests after surgery showed it was in fact a rare, fast-growing soft tissue cancer.

The cancer, called undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma, is more common in older adults and can hide behind signs of infection. The report walks through the scans, tissue tests, and wide surgery used to clear it. Later scans found spots in her lungs, which led her to a major cancer center. The case warns doctors to rethink lumps that fail standard care.
pmc-13359005:
Vasileios T. Stavrou and co-authors test exercise at home for a scarring lung disease in a 2026 report. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis makes travel to a rehab center hard for many patients. Their service offered a four-week supervised exercise program by video link, then watched what happened over four weeks with no training.

Thirteen patients took part and finished about 92 percent of their sessions, with no exercise-related harms. Walking distance rose by about eight percent after training, and physical health scores improved too. Both gains faded once training stopped. The report supports home programs as safe and workable, while showing that benefits need upkeep.
pmc-13359105:
Wangfei Yang and co-authors apply knot theory to floppy proteins in a 2026 study. Intrinsically disordered proteins never settle into one shape, so standard tools struggle to describe them. The team measured how tangled these proteins are, using two numbers borrowed from the math of knots, across more than 28,000 simulated examples.

One measure mostly tracks how compact a protein is. The second catches deeper tangling that simple measures miss, and it links to what the protein does. Grouping proteins by these features revealed regions rich in certain functions. The work offers a fresh language for a class of proteins tied to many diseases.
pmc-13359605:
Yi-Teng Hung and co-authors pilot a skin treatment for melasma in a 2026 study. Melasma causes stubborn brown patches, often on the face, and no single treatment leads the field. Microneedle radiofrequency, which sends heat through tiny needles, has been tried recently. The team tracked its effects with a standard severity score and with coherence tomography scans that image skin layers.

Only five patients are detailed, split into response groups after treatment. Scans showed pigment clumps breaking up and spacing out, and fewer pigment-handling cells. Two patients reached a fair response and three a poor one. As a pilot, the study mainly maps how the skin changes, to guide larger trials.
pmc-13359705:
Zoltán Kiss and co-authors chart cancer in Hungary across the COVID-19 years in a 2026 study. Using nationwide health insurance data, they compared cancer cases and deaths before the pandemic (2011 to 2019), during it (2020 to 2021), and after (2022 to 2023). Diagnosis had already been slowly declining before the virus arrived.

During the pandemic years, new diagnoses fell sharply below expectation. The steepest drops hit slow-growing cancers that routine screening finds, among them cancers of the prostate, kidney, and skin. By 2022 and 2023, detection partly recovered for some of these. The record helps health planners judge the pandemic's hidden cancer cost and the backlog still to clear.
pmc-13361805:
Burak Manay and co-authors studied swallowing in brain-injured patients with tracheostomies in a 2026 paper. Swallowing trouble is common after traumatic brain injury, and a breathing tube in the neck adds its own complications. The team reviewed 80 patients who used a speaking valve, which lets air reach the voice box. Patients were grouped by tube type: with or without a small window opening.

A camera exam rated how each patient swallowed, and a standard scale graded food residue left in the throat. Airway narrowing was graded on a classic scale. Layered analysis asked whether tube type itself links to residue once narrowing and other health traits are counted. Answers can guide tube choice and feeding safety for a group at risk of food entering the lungs.
pmc-13361905:
Valéria Tavares and co-authors studied a vitamin D gene variant and cancer wasting in a 2026 paper. Cancer cachexia is a syndrome of muscle loss, inflammation, and poor treatment tolerance that shortens lives. People differ widely in who develops it, hinting that genes play a part. Vitamin D guides muscle growth and calms inflammation through its receptor, so the team examined one common variant of that receptor gene.

The cohort held 140 adult cancer patients. The variant, called rs731236, changes how active the receptor is. The team tested whether it tracks with cachexia risk and with overall survival. A gene that flags high-risk patients could guide earlier nutrition and anti-inflammatory care, when wasting is still reversible.
pmc-13362405:
Warinda Prommachote and co-authors offer a 2026 computer-based study that hunts for new ways to weaken Staphylococcus aureus, a germ that often resists standard drugs. Instead of killing the germ, their plan blocks a surface protein it uses to grab iron from blood. They screened look-alike small molecules on a computer and ranked how well each one fit that protein.

Two lead molecules bound the target tightly and stayed stable in long computer runs that mimic real motion. Both passed basic drug-like checks, but one showed more risk signs for the liver, heart, and kidneys. The authors flag the safer one as the better pick, while stressing that lab tests must confirm these computer results.
pmc-13365605:
Juliani Juliani and co-workers probe in 2026 if half loss of a cell clean up gene is enough to weaken the gut wall. Full loss in gut skin kills mice by gut swell. Half loss is more like the dips seen in some human ills. The team breeds mice with half the gene in gut skin.

Half loss mice keep calm clean up, but their cell frame shifts and their small gut runs short. In the large gut, slime cells thin and slime drops. A harsh chem test then hits them hard, with more weight loss and worse gut harm. Half loss leaves the wall frail.
pmc-13369605:
Reema Mohammad Munshi and others ask whether age shapes the risk of hospital admission caused by medicines in a 2026 review.
