They searched eight major research databases for studies from January 2000 to March 2025, keeping adult studies that reported age for both admitted patients and a comparison group. Two reviewers screened each study, and a third settled disagreements.

The team pooled risk figures for adults aged 16 to 64 against those aged 65 and older. They also compared average ages of people admitted for medicine-related reasons with people admitted for other causes. The review pulls scattered evidence into one view, so care teams can see which age groups face the most risk and where safer prescribing and closer checks could prevent harm.
pmc-13371705:
Sameera Wijayawardhana and colleagues lay out a plan to review bone age methods in children across ethnic groups in a 2026 protocol paper. Hand and wrist X-rays are widely used to judge biological maturity when exact age is unknown or when endocrine, genetic, or developmental disorders are suspected. Yet skeletal maturity varies by ethnicity, casting doubt on universal reference charts.

The planned review will search five major databases, screen studies with two independent reviewers, and pool results on method accuracy by ethnicity. Quality will be assessed and results reported with a PRISMA flow diagram. Because this is a protocol, no findings are reported yet. The completed review should tell clinicians which bone age charts travel safely across populations and which do not.
pmc-13373305:
Smith and colleagues tested in 2026 whether oxidants made naturally in the body can switch off p16INK4a, a tumor guard protein that brakes cell division. Earlier work showed that oxidizing the protein's single cysteine, a sulfur-bearing building block, folds it into inactive amyloid fibrils, rope-like clumps. The team exposed lab-made p16 to five body-relevant oxidants and tracked the change with gels, dye tests, mass measurement, and electron microscopy.

Two oxidants, peroxymonocarbonate and hypothiocyanous acid, drove the protein to pair up through its cysteine and then form amyloid fibrils. The other three, including hydrogen peroxide, were weaker and mainly produced shapeless clumps instead. The split shows that not all oxidative stress is equal for this guard protein. The authors suggest such selective switching could help explain how long-term oxidative strain in tissue quietly disables a key brake on cancer.
pmc-13373605:
Sarah Cook and co-authors made a free kit for social media hiring into drug trials in a 2026 paper. Trials often miss their sign-up goals, and social feeds give a new way to reach people. Many teams lack clear steps for that work, though.

The kit was built by a hub for hiring craft, shaped by user views and years of team know-how. It gives best steps, tips for each feed type, and forms teams can adapt. Kit pages walk a team from plan to posts to checks on what worked. The aim is more fair and full sign-up, so trial results speak for all.
pmc-13373805:
Katherina Petrou and colleagues comment on new molecular signs of heat stress in coral symbionts in a 2026 commentary. The piece responds to work by Johnston and colleagues on infrared microspectroscopy signatures of thermal stress in the algae that live inside corals. Bleaching, driven by marine heatwaves, is now frequent and is stripping reefs of heat-sensitive species.

Some corals tolerate heat better, and some shuffle to tougher algal partners, but warming outpaces natural adaptation, at high cost to biodiversity. The commentary frames assisted evolution, including selective breeding and genetic interventions, as a way to speed adaptation. New molecular signatures could help researchers spot tolerant symbionts early and choose breeding stock for reefs that must survive warmer seas.
pmc-13377005:
Irene Best and co-authors review qualitative research on the distress that accompanies delirium in hospitalised older adults. Delirium affects up to half of older inpatients and is often missed or mistaken for depression or dementia. Their 2026 scoping review organises the evidence using the Theory of Unpleasant Symptoms, a framework linking symptom influences and consequences.

Fourteen studies with qualitative or mixed designs were included, covering patients, their care partners, and nurses, since distress extends to witnesses as well as patients. The framework sorted factors that shape the distress and what follows from it. The reviewers found the experiences of care partners and nurses understudied, as were patients whose delirium sits on top of dementia. How the distress changes from acute care through to long-term care also remains unclear. They map these gaps for future qualitative work.
pmc-13377805:
Kiana Yousefipour and others review repurposing melatonin as an adjunct for gastrointestinal cancers in a 2026 paper. Gastrointestinal cancers are common and often carry poor prognosis, while chemo toxicity and low compliance limit treatment. Melatonin, a hormone with low toxicity, shows antitumour effects by modifying signals pathways, blocking growth and spread, triggering cell death and self-eating, and cutting oxidative stress.

The review traces melatonin action across gastrointestinal cancers, emphasising its power to boost chemo effect while reducing toxicity. Because melatonin is already well characterised, it could be used off-label as an adjunct to improve prognosis and quality of life. The work gathers the gene case for trials testing melatonin alongside standard gastrointestinal cancer therapy.
pmc-13379505:
Luisa Rezende Batista and co-authors map the literature on diagnostic delay in rare diseases and its repercussions for patients. Rare diseases are often diagnosed late because they are uncommon, variable, and unfamiliar to many clinicians. Their 2026 scoping review follows standard reporting guidance and covers studies published between 2010 and 2025.

Twenty-three studies from thirteen countries were included, with a concentration in Europe and publication rising in recent years. Reported consequences of delay included psychological distress such as anxiety and frustration, misdiagnosis and inappropriate treatment, disease progression, heavier healthcare use, reduced quality of life, social isolation, and financial burden. The authors conclude that cutting delay needs coordinated public health effort, better diagnostic infrastructure, and more professional training, so patients reach earlier diagnosis, better outcomes, and timely genetic counseling for their families.
pmc-13380405:
Finian M O'Malley, Amelia Street, and Kush Deshpande describe a 2026 quality improvement project on handover notes when patients move from intensive care to a ward. That move carries risk, and local rules require the verbal handover to be documented with its time. In practice, recording was patchy.

Working in a large hospital in Sydney, Australia, the team first measured one week of discharges. It then introduced changes over two days: a visual prompt, a meeting reminder, and digital messages. The design drew on human factors ideas to cut mental load. A repeat check four weeks later measured whether documentation became more frequent and more complete.
pmc-13382005:
Lv and colleagues measure forever chemicals in the fluid around women's eggs, in a 2026 multicenter fertility study across China. Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, PFAS, persist in the environment and may harm reproduction. The team quantified 20 PFAS in follicular fluid from 1,301 women undergoing assisted reproduction in eight regions. They then linked levels to live birth, pregnancy loss, hormone measures, and egg and embryo development, combining center-specific models and correcting for multiple comparisons in the pooled analysis.

Both legacy and newer PFAS appeared, with PFOS contributing 19 to 40 percent of total concentration and PFOA 23 to 37 percent across centers. Levels ran higher in eastern and southern China. Higher PFOS was linked with biochemical pregnancy loss, at a relative risk of 2.10 per natural-log unit increase in concentration. Several PFAS also tracked with lower luteinizing hormone, higher progesterone, and thinner womb lining. Aquatic foods emerged as a dietary contributor worth attention.
pmc-13382905:
Zhang and colleagues build BattFailScholar, a language model system augmented with a battery failure knowledge graph, in 2026 energy research. Diagnosing why batteries fail demands experts or data-hungry learning that generalizes poorly and explains nothing. Their framework assembles a knowledge graph linking material properties, sensor signals, and failure pathways from incidents. A retrieval method feeds relevant knowledge into the language model's reasoning, so diagnoses cite established failure chains instead of improvising stories from text patterns.

Experiments showed a 19.7 percent improvement in language-model-based diagnosis over the unaugmented baseline. The system reached 86.2 percent accuracy in identifying failure mechanisms or causes in the set. Gains were strongest on long-tail problems, rare failure modes where training data are thin and ordinary models flounder. Zhang positions the system as diagnostic support for research and development teams, and as a tool for discovering failure chains that review might miss in incident records.
pmc-13383905:
Xuejun Du's team built a sheep model of knee osteoarthritis and piloted focused ultrasound for pain, in a 2026 study. Knee osteoarthritis lacks good non-surgical pain options, and large-animal models matching human joint anatomy were needed. The team induced osteoarthritis in the right knees of nine sheep with monosodium iodoacetate injections on days 8 and 29, tracking them for 12 weeks.

Treated knees developed joint space narrowing, osteophytes, cartilage erosion, and disrupted architecture, confirming the model. Only two sheep developed persistent pain behaviors, and in those, MRI-guided focused ultrasound between weeks 6 and 8 improved pain scores and activity without added harm. The pilot supports larger controlled trials of ultrasound pain therapy.
pmc-13384005:
Bettina Csilla Budai and colleagues pool trial evidence on immune-support feeding in gut cancer surgery in a 2026 review. Special formulas with arginine, nucleotides, and omega-3 fats aim to cut problems after operations. The team searched three databases and gathered 90 randomized trials, with 55 fit for combined analysis covering 7,462 patients.

Patients given the immune formula around surgery had lower odds of joint leaks between bowel ends. Infection odds also fell across lung, urinary, wound, and blood infection outcomes. Hospital stays shortened by about two and a half days on average, which supports the formula as the best-tested option in this field.
pmc-13385005:
Kristina Maria Belakova and a large team study two families with low fibrinogen, a clotting protein shortage, in 2026 work. Clotting tests, a stiffness-based assay, gene analysis, and protein modeling were combined. In one family, an 18-year-old with mild bleeding carried two variants in the FGB gene at once.

One variant tracked with lower fibrinogen levels, while the other appeared in relatives with few or no symptoms. In a second family, the milder variant came with near-normal clot stiffness scores. Modeling suggested mixed structural effects, which helps explain why the same gene changes can yield such different clinical pictures.
pmc-13385905:
Sungwook Choi's team watched line defects guide metal particle exsolution in a doped perovskite, in a 2026 study. Self-assembled metal particles exsolved from host oxides excel in catalysis, but dopant transport pathways and defect interactions stayed hidden in the bulk. The team used in situ Bragg coherent X-ray imaging and electron microscopy during reduction of ruthenium-doped barium cerate.

Line defects nucleated in the bulk interior and propagated to the surface during reduction. Ruthenium dopant correlated specifically with mixed line-defect formation, and these defects acted as mobile carriers taking dopant to the surface. The pathway explains exsolution site, density, and spread, guiding design of more active and stable catalysts.
pmc-13386605:
Shao and colleagues race nine machine learning algorithms to predict which intensive care patients will develop sepsis after the first day, in 2026 informatics research. Sepsis strikes up to 30 percent of ICU patients and rewards early treatment. Using the MIMIC-III database, the team excluded patients septic within 24 hours, leaving 1,634 patients, of whom 349, or 21.4 percent, developed sepsis. Features were selected automatically, class imbalance was corrected in training, and models were judged on discrimination, calibration, and clinical usefulness.

The gradient boosting model XGBoost-DART won the comparison, reaching an accuracy score of 0.881 on the discrimination scale. It posted the best accuracy, at 0.847, and specificity of 0.897 among the nine algorithms. Rival models' scores ranged from 0.794 to 0.881 across the evaluation. Decision-curve analysis showed the model delivered the greatest net benefit over the broadest span of risk thresholds. Shao concludes models can flag deteriorating patients a day ahead reliably enough to guide monitoring intensity.
pmc-13386905:
Ying Wang and a large team show gut bacteria reaching the pancreas drive early islet cell death in diabetic mice in 2026 work. The drug streptozotocin damages the gut barrier while it triggers diabetes, a pairing the team untangled. Mice raised germ-free let them test whether bacteria themselves were required for the injury.

In normal mice, the drug broke the barrier, bacteria crossed to the pancreas, and insulin cells died. Germ-free mice had leaky barriers too, yet no islet death, which isolates the bacteria as the essential step. Transplants of altered gut communities reproduced the crossing and the damage.
pmc-13387305:
Shadi Sedgh-Gooya, Ahmad Mohebbifar, and Mehran Torki feed laying hens added chromium and zinc in a 2026 trial. The trial ran 216 hens aged 42 weeks on six diet mixes for twelve weeks in a factorial design. Three chromium levels crossed with two zinc levels let the team split single and joint effects.

Chromium failed to help laying, and hens without it laid more eggs with greater egg mass in the results. Zinc thickened shells while chromium thinned them, and their pairing set yolk color at its peak. Blood albumin rose with both minerals, while zinc lowered blood triglycerides, the authors report.
pmc-13387405:
Naveen Gowda and colleagues assess brace-augmented knee ligament surgery for severe rotational instability in a 2026 cohort study. Patients had complete ACL tears with the highest grade of pivot shift before surgery. The operation used a hamstring graft reinforced with a synthetic FiberTape brace to shield early healing.

Forty-three patients finished the study at a tertiary center, with function scored over twelve months. All knee scores improved steadily and significantly, and most patients reached excellent function by one year. Hands-on stability tests showed rotational control restored in the examined knees, the authors report.
pmc-13390205:
Sonia Servitja's team analysed long-term results for 8,825 Spanish patients with hormone-sensor-positive, HER2-negative early breast cancer, grouped by relapse risk. Endocrine therapy with or without CDK4/6 inhibitors is now standard for intermediate- and high-risk disease, but real-world long-term relapse data matter for prescribing choices.

With a median follow-up near eleven years, ten-year invasive disease-free life span ran 53.8 percent in the high-risk group, 73.8 percent in the intermediate group, and 84.0 percent in the low-risk group, with overall life span following the same gradient. High-risk relapses peaked in years two to three with a second peak at year seven, sharpening the case for extended vigilance.
pmc-13393605:
Jan Coveliers and four colleagues revisit claims that pumping blood back through an arm artery, rather than a leg artery, unloads the heart better during veno-arterial ECMO. The circuit is a rescue loop that takes over heart and lung work. Their letter urges caution about reading a common pressure measure, the pulmonary artery occlusion pressure, as a direct stand-in for left heart loading under such support.

Under ECMO that pressure blends two opposing forces: the circuit drains blood away, easing filling, while pumping into arteries raises the resistance the weakened heart must push against. In the data they re-examine, higher circuit flow raised pressures in the arteries and lowered the heart's own output and ejection measures. The headline pressure stayed flat. That pattern suggests the circuit was taking over rather than the ventricle resting. Arch anatomy, they add, further complicates any simple unloading story.
pmc-13393805:
Huan Cao and six colleagues decoded how prostate cancer enhancers, the DNA switches that boost gene activity, cooperate inside the three-dimensional folding of the genome. Pooling two hundred one datasets of an active enhancer mark across prostate samples, they pinpointed over three thousand cancer-specific enhancers. Ultra-fine mapping of contacts at one representative locus then showed those enhancers weaving highly nested connections with promoters, forming a multi-linked hub absent from normal prostate cells.

Deleting enhancers one by one with CRISPR split them into classes. Removing the central enhancer collapsed activity and architecture across the whole hub, slowing growth, while deleting a redundant one changed little because neighbours rewired their contacts to compensate. The pioneer factor FOXA1, switched on in prostate cancer, binds these enhancers and tunes the classes differently. The authors argue enhancer teamwork, not single switches, drives the cancer programme.
pmc-13393905:
Mahmoud A F Khalil leads an eight-author study of drug-resistant Klebsiella pneumoniae hiding in the guts of children hospitalised with COVID-19 at a tertiary hospital in Fayoum, Egypt. Gut carriage of such bacteria raises the risk of later infections elsewhere in the body, and pandemic antibiotic use fanned resistance. Stool from seventy-one young patients was cultured on selective media, and isolates faced drug panels, resistance gene hunting, and biofilm tests.

Half the children carried the bacterium, and every isolate was resistant: twenty-two shrugged off carbapenems, the last-line drugs, and fourteen produced broad-spectrum beta-lactam destroying enzymes. Two carbapenemase genes split the resistant group almost evenly. All isolates still answered to colistin, and biofilm formation was common in both groups. The authors call for routine carriage screening, tighter antibiotic stewardship, and stronger infection control in children's hospitals.
pmc-13394605:
Ping Wang and co-authors show, in 2026, that the daily clock in cotton plants times their defence against a soil fungus. The fungus, Verticillium dahliae, wilts cotton and cuts yield. Night-time resistance proved strongest, shaped by microbes around roots and by a hormone signal named jasmonic acid. A clock part named GhLUX held down brake genes called JAZ, which freed the hormone signal at night.

Plants with extra GhLUX fought the fungus better in field trials. They also gave more fibre, and the fibre was of better quality. Attack by the fungus sped the clock up and disturbed night microbes. The authors suggest clock tuning could guard crops without trading away harvest.
pmc-13395405:
Mei Lu and co-authors build, in 2026, a questionnaire that asks heart failure patients how comfortable their mouths feel. Mouth discomfort is common in this illness and can cut eating, speech, and life quality. Older tools let clinicians grade the mouth but miss what patients feel. The team drafted items from papers, patient talks, and expert rounds, guided by a comfort theory.

A final form of 24 items was tested in 190 hospital patients across three sites. Expert scores for item fit ran high, and answers hung together well. Factor maths found four parts that match the theory. Scores tied only weakly to a clinician scale, as hoped. More tests are planned.
pmc-13395905:
Marina Gasparini, Nicola Vanacore, and Valentina Moro trace, in 2026, the past and future of mind testing for dementia care. Testing grew from bedside craft to fixed batteries, then to remote and digital tools sped by the pandemic. The authors warn that unsupervised digital tests can mislead, as when video calls inflate deficit scores. Sound testing still rests on watchful clinical eyes.

Their call is to fuse new tech with personal, expert-led checks. Tailored tests, scans, and body signals should back one another, not stand alone. AI tools need expert hands on the wheel. The piece asks for fresh studies on how to blend old craft and new tools well.
pmc-13397005:
Gyutaek Oh and co-authors tested whether giving medical chatbots more thinking time at the moment of use, rather than more training, makes them better, and which strategy fits which model. Their 2026 evaluation covers large language and vision-language models working on medical tasks.

Test-time scaling covers tricks such as sampling many answers and voting, or letting a model reason in longer chains before replying. The team varied model size and task difficulty, and also probed whether models cave when a user pretends to clinical authority and pushes a wrong answer. Results are meant to guide hospitals on when extra computation buys accuracy and when it merely buys confidence.
pmc-13397705:
Soutrik Kundu and colleagues measure how leg length changes when a knee replacement straightens a bent leg. Their 2026 study reviews 237 primary knee replacements by one surgeon between August 2024 and July 2025. A leg that ends up longer or shorter can sour how the new joint feels and works.

Most knees (215) bowed inward before surgery, while 22 bowed outward. Full-length standing X-rays gave hip-knee-ankle angles and leg lengths before and after the operation, and bending stiffness was checked by hand in clinic. Statistical models then sorted which fixes (sideways straightening or releasing a bent knee) best predict the length change, guiding surgeons on what to warn patients to expect.
pmc-13397905:
Sayema Naaz and colleagues find that a virus infecting Salmonella bacteria triggers the bacteria to ship out small RNAs in membrane bubbles. Their 2026 study uses RNA sequencing on infected and uninfected cells and on the vesicles those cells shed. The bubbles, about 120 nm wide, carry proteins, DNA and RNA and take part in talk between cells and in defence against viruses.

Infection with phage P22 crashed small RNA levels inside the bacteria, to an average of just 15.6 percent of normal. At the same time, transfer RNA levels rose by 72.7 percent across the cell, a mirror-image shift. The pattern suggests selective packing of RNA into vesicles during attack, a possible bacterial counter-move worth probing further.
pmc-13398005:
Hayato Miyasaka and co-authors ask which tissues at the back of the ankle decide whether a patient can deep-squat after fracture surgery. Their 2026 study covers 53 patients, average age near 49.5 years, split evenly by sex. Deep squatting underpins daily life and sport, yet many patients lose it after an ankle break is fixed.

Ultrasound measures captured stiffness of the calf muscle and Achilles tendon, plus image brightness in a deep toe-bending muscle and the fat pad behind the joint. Joint range and strength were tested too, and each patient attempted a deep squat. Modelling and accuracy curves then singled out which tissue traits best predict who stays stuck above the squat.
pmc-13398105:
Gjertrud Moe and colleagues listen to young people who arrived in Norway alone as refugees and now manage health and daily life in settled towns. Their 2026 study draws on deep interviews with nineteen people aged 18 to 25 from Afghanistan, Eritrea and Syria. Once housed, these young adults must book their own care and run their own routines, often while supporting family far away.

Read through Honneth's theory of recognition, the interviews show strength in daily coping alongside a tender spot: few close, loving relationships nearby, which dents self-confidence. Participants asked that everyday services weave plain care and recognition into routine contact. Schools, clinics and caseworkers, the authors suggest, are health support whether they name it or not.
pmc-13398505:
Yara E Sanchez-Corrales and colleagues separate mother and fetus contributions to severe preeclampsia, cell by cell and place by place. Their 2026 study profiles tissues of the fetal-maternal interface across gestation, adjusting for age in a preterm third-trimester group. The disease's roots run beyond the placenta into membranes and womb muscle, a spread older studies blurred.

The placenta showed joined signatures of low oxygen, skewed vessel-growth signals, scarring and off-kilter metabolism. The mother's tissues carried immune marks (strained mitochondria and interferon signalling) reaching the myometrium and membranes, matching her body-wide inflammation and vessel trouble. Fetal cells also interacted poorly with vessel cells in the womb wall, adding a two-sided picture of the disease.
pmc-13398605:
Amanda Andrade do Rosário and co-authors investigate a dog leishmaniasis outbreak on São Paulo's peri-urban fringe. Their 2026 study checks twelve dogs for infection and traps sandflies in the Perus district using Shannon and light traps. The parasite Leishmania infantum causes visceral disease in dogs and people, and finding which fly carries it locally shapes control work.

Four dogs tested positive on both a rapid test and ELISA for the parasite. Of 8,354 sandflies caught, the species Nyssomyia whitmani made up 98.2 percent of the haul, and its females carried DNA of both Le. infantum and Le. braziliensis in the lab checks. That double finding ties the district's outbreak to a fly long suspected in wider transmission.
pmc-13399105:
Luyan Zhao, Na Song, Lei Wang, and Jinsong Wu studied how wild tobacco balances defense against growth when a fungus attacks, in a 2026 plant biology paper. The hormone jasmonate switches on defenses in Nicotiana attenuata but also slows growth. The team traced this trade-off to a transcription factor they call NaERFIDOG, which sits under the control of the MYC2 regulators.

Plants with NaERFIDOG silenced or knocked out suffered more damage from the fungus Alternaria alternata yet grew larger, while plants making extra NaERFIDOG resisted the fungus and stayed smaller. The factor switches on genes that produce scopoletin, jasmonate itself, and related compounds, and it turns down production of gibberellin, a growth hormone. Raising scopoletin and lowering gibberellin each contributed to both the stronger defense and the slower growth. The authors map a chain from jasmonate through MYC2 and NaERFIDOG that explains how the plant puts defense first.
pmc-13399205:
Vijayalakshmi Sivapurapu and colleagues describe, in a 2026 letter, the anesthetic care of a pregnant patient whose kidneys had nearly failed. The 23-year-old woman had stage 5 chronic kidney disease and developed superimposed preeclampsia, a dangerous rise in blood pressure during pregnancy. She needed a planned caesarean delivery at about 34 weeks. Her team had to balance fluid, blood pressure, and drug clearance in a body that could not remove waste normally.

Before surgery she received repeated dialysis sessions and several blood transfusions for severe anemia, plus blood pressure medicine. The team chose spinal anesthesia over general anesthesia, using a small dose of bupivacaine with fentanyl, and treated the expected blood pressure dip with phenylephrine boluses. A 1500-gram baby was delivered with good Apgar scores. Ultrasound-guided abdominal wall blocks plus paracetamol kept the mother comfortable afterward. She recovered in intensive care with stable kidney numbers.
pmc-13400105:
Maxime Dubosq-Lebaz and an international steering committee convened 35 experts to define when dissolvable drug-eluting scaffolds make sense for blocked arteries below the knee, in a 2026 consensus study. With no guidelines to lean on, the panel used the RAND/UCLA appropriateness method and a modified Delphi process to rate 114 clinical scenarios spanning lesion features, patient factors, and health-system conditions.

Strong consensus, over 80 percent agreement, emerged for 44 scenarios, or 38.6 percent of the set. Another 35 reached partial consensus and 35 reached none. The strongest support backed scaffold use in limb-threatening ischemia of Rutherford grades 4 to 6, in vessels at least three millimeters wide, for lesions up to sixty millimeters. Support also required thorough vessel preparation and experienced centers with advanced imaging. The authors present the map of agreement and disagreement as both a practice guide and a research agenda.
pmc-13400205:
Raphaël Bentegeac and colleagues randomized clinicians tackling hard kidney cases to work with or without a large language model's feedback, in a 2026 trial. Ninety-seven participants from nine countries, three-quarters of them nephrologists, completed 556 evaluations of multimodal vignettes. Fifty-three worked with AI assistance and 44 without. The workflow gave the assisted group a high-reasoning model's suggestions after their initial answer, letting them revise.

Assistance worked. The chance that the correct diagnosis sat in a clinician's top three was 57.5 percent with AI against 37.2 percent without, an adjusted odds ratio of 2.8 that was highly significant. Within the assisted arm, accuracy jumped from 25.4 percent before seeing suggestions to 57.5 percent afterward. Of initially wrong answers where the model was right, 47.8 percent got corrected. The authors present the trial as realistic-setting evidence that LLM feedback improves specialist diagnostic accuracy.
pmc-13400605:
Zhenheng Wu and colleagues trace, in 2026, how gallbladder cancer spreads through lymph vessels, the drainage network cancers often use to reach lymph nodes. Gallbladder cancer is the most common bile tract cancer and spreads this way often, yet the mechanism was poorly understood. A signaling molecule called CCL21 stood out.

CCL21 levels ran high in these tumors and tracked with denser lymph vessels and more node spread. Lab and animal experiments confirmed its receptor pathway drives new lymph vessel growth. The pathway works by altering a chemical mark on the message for a growth factor, VEGF-D, through an enzyme that removes such marks. Blocking that editing step lowered the growth factor, revealing a chain that could be targeted.
pmc-13401205:
Dalia Eid and co-authors report a 2026 retrospective evaluation of two skin lesion referral routes in one dermatology service: face-to-face clinics and teledermoscopy, where lesion images are reviewed remotely. Referrals for suspected skin cancer keep rising, and the service deliberately split patients by risk.

Over July to December 2025, 201 patients with 207 index lesions went through face-to-face clinics, while 378 patients with 415 lesions used teledermoscopy, all assessed by the same dermoscopy-trained consultant. Most face-to-face referrals, 175 of 201, were urgent suspected cancer referrals, and 57 of 207 lesions proved malignant. The authors compare discharge rates and malignancy yield between the routes as headline outcomes, treating other comparisons as exploratory.
pmc-13401305:
Mohammed Saeed-Zidane and co-authors published a 2026 cattle genomics study combining whole-genome data with tissue-specific gene expression, centred on the NF-kappaB pathway, a master switch for immune defence. Large sequence resources now let researchers map genetic differences and expression patterns across a whole species.

Using the 1000 Bull Genomes Project, the team flagged strongly differentiated variants in NF-kappaB-related genes including CD14, NF-kappaB1, IL-1beta, and BAFFR. They then measured expression of selected pathway genes in four tissues tied to defence and metabolism, in bulls and cows of two breeds. Expression was strongly tissue-dependent: intestinal tissues showed lower levels of several innate immune genes, while CD14 stood out in liver comparisons. Breed and sex effects varied gene by gene rather than following one pattern.
pmc-13401405:
Nitin Mehta, Abhishek Sengupta, Hitesh Grag, and Deepak Joshi describe a 2026 surgical technique for double-bundle anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction using two hamstring tendon grafts with hybrid fixation. Rebuilding both of the ligament's bundles follows the knee's anatomy more closely. It also covers the ligament's footprint on femur and tibia more fully.

In their method, the semitendinosus tendon is doubled and stitched over a suspensory TightRope device for the anteromedial bundle. It is made into three strands if it comes in under 8 millimetres wide. The gracilis tendon becomes a four-strand graft for the posterolateral bundle, prepared with the GraftLink technique at 6.5 centimetres. One bundle uses suspensory fixation throughout; the other mixes a femoral suspensory device with tibial interference fixation. The authors link the setup to a better hold against twisting.
pmc-13401605:
Markus Heidrich and co-authors present a 2026 deep learning model, Image2Count, that predicts rich single-cell protein and RNA expression from just four low-plex immunofluorescence images. Mapping the tumour immune microenvironment in depth can sort patients by likely treatment response, but high-plex spatial methods are costly and hard to use clinically.

The model learns visual features of cells in a contrastive way and uses graph neural networks over cell graphs to infer full expression profiles from the sparse images. It was evaluated on three datasets: an ovarian cancer set with 72-plex regional protein counts, a colorectal cancer set with 25-plex single-cell imaging. A lung cancer set with 960-plex single-cell RNA data. The authors report it can recover distinct spatial expression patterns, pointing toward cheaper precision oncology guidance.
pmc-13401705:
Robert K Reeks, Onyansaniba K Ntim, and Eric S Donkor wrote a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis of non-typeable Streptococcus pneumoniae carriage. These pneumococcus strains lack a detectable capsule, so ordinary serotyping misses them, yet they help spread resistance genes and fill gaps left by vaccine-targeted types.

The team searched PubMed, Scopus, Web of Science, Google Scholar, and ScienceDirect through May 2025. They sought studies reporting carriage, molecular typing, or resistance profiles. Work followed PRISMA guidelines, and quality was rated with an adapted Newcastle-Ottawa scale. Forty studies from 23 countries qualified. The analysis pooled carriage prevalence and resistance estimates and probed differences with subgroup and meta-regression work. The authors note one built-in weakness: only open-access articles with free full text qualified, which may have skewed the evidence base.
pmc-13402305:
Chen and co-authors hunt, in 2026, for blood proteins linking HIV-related inflammation to stroke, using targeted plasma proteomics in a nested case-control study. People with HIV face elevated stroke risk beyond traditional factors even on antiretroviral therapy. The study compared 135 people with HIV who had suffered stroke, mean age 64.2 years and 85.9 percent ischemic cases, against two matched control groups of 135 each, and followed 37 more who later developed stroke.

Of 184 measured cardiovascular proteins, 16 were associated with stroke in people with HIV, centered on the tumor necrosis factor receptor superfamily. Four TNFRSF members were tightly inter-correlated, with correlation coefficients above 0.77, and their combined module carried an adjusted odds ratio of 1.75 for stroke in the analysis. Levels climbed in steps from HIV-negative controls through HIV-positive controls to stroke cases, and longitudinal samples confirmed the proteins rose after stroke. The authors offer the coordinated TNFRSF signature as candidate biomarkers.
pmc-13402605:
Nicholas G Cicero and colleagues show that the sleeping visual cortex does not merely mute light signals; it flips them. Some light leaks through closed eyelids, and the thalamus is usually cast as the gate that blocks senses during sleep. Using EEG and fMRI together, the team flashed brightness-changing patterns at sleeping volunteers and watched each relay station in turn.

Responses in the visual thalamus stayed intact through the light sleep stages N1 and N2. In early visual cortex, though, signals were strongly suppressed and even inverted: brighter input drove the cortex downward, a deactivation pattern. The authors credit local inhibitory circuits for that flip, suggesting the cortex itself enforces sensory isolation early in sleep rather than leaving the job to the thalamus. The finding reshapes how sleep gating is pictured.
pmc-13403505:
Yuan Zhou and colleagues tested in 2026 a pressure-driven way to deliver tumor-fighting immune cells into rat brain tumors. Cells taken from a tumor can attack it, yet getting enough of them deep into brain tissue is hard. A slow pressure infusion can push fluid past the blood-brain barrier.

Rats given the pressure method had immune cells spread wider through the tumor than rats given a plain needle dose. Tumors grew more slowly, cell-death signals rose, and treated rats lived longer. Healthy rats showed no clear harm in the short check window. The team calls the result an early proof of concept for local brain therapy.
pmc-13403605:
Therese Phua and colleagues unraveled a 2026 case where a thin membrane web in the spine caused sudden leg paralysis. A 62-year-old man felt sharp chest-level back pain, then lost leg strength within hours. Such webs usually cause slow decline, so the team first doubted the web was to blame.

Later scans showed the web had grown and the cord's front part lacked blood flow. The web sat in a zone with naturally thin blood supply, which likely sped the harm. Urgent surgery to free the cord brought partial recovery. Webs belong on the list for sudden cord failure.
pmc-13404005:

pmc-13404105:

pmc-13404205:

pmc-13404305:

pmc-13407605:

pmc-13408005:

pmc-13408105:

pmc-13408405:

pmc-13408505:

pmc-13408705:

pmc-13408805:

pmc-13410305:

pmc-13410705:

pmc-13410805:

pmc-13411905:

pmc-13412005:

pmc-13412605:

pmc-13415505:

pmc-13415805:

pmc-13415905:

pmc-13418505:

pmc-13418705:

pmc-13420205:

pmc-13420305:

pmc-13420705:

pmc-13422805:

pmc-13423505:

pmc-13424005:

pmc-13425405:

pmc-13426205:

pmc-13426505:

pmc-13426705:

pmc-13427505:

pmc-13428005:

pmc-13428405:

pmc-13429105:

pmc-13430805:

pmc-13432405:

pmc-13432705:

pmc-13432905:

pmc-13433905:

pmc-13434305:

pmc-13434505:

pmc-13434705:

pmc-13435605:

pmc-13435705:

pmc-13436105:

Each ten percent more European ancestry came with a slightly higher risk, but the link was not statistically significant. A pooled analysis with three American cohorts was also inconclusive and inconsistent across studies. Removing one cohort, the Women's Health Initiative, left a modest significant link with no inconsistency. The authors say ancestry may play a small role, but the evidence stays mixed and cohort-dependent.
pmc-13436405:
Melina Pedroso Merlone and coauthors tune artesunate dosing against brain malaria in mice in 2026. Infected mice got one of four dosing plans on day five, from split daily shots to slow pump delivery. Parasite counts and survival grade each plan.

Slow delivery after a loading shot cut parasites by 97.2 percent in one day, yet half the mice relapsed. Twice daily shots cut parasites by 90.5 percent with no relapse. A stronger first day variant saved forty two percent of mice in rescue runs. Platelet counts stayed low under all plans. Split dosing suits add on therapy trials, the team concludes.
pmc-13437205:
Eunseon Jeong and colleagues built a deep learning tool that finds and counts paramagnetic rim lesions in the brains of people with multiple sclerosis. Their 2026 study trained a three-dimensional network on a special MRI method that maps tissue magnetic traits, using scans from patients suspected of having the disease.

Two setups were compared: the magnetic map alone, and the map paired with a second common scan type. In the first test set, the map-only model caught more lesions and made fewer false calls. In a later group, both setups found every affected patient, though lesion-level scores dipped for each. A separate group of 117 patients linked a higher counted rim burden to poorer thinking scores. The authors say the single-scan route keeps the work simpler while matching the paired version, and they propose the counted burden as a marker worth tracking in MS care.
pmc-13437305:
Nathaniel McLaughlan and colleagues describe lessons from Operation Oasis, a virtual resilience program built for military health workers during the COVID-19 pandemic. A weekly music session called Human Jukebox let workers request songs and share thoughts online. Their 2026 case study sorts 404 anonymous chat messages posted across two years of that session.

Music appreciation was the most common theme, appearing in forty-three percent of coded messages. Positive feeling, gratitude, memories stirred by songs, and a sense of social connection filled out the top five themes. Writers described lifted moods, quiet reflection, and feeling close to colleagues at a time of strain and separation. The authors also share what the organizers learned about setting up and running such a program online. They argue that simple, arts-based gatherings can support staff well-being, and they offer the record as a guide for facilities weighing similar efforts in future crises.
pmc-13439005:
Aarts and colleagues published a 2026 study on how much energy patients with a muscle disease need. Myotonic dystrophy type 1 weakens muscles and changes body makeup over time. Diet plans rely on formulas that guess daily calorie burn from body data. The team checked those formulas against measured burn in 15 patients.

Standard formulas overshot real burn by about 100 to 165 calories daily. Matched healthy controls showed no such skew in their formula checks. A formula built on body makeup hit the true value almost exactly. Patients also moved less, with activity levels well below control values. Diet advice should use body makeup and low activity, the authors say. Better estimates could stop slow weight gain in this patient group.
pmc-13439305:
Bardak and colleagues pooled trials in 2026 on bowel cleaning drinks for colonoscopy in older adults. A colonoscopy is a camera exam of the large bowel, and it needs a clean bowel to work well. The team compared low-volume sulfate drinks with low-volume polyethylene glycol drinks plus vitamin C, using six trials with 682 patients aged 65 or more.

Satisfaction scores modestly favoured the sulfate drinks, while willingness to repeat the drink was similar. The authors say sulfate drinks may be a wise choice when finding lesions matters most, given equal cleaning and safety.
pmc-13439605:
Ester Martínez-Renau and a large team compare microbes living on bird skin and in the preen gland across species, ages, and nest types, reporting in 2026. Feathers and skin form a first defence against infection, seeded partly by oily secretions from the uropygial gland near the tail. Birds spread those secretions while preening. Bacterial communities differed clearly by species, and nestlings carried richer mixes than adults, mainly on gland skin. Birds nesting inside cavities held more varied and uneven communities than open-cup nesters, an effect strongest in adults and secretions. Cavity nesters also carried relatively larger glands, hinting at more preening effort. Nesting habits and age thus shape the microbial shield birds wear.
pmc-13440105:
Jie Wang's team traced a CA9-driven chain in 2026 that accelerates colorectal cancer through neutrophil traps. Blocking this CA9-ITGB1-CXCL8 axis emerges as a therapeutic idea. Colorectal teams get a complete immune mechanism with a druggable target, still preclinical.
pmc-13440505:
João Pedro Rocha Nogueira and colleagues describe the field investigation of a confirmed West Nile virus case in an infant in Mato Grosso, Brazil, reporting in 2026. The mosquito-borne virus circulates in birds and usually leaves people without symptoms, though rare cases invade the nervous system. The infant's illness began in mid-December 2025, and spinal fluid testing confirmed the virus days later. A three-day investigation in February 2026 combined case review with door-to-door searching.

Interviewers reached 112 residents near the case. Twenty-nine reported symptoms, and eight of them described neurological complaints. Surroundings favoured mosquito breeding, raising concern about local transmission. West Nile virus has been confirmed in Brazil since 2014, with about one hundred ten human cases logged in the following decade. The authors urge joined human, animal, and environmental surveillance with wider laboratory and insect investigation in the territory.
pmc-13440705:
Takuji Igarashi and colleagues report a fatal case where a gut bacterium seeded an abscess inside a recent brain bleed, publishing in 2026. Abscess forming at a haemorrhage site is exceedingly rare, and Bacteroides fragilis is an oxygen-hating gut resident seldom blamed. Their patient, an 86-year-old woman, arrived with bleeding in the right back of the brain plus body-wide inflammation signs. Abdominal scans suggested inflamed bowel pouches, a plausible entry point for the germ.

She first developed meningitis from the same bacterium under conservative care. Sixteen days after the stroke, swelling around the bleed ballooned and her condition crashed. Emergency surgery found pus inside the blood cavity, and cultures confirmed the organism. Despite surgery and targeted antibiotics, infection spread to brain tissue and the fluid channels, and she died. The authors advise contrast imaging whenever fever and decline persist after brain haemorrhage.
pmc-13441505:
Qiutong Lu and colleagues improvise a rescue tool from spare parts to extract a fragile foam object lodged in the rectum, reporting a 2026 case. Their patient, a 51-year-old man, arrived after the object had been retained for a day and a community hospital attempt had already failed. Scans showed bowel swelling but no dense object, matching foam's faint signature. Urgent scope examination found the large foam body at the rectosigmoid junction, where the colon bends.

A standard snare slid off the soft, slippery surface, and grasping forceps could not hold it either. The team folded a guidewire through the metal outer sheath of a stone-crushing device, building a homemade gripper. That improvised tool seized the friable object firmly and removed it whole. The authors offer the construction as a fallback when stock retrieval gear fails on soft, fragile foreign bodies.
pmc-13441905:
Kivian Obed Matamoros Padilla and colleagues profile stroke in young Honduran adults at a national referral hospital, reporting a 2026 case series. Stroke is rising in the twenty-to-fifty-four age band worldwide, and local Central American data are scarce. Seventy patients aged eighteen to fifty-five were studied with examinations, laboratory tests, brain imaging, and neck and brain vessel ultrasound, including a bubble test for heart shunts.

Young adults made up thirty percent of the stroke cases assessed. Women formed the majority, and average age sat in the early forties. High blood pressure history led the risk list, followed by diabetes and migraine. Most strokes were ischemic, with clots from the heart the top identified mechanism. A heart shunt turned up in a notable share of those tested. Death claimed about one case in six. The authors highlight modifiable risks that local prevention could target.
pmc-13442605:
Majlinda Naco and colleagues recount sleep-drug care for a 65-year-old woman with a giant belly tumor in a 2026 case report. The ovarian growth weighed about 21 kg and filled most of her belly, pressing on organs and chest parts. Surgery removed the growth along with her womb, belly fat apron, and appendix.

The mass squeezed her main belly vein, so body shifts on the table swung her blood pressure hard. Direct pressure checks inside the belly forced quick changes to both the drug plan and the cut plan mid-surgery. She came through the full course well in the end. The team stresses joint planning across surgery, sleep-drug, and watch teams, plus lung prep and close line checks, when a mass of this scale goes to the table.
pmc-13442705:
Xuejun Liu and colleagues study why time stress feeds reliance on AI text tools among graduate students in a 2026 survey. Replies came from 1,157 students, and the team traced paths from time stress to tool reliance through mind states. Profile sorting then split students into groups by how their reliance formed.

Time stress fed reliance through two side paths, worry about research and faith that tools boost output. The worry path held a 41.22 percent share of the total link in their model. Four profiles emerged, from an all-low group at 5.77 percent of students to a dual-high group near two-fifths. Sex, study year, and critical thought marked who fell where. The authors warn that stress care and thought training may cut heavy reliance more than bans can.
pmc-13443105:
Ronak Nikbazm and coauthors report a 2026 case-control study of premature ovarian insufficiency, the loss of ovarian activity before age 40, seeking blood markers that flag the illness early. The team compared 38 affected women with 38 controls on body measures, the protein chemerin, follicle stimulating hormone, blood fats, and cardiometabolic indices.

Chemerin, total cholesterol, and triglycerides each separated cases from controls only moderately, but a joint model reached strong discrimination, with 94.7 percent sensitivity and 76.3 percent specificity. Schooling, activity level, and several blood measures also linked to the illness. The joint panel looks promising as a screening aid, though larger and more diverse cohorts must confirm the cutoffs before clinical use.
pmc-13443505:
Rebekah Erin Strong and colleagues make primary amines from alcohols inside charged microdroplets in a 2026 paper. Amines serve as core building blocks, yet classic routes need guard groups or harsh reducers. Their spray rig makes ammonia from air nitrogen on the fly, right inside the droplets.

The fresh ammonia swaps the alcohol's oxygen group for a nitrogen group in one pass. Adding hydrazine as a twin ammonia source lifted yields more than tenfold in their runs. Three spray setups faced off, from twin spray with hydrazine to solo sprays at high and low flows. NMR reads confirmed the swap at the same carbon spot. The authors pitch droplet chemistry as a mild route that skips harsh goods and rare catalysts.
pmc-13443605:
Huacen Wang and colleagues build a paper-thin flexible robot for work on huge structures in a 2026 paper. Ships and planes need cutting and checks in place, yet stock robots are heavy and may harm weak skins. Their robot is 970 micrometers thick and weighs 19.7 g, driven by a two-way electric actuator on flex circuits.

Sticky electric feet let it climb flat, curved, and upright faces with path repeat marks near 21.7 micrometers of drift. Top speed hit 290 mm per second in their runs. Loads reached more than four times its own weight, and a 3 kg drop failed to kill it. Trials showed gap checks, curved grinding, and micro spark cutting. The authors pitch the platform for tight, delicate work zones.
pmc-13444105:
Aleksandra Ferenc-Mrozek and colleagues demonstrate a 2026 biophysics finding that the DcpS scavenger enzyme, known for stripping caps from decayed messenger RNA, can misfold into amyloid-like fibrils in the lab. The team tested human and worm versions of the protein, plus a mutant tied to Al-Raqad syndrome, tracking phase separation and fibril growth.

Both species' proteins formed fibrils, and the disease-linked mutant aggregated faster than the normal protein. Liquid-liquid phase separation appeared to precede fibril formation and may explain the odd kinetics, including a missing lag phase. The work links DcpS aggregation to possible loss of function in disease, though physiological relevance in living tissue remains to be shown.
pmc-13444305:
Moeza Zulfiqar and colleagues report a 2026 cross-sectional study of treatment adherence among 401 women with polycystic ovary syndrome treated at hospitals in Lahore, Pakistan. The team used structured questionnaires to grade adherence and test links with social and clinical factors.

Only 21.4 percent reported full adherence, while 50.6 percent were partial and 27.9 percent non-adherent. Socioeconomic status and body mass index predicted adherence, with upper-middle-class women less likely to adhere than upper-class women. Limited knowledge, side effects, and cost led the barriers, pointing to education, financial support, and system fixes as remedies.
pmc-13444505:
Denis Qirinxhi and colleagues track a giant liver hemangioma that shrank on its own over three years in a 2026 case paper. A 53-year-old woman had the lump found by chance during checks for vague belly discomfort. MRI scans across three years, from February 2022 to January 2025, charted its course.

Classic scan marks confirmed a cavernous hemangioma at each visit. The lump first grew, from 14.1 cm long to 15.9 cm at the mid scan, then fell to 8.0 cm by the last scan. Volume loss topped 80 percent across the full span, with no drugs, surgery, or needle work in between. She stayed well, with clean labs and no cancer signs. The authors back watchful care for stable giants with classic marks.
pmc-13445205:
Atsushi Musha and colleagues present a 2026 case report on carbon-ion radiation therapy for a rare jaw tumor, ameloblastic fibrosarcoma of the upper jaw, in a patient who declined radical surgery. The 68-year-old woman arrived with nasal congestion, tooth pain, and a watering eye, and biopsy confirmed the tumor in the left maxillary sinus.

With no standard treatment or guidelines for this rare tumor, the team planned a two-stage carbon-ion course totaling 70.4 gray in 16 fractions, shrinking margins midway to spare the eye, brain, and jaw muscles. The report offers a treatment path for inoperable cases, though the record shown covers planning rather than long-term outcome, so efficacy remains an open question.
pmc-13445505:
Jiaying Zhao and colleagues ask why some skull and face bones harden well while nearby zones lag, in a 2026 study of bone growth. Citrate, a small molecule in bone, shapes the crystals that give bone its strength. The team found citrate piling up in just the zones that harden most.

Gene readouts split hard and soft zones along two lines: a growth signal chain and the cell's primary cilium, a tiny antenna-like part. Citrate switched the signal chain on, and the chain in turn fed citrate build-up, a loop that raised bone cell activity. Working with the cilium, citrate steadied young mineral clusters. The pattern hands bone repair work a new metabolic lever to test.
pmc-13446005:
Bárbara Dieck-Gutiérrez and colleagues report a young woman found to carry three rare belly vessel squeeze conditions at once, published in 2026 with a review of past reports. One condition presses the gut's main artery under a chest ligament, causing pain after meals. The second narrows the gap where the gut passes between two vessels, blocking food and driving weight loss.

The third presses the left kidney vein between the aorta and a gut artery. Each condition is uncommon alone, so the triple match is a true rarity that tests diagnosis and care. Surgery treated her case with success. The report walks through scan choices and treatment paths, urging doctors to keep these squeezes in mind when belly pain defies easy answers.
pmc-13446105:
Haoming Huo and colleagues sharpen a sound-and-light imaging method by borrowing fine vessel maps from a sister technique, in a 2026 study. Photoacoustic imaging reads light absorbed in tissue as sound, giving depth and contrast, yet its detail is capped by sound spread, and partial views smear the picture. Ultrasound tracking of single bubbles can map vessels far more finely.

Their method folds those sharp vessel maps into the rebuild of photoacoustic data, weighting the smoothing by region. Tests ran on computer models, tissue-like phantoms, and the living mouse brain. The new rebuild cut blur, raised contrast, and kept blood oxygen maps tighter and truer than the standard rebuild. Vessels that once blurred into haze stood out, which widens the method's use in brain and tumor studies.
pmc-13446305:
Iovino and colleagues argue for combining two immunotherapies that each fail on their own. Their 2026 commentary discusses bispecific T-cell engagers, or BiTEs. These antibody-like drugs drag T cells onto tumour cells. The authors pair them with donor stem cell transplant, which can cure blood cancers through the graft-versus-tumour effect. Both approaches lose effectiveness over time in many patients.

BiTEs depend on the patient's own worn-down T cells, which heavy pretreatment leaves exhausted, while transplant relapse remains common, especially when disease is not fully cleared beforehand. Their proposal is to give BiTEs around the transplant window, redirecting fresh donor lymphocytes against the cancer instead. They frame donor cells as an immunologic dream team for the engagers: unexhausted, abundant, and already primed to attack. The piece maps the rationale and obstacles for trials of this combination.
pmc-13447105:

Three-dimensional computer models tested how Venus rock behaves under heat and stress, then let the land relax after stretching ended. Wide flank uplifts matched young or still active rifts best, not old inactive ones. Three named chasm regions on Venus show that same pattern. Their shapes also imply faster stretching than often assumed, possibly linked to hot rising rock deep below the surface.
pmc-13447305:
Lorena Bejarano-Hernández and co-authors review HPV vaccination in adults in 2026, asking whether programmes should reach beyond teenage girls. Vaccination linked to lower infection and persistence in several reports, while estimates for high-grade cervical changes varied widely across studies. pmc-13448805:
Wei Guo and coauthors screen a 2026 hope strain for a killed Coxsackie B4 vaccine, a virus behind hand, foot, and mouth disease, brain-lining swelling, and links to type 1 blood-sugar illness. pmc-13451905:
Anmut Assemie and Beyene Bashu Haile test in 2026 whether garlic and ginger extracts kill mosquito young in water. pmc-13452105:
Ahmad Almadani and a large team measure in 2026 how often sexual trouble and distress ride along with depression at a Riyadh hospital. Distress tied to marital state, extra mental ills, and smoking history. The authors say these hidden burdens deserve plain talk in depression care, since they weigh hard on daily life.
pmc-13452305:

pmc-13453005:

The gap held after the team adjusted for sex, age, priority group, and region. The authors call the pattern a sign of real access barriers and urge stronger outreach so future vaccine drives reach migrants on time.
pmc-13453605:
Yukiyoshi Sumi and others set burnout cures for trainee doctors side by side in 2026, pooling trial data. Burnout in training harms doctors and patients, yet which cure helps most was not clear. The team trawled five data banks in Feb 2025 and logged the plan first.

Scores covered worn-out feelings, cold detachment, weak efficacy, and whole burnout, ranked by network stats. The rank shows which cures merit first use in training plans. Hospitals gain head-to-head proof to shield trainees and, through them, patients.
pmc-13454205:
Guilherme Lepski and six co-authors report a compassionate use case of a patient's own bone marrow stem cells in long standing brain damage from oxygen loss. Their 2026 report works under national regulatory oversight, with cells grown under strict manufacturing and safety testing, then delivered into the spinal fluid.

Small gains showed in hearing, vision, and arousal, and the patient began a first repeatable yes no signal by blinking. Muscle stiffness eased a point in some groups, and no side effects appeared. pmc-13454505:
Ackermann, Reiner, and Kruss review new light-based sensors for brain signaling chemicals in this 2026 paper. pmc-13455205:

pmc-13455305:

The authors frame mint as a potential resistance reservoir needing wider surveillance of market produce.
pmc-13455405:

pmc-13457005:

pmc-13457105:

pmc-13457205:

Because treatment eras, not randomization, defined the groups, the authors call for a prospective trial to confirm the effect.
pmc-13457905:
Shalin S Bhatt and a large team searched donated human bodies for lymph vessels where the central and peripheral nervous systems meet in the neck. They then tested harvested tissue with a stain for podoplanin, a marker on lymph vessel walls.

pmc-13458005:
Dlkhwaz Hama and Karzan Mohammed Hawrami report a nutrition study, published in 2026. It measures iodine and selenium intake in 201 healthy adults. Thyroid function was also measured. Dietary iodine was not independently linked to thyroid-stimulating hormone levels after adjustments. The authors urge monitoring of iodised salt use. This matters where staples dominate the diet.
pmc-13458605:

pmc-13483705:
Juliet Nwamaka Ozioko-Agbo tests a soursop seed extract against prostate enlargement in rats, combining animal, chemistry, and computer evidence. Published in 2026, the work first profiles the extract and checks its antioxidant strength and short-term safety. Thirty male rats then received testosterone to enlarge the prostate, followed by the standard drug finasteride or one of three extract doses.

Testosterone treatment disturbed blood chemistry, blood counts, and prostate tissue structure in the untreated group. Extract treatment moved several of those measures back toward normal, including a prostate marker and hormone levels, in a dose-aware pattern detailed in the full report. Computer modeling pointed to blocking of the same hormone-converting enzyme that finasteride targets. The combined evidence supports further study, while stopping short of any human claim.
pmc-13486005:
Albert Assad builds a bedside formula that converts how far an enlarged spleen can be felt into an estimate of its true volume. Published in 2026, the post hoc analysis pools data from two phase 3 trials in myelofibrosis, a marrow disease where spleen growth tracks severity and treatment response. Imaging measures volume precisely yet is not always available in routine clinics.

Mixed-model regression tested felt spleen length alongside weight, height, age, and sex as predictors of scanned volume. Felt length plus patient height gave the best-fitting model, since length alone does not scale proportionally with volume. A standardized conversion lets researchers and observational clinics translate quick physical exam findings into the volume language that trials speak, without pretending the estimate replaces imaging.
pmc-13486405:
Hongqin Jia reports a 2026 case of a fast, grave tumor in the eye socket of a small child. The patient was a girl aged 20 months. Her left eye bulged fast as a mass grew behind the ball. Scans showed the mass at about two centimeters wide, with slight wear of the bone at its edge.

The tumor was cut out in pieces. Drug care and radiation care then gave brief control at best. Tissue checks showed big cells of the rhabdoid type. A key guard protein, INI1, was lost, and gene tests found a flaw in the SMARCB1 gene. Marker stains broke the usual mold, with one mark present and one absent. Growth came back in three months and spread to the brain. The child died 34 months after first surgery.
pmc-13486505:
Abdipour and colleagues stabilized a highly expansive clay by mixing in steel furnace slag and sludge from water treatment plants, two wastes that usually burden landfills. Expansive clays swell and shrink with moisture, cracking foundations and roads. Their 2026 study blended slag at up to 30 percent and sludge at up to 30 percent, cured samples for up to 56 days, and measured strength, stiffness, and swelling.

The best blend combined 30 percent slag with 20 percent sludge and transformed the clay's behavior in the reported tests. Compressive strength rose more than fourfold, reaching about 2,800 kilopascals at the longest curing time. Swelling potential collapsed from 270 percent in the raw clay to only 8 percent in the optimized mix. Microscope and X-ray analyses showed cement-like gels binding the particles. Abdipour presents the pairing as a genuine synergy, not just dilution.
pmc-13486805:
Zachary C E Hawley and a large co-author group combine two gene-silencing technologies to treat the SOD1 form of ALS more safely. Published in 2026, the program delivers an artificial microRNA against the toxic SOD1 gene by virus into spinal fluid, then adds a second antisense drug. A primate safety finding anchors the report.

Immune suppression after the viral delivery prevented the dorsal root ganglion toxicity that has haunted this route, and protection lasted beyond 300 days even though suppression stopped at ninety days. Fluid delivery alone distributes unevenly and raises side effect risk, which motivates the layered approach tested in the SOD1 mouse model described in the study title. Stacking a durable viral silencer with a tunable antisense drug could give steadier gene knockdown at lower risk.
pmc-13488205:
Emmanuel Chilanga studies soybean porridge for young children in rural Malawi in a 2026 community experiment in Dowa District. Poor protein intake fuels stunting, and soybeans grow locally with rich protein. Four local varieties were prepared five ways, from untreated to soaked, roasted, dehulled, or dehulled then roasted, and protein was measured in the laboratory. Sixty caregivers tasted the porridges at child clinics and rated aroma, flavor, texture, and overall liking.

Removing the hull gave the highest measured protein, while soaking gave the lowest in the reported tests. Caregivers liked the dehulled-and-roasted porridge best overall, with plain dehulled close behind. Combining nutrition and taste, the author favors dehulling, with roasting added, as a practical home method families will actually use.
pmc-13489705:
Zongting Gu and co-authors build a prediction tool for survival after surgery for duodenal adenocarcinoma, a rare cancer of the small intestine's first section. Their 2026 multicentre study develops a nomogram, a scoring chart, from 2,289 patients who had curative surgery in China's National Cancer Center database between 2012 and 2022.

A variable-selection method chose eight predictors from eighty-nine perioperative factors, including changeable surgical factors such as transfusion and operating time. The model predicted one-, three-, and five-year survival more accurately than traditional models, and an external hospital cohort of 335 patients confirmed its performance. A cutoff split patients into low- and high-risk groups with clearly different survival. The authors present the tool, also released as a web calculator, as support for counselling, follow-up planning, and discussions about further treatment, not as a replacement for staging and clinical judgement.
pmc-13491605:
Saullo Queiroz Silveira leads a ten-author team reporting a 2026 randomized trial on ventilator settings during weight-loss surgery performed through small incisions. Patients with obesity face lung stress under anesthesia when air pressure is poorly set. The trial tested whether a lung recruitment maneuver plus pressure-guided adjustment of PEEP, the pressure kept in the lungs between breaths, would prevent high driving pressure.

Seventy-eight patients were split among three strategies combining recruitment, guided adjustment, or fixed pressure. During the gas-inflated phase of surgery, high driving pressure struck far fewer patients in the guided group before and after recruitment. Blood pressure measures and later lung complications did not differ between groups. Careful pressure titration improved breathing mechanics during surgery without proven benefit afterward.
pmc-13491705:
Bing Ma and Lihong Zhang examine in 2026 whether cells aged prematurely by chemotherapy predict relapse in acute myeloid leukemia. Treatment forces some leukemia cells into senescence, a halted state, yet those cells release signals that may shelter surviving cancer. The single-center study followed 128 newly diagnosed patients treated with standard induction chemotherapy between 2019 and 2023.

Bone marrow checks before and after treatment measured aging markers such as p16INK4a and p21Cip1 plus the secreted signals IL-6 and IL-8. Patients with a high senescence burden after treatment relapsed sooner and died earlier, with median survival roughly a year shorter than the low-burden group. High IL-6 and high p16INK4a each independently predicted poor outcomes. The authors propose drugs that clear senescent cells as a future addition to leukemia care.
pmc-13491805:
Fang Wang and Ling Zhou model in 2026 why boredom-prone teenagers' minds wander so often, surveying 3,736 adolescents at seventeen schools in Guangdong Province, China. The average participant was about fifteen years old. Questionnaires measured proneness to boredom, mobile phone addiction, sensation seeking, and everyday mind wandering, and structural modeling tested how the traits connect.

Boredom proneness predicted more mind wandering, and phone addiction carried part of that effect, as if bored teenagers reach for their phones and then drift further. Sensation seeking strengthened the link between boredom and phone addiction, so thrill-hungry students showed the pattern most clearly. Because all measures came from one moment in time, the authors avoid causal claims and suggest interventions that teach boredom regulation and healthier phone habits.
pmc-13493505:
Naghmeh Nademi and five colleagues build in 2026 a wound dressing that fights bacteria, conducts electricity, and releases antibiotic on schedule. The film blends gellan and agar gels with chopped electrospun fibers carrying a conductive polymer-graphene mix, plus particles loaded with ciprofloxacin. Conductivity matters because gentle electrical cues are thought to help tissue repair.

The best fiber recipe, using one and a half percent of the conductive blend, delivered the highest conductivity and noticeably strengthened the film's stretch resistance and stiffness. Drug release followed a steady first-order pattern rather than dumping its payload at once. Growth halos in culture dishes confirmed killing power against both Staphylococcus aureus and Escherichia coli, stronger against the latter. Swelling and breakdown behavior also suited wound contact, and the authors propose trials in living tissue.
pmc-13493705:
Antonio Martorell and two colleagues argue in 2026 that hidradenitis suppurativa staging misses much of the disease because it counts a tunnel as active only when it drains pus. Their prospective study paired clinical examination with high-frequency ultrasound and Doppler flow imaging across 312 tunnels in eighty-four patients at three centers. Each tunnel was classed by depth and shape before its clinical signs were matched against blood flow inside its walls.

Doppler found active blood flow in ninety-one percent of tunnels, including most that never drained. Draining tunnels always showed flow, yet two bedside patterns predicted flow nearly as well in dry tunnels: pain combined with redness, or pain combined with firmness. Shallow dermal tunnels, though never draining, were inflamed in most cases and often painful and red. The authors propose widening the definition of an active tunnel to catch a treatable early window.
pmc-13493805:
Zhong and colleagues modelled a 2026 land use study for Sichuan Province in China, tracking how land change moves the carbon stored in soils and vegetation. Balancing growth with ecological protection is central to China's dual carbon goals. Their coupled model links land simulation, carbon accounting, and a driver analysis tool.

Between 2000 and 2020 Sichuan lost a large amount of stored carbon, with declines centred on the middle and south of the Sichuan Basin. Zhong found vegetation greenness was the strongest single driver of carbon patterns, and its effect grew stronger when combined with elevation. Looking ahead, natural trend and economy first scenarios kept losing carbon through 2060. Only the ecological conservation scenario reversed the trend, gaining a substantial amount by 2060.
pmc-13493905:
Kocabıyık, in a single-author 2026 study, builds a mathematical model of chikungunya, the mosquito-spread virus that causes fever and long-lasting joint pain. Standard epidemic models treat time as uniform and forget the past, but real outbreaks show memory, where earlier conditions shape later spread, and bursts at many timescales. The new model combines fractional derivatives, a calculus that weights history, with fractal time, which stretches and compresses the clock.

The author proves the model's solutions stay positive and bounded, works out its resting states, and computes the basic reproduction number, the threshold deciding whether an outbreak grows or fades. Analysis shows the system switches stability exactly at that threshold, as theory expects. Simulations then show the memory and fractal settings bending the epidemic curves away from classical predictions, lingering longer in some regimes. The author argues such models fit real outbreak shapes better.
pmc-13494205:
Maureen M Black and Chessa K Lutter set out, in a 2026 article, a plan for programs that join nutrition with early child development in poor settings. Millions of young children in low- and middle-income countries grow and learn below their potential, held back by poor diets and few chances to learn. Few big efforts support food, growth, learning, and caregiving together.

The authors propose six tests any such program should pass. Goals should rest on theory and proven methods, and the program should reach the children most at risk with content that fits their age and culture. Staff need training and support, with checks on quality. Families, communities, and officials should hold active roles, and outcomes should be tracked with simple tools. Lasting funding and updated policy round out the list. A joint partner team, guided by steady data feedback, would steer the system.
pmc-13494605:
Kaori Koga and colleagues report a 2026 phase 3 trial in Japan of a flexible hormone pill routine for painful periods, known as dysmenorrhea. The pill pairs desogestrel with a low dose of ethinylestradiol. Rather than fixed monthly cycles, users take the pill for 24 to 80 days in a row, then pause for four days, choosing the rhythm themselves. The trial ran at 21 centers with a blinded phase and an open follow-up.

The study enrolled 211 women with regular cycles and period pain, giving most the drug and the rest a placebo. Pain scores fell far more on the drug through day 84, and days of strong pain shrank. Over eighty percent on the drug reported feeling better, against under thirty percent on placebo, and satisfaction scores ran higher. Bleeding between periods, colds, and nausea were the most common side effects, and no deaths occurred.
pmc-13495305:
LiLi Deng and a large team review, in a 2026 article, how fat-based nano carriers could carry Chinese herbal compounds into the brain against Alzheimer's disease. The disease tangles memory through amyloid plaques, tau tangles, inflammation, and oxidative stress, and current drugs ease symptoms only. Several plant compounds from traditional Chinese medicine guard nerve cells on many fronts, yet they break down fast and cross the blood-brain barrier poorly.

The review weighs carrier types, from liposomes and cell-shed exosomes to solid and mixed fat particles, for stability, barrier crossing, and brain build-up. Fresh tactics add guided targeting and disguise, such as coating particles in cell membrane so the body treats them as its own. The authors also face the blocks ahead: mass production, quality checks, rules, and long-term safety. They frame the platforms as a promising scaffold needing hard proof before clinic use.
pmc-13495405:
Enyu Xu and a large team track, in a 2026 study, six years of malaria mosquito ecology across city and country sites in eastern China. China has ended local malaria, yet the vector Anopheles sinensis remains, and how weather, farming, and city growth steer it was a knowledge gap. Nets and light traps logged biting and density from 2016 to 2021 under a One Health frame joining human, animal, and land factors.

Nearly fifty thousand mosquitoes were counted, confirming the species' dominance. Heat ruled: rural biting peaked near twenty-eight to thirty degrees a month later, and rain showed threshold effects. Crops raised risk slightly, while cattle and buffalo nearby shielded people by drawing bites. Dense city living, oddly, suppressed the mosquito. Male-skewed local populations raised rural biting. The authors say control must be tuned separately for city and country, since the drivers diverge.
pmc-13498505:
Martino Azzi and others follow cardiometabolic risk over ten years of testosterone-based gender-affirming hormone therapy in transmasculine adults. In 2026, the single-center long-term cohort tracks fifty-seven people who completed a decade of yearly examinations, blood tests, and body composition tests. Long-term energy effects of prolonged male hormone were earlier poorly documented.

Blood protein rose early then stabilized, while glucose, insulin, and blood pressure changed little. Lipids worsened throughout, with higher LDL, total blood fat, and blood fats and lower HDL, with rising weight, waist tests, lean mass, and trunk fat. No major heart and vessel events occurred, and one participant developed atrial fibrillation. The authors recommend ongoing tracking, risk treatment, and lifestyle support.
pmc-13499705:
Walsh and colleagues forecast demand for community-based health and publicly funded social care tied to frailty, in a 2026 modeling study. The forecast covers people aged fifty and over in England from 2025 to 2040. Evidence on hospital and primary care demand was good, but community services were unquantified. The team derived contact rates by age and frailty index from North-West London cohort data, then ran a system dynamics simulation nationally.

Walsh projects use rising over the sixteen years, with mental health contacts up about a sixth and community health and social care contacts up about thirty percent each. Preventing frailty could save hundreds of thousands of social care contacts. Slowing progression could save tens of thousands of health contacts, yet both gains are partly swallowed by population ageing. Because so many people already live with mild frailty, the authors conclude demand will grow regardless and planning must assume it.
pmc-13500505:
Huimin Hou and colleagues trace in 2026 how the conservation capacity of Lanzhou, a dry northwestern Chinese city, changed between 2000 and 2023 and what drives it. This ecosystem service, the landscape's ability to hold and regulate water, buffers scarcity and climate stress.
