The team combined land use, weather, and socio-economic series with a land change model, an ecosystem service model, and an interpretable machine learning method that attributes influence to each driver. Scenarios were then projected to 2050.

Capacity fluctuated strongly year to year without a significant long-term trend, sitting highest in northwestern and southern mountains and lowest in central river valleys and the southeast in their maps. Soil water content, rainfall, and vegetation greenness pushed capacity up, while human activity intensity was the dominant drag, with drivers interacting in nonlinear ways. Future patterns stayed spatially similar, though total volume depended heavily on the climate and development path chosen.
pmc-13500805:
A. Vijay reports a 2026 simulation study of a wireless system proposed for future 6G networks. The design combines multiple-antenna MIMO transmission with multi-carrier code division multiple access, a scheme that lets many users share the same frequencies. Artificial intelligence runs at the network edge, close to users, so decisions stay fast. Deep reinforcement learning adjusts spectrum and power settings as conditions change, while successive interference cancellation separates overlapping signals from different users.

The system was implemented in MATLAB and compared with plain MC-CDMA, MIMO-OFDM, and hybrid precoding designs. Simulations reached a spectral efficiency near 32.7 bits per second per hertz and an energy efficiency near 14.8 bits per joule. Signal quality rose to about 34 decibels, and the bit error rate fell to one in a hundred thousand. Vijay presents the design as a scalable option for very dense 6G networks where interference and energy use are central problems.
pmc-13501605:
Yajia Wang leads a seven-author team reporting a 2026 materials study of a powder that seals open eye injuries without stitches. Open globe injuries, full-thickness wounds of the eye wall, need repair within about a day, yet suturing is slow and demands specialist skill. The powder combines two oppositely charged polymers, polyethyleneimine and polyacrylic acid. On contact with the wet surface of a wound it soaks up interfacial water and the polymers clump into a hydrogel that bonds directly to tissue.

Laboratory tests showed strong tissue adhesion and good mechanical properties, and cell experiments together with animal studies indicated friendly biological behaviour. In animals the powder sealed irregular damage on both the cornea and the sclera, the eye's clear front window and its white outer coat. The authors present the polyethyleneimine and polyacrylic acid powder as a fast first-response option for eye trauma care.
pmc-13503805:
Haixia Zhai and four colleagues present a tool that finds loops in folded DNA inside the cell core, in a 2026 paper. Loops bring far-apart gene switches next to the genes they control. Broken loops can cause birth defects and cancer, yet spotting them in noisy map data is hard.

The tool, called TM-Loop, joins three data types: contact maps, open-chromatin reads, and binding data for a key loop protein. A transformer network, which weighs links across the whole input, reads the joined data. Two-stage filtering and guided grouping cut false hits. In tests it beat older tools on overlap scores, protein enrichment, and match with known 3D shapes. The code is posted in public for other labs to use.
pmc-13503905:
Armin Behfrouz and Maryam Tahmasebpoor improve a natural mineral so it pulls more ammonia from wastewater, in a 2026 study. The mineral, clinoptilolite, is common and cheap, yet in raw form it takes up ammonia poorly. Chemical treatment can sharpen its appetite.

The team tried four treatments; a sodium aluminate wash worked best, reaching high uptake under mild alkaline conditions. They then bound the treated powder into beads with a polymer glue for easy handling and reuse. The beads kept about three fifths of the powder's capacity and stayed firm in use. Standard uptake curves fit the data well. The beads held up over repeat cycles, which suits plant-scale trials.
pmc-13504005:
Francisco Rodrigues dos Santos leads a team explaining a heart tracing that points to poisoning by an old drug, in a 2026 case answer. The drug is digoxin, used for heart rhythm and failure, with a narrow safe range. The tracing came from a woman whose care team had missed the drug in her recent records.

The tracing showed a junctional rhythm with the upper and lower heart chambers beating apart, a short QT span, and a scooped dip in the ST segment, a classic digoxin mark. Blood tests found the drug at a level far above the toxic line. Further checks showed she had taken it on purpose. Care centered on fixing her high potassium, close support, and antibody fragments that bind the drug. Her tracing returned to normal as drug levels fell.
pmc-13504805:
Hassan and colleagues surveyed 426 licensed dentists in Erbil City, Iraq, about teledentistry, treating and triaging dental problems remotely, and found a profession that has barely begun. Knowledge was poor in nearly two thirds of respondents and practice poorer still, with attitudes mostly neutral rather than hostile. Their 2026 cross-sectional study scored knowledge, attitude, and practice separately, then modelled what predicts doing well on each.

Knowledge was the linchpin: dentists with good knowledge were many times likelier to practise teledentistry well, and qualification level separated the knowledgeable from the rest in the analysis. Women and knowledgeable dentists held more positive attitudes, while each added year of age slightly raised the odds of good practice. The top barriers dentists named were fearing patients would not accept remote care and lacking formal training, each cited by about five in six respondents. The authors prescribe curriculum reform and clear professional guidance as the fix.
pmc-13505105:
Haruna Ushimura and others test whether oral motor function relates to daily living ability in older adults. In 2026, the one-time study covers one hundred people aged seventy to eighty-five, classified by Barthel Index into seventy-nine with good and twenty-one with poor daily living ability. It tests oral diadochokinesis, tongue pressure, chewing performance, and remaining teeth. Tongue and chewing decline tracks frailty and disability.

Oral diadochokinesis scores for pa, ta, and ka came out lower for the poor-ability group and remained independently linked after age adjustment. Chewing performance was lower too but lost significance after adjustment, and tongue pressure and tooth count showed no correlation. Discrimination was modest, with areas under the curve of 0.66 to 0.67, so oral motor tests alone cannot screen for disability without long-term testing.
pmc-13507105:
Qian Gui, Beijia Liu, Yue Wu, and Gui Yu examine, in 2026 work, whether a psychological frailty score predicts new heart and metabolic disease in older Chinese adults. Data come from a national aging study and cover 4060 people aged 45 or older who began free of diabetes, heart disease, and stroke. The score blends distress, thinking, memory, and felt physical weakness across fifteen items.

Over a median follow-up of twenty-four months, higher scores meant higher risk of the combined outcome and of each disease alone. The link was strongest for stroke. Adding the score to standard risk factors sharpened prediction for the combined outcome and stroke. Mind and mood health may deserve a place in risk checks.
pmc-13507205:
Hugo Gizardin-Fredon and colleagues present 2026 work on a faster way to map protein partnerships by chemically linking partners before mass spectrometry reads them. Many key partnerships are brief and weak, so linked pairs are rare and hard to detect in complex samples. Their workflow sorts ions in gas phase with an electric waveform method before reading, which thins the crowd.

In human cell extract, the method found 1269 links covering 213 partnerships from under twenty micrograms of sample, with no liquid sorting steps. Tests also covered a purified three-protein complex and sparse spliceosome samples, the machines that edit RNA messages. Better link detection at small scale could bring partnership mapping into routine structural biology.
pmc-13508005:
Vaishali Singh and five co-authors study whether a low dose of ketamine eases pain after spine fusion surgery, in 2026 work at a large hospital in Srinagar, India. Pain control after this surgery aids healing, yet opioids carry clear limits. The team followed 44 patients split into two equal groups. One group received a steady low-dose ketamine drip during and after surgery. The other group received standard pain drugs without ketamine.

Pain scores were lower in the ketamine group at several points in the first day after surgery. The strongest gains came at four and six hours. Ketamine patients also used far less opioid medicine over 48 hours, reported higher satisfaction, and left hospital sooner on average. No major added side effects stood out in this small group. The authors see ketamine as a useful part of a mixed pain plan, above all in early recovery.
pmc-13508205:
Louis Odeigah and five co-authors review three years of infertility cases at a teaching hospital in Ilorin, north-central Nigeria, in 2026 work. Causes of infertility in Africa may differ from patterns in wealthier countries, the team notes. They pulled records for 797 women treated at the hospital's clinics between 2016 and 2018. Files gave causes, related health factors, and whether infertility was primary or secondary. Statistical tests then weighed which factors linked most strongly to each pattern.

The women's average age was near 33 years. About a third had a menstrual disorder, and one in five had past pelvic infection. More than half were married to men whose semen tests came back abnormal. Past womb scraping surgery stood out as the strongest single factor tied to the type of infertility. The authors stress that male factors now lead the picture locally, so couples should be assessed together from the start.
pmc-13508305:
Byron Rusnak, Lilijana Sarabia Oliver, Kyle Procopio, and Adrienne Roeder study how a small plant keeps the green sepals around its flowers evenly sized, in 2026 work. Sepals must close neatly to shield the young bud. A mutant plant, called drmy1, breaks that evenness: outer sepals overgrow and inner ones lag, leaving buds open. The team read gene activity cell by cell and by location in young buds. Imaging with a glowing reporter then tracked a hormone signal group called brassinosteroids.

The hormone signal ran high and uneven in the mutant's young sepals. Crossing the mutant with hormone-pathway mutants, or dosing it with the hormone or a hormone blocker, restored balance. Extra hormone favored the inner sepals, while blocking it trimmed the outer ones. The work shows the missing gene normally keeps hormone signaling in check so all sepals grow in step.
pmc-13508805:
Dadashpour and colleagues compared five machine learning methods in 2026 for identifying type 2 diabetes and the factors tied to it. They used a public dataset of health records for nearly 100,000 people, testing models that included logistic regression, a neural network, and a random forest.

The gradient boosting model called XGBoost performed best, reaching 96 percent accuracy and a near-perfect discrimination score. An explanation method ranked the strongest predictors: hemoglobin A1c, a long-term blood sugar measure, came first, followed by blood glucose, age, body mass index, and sex. The authors note the ranking fits known diabetes biology. They caution that the results need testing in independent patient groups before clinical use.
pmc-13509805:
Cejalvo-Lapeña and colleagues pooled in 2026 the animal evidence on brown seaweed compounds as antioxidants. Phlorotannins, polyphenols from brown macroalgae, show antioxidant and inflammation-calming activity in the lab, but animal proof is mixed. The team searched four databases for in vivo studies. Of 415 records, twenty-two studies in zebrafish embryos, mice, and rats qualified, covering extracts, fractions, and pure compounds.

In zebrafish, the compounds reduced reactive oxygen, fat oxidation, and nitric oxide output. One enzyme, glutathione peroxidase, showed no consistent pooled effect. Bias checks found unclear reporting of chance assignment, hidden grouping, and blinding in many studies. The authors call the protective signal promising but uncertain. They warn the mix of models and preparations blocks direct translation to human use.
pmc-13510105:
Walton and Strickland reviewed in 2026 therapies that target the complement system in glioblastoma, the most common and deadly primary brain tumor in adults. Complement is a blood-borne defence network, but in this tumor it plays a double role. It aids attack on cancer cells while also sending calming signals that shield the tumor. The team graded 41 studies, from cell and animal work to patient observations.

Walton found most work clusters on a few targets, such as the C3b tagging step and the C5a signal and its receptor. Only five animal survival studies were alike enough to compare, and they were too different to pool. Certainty of evidence was rated very low, so the authors frame complement drugs as a hypothesis needing standard models and proper trials.
pmc-13511005:
Ying Yan, Xi Lan, Huaxi Mai, Hao Tan, and Yanchun Liang review how the drug dienogest eases pain from endometriosis, in 2026 work. In this condition, tissue like the womb lining grows outside the womb. Pain is the most common complaint in this disease, and its roots mix misplaced nerve fibers, a sensitized central nervous system, immune and inflammation imbalance, and low-oxygen stress in lesions. The team searched two major databases for work through May 2026.

Dienogest, a modern hormone drug that targets progesterone receptors, lowers estrogen levels and calms inflammatory responses. It also adjusts nerve growth signals, tempers central sensitivity, and changes how cells in the lesions behave. Clinical studies report decent long-term safety and tolerability for the drug. The authors present it as an effective option for endometriosis pain, grounded in those paired mechanisms.
pmc-13511305:
Hu and colleagues reviewed the mixed evidence on isoflurane, a used anesthetic gas, and thinking ability, in their 2026 article. They offer a model built on two axes, dose and age, to make sense of it. Older accounts stress harm: nerve cell death, oxidative stress, and brain inflammation. Yet studies report that low doses at certain life stages sharpen memory. The authors argue dose and age together decide which face the drug shows.

Hu sorts evidence across young and mature life stages. brief low-dose exposure improved maze scores in young mice, with changes in a memory-related receptor. Across settings the drug engages shared pathways, including an inflammation axis and growth signaling, meeting at cell-death and synaptic plasticity proteins such as brain-derived neurotrophic factor. The framework aims to guide safer anesthesia practices and steps that protect thinking after surgery in at-risk patients.
pmc-13513705:
Dolev Fabrikant and colleagues describe fossil planthoppers from about 100 million years ago whose mouthparts worked like bendy drinking straws. The insects, trapped in amber, carried feeding tubes longer than their bodies, ending in a finely folded segment.

Using micro-CT scans, 3D X-ray images, the team read the fine folds as a bend-without-kinking device, like a vacuum hose. That flex likely let the insects probe deep bark cracks for plant fluids that stiff mouthparts could not reach. The tip may also have swollen like a wall plug to anchor the insect while it fed. Similar folded straws arose in unrelated Cretaceous insects, Fabrikant notes, hinting at lost feeding tricks of ancient forests.
pmc-13516005:
Saroukhani and colleagues compared in 2026 how synthetic dialysis grafts perform in the groin versus the upper arm. Patients on hemodialysis need reliable blood access, and when a natural fistula is not possible, surgeons implant a plastic graft tube. Upper arm sites are preferred, but some patients exhaust those options, so the team asked whether groin grafts last as long and cause similar problems.

Their cross-sectional study covered 213 patients treated between October 2018 and October 2020 and followed for at least two years, with 183 upper extremity grafts and thirty groin grafts. Patency, the time a graft keeps working, did not differ significantly between the sites, and rates of infection, ischemia, nerve damage, and clotting were also similar. The authors conclude groin placement is a viable alternative when upper arm access is unsuitable, while calling for studies with standard materials and longer follow-up.
pmc-13516805:
Esli Janai Flores-Palma leads a twelve-author team profiling proteins in childhood leukaemia that resists first-line drugs, in a 2026 retrospective analysis. B-cell acute lymphoblastic leukaemia is the commonest childhood cancer, and ten to twenty percent of patients relapse when induction drugs fail. The team ran mass spectrometry on bone marrow samples taken before treatment, comparing children who responded to vincristine and methotrexate with those who did not.

Nonresponders carried a distinct protein pattern before any drug was given. The shifts centred on the cell's skeleton and its movement, on nucleic acid handling, DNA repair, and RNA processing. Two proteins, thymidine phosphorylase and gelsolin, stood out as consistently raised in nonresponders, patient by patient. Flores-Palma's team names them candidate warning markers of built-in resistance. Validation by other methods in bigger, independent groups must come before clinical use.
pmc-13517405:
Aydın and co-authors ask whether botulinum toxin reshapes the tissue around spastic muscles, not just the nerves. Their 2026 retrospective ultrasound study follows 37 stroke patients treated with botulinum toxin type A for focal spasticity. Fascial thickness, the connective tissue wrapping the muscles, was measured before treatment, at three weeks, and at three months in the injected regions, alongside standard clinical scores.

Fascial thickness fell significantly across all evaluated regions after injection. Most sites thinned by week three and stayed thinner at month three, while three deeper layers kept thinning through the full period. Clinical measures moved in parallel: spasticity scores and upper-limb motor scores improved significantly, though recovery staging did not change. The authors suggest the toxin's benefit partly reflects fascial remodelling, a structural effect beyond nerve blocking, and propose ultrasound fascial measurement as a monitoring biomarker.
pmc-13517505:
Muhammad Farid leads a nine-author review of measles and rubella across the WHO Eastern Mediterranean Region in a 2026 analysis. The two diseases serve as tracers of how well vaccine systems work, and pandemic disruption tore gaps in coverage. The team examined surveillance, coverage estimates, and elimination status for all twenty-two countries and territories over 2023 and 2024.

Regional measles incidence crept up, and rubella more than doubled per million people. Big outbreaks in Yemen, Iraq, and Afghanistan drove much of the rise. First-dose coverage held near eighty percent, second-dose near seventy-five, and only nine countries cleared ninety-five percent on both. Zero-dose children and dropout between doses kept transmission alive. Farid's team judges the region off track for 2030 elimination and urges equity-first catch-up, stronger surveillance, and faster outbreak response, above all in fragile, conflict-hit settings.
pmc-13517705:
Krisztián Németh leads a nine-author review, the second of two parts, tracing collagen fragments from the gut through the whole body in a 2026 article. Collagen supplements are usually sold for joints and skin, but digested fragments travel widely. In the gut they help seal the lining, nudge the resident microbes, and change bile, the liver's digestive fluid, which in turn talks to appetite, blood sugar, fat, liver, and brain.

The authors grade the findings honestly. Firmest ground: joint disease in dogs and horses, plus taurine, a separate nutrient working through bile, for a reversible heart condition in some dog breeds. Lab hints about fat burning, memory, and clotting remain unconfirmed in animals. Németh's team frames diet as a shared gut-bile signalling system that collagen and taurine each tune differently, relevant across pets, horses, and livestock.
pmc-13518805:
Yujie Chen and six colleagues unveil CAPO in 2026, a yeast platform that makes gene activity tunable and predictable. Engineers often combine promoters, DNA switches that set gene output, only to find behavior changes in new combinations. CAPO instead uses synthetic promoters that stay silent until guide RNAs bring in a dCas9-VPR activator.

Each gene's output is dialed by guide RNA amount, set through defined T7 promoters, while channels stay independent of one another. Output reached levels matching strong natural yeast promoters with little background leak, and strength order held across genes. The team programmed broad fluorescence colors and quickly optimized production of lycopene and 3-hydroxypropionic acid, showing practical range.
pmc-13520305:
Ava Safaroghli-azar leads a 2026 laboratory study of AU2-94, a drug designed to block only the CDK4 protein in prostate cancer. Earlier drugs block CDK4 together with CDK6, so the team tests whether a narrower drug keeps its strength while working in cancers that resist standard care.

AU2-94 slowed growth across prostate cancer cells with varied hormone sensitivity, plus organoids and mouse tumours. In cells with intact RB protein, the drug lowered RB activity and quieted growth programmes. Combinations with hormone therapy, chemotherapy and a PI3K blocker were also tested. Readers get a detailed early case for selective CDK4 blockade before any human use.
pmc-13520705:
Sadaf Khursheed Baba and colleagues outline in 2026 a term-long course in cancer biology for undergraduates. Students run a real lab project on HPV-linked cervical cancer. They also learn science writing in a structured way. The class silenced a candidate gene in cancer cells and tracked gene activity.

All students finished the full lab workflow. Gains covered lab skills, data work and reading of primary papers. Writing support led to student names on a published review article. That step links bench work with scholarly output. The group was small. The design is still offered as a model that other schools can scale.
pmc-13522005:
Ling-Gen Xiong and colleagues derive in 2026 breast cancer subtypes from microscope image features, then trace a key gene's spatial pattern with single-cell and spatial gene data. Image traits from tumour slides numbered 1,406, narrowed to 25 core features for clustering.

Two subtypes emerged, with one tied to advanced disease and poorer outlook. A splicing-related gene called ESRP1 stood out as raised in that harsher subtype. Spatial maps placed the gene inside tumour zones alongside epithelial and support cells. Communication analysis cast support cells as hubs in a growth-factor network in gene-rich regions, suggesting a microenvironment role worth targeted study.
pmc-13523205:
Peerapen and co-authors test chlorogenic acid, a coffee bean compound, against the kidney scarring that kidney stones set in motion. Calcium oxalate crystals, the main ingredient of most stones, prod kidney lining cells into epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition, a shape-shifting step toward fibrosis where cells loosen their seals and turn spindle-like. Their 2026 cell study exposed dog kidney cells to the crystals with and without the acid, then measured shape, barrier strength, identity markers, and the cell's full protein inventory.

The crystals duly triggered the transition, raising the spindle index and a mesenchymal marker while the electrical resistance across the cell sheet, a seal quality measure, fell. Chlorogenic acid prevented every one of those changes when given before or with the crystals. The authors suggest a dietary compound might interrupt stone-driven fibrosis early.
pmc-13523305:
Mingjie Xu, Hao Cheng, and Lijian Xu report a rare gut cancer that mimics another cancer type in a 2026 case report. An eighty-two-year-old man had persistent black stools and severe anemia. Imaging found multiple lesions in the stomach and small intestine, and surgery removed several bowel segments. Under the microscope the tumors formed solid sheets of epithelium-like cells with extensive bleeding, and they stained for an epithelial marker, imitating poorly differentiated carcinoma.

Stains for blood vessel markers were also strongly positive, pointing to epithelioid angiosarcoma, a cancer of vessel-lining cells. Gene sequencing found amplification of the MYC gene, usually associated with radiation-linked cases, although this patient had no prior radiotherapy. He died three months after surgery. The authors propose MYC amplification as a possible driver and marker of aggressive behavior in primary cases.
pmc-13523405:
Margaret Kurop, Hekmat B Khoukaz, and William P Fay present an electrocardiogram puzzle in an eighteen-year-old woman in a 2026 case report. She arrived at the emergency department with nausea, fatigue, and tremor, and her heart tracing showed inverted T waves in the chest leads. In adults such changes often suggest reduced blood flow to the heart, yet in a young patient other causes move up the list. Her history included depression treated with medication.

The teaching point centers on lithium toxicity. Because lithium resembles sodium and potassium chemically, it interferes with the channels and pumps that set heart cell electrical activity, in both slow nodal tissue and fast conducting tissue. The resulting tracing changes most often include T-wave inversion and lengthening of the QT interval, a pattern clinicians should recognize in patients taking lithium.
pmc-13524605:
Alfaro Hudak and colleagues examined whether the time adults spend on responsibilities squeezes out home food preparation, a question sharpened by new dietary guidelines urging whole, minimally processed foods. Their 2026 study first surveyed United States adults about which daily activities count as responsibilities. They then linked national time-use data from 2014 to 2016 and 2022 to 2023 to examine cooking time across household types.

Alfaro Hudak found households with children spent the most time on both responsibilities and food preparation, while single parents cooked less than two-parent households. More responsibility time was linked to slightly less cooking in every household group, a small per-hour effect that households seem to resist by protecting cooking time. Accumulated across realistic differences, though, the loss reached a meaningful share of average preparation time. That suggests many households already cook near their feasible minimum and need time relief, not just dietary advice.
pmc-13526205:
Parissa J Ballard and colleagues examined how civic life relates to health among United States school students. Published in 2026, the study surveyed 1,286 students in grades six through twelve, average age near fifteen, between fall 2021 and spring 2025. Civic engagement covered actions, attitudes, and skills, while health covered physical, mental, and overall well-being, split by race and gender groups.

Whole-sample averages hid distinct subgroup patterns. Girls, transgender, and gender-diverse students showed more positive links between civic engagement and health than boys did. Political participation and civic discussion, by contrast, linked more negatively to health for students of color than for White students. A sense of community, by contrast, linked positively to health for every group. The authors urge programs tuned to these intersections rather than one-size civic prescriptions.
pmc-13527905:
Jian Wang and eleven colleagues report a 2026 experiment on whether melatonin can protect cotton seeds from cadmium, a toxic heavy metal that builds up in farm soils. Working with the cultivar Nongda 601, the team compared plain seeds with seeds given melatonin, cadmium, or both together, then sequenced gene activity to see how the hormone changed the response.

Cadmium alone slowed germination, raised damaging oxygen byproducts, and disturbed the seed's own hormone balance. Adding melatonin restored enzyme activity that breaks down stored starch, lowered the harmful byproducts, and shifted hormone levels back toward growth. Gene data pointed to antioxidant defenses and a plant chemical pathway called phenylpropanoid biosynthesis. The findings may guide cotton growing on polluted land.
pmc-13528005:
Cagri Ates and Onur Karaaslan report a 2026 prospective study of fetal heart function in growth-restricted pregnancies. Telling a naturally small fetus from a truly restricted one is hard. Standard Doppler blood-flow tests can look normal until late. The team used a modified heart performance index on 157 pregnancies at or past 32 weeks. Fetuses were grouped by belly size percentile.

Usual Doppler measures and fluid levels did not differ among groups. Heart timing measures did. Fetuses below the tenth percentile showed longer contraction and relaxation phases and higher index values. That pattern signals early heart strain. Borderline fetuses between the third and tenth percentiles looked much like those below the third. The authors suggest the index adds useful warning where Doppler stays silent.
pmc-13528105:
Qianqian Wu and seven colleagues delete a gene in a pig and human pathogen to see what it does in a 2026 study. The germ is Streptococcus suis serotype 2. The gene makes a small enzyme that strips phosphate tags from proteins. Such enzymes help build capsules in related germs. The team built a mutant missing the gene and compared it with the normal strain.

The mutant grew a bit slowly in mid-phase. Its capsule ran thinner, with about twelve percent less capsule sugar. Colony looks, cell sticking, and dodging of immune eating stayed normal. Mouse infections were no milder than with the normal germ. Lab tests showed the enzyme cannot strip the expected partner protein. The authors conclude the enzyme trims the capsule but is not vital for disease. They warn against copying mechanisms between cousin species.
pmc-13529805:
Sina Ghanbari and eight colleagues hunt durum wheat lines that yield steadily under rain-fed farming in a 2026 study. They grew 118 inbred lines from a cross between a drought-fit Iranian cultivar and a protein-rich landrace. Four sites in Italy and Iran hosted the trials. Both grain yield and grain protein were scored. Several stability methods ranked the lines.

One line, ZD-050, gave the top yield at about 3.9 tonnes per hectare. Another, ZD-032, led protein at about 14.3 percent. Rankings shifted by method, as expected. Yield-focused and dynamic methods still put ZD-050 near the top. It kept moderate protein while adapting widely. Gene, place, and their interplay all shaped both traits strongly. The authors nominate ZD-050 for breeding programs chasing steady harvests without rain insurance.
pmc-13529905:
Simran K Chandawarkar and Ibrahim Amjad review lasting harm from dermal fillers in a 2026 synthesis of published evidence. Fillers lift and reshape facial tissue, and most side effects stay minor. Rare lasting injuries, by contrast, can change a life, so the authors trace why they happen and how clinics might prevent them.

Their search followed PRISMA guidance across PubMed reports from 2000 to 2024. Blindness, stroke, lasting inflammation, and tissue death emerged as the gravest outcomes, tied mainly to injection site, technique, and product choice. Hyaluronic acid products stayed favored because their effects can be reversed.
pmc-13534405:
Mehedi Hasan Meraj and colleagues present in 2026 CAE-BrainNet, a model that sorts brain tumours from MRI scans into four classes. Past models often covered few classes, lacked clear explanations, and skipped firm statistical checks. Their system blends three image networks and weights each one by tumour class through a learned attention step.

The model reached very high accuracy on its main test set and kept healthy tissue calls highly specific. On a separate dataset it still scored high without retraining, and tests confirmed gains were not chance. Visual maps show which scan areas drove each call for clinicians.
pmc-13536705:
Souhaib Atri and colleagues recount an unusual trauma recovery in a 2026 case report involving a complete cut through the common bile duct. A 29-year-old man arrived with a stab wound through the chest and abdomen, severe liver injury, and active bleeding. Emergency surgery controlled bleeding and drained bile, yet a later bile collection still required drainage. What followed avoided the major rebuilding operation that such injuries usually need.

Scans two months later showed a new natural channel between the bile duct and the small intestine that allowed bile to drain inside the body. Because liver tests stayed normal and no blockage appeared, surgeons chose close follow-up instead of reconstruction. One year later the patient remained well without symptoms. The authors present careful staged care plus watchful follow-up as a workable path in rare cases like this one.
pmc-13538305:
Myriam V. Thoma and colleagues test two accounts of how early-life hardship shapes mental health in old age in a 2026 study. One account predicts steady harm with each added hardship, while the other predicts a curved pattern where moderate hardship toughens people. A total of 211 older adults with an average age near seventy years took part, split between a high-hardship group and a lower-risk comparison group. Past-year mental disorders were counted.

About six in ten participants qualified for at least one past-year disorder diagnosis, with higher shares in the high-hardship group. Disorder counts rose steadily with hardship level, fitting the straight dose pattern. No curved toughening pattern appeared. The authors conclude that early stress casts a long shadow and stress prevention across life deserves priority.
pmc-13538405:
Yaan-Kit Ng and colleagues map protein interaction changes in muscle insulin resistance in a 2026 study combining two mass measurement methods. Protein partnerships shift with disease, yet counting those shifts body-wide has been hard. More than seven thousand unique partnerships among over five thousand proteins were quantified in muscle, with and without fresh insulin stimulation after chronic resistance developed. Network changes were compared with plain protein level changes.

Interaction rewiring dominated the response, outweighing level changes alone. A hub for protein folding and bond handling inside cell compartments stood out as disturbed. Follow-up work tied one partner, PDIA6, to sulfur oxidation control and insulin sensitivity itself. The authors present living-tissue interaction mapping as a powerful lens on disease workings.
pmc-13538705:
D Gavars and colleagues probe single tiny wires of mixed copper and zinc oxides for infrared harvesting in a 2026 scope study. The cheap, common oxides form junction wires mostly studied for visible light, leaving infrared response untested. Wire arrays grown on copper foil were steered inside an electron scope while current flow and light response with no power applied were recorded.

The wires acted like diodes, confirming a working junction between the oxide types. A strong current appeared under infrared light with no applied voltage, traced to a heat-driven effect. Voltage per degree, power factor, and response speed all reached solid levels. The authors see promise for tiny power units running on small heat gaps in wearable gear and sensors.
pmc-13539905:
Lu and colleagues wrote a 2026 review on how gut microbes may shape Alzheimer's disease. Gut microbes and the brain trade signals through nerves, immunity, and chemistry. The review gathers how microbe imbalance may feed the disease's core damage. Most evidence so far comes from animal models and human correlations.

Microbe products include short fatty acids and breakdown bits of dietary protein. Imbalance may spark brain inflammation and oxidative stress, the review argues. Those paths tie to the sticky plaques and tangles of Alzheimer's disease. Multi-layer gene and chemical maps sketch patient-specific microbe patterns now. Gut-targeted steps remain promising but unproven for patients, they caution. Human proof of cause still lags behind the animal evidence base.
pmc-13540905:
Song Qu and colleagues describe new stem cells in a 2026 resource paper. The cells came from a young girl with Angelman syndrome. That is a severe developmental disorder. Most cases follow the loss of a stretch of chromosome 15. The lost stretch comes from the mother. It silences a gene called UBE3A in the brain.

The team reprogrammed her blood cells into stem cells. The cells kept a normal chromosome set. They also showed the standard markers of stemness. They could form all three early tissue layers. The team then turned them into neural stem cells. Those cells offer a base for drug screening work.
pmc-13542205:
Ibone Labiano and colleagues report a pilot study in 2026. Blood tests hunted leftover cancer DNA after surgery. The cancer was localised colorectal cancer. The goal was catching minimal residual disease early. Scans cannot see such tiny traces. Forty-seven patients joined, all with high-risk tumors.

Tumor tissue was sequenced first for each patient. Plasma was drawn four weeks after surgery. Judged by blood alone, the test caught few relapses. It cleared most patients who stayed well. Adding tissue results lifted detection a lot. Accuracy rose markedly as well. Agreement between tissue and plasma stayed low. Lung relapses escaped detection entirely.
pmc-13546705:
Md. Royhan Gofur and co-authors profiled in 2026 three accessory sex glands of male mice, structures whose secretions support sperm and fertility but which lack thorough measurement in this common laboratory animal. Six adult mice provided tissue from the vesicular, bulbourethral, and preputial glands for size and structure measurements, gene checks, and staining for three membrane proteins from the Eph family.

Each gland showed a distinct architecture, from folded linings to lobed, sebaceous tissue. EphB4 and its partner ephrin-B1 appeared in all three glands, while EphB2 showed up only in two, and the proteins sat mainly in basal or secretory cells depending on the gland. The authors offer the measurements as baseline data and suggest these proteins help regulate gland structure.
pmc-13547305:
Dominika Zaremba and a cross-national team ran a preregistered experiment in 2026 on whether stirring climate emotions moves people to act. More than a thousand participants each in Poland and Norway read stories designed to evoke anger, compassion, or hope about climate change, or neutral stories. Afterward they could work at a tedious task that benefited an environmental cause or donate money, two concrete measures of pro-environmental behavior.

Against expectations, the emotional stories changed neither effort nor donations compared with the neutral ones. Age was the steady predictor instead, with older participants giving more of both. The authors suggest future work needs more natural or immersive emotional material, longer exposure, and tasks matched more closely to the feelings raised.
pmc-13548705:
Liang Zhou and colleagues compare two rival definitions of sepsis in children at one intensive care unit, in a 2026 retrospective study. The older definition rests on body-wide inflammation signs, while the 2024 Phoenix criteria center on organ dysfunction. Reviewing just over a thousand infected children admitted in Chongqing between 2020 and 2023, the team scored every child under both systems and compared agreement and death prediction.

The two definitions overlapped poorly, agreeing only weakly. About three fifths met the older criteria, nearly three quarters met Phoenix, and fewer than half met both. Children meeting neither almost always survived. After adjustment, Phoenix status strongly predicted death within twenty-eight days, while the older criteria predicted nothing independently, and Phoenix separated survivors from non-survivors far better. The authors back Phoenix for judging risk in infected children.
pmc-13550605:
M. Trinidad García-Barceló, with six colleagues, published a 2026 study of gases given off by a lung germ. The germ, Pseudomonas aeruginosa, infects people with weak lungs or cystic fibrosis. Finding it now often needs invasive tests. The team asked whether the gases it releases could give it away. They profiled gases from 48 clinical samples with a lab instrument.

All samples shared three gases not reported before, a sign of shared germ chemistry. Samples from long-term infections made more fatty gases. Samples from short, sharp infections made more ring-shaped gases. Related samples taken over time from the same patients changed their gas mix. A gene switch called LasR also shaped which gases appeared.
pmc-13550805:
Maximilian Philip Wessendorf, leading eleven colleagues, published a 2026 evaluation of a two-day training course in micro-ultrasonography for prostate cancer. The imaging method can flag clinically significant cancer, yet new readers often miss cases. Twenty participants with limited experience took lectures and supervised case practice in Mannheim, then read biopsy-confirmed test cases before and after training.

Accuracy rose from about half of cases correct to roughly two thirds, and sensitivity climbed sharply as well. The share of negative calls that proved right also improved, while specificity barely moved. A risk scoring system performed better after training too, and the gain repeated across two separate sessions, which the authors read as evidence that structured practice helps novices manage patients more soundly.
pmc-13550905:
Ghinwa S. Majid, with co-authors including Ahmed S. Abdulamir and Iman M. Aufi, published a 2026 study building a cheaper test for two herpesviruses in donated blood. Antibody screening can miss Epstein-Barr virus and cytomegalovirus during early infection, so the team designed a multiplex real-time PCR test that detects both viruses' DNA at once. Blood came from 1,000 apparently healthy Iraqi donors, pooled ten at a time.

The home-built test found rates close to a commercial kit, with Epstein-Barr virus common in pools and cytomegalovirus uncommon. Sensitivity and specificity were high for both viruses, while cost ran near a tenth of the commercial kit. The authors argue such pricing matters for safer transfusion in lower-resource settings.
pmc-13551705:
Martin Baxmann, Márton Zsoldos, and Krisztina Kárpáti published a 2026 review of AI in orthodontic planning. Orthodontists must decide on tooth removal, jaw class, and treatment type. Their calls often differ from each other. The team searched six databases to October 2025. They kept studies that used real patient data and rated each study's bias risk.

Nineteen studies qualified for the review. Most tested learning models for removal and jaw class calls. Reported accuracy often passed 80 percent against expert calls. Rule-based systems showed their reasoning more clearly. Data-driven models often scored higher. Bias was mostly moderate to serious, driven by backward-looking designs. The team urges tests in new clinics before real use.
pmc-13551805:
V P Ansar Ahamed, Abhay Mudey, Abhishek Joshi, and T Athila Jasmine published a 2026 case report from rural India. A 75-year-old farmer had lived with a swollen leg and scrotum for about seven years. He came to a rural screening camp with two days of fever. He also had type 2 diabetes, found at the camp. Care took place at a rural medical college.

A blood smear showed young worms, the offspring of a filarial parasite. An ultrasound showed the classic dance sign of the worms. Care combined sugar control, drugs for the infestation, and limb hygiene advice. Staff also counseled him on mosquito control and follow-up. The team argues for joining worm disease checks with chronic disease care in rural programs.
pmc-13556005:
Min-Jeong Kim and Joo Hwan No screened in 2026 for drug leads against Naegleria fowleri, the amoeba that causes a usually fatal brain infection. Treatment options for primary amoebic meningoencephalitis remain very limited. The pair tested a library of 126 compounds that inhibit cyclin-dependent kinases, a family of enzymes that control cell division, against the amoeba's feeding stage.

Twenty-three compounds proved active, and five stood out with strong potency at low doses. Sequence searches then found five CDK-like proteins in the amoeba, and one resembled a related parasite kinase closely enough to model in three dimensions. Computer docking placed all five lead compounds inside its predicted binding pocket, and simulations held them stable. The study gives drug hunters a concrete protein target and a short list of starting compounds.
pmc-13556105:
Seraki Miyamoto and ten colleagues validated in 2026 a Japanese version of a scale that measures distress about death and dying in people with advanced cancer. The Death and Dying Distress Scale is used internationally, but a translated tool must prove itself in its new language. Two hundred Japanese patients with advanced cancer completed the scale alongside measures of depression, anxiety, quality of life, symptom burden, and spiritual wellbeing.

Factor analysis settled on a three-part structure after one weak item was dropped, leaving fourteen questions. Each part scored consistently, and the confirmatory analysis fit the data adequately. Scores rose with depression, anxiety, and symptom burden, and fell as quality of life and spiritual wellbeing rose. Family and social wellbeing showed no such link. Clinicians in Japan gain a checked instrument for a hard conversation topic.
pmc-13558605:
Eliana Vivas, Chengyan Ji, and Lelys Bravo de Guenni proposed in 2026 a wavelet method for forecasting drought. The method breaks both the weather drivers and the drought record itself into waves of different speeds. A common flaw in such decomposition is leakage, where future information sneaks into training. Their design applies the transform inside moving windows of past data only, keeping the forecast honest, and tests it on seventy-six years of Illinois drought records.

The joint decomposition model often beat simpler wavelet and naive baselines, cutting one error measure by up to about a quarter and calling the direction of change more accurately. Seasonal bootstrap intervals quantified the uncertainty around each gain. Because drivers and target are split into the same frequency bands, users can see which slow or fast climate rhythms carry the drought signal. The authors present interpretability as the method's chief prize.
pmc-13559105:
Xiaocheng Wu and colleagues published a 2026 narrative review on probiotics for asthma, with attention to delivering them through the airways rather than by mouth. Asthma involves long-standing airway inflammation shaped by genes, immunity, and environment. Changes in the microbes living in the airways track closely with the disease, which raises the question of whether helpful bacteria could calm it.

The reviewers searched PubMed for work from January 2007 to February 2026. Animal studies show swallowed probiotics can ease asthma symptoms, though human results conflict, partly because strains, doses, and patient groups differ. Breathing probiotics in has shown benefit in animal experiments, and the bacteria might also ferry anti-asthma drugs into the lung. The authors judge the strategy promising yet still preclinical, with delivery, safety, and product standards unresolved.
pmc-13559805:
Manuela Araque and colleagues examine how social conditions track with metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease in the All of Us research database. Their 2026 cross-sectional analysis identified cases by diagnosis codes, excluded other liver diseases and heavy alcohol use, then matched cases to controls by age and race or ethnicity. The matched sample held 57,895 participants, with full survey data for 16,666.

People with the liver disease were more likely to report incomes at or below $35,000 and schooling below high school level. They also scored higher on social isolation, neighborhood disorder, perceived stress, food insecurity, and transportation insecurity, each gap statistically significant. The authors note the disease already affects roughly a third of the world's adults by current estimates. They call for research on how these social factors combine to drive risk and progression, rather than treating each factor in isolation.
pmc-13560305:
Young Sun Hwang and three colleagues explore why lab-grown human primordial germ cell-like cells split into distinct states. Their 2026 study centers on DND1, a protein whose production from its message varies between cells. Dual fluorescent reporters, single-cell sequencing, and functional assays tracked what the DND1-positive state means for these early germline cells.

DND1-producing cells were rich in RNA regulation machinery, including genes tied to processing bodies and translation control. They divided slowly, exited the cell cycle, and raised the brake protein P27 in their nuclei. At the same time they kept stable expression of genes the germline needs for later differentiation. Adding the signal BMP2 steadied DND1 production without changing its message level or growth rate. The authors conclude that control after transcription coordinates cell cycle behavior with germ cell identity during development.
pmc-13560405:
Ömer Faruk Turan and three colleagues analyze emergency care at a Turkish national hospital deployed for the 2025 Hajj pilgrimage in Makkah. Their 2026 retrospective study covers a mission serving 84,942 Turkish pilgrims between April and July 2025. Operational data from such independent national missions are rarely published.

Nearly ten thousand pilgrims, 11.7 percent of those served, made 13,360 emergency visits. Respiratory illness dominated at about half of presentations. Referrals to higher care stayed low overall, yet heart and neurological problems, small shares of visits, supplied outsized shares of referrals. Age was the strongest referral predictor, with pilgrims seventy-five and older referred at roughly fourteen times the adjusted odds of younger groups. Repeat visitors also faced higher referral risk. Mortality ran at thirty-four per hundred thousand pilgrims. The authors recommend age-based planning and stronger advanced life support.
pmc-13561105:
Yu Sakamoto and colleagues measure the thermal strain of recreational runners racing in tropical heat. Their 2026 study follows 162 runners through ten- or twenty-one-kilometer events in warm, humid conditions near twenty-seven degrees with humidity in the high eighties. Core temperature, heart rate, skin temperature, and fluid balance were tracked in real time for subsets of the field.

Peak core temperatures averaged about 39.4 degrees in both races, with some runners crossing forty-one. Heart rates peaked near maximal values, and half-marathoners lost about two and a half percent of body mass. Four factors independently fed peak core temperature: the temperature a runner started at, mean heart rate, body surface area, and average speed, together explaining about half the variance in the reported model. Age and finishing time did not matter. The authors aim the findings at safer mass-participation racing in the heat.
pmc-13561205:
Sumet Kumar and colleagues pooled trial evidence on lorundrostat, a new drug for high blood pressure that stays high despite several medicines. Lorundrostat blocks the making of aldosterone, a salt-holding hormone, while leaving related hormones alone.

Three trials with 1,568 patients compared the drug against placebo, a dummy treatment with no active drug. On average, systolic pressure fell about 8.4 points more on lorundrostat, and diastolic pressure fell about 3.8 points more. Side effects came more often on the drug, notably low pressure and high potassium, though serious harms were not clearly higher. Kumar says the drug looks promising but larger, longer trials must confirm its safety.
pmc-13562205:
Marie Linderup Funck and six colleagues measured frailty in older adults booked for planned bone and joint surgery in Denmark. Frailty means a body with little reserve, so stress such as surgery hits harder. Their 2026 study covered 519 people aged 65 and older, most booked for hip or knee replacement, and graded each person's health from medical records before surgery.

About one in four patients was pre-frail, and a small share was moderately frail, while none was severely frail. Both groups spent more days in hospital during the 90 days after surgery than patients who were not frail. Spotting this weakness before surgery, the authors argue, lets care teams plan support across clinics and wards and head off complications.
pmc-13562505:
Haohao Wang and six colleagues tackle a deep coal mine problem: the floor of a kept roadway bulging upward unevenly under shifting pressure. The roadway runs beside a mined-out area, and cutting the roof to relieve stress makes the load lopsided. Floor heave then warps the passage and raises upkeep costs. The 2026 study combines a scaled physical model, a mathematical failure model built on earth-pressure theory, and measurements underground at the Zhaogu No. 1 Mine.

Model tests traced how floor strain spread from shallow layers downward after roof cutting. The team proposed a pressure-balancing support scheme: pre-split the roof, fit yielding supports that give under load in roof and walls, and brace the floor with an inverted beam. In the field, the scheme cut floor heave by 46.1 percent against an uncontrolled section. Theory, model, and mine data agreed.
pmc-13563805:
Mohammed Azhar Hussain and two colleagues pair continuous glucose monitors with meal records to see how diet mix and meal spacing move blood sugar in Indian adults with type 2 diabetes. Swings in glucose, beyond the average marker, drive complications on their own. Their 2026 study kept 47 adults who wore a sensor for ten to fourteen days. Food diaries supplied carbohydrate, protein, and fat shares, plus meal gaps. Sensor metrics captured time in range, time above it, and variability.

Carbohydrates dominated the story. Eating more tracked with higher variability, more time above range, higher average glucose, and less time in range. Longer gaps between lunch and dinner, and between breakfast and dinner, linked to more time in range in simple looks. Those timing links faded once total intake and body weight entered the models. The authors advise cutting carbohydrate share first, and call for trials to test meal timing.
pmc-13563905:
Yinchun Huang and seven colleagues ask whether the chromosome pattern in Turner syndrome predicts heart and metabolic trouble in girls and young women. Turner syndrome follows the loss of one sex chromosome, fully in some patients and in mosaic or structural patterns in others. Their 2026 review covered 289 patients assessed at one centre between 2016 and 2023, split into 149 with the single-X pattern and 140 with mosaic or structural variants. Ultrasound scans and blood tests supplied the comparison.

Heart disease appeared in 32.9 percent of the single-X group against 18.6 percent of the others, and the gap survived adjustment for age, weight, cholesterol, and insulin resistance, at odds of 1.88. Aortic widening by the size index was equally common in both groups. Cholesterol clustered in the single-X patients, and LDL cholesterol tracked with structural disease. The authors advise karyotype-aware surveillance, while conceding that scan differences were small and need multicentre confirmation.
pmc-13569505:
Lauren Fernandes and co-authors map, in a 2026 scoping review, interventions that fix inappropriate prescribing for older adults in emergency departments and acute geriatric units, where many medicines and frailty raise risk. Searches across major databases and grey sources from 1991 to 2025 found twenty-one studies, only four of them randomized trials.

Eighteen interventions fell into pharmacist-led medication reviews, computer decision support, staff education, or combinations of those. Inappropriate prescribing was often the main measure, yet few studies reported whether patients actually fared better. The map exposes a field rich in process checks and poor in outcome proof, guiding where future trials should aim.
pmc-13572405:
Abhijit Bhowmik, with eight colleagues, reports a 2026 study of fly ash mixed into an aluminium alloy to cut wear. Fly ash is a fine waste from coal plants. The alloy, AA8011, gains a harder filler when ash is stirred into the melt, which may save energy and raw stock in parts that rub.

The team cast mixes with 0, 4, 8, and 12 percent ash by weight and rubbed pins against a disc under dry conditions. A Taguchi test plan and a grey relation method weighed wear rate, friction force, and friction level together. The best run used 8 percent ash, a 30 newton load, a slide speed of 3 metres per second, and a 3,200 metre slide path. Load shaped the outcome most, at near 49 percent of the effect in the variance checks.
pmc-13572505:
Udomporn Manupibul, with four colleagues, reports a 2026 pilot test of a wearable system that reads how people walk. Lab gait rigs are costly and fixed in place, so the team built SMART F-IMU, which joins motion sensors with flexible foot force pads. The test asked whether it can spot gait shifts tied to body weight outside a lab.

The system estimates ground force, joint angles, and step timing as a person walks. The overweight and obese group took longer strides and spent more time in stance, swing, and double support than the normal-weight group. Their step rate fell, and many joint angles at key gait moments differed with large effect sizes. The authors say the kit can track joint motion in daily life over time. That opens a path to low-cost checks in real settings.
pmc-13573105:
Trofimova and colleagues investigate in 2026 why certain boron bonds survive in molecules where they should quickly fall apart in water. They work with MIDA boronates, compounds in which a protective ligand grips the boron atom loosely enough to let go when needed.

That loose grip, called hemilability, has already let chemists isolate boron species once thought too fragile to exist. The study shows that under acid, the group attached to boron can migrate, leaving boron bound to nitrogen across different oxidation states. Most strikingly, a boron-nitrogen compound with an azide group formed in preference to the aminoboronate that energy arguments favored. That defied the expected easy escape route of releasing nitrogen gas. The authors present these stabilized boron bonds as versatile building blocks for wider use in chemistry.
pmc-13574505:
Seo writes in this 2026 editorial about two menopausal burdens that hormone therapy handles poorly: broken sleep and urinary incontinence. He comments on a systematic review and meta-analysis by Martins and colleagues, published in the same issue, on exercise as treatment for both.

Seo summarizes the review's findings: for sleep, exercise outperformed the comparison interventions. Mind-body practices like yoga and Pilates matched conventional aerobic and strength training, with the largest effects in programs running at least three times weekly. For incontinence, the pooled estimate missed statistical significance, yet pelvic floor strengthening showed a distinct effect. Seo reads this as proof that matching the exercise to the symptom matters more than simply exercising more. He also praises the review for treating the two symptoms as an interacting pair, since night-time urination fragments sleep and embarrassment deepens isolation.
pmc-13575005:
Rajiv Yeravdekar and Alaka Chandak report screening results for Indian university students in a 2026 study. Young adults are often seen as low risk, yet these years are when food and health habits set in. The pair reviewed records from a campus health screening programme.

The records covered 13,628 students aged 18 to 30 screened between June 2023 and May 2024. Close to half were overweight or had obesity, and 53 percent met World Health Organization cut-offs for anaemia. High blood pressure readings were common too, more so in men than women. Being male linked with both anaemia and high readings in adjusted models. The authors urge universities to run routine screening with follow-up care.
pmc-13576305:
Takashi Watanabe leads a 2026 study of immune side effects from checkpoint inhibitor therapy in lung cancer. These drugs free the immune system to attack non-small cell lung cancer, yet they can also trigger inflammation in healthy organs. The team reviewed five years of cases at a Japanese university hospital to find what shapes that risk.

Among 203 patients, 92 had at least one immune side effect, with lung inflammation the most common, followed by thyroid problems. One factor stood out in reverse: patients with heart failure developed side effects far less often, with a risk near one third of others. The link held under a second method that accounts for competing risks. A related model swapping in use of certain heart drugs also showed a link. The authors suggest heart history belongs in monitoring plans.
pmc-13576805:
Luxi Yu, Antonio del Rio Chanona, and Cleo Kontoravdi present a method for carrying a cell culture model from one setup to another without rebuilding it, in a 2026 bioprocess paper. Mechanistic models of CHO cell culture are usually tuned to one cell line, scale, or set of conditions, which limits their reach. Their tool is the ensemble Kalman filter, borrowed from weather forecasting.

The filter folds live process measurements into the model step by step, updating uncertain rate constants and predicting the culture state together. A model tuned on one system could then adapt to a new one from a single experiment. The shifting parameter sets double as a sensitivity map, showing which rates matter under new conditions and when. Tests on six datasets across scales, cell lines, temperatures, and feeding plans reconstructed behaviour well, with forecasts improving as data grew.
pmc-13577905:
Zhong Cao leads a 2026 study pricing the global economic cost of depression from 2025 to 2050 across 154 countries. Depression already ranks among the largest causes of disability worldwide. The team built a macroeconomic model from World Bank and Global Burden of Disease 2021 data, tracking how the illness cuts labour force participation, schooling, and work experience by age and sex.

The projected bill comes to 12 trillion US dollars over the period, equal to 0.460 percent of world output each year. Counting deaths by suicide attributed to depression at an assumed upper rate lifts the total to 14 trillion dollars in the same accounting. The United States and China carry the largest absolute burdens, while North America loses the most relative to its economy. Lost work and productivity drive most of the cost. The authors argue treatment pays for itself in output.
pmc-13582405:
Hesham Salah El-Din Taha and colleagues report a high-stakes rescue of a man whose lung arteries were chronically blocked. A 55-year-old West African man first showed up with a large saddle embolus. It fully blocked the left lung artery and nearly blocked the right. He later came back in shock, with oxygen at 81 percent. Surgery to strip the clots was judged unsuitable at that stage. This 2026 case report describes the catheter-based alternative.

With veno-arterial ECMO, a heart-lung support circuit, backing two sessions, operators reopened both arteries with aspiration, wires, balloons, and a stent. Mean pulmonary artery pressure fell from 89 to 59 millimetres of mercury by the second session. The authors present ECMO-supported intervention as a viable path when chronic central blockage and shock rule out surgery.
pmc-13582705:
Regina Molnár and colleagues studied how foreign med students in Hungary settle into local life. They used Berry's model of four paths: blending with both cultures, keeping one's own culture apart, dropping one's own culture, or drifting from both. Of 326 students, near half took the blend path and just over half kept apart, while the other two paths were rare. The work thus sets the two big groups side by side.

Men, early-year students, non-drinkers, and students with less stress blended in more. Non-smokers and students who shunned shrink visits, oddly, blended in less. Schools can use these trends to shape help that lets foreign students fit in well and stay well in mind and body.
pmc-13582805:
Shamaila Zafar and Jay S. Schneider propose that Parkinson's disease is, at root, a failure of the brain's sleep-driven clearance system. Parkinson's involves alpha-synuclein build-up and steady nerve loss, and sleep and body-clock disruption are common long before motor symptoms dominate. This 2026 review unites two clearance routes: autophagy, the cell's internal recycling, and glymphatic transport, the brain's external wash, across neurons, glia, and the blood-brain barrier.

When sleep architecture and circadian timing fall out of sync, both routes falter, proteins pile up, and pathology spreads. The authors frame sleep-circadian trouble as an upstream driver rather than a side effect, and suggest that restoring healthy sleep rhythms could improve clearance and support disease-modifying strategies.
pmc-13583205:
Ahmed Abdelmaksoud and colleagues ask in a 2026 study whether people with trisomy 21, the condition also known as Down syndrome, face a higher risk of gout. Gout is a painful joint illness caused by uric acid buildup, and high uric acid had already been noted in this group. Proof of a gout link, though, rested on a handful of case reports.

Using health records from a large United States network, the team compared more than 30,000 people with trisomy 21 against matched people without it. Gout showed up in close to three in a hundred patients with the condition, about triple the rate in the comparison group. The higher risk held across age, sex, and racial groups, and the authors urge more work on why it happens and how to screen for it.
pmc-13584505:
Jamaal Ibrahim, Sahardiid Abdilahi, and Mohamed Osman measure anemia among people with HIV in Jigjiga, Ethiopia, in this 2026 paper. Anemia, a lack of healthy red blood cells, drains energy and shortens life for people on HIV treatment. Their clinic-based study covered 392 patients on antiretroviral therapy at public facilities, surveyed over one month in 2023 with blood tests and a set questionnaire.

Close to four in ten patients had anemia, and nearly all of those cases sat in the moderate band. Being female, carrying another infection on top of HIV, and eating a narrow range of foods each raised the odds clearly. The authors call anemia a moderate public health problem at these sites and urge targeted help for women, faster treatment of extra infections, and food advice for patients with poor diets.
pmc-13587305:
Haimanot Andualem Ayalsew and colleagues compare balance in schoolchildren with and without hearing loss in Addis Ababa. The inner ear houses both hearing and the balance organs, so children who cannot hear well may also wobble more, yet balance is rarely checked in this group. Their study tested 148 children aged 7 to 18, half with hearing impairment and half matched peers with normal hearing, on standing, reaching, and a child balance scale.

Children with hearing loss scored lower on every test, in still standing with eyes open or shut, in reaching, and on the full scale. The gap held for boys and girls alike. The authors argue that balance checks belong in the routine care of children with hearing impairment, so that training and support can start before falls and missed play shape their school years.
pmc-13592305:
Florian Maurer leads a 2026 team watching single platinum particles dissolve into lone atoms on ceria supports, then tying that decay to catalyst performance. Platinum on ceria anchors many clean air and chemical catalysts, yet under oxygen the particles can scatter into single atoms and lose punch. Using an electron microscope that works inside gas, the team timed the shrinking of individual particles on shaped ceria cubes.

Neighboring particles and flaws in the support slowed the scatter, while each particle lost volume at a steady rate regardless of starting size. Those atomic scale rates matched the fall in whole catalyst activity closely enough to forecast it. Maurer and the team call this a first step toward predicting catalyst life from particle kinetics.
pmc-13592605:
Chung-Fen Tsai leads a team comparing brain bleeds in 202 Taiwanese patients by where the bleed sits and what caused it. East Asians face higher rates of this stroke type, yet most past data come from Western patients. The group recruited acute cases at two large hospitals, recording risk factors, gene variants, scans, and early thinking tests. They then contrasted bleeds near the brain's surface with deeper ones, and amyloid linked bleeds with others.

Surface bleeds came with older age, larger volume, worse awareness, higher one month death rates, and weaker early cognition. Deep bleeds tracked far more often with high blood pressure. Early thinking scores tied to age, schooling, awareness, stroke severity, bleed size, and small bleed burden near the surface. Tsai and the team urge location aware care and study.
pmc-13592705:
Denise Fuchten and four colleagues check how much tinnitus distress questionnaires overlap in content with depression questionnaires. The two states correlate strongly, and shared items can blur what a score really measures. Six tinnitus scales and seven depression scales were taken apart item by item. Each item's concepts were linked to categories in a global functioning classification, and overlaps were counted at the shared category level.

Depression scales covered fourteen categories, tinnitus scales twenty three. Seven categories appeared in both families, spanning energy, sleep, attention, emotion, thought, social life, and leisure. Overlap ran from about a tenth between the least similar pair to near total for one depression subscale. Fuchten and the team advise picking scales with the study question, not habit, in mind.
pmc-13593705:
D. Pamei and co-authors measured how broken teeth from accidents affect daily life for young patients at a large hospital. Their 2026 study enrolled 266 children and teenagers aged eight to sixteen. All had injured their teeth within the previous year. The team scored the impact with a standard questionnaire on oral effects on daily performance.

Front upper teeth took the most damage, usually as uncomplicated crown fractures, and about a third of injuries were severe. Hardly anyone arrived quickly: only a small minority got emergency care within a day. Nearly all the children were aware of the broken teeth, most reported sensitivity, and two thirds disliked how their teeth looked. Eating, cleaning the mouth, smiling freely, and mixing with friends all suffered. Severe overall impairment, seen in about a quarter, tracked with worse injuries, repeated trauma, soft tissue wounds, and appearance concerns.
pmc-13594405:
Ida Steiro leads a ten-author team asking whether bispecific antibody therapy for multiple myeloma weakens the T cells' memory of past infections, helping explain why treated patients suffer more infections. The therapy joins T cells to a target called BCMA on myeloma cells. The team tested T cells from healthy donors. The cells were grown with the engager drug pavurutamab and with myeloma cells.

Those T cells still killed myeloma cells well, yet their responses to common pathogen fragments dropped compared with untreated cells. A small exploratory check of blood from four patients responding to the same class of therapy pointed the same way, with reduced pathogen-specific memory responses. The authors are careful to call the observation preliminary, urging a larger study to confirm whether this immune dulling truly drives the infection burden.
pmc-13597505:
Ahren Hart and co-authors publish an open dataset of real-world 5G performance across Glasgow, gathering 720 outdoor measurements in fifteen neighborhoods over three days in April 2025. All four major British operators and two flagship phones were used, giving the 2026 release a neighborhood-level view that operator maps rarely supply.

Citywide averages came to roughly six hundred seventy megabits per second down and one hundred sixty-five up, with a ping near twenty-two milliseconds. Individual readings swung from under fifty to over twelve hundred megabits, a variability the authors stress is the honest face of shared urban spectrum. One operator posted the highest median download, suburbs beat the city core, and signal strength barely predicted speed at all. The openly licensed dataset is offered for coverage modeling, smart city planning, and as a 2025 baseline against which future 6G claims can be judged.
pmc-13598105:
Alice Vivien Barchet and colleagues recorded brain signals from sixty-three adults aged nineteen to seventy-one as they picked a target voice out of competing talkers, asking why comprehension frays with age. Their study combined fine-grained behavior with models of how the brain tracks each speech stream.

Older listeners' weaker performance came with stronger brain tracking of the distractor voice, hard evidence for a filtering failure: the aging auditory system lets the wrong speaker in. Yet older adults also leaned harder on word-level linguistic knowledge, at both the behavioral and neural levels, and that reliance paid off, offsetting the leakier filter and supporting comprehension. The authors frame successful aging listening as a trade. Degraded bottom-up selection is compensated by richer top-down prediction. Hearing support might aim to restore that balance. Merely amplifying sound is not the goal.
pmc-13601105:
Anne Kristin Fischer and three colleagues present a 2026 German-language case report on a liver change that mimics a tumor. The condition, massive ductular reaction, is extensive liver remodeling triggered when local blood flow through liver veins and sinusoids is blocked, starving the area. A cancer growing into vessels is often the cause, though cirrhosis or widespread liver cell death can also produce it.

Their patient was a 68-year-old man followed for fatty liver cirrhosis, in whom imaging found a large mass in liver segment VIII. Scans suggested an atypical liver cancer possibly spreading into small vessels, and the tumor board advised surgical removal. The report walks through the imaging in detail, from ultrasound to contrast MRI and CT. Because imaging cannot always separate this reaction from cancer, the authors stress that a biopsy may be needed before treatment decisions.
pmc-13607205:
Robert Mîndreanu leads an eight-author systematic review asking whether the epilepsy drug levetiracetam changes oxidative stress markers in people. Oxidative stress is tied to epilepsy, but seizures, diet, illness, and treatment all move the same markers, making drug effects hard to isolate. The team searched four databases and sorted human studies three ways: change within a person, patients versus healthy controls, and levetiracetam versus other seizure medicines.

Eleven non-randomized studies contributed 297 participants with usable data. Where effect sizes could be calculated, they came out wide, pointed in inconsistent directions, or rested on designs unable to credit the drug. Definitions, matrices, assays, and reporting varied so much that pooling was ruled out. Certainty rated very low throughout. Dropping one study that failed a source check changed nothing. The message is negative: current literature can neither support nor refute a redox effect for this widely used medicine.
pmc-13611505:
Zixin Wang leads an eight-author team fixing a quiet mismatch in aerial detection. A drone photo's feature maps keep nominal resolution even when blur or coarse sampling destroys the fine detail. Their interface, PIR-SBFR, routes each scale's features by two separate judgments. One asks how much detail the scene demands, which a visual branch estimates. The other asks how reliable the observation is, which a fixed analytic rule derives from sampling, sharpness, and noise, with no sensor-specific calibration.

Average precision rose from 62.98 to 65.52 percent on the DIOR benchmark and from 29.58 to 32.10 percent on an AI-TOD-v2 split. Three rival tiny-object detectors landed between those endpoints. The interface also lifted three host detectors by about two points, won under all 27 controlled quality conditions, and ran at a median 19.55 milliseconds on a Jetson board. The authors claim acquisition-aware routing as a practical upgrade.
pmc-13612305:
Sujogya Kumar Panda leads an eight-author team prospecting the leaves of Limonia acidissima, the wood apple tree of South Asian folk medicine. With drug resistance rising, the team extracted leaf compounds in acetone, ethanol, and water, screened them against microbes, and followed the strongest extract. Four compounds emerged, including kaempferol, luteolin, and a biphenanthrene reported from this plant for the first time.

All four isolates killed Gram-positive bacteria, with weaker action against Gram-negative bacteria and yeast. The four also showed moderate worm-killing activity and selective toxicity toward some cells. Computer docking ranked the kaempferol derivative afzelin as the strongest, most consistent binder across microbial targets, with luteolin close behind. The authors present the leaves as a source worth developing, and the two lead compounds as candidates for deeper testing. The study supports the plant's traditional uses, now tied to named molecules.
pmc-13616005:
André O. Soares and colleagues gather in 2026 the long-term studies linking fatty liver disease with chronic kidney disease, and test whether a recent renaming of the liver condition changes the answer. Fatty liver tied to metabolism is now called metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease, replacing the older non-alcoholic label. From 2,099 papers found across four databases, twenty long-term studies in adults free of kidney disease at the start qualified.

The pooled work asks how often new kidney disease appeared in people with fatty liver against those without, under each naming scheme. Incidence studies through June 2025 fed the analysis. A firm link would mean liver clinics should watch kidney numbers as a matter of routine, and kidney clinics should ask about the liver. The naming comparison guards the answer against a change in labels rather than biology.
pmc-13616605:
Ami Aoyama leads a team studying in 2026 two sugar-processing proteins as possible forecast markers in lung adenocarcinoma of dogs, a rare and aggressive cancer with no settled molecular predictors.
